title: Size-4 numerators are PROVED in F_q[T]: F_4[T] with A=T, F_2[T] with A=T²
connection: The two function-field analogues whose numerator has the same norm as 4 (|A| = 4: q=4,deg A=1 and q=2,deg A=2) are theorems (FUNCTIONFIELD_ES Thm 6.1, 6.3), proved by a FINITE congruence covering. Over Z a finite covering is impossible (Mordell square classes).
why: Pinning down exactly which Z-obstruction each FF proof dodges isolates the one ingredient Z lacks; it is the cleanest 'proved twin' of ES.
first_step: Tabulate for Thm 6.1/6.3 every covering family and mark which uses char-2 cancellation vs absence of the square-class obstruction (FUNCTIONFIELD_ES §6 'Why this exists over F₂').
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

analogues-0001.world: A. Function fields F_q[T] and polynomial rings

title: Char-2 cancellation ↔ signed ES with a size-controlled negative term
connection: In char 2 two monic denominators of equal minimal degree cancel at ∞ (m = 2), which is what the F₂ identities exploit. Over Z the closest mechanism is 1/x − 1/x' with x' ≈ x, i.e. signed ES where the negative term is tiny.
why: If the F₂ identities lift to signed integer identities whose sign defect is confined to a small term, the remaining task is a 'sign repair' problem, which is a different and more concrete integer statement.
first_step: Lift the F₂[T] identity of Thm 6.1 coefficientwise to Z[T] (T ↦ integer), record which term goes negative, and measure its size relative to 4/n.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

analogues-0002.world: A. Function fields F_q[T] and polynomial rings

title: Rate comparison: FF density-zero failures (Thm 5.3) vs Vaughan's exceptional-set bound
connection: At fixed q the FF failures have density 0 via a one-prime identity plus Dirichlet/RH in F_q[T]; over Z Vaughan gives #exceptions ≤ N exp(−c log^{2/3} N). The FF proof uses RH (Weil), so its rate may be a power saving.
why: A power-saving rate in FF suggests what GRH would buy over Z; a GRH-conditional power-saving ES exceptional bound would be a new (conditional) integer theorem.
first_step: Extract the explicit rate in FUNCTIONFIELD_ES Thm 5.3; then check whether a GRH-conditional ES exceptional-set bound with power saving exists in the literature (search 'Erdős–Straus exceptional set GRH').
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

analogues-0003.world: A. Function fields F_q[T] and polynomial rings

title: q→∞ failure (Thm 2.1) ↔ few numerators per prime (Luca–Pappalardi, Mond–Portier A₃(p))
connection: ES_q(A,P) fails for a proportion → 1 of P as q → ∞ with deg P fixed; over Z, Σ_{p≤x} A₃(p) ≍ x(log x)³(up to loglog), so a typical p has only polylog numerators m with m/p a 3-term sum.
why: Both say 'numerator size vs denominator size' governs a phase transition; the Z regime m ≍ p^δ is the analogue of q→∞ and its failure would be the integer twin of Thm 2.1.
first_step: Read Mond–Portier 2201.11805 and check whether the proof shows A₃(p) is supported on m ≤ (log p)^C for most p — if so record the integer 'Thm 2.1'.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

analogues-0004.world: A. Function fields F_q[T] and polynomial rings

title: Sign-subgroup world: positivity = leading coefficient in a subgroup H ≤ F_q^*
connection: Monic (H = 1) is Hayes' choice; H = F_q^* is the trivial sign-free problem. Taking H = squares (index 2) mimics Z, whose sign group {±1} has index 2 in nothing but whose 'positive' half is index 2 in Z∖0.
why: Interpolating H shows whether hardness is controlled by the index of the cone; an index-2 cone FF problem might be the most faithful model of ℕ ⊂ Z.
first_step: Run the existing ffl_* search with leading coefficients restricted to squares for q = 3,5,7, deg P ≤ 8, and compare failure counts to the monic version.
refs: Hayes, 'Explicit class field theory in global function fields'
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

analogues-0005.world: A. Function fields F_q[T] and polynomial rings

title: Constant numerator 4 fails in char ≥ 5 because leading coefficients are 1,2,3 ↔ 'x > n/4' archimedean bound
connection: Prop 1.2: 4/P with monic denominators fails for every P in char ≥ 5 (sum of three monic reciprocals has leading coefficient 1,2,3). Over Z the analogue is the archimedean bound x ≥ n/4 that makes m ≥ 4 the first hard numerator.
why: It shows that '4 > 3' is the genuine source of hardness; the integer statement 'm ≤ 3 trivial, m = 4 hard' has an exact FF mirror, which supports using FF degree bookkeeping as a model of archimedean size.
first_step: Write the dictionary entry 'leading coefficient count ↔ number of terms ≥ numerator' and check whether k-term m/n with m ≤ k is trivial in both worlds (it is over Z: m/n = Σ 1/n).
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

analogues-0006.world: A. Function fields F_q[T] and polynomial rings

title: Large-q monodromy (Bary-Soroker style) for 'divisor of A·C·P+1 in a residue class'
connection: Over F_q[T] with q → ∞, factorization types of P-tied polynomials such as A·C·P + 1 become equidistributed via full symmetric monodromy; ES Type II needs a divisor of 4Cp+1 in class −1 mod 4C over Z.
why: A large-q theorem would show the 'divisor in class' event behaves like a random permutation event; it localizes which part of the Z problem is genuinely arithmetic (finite q).
first_step: Check whether Bank–Bary-Soroker–Rosenzweig ('Prime polynomials in short intervals and in arithmetic progressions') or Bary-Soroker's divisor results cover 'has a divisor ≡ −1 mod 4C'.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

analogues-0007.world: A. Function fields F_q[T] and polynomial rings

title: Keating–Rudnick variance in F_q[T] as model for the variance of Type II counts over C
connection: Variance of arithmetic functions in FF arithmetic progressions is computed exactly via random matrix theory for q → ∞. The fixed-p ES count Σ_C #(divisors of 4Cp+1 ≡ −1 mod 4C) is a sum of divisor-in-AP indicators.
why: A matrix-integral prediction for the variance gives a principled lower-tail model; lower tail at fixed p is exactly the ES question.
first_step: Check whether Keating–Rudnick 'squarefree / divisor function in arithmetic progressions over F_q[T]' covers d(n) restricted to a class; adapt to the Type II sum at q→∞.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

analogues-0008.world: A. Function fields F_q[T] and polynomial rings

title: Profinite sterile points: FF x* in ES₃(T²) vs non-square sterile profinite integers
connection: FF_STERILE_* constructs a profinite point x* of ES₃(T²) where every covering family fails (Haar-null set). Over Ẑ the odd squares are sterile for certificate lines; are there non-square sterile points in Ẑ?
why: If Ẑ has only square-type sterile points, ES reduces to squares-plus-growth; if it has others, they are new candidates for hard primes.
first_step: Mirror the FF construction in Ẑ: run the certificate-line covering tree mod 840·k and look for profinite branches avoiding all lines that are not square classes.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

analogues-0009.world: A. Function fields F_q[T] and polynomial rings

title: FF reciprocity sign (−1)^{deg·deg·(q−1)/2} may resurrect a T1-type square obstruction for q ≡ 3 (mod 4)
connection: T1 (empty certificate lines at odd squares) is a quadratic-reciprocity effect over Q. FF quadratic reciprocity carries a sign depending on degrees and q mod 4, so odd-degree squares in F_3[T], F_7[T] may carry a T1 analogue.
why: If a T1 analogue appears exactly when the reciprocity sign is non-trivial, T1 is pinned to the sign in reciprocity, the 'archimedean' part of Q's reciprocity.
first_step: EXSET_FUNCTION_FIELD Thm 1.3 already shows squares fail U_q for q ≡ 3 (mod 4) — start there. For q = 3, 7 enumerate certificate lines at P = Q² with deg Q odd vs even (deg ≤ 6) and test emptiness; compare FUNCTIONFIELD_ES2 §3 (degree parity).
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

analogues-0010.world: A. Function fields F_q[T] and polynomial rings

title: Positivity at a finite place: cone = polynomials with constant term 1
connection: Replace 'monic' (sign at ∞) by 'X(0) = 1' (sign at the place T). This cone is multiplicatively closed but contains elements arbitrarily close to 1 T-adically, i.e. it is not discrete at its sign place.
why: The other_rings principle predicts collapse to a finite covering when the cone is not discrete at the sign place; checking it in a new world tests the principle.
first_step: Search for e with e = 1/U + 1/V, U,V in the cone, e ≡ 'class 3' modulo the analogue of 4 (T²?) — try q = 3,5 by brute force.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

analogues-0011.world: A. Function fields F_q[T] and polynomial rings

title: Genus-1 coordinate rings: ES over F_q[x,y]/(E) with sign at the point at infinity
connection: Drinfeld–Hayes rings with nontrivial class group: a 'prime' P generates a non-principal ideal in general, so 4/P is not even an element unless P is principal; ES becomes a statement about principal primes or ideal classes.
why: Separates the role of the class group (trivial for Z) from the role of the cone; if ES fails only in non-trivial class-group rings, class number one is part of the mechanism.
first_step: Pick an elliptic curve over F_3 with A = F_3[E∖O], enumerate principal primes of small degree and run the e-slice search with sign-normalized denominators.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

analogues-0012.world: A. Function fields F_q[T] and polynomial rings

title: Sign groups at ∞: {±1} for Q versus F_q^* for monic F_q[T] in ray class groups mod m·∞
connection: With the sign at ∞, the ray class group mod m of F_q[T] is (F_q[T]/m)^* (Carlitz), and dropping the sign quotients by F_q^*; for Q the analogous groups are (Z/m)^* and (Z/m)^*/{±1}. (The narrow class groups themselves are trivial in both cases, since every ideal has a positive/monic generator.) So the 'sign part' of ray class groups has size 2 over Q and q − 1 over F_q[T].
why: ES-type certificate conditions are ray-class conditions; if FF hardness scales with the size of the sign part, Q (sign part of size 2) sits in the most constrained-sign regime.
first_step: Compute, for q = 3, 4, 5, 7, the failure rate of ES_q(T, P) at deg P = 6 against q − 1; fit.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

analogues-0013.world: A. Function fields F_q[T] and polynomial rings

title: Large-degree numerators A = T^k ↔ Schinzel m/n with m → ∞
connection: In FF the numerator degree k plays the role of log m. Families with k→∞ at fixed q correspond to m/n problems with growing m (Schinzel), where Vaughan-type density results still hold over Z.
why: If ES_q(T^k,·) has a uniform-in-k density theorem in FF, it predicts the right uniformity in m for Z, i.e. a quantitative Vaughan for m ≤ (log n)^c.
first_step: From existing FF data, tabulate failure density at fixed q=3 as k = 1..4 grows and compare with Z data for m = 4..12.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

analogues-0014.world: A. Function fields F_q[T] and polynomial rings

title: Lang–Weil/Ax ultraproduct of F_q[T]: ES in a pseudo-finite polynomial ring
connection: The ultraproduct of F_q[T] over q has a pseudo-finite constant field; ES over it is decided by Lang–Weil point counts on the fixed-degree ES variety, giving failure (Thm 2.1) for standard degree.
why: Clarifies that the FF 'q→∞' world is a model-theoretic limit with exact point-count control, which Z lacks; any Z proof must use non-uniform information in p.
first_step: Write the first-order formula ES_deg≤d(P) and verify via Lang–Weil that its truth in the ultraproduct matches Thm 2.1's density.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

analogues-0015.world: A. Function fields F_q[T] and polynomial rings

title: Mason–Stothers in F_q[T] vs abc over Z for size of largest ES denominator
connection: abc is a theorem in F_q[T] (Mason–Stothers, under the usual hypothesis that not all of a, b, c have zero derivative — i.e. excluding p-th-power cases like T^p + (1 − T)^p = 1); applied to ES identities it bounds degrees of solutions. Over Z, abc would bound sizes of x,y,z from below/above in terms of rad(xyz·n).
why: Size bounds feed every search strategy; an FF theorem with its Z-conditional twin may reveal a forced-size window for solutions.
first_step: Apply Mason–Stothers to xy·4z = n(xy+yz+zx) rearranged as a+b=c and derive the degree inequality; check its integer form under abc on the computed ES solutions.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

analogues-0016.world: A. Function fields F_q[T] and polynomial rings

title: Mordell–Schinzel proves ES FALSE over Z[T] (eventual positivity) at P = mT + r² (gcd(m, r) = 1, odd values)
connection: Over Z[T] with cone 'positive leading coefficient', a solution at P = mT + r² with gcd(m, r) = 1 (and P taking odd values; e.g. 4T + 4 = 4(T+1) is trivially solvable: 4/(4T+4) = 1/(2T+2) + 1/(4T+4) + 1/(4T+4)) would be a polynomial identity covering a square class, excluded by Mordell–Schinzel. So Z[T] is an analogue world where ES is provably false.
why: It certifies that any proof over Z must be non-uniform in n (cannot come from a single polynomial family per class); Z[T] is the 'false twin' to set against the FF 'true twins'.
first_step: Check whether the Mordell–Schinzel argument extends to Z[T] with merely eventual positivity of denominators (not positivity for all T ≥ 0).
refs: Elsholtz–Tao arXiv:1107.1010 (discussion of Mordell's square-class result)
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

analogues-0017.world: A. Function fields F_q[T] and polynomial rings

title: Which non-square classes (m, r) admit an ES polynomial identity?
connection: Mordell–Schinzel excludes square r mod m. For non-square r, is there always an identity 4/(mT + r) = Σ 1/X_i(T) over Z[T]? Over 840 Mordell finds identities for all non-square classes; for general m this is the polynomial world's version of ES.
why: A complete answer in Z[T] separates exactly the polynomial-identity (B1) part of ES and would show whether non-square classes are always B1-coverable.
first_step: Brute-force Type I/II identities for m ≤ 2000, all non-square r, recording uncovered (m,r); check Elsholtz–Tao §2 for a stated answer.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

analogues-0018.world: A. Function fields F_q[T] and polynomial rings

title: Two-variable identities for primes represented by a non-principal binary form
connection: Primes p = f(S,T) for a non-principal form f (e.g. disc −23, h = 3) form a non-congruence set. A polynomial identity 4/f(S,T) = Σ 1/X_i(S,T) in Z[S,T] would cover a non-abelian Chebotarev set.
why: It would be a certificate family outside the abelian (congruence) world where Mordell's obstruction lives; the obstruction then concerns which forms represent squares.
first_step: Search ansätze X_i quadratic/quartic in (S,T) for f = 2S²+ST+3T² by solving coefficient equations with a Gröbner basis or LLL.

analogues-0019.world: A. Function fields F_q[T] and polynomial rings

title: Identity for 4/(S²+T²) restricted to a cone avoiding Pythagorean pairs
connection: Primes ≡ 1 (mod 4) are exactly the primes S² + T². A Z[S,T] identity valid on a cone would prove ES for the primes in it; Mordell–Schinzel-type obstruction bites at (S,T) with S²+T² a square (Pythagorean pairs).
why: Asking whether the obstruction is only at Pythagorean points turns T1 into a statement about rational points on the conic S²+T² = R², a geometric handle.
first_step: Prove or refute: no identity in Z[S,T] can be valid on any Zariski-dense set of (S,T); test small-degree ansätze numerically.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

analogues-0020.world: A. Function fields F_q[T] and polynomial rings

title: ES over R[T] with lc > 0: the real-closed-coefficient world
connection: Over R[T] with positive leading coefficients there is no integrality of coefficients, so ES becomes a semialgebraic condition on the solution variety, like the q → ∞ limit but with an ordered constant field.
why: Separates 'ordered field at the sign place' from 'finiteness of the constant field'; if R[T]-ES is trivial, the Z difficulty is all integrality.
first_step: Check whether A/P = Σ 1/X_i with monic-real X_i always has solutions for deg A = 1 (dimension count + sign of leading terms).
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

analogues-0021.world: A. Function fields F_q[T] and polynomial rings

title: Zaremba over F_q[T] (Niederreiter-type results) ↔ continued-fraction length form λ(p) ≤ 3
connection: ES₅ says ES ⇔ λ(p) ≤ 3 for a continued-fraction length. In F_q[T], Zaremba-type statements (all partial quotients of degree 1) are known for small q; the length-3 statement is a much weaker FF analogue.
why: An FF proof of 'some a/P has length ≤ 3 in the ES₅ sense' via degree bookkeeping would show which step needs archimedean size over Z.
first_step: Check whether Niederreiter (1987) proved Zaremba for F_2[T] and F_3[T]; then state ES₅ in Artin's FF continued fractions and test deg ≤ 10.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

analogues-0022.world: A. Function fields F_q[T] and polynomial rings

title: Nagao amalgam: SL₂(F_q[T]) is not finitely generated — the words form of ES changes shape
connection: ES ⇔ certain short SL₂(Z) words; SL₂(F_q[T]) is an amalgam (Nagao) of GL₂(F_q)-type and Borel pieces and is not finitely generated, so word length is replaced by degree.
why: If the FF words problem is trivial via the Borel piece, it shows that ES words over Z draw their difficulty from SL₂(Z)'s finite generation.
first_step: Translate the SL₂ word form of ES to SL₂(F_q[T]) and check whether Borel elements produce solutions for all P.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

analogues-0023.world: A. Function fields F_q[T] and polynomial rings

title: Function-field large sieve on the ES certificate set (Hsu-type FF large sieve)
connection: The FF large sieve is sharp with explicit constants. Applied to 'P avoiding all certificate classes for moduli ≤ Q', it bounds the FF exceptional set; Z has the same inequality with worse explicit constants.
why: The FF large-sieve bound can be compared directly with the FF exceptional count computed exactly, calibrating how lossy the Z large-sieve route is.
first_step: Compute the FF large-sieve prediction for q=3, A=T, deg ≤ 12 and compare with the exact failure counts in data/ffl.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

analogues-0024.world: A. Function fields F_q[T] and polynomial rings

title: Katz monodromy for Kloosterman/Salié-type sums in ES Type II counts at q → ∞
connection: Type II counts at fixed P are sums of incomplete Kloosterman/Salié-like sums; over F_q[T] with q→∞, Katz's equidistribution gives square-root cancellation with known monodromy groups.
why: If the relevant monodromy is computed, it predicts the fluctuation law of the fixed-p count over Z (Katz–Sarnak style) and so the lower-tail behaviour.
first_step: Identify the exact exponential sum in the FF Type II count (FUNCTIONFIELD_ES §4) and look up its geometric monodromy in Katz 'Gauss sums, Kloosterman sums and monodromy groups'.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

analogues-0025.world: A. Function fields F_q[T] and polynomial rings

title: Squares in F_q[T] are not obstructed: compute ES at P = Q² to see what 'unobstructed squares' look like
connection: FF has no T1 at squares (odd q), so ES_q(A, Q²) is solved by ordinary certificates. Comparing the certificate types used at FF squares vs non-squares shows which Z certificates would be needed at odd squares.
why: Z's odd squares are known ES-true but certificate-line-empty; the FF certificates at squares are a template for what a 'non-line' solution at a Z square looks like.
first_step: For q = 3, A = T, list solutions at P = Q², deg Q ≤ 4, classify by Type I/II and certificate line; compare with Z solutions at 25, 49, 121.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

analogues-0026.world: A. Function fields F_q[T] and polynomial rings

title: Drinfeld modular curves X₀(P) point counts as ES solution counters
connection: Type II ES data at P correspond to points on modular-type curves in FF; Drinfeld modular curves have explicit point counts (Gekeler). If the ES count at P equals a Hecke eigenvalue sum, Ramanujan bounds (Drinfeld) give lower bounds.
why: A lower bound from a Ramanujan-type identity is the only FF mechanism that would directly transfer as 'pointwise' information over Z.
first_step: Test numerically in F_3[T] whether #ES-solutions(P) correlates with a_P of some Drinfeld modular form of small level (fit against Gekeler's tables).
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

analogues-0027.world: A. Function fields F_q[T] and polynomial rings

title: F_q[T] with q = p prime vs prime power: does F_4 behave like F_2 or like F_3?
connection: Thm 6.3 (F₄, A = T) and Thm 6.1 (F₂, A = T²) are both char 2. Comparing F₄ with F₉ (char 3) and F₂₅ isolates characteristic from field size.
why: Disentangles 'char 2 cancellation' from 'small q', which decides whether the |A| = 4 analogues are char artefacts.
first_step: Run the existing covering-tree search for q = 9, A = T (|A| = 9) and q = 3, A = T² to deg 8 and report covering success.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

analogues-0028.world: A. Function fields F_q[T] and polynomial rings

title: ES over F_q[T] for P = composite: does the reduction to primes hold?
connection: Over Z, ES for n follows from ES for any divisor of n. Over F_q[T] the same divisor-closure holds, but FF exceptions may be prime-only; check if all composite exceptions inherit from prime factors.
why: If FF exceptions are not divisor-closed in the obvious way it reveals an error in the dictionary (e.g. NC/degree conditions break the divisor reduction).
first_step: Check: if Q | P and ES_q(A,Q) holds with NC, does ES_q(A,P) hold with NC? (degree condition changes) — one-line lemma.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

analogues-0029.world: A. Function fields F_q[T] and polynomial rings

title: Riemann–Roch dimension count of the ES variety at fixed P in FF
connection: The space of solutions of A/P = Σ 1/X_i with bounded degrees is a variety whose expected dimension is −k (BRAINSTORM ff §4). Riemann–Roch on the ES surface's fibration gives exact dimension of families.
why: Over Z the analogue is the log² p expected count; RR gives an FF exact formula that could reveal a hidden term (e.g. a constant correction) that also exists over Z.
first_step: Compute for q = 3 the generating function of #solutions by degree and compare with the expected-dimension prediction; look for a polynomial-in-q correction.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

analogues-0030.world: A. Function fields F_q[T] and polynomial rings

title: Function-field Bombieri–Vinogradov at level beyond 1/2 (Sawin–Shusterman style)
connection: Sawin–Shusterman proved FF results (e.g. level of distribution beyond 1/2 for primes, twin-prime-type statements for large q) unavailable over Z. ES-type existence at a given P via primes in progressions could follow in FF.
why: If an FF ES-for-all-P proof needs exactly a level-θ > 1/2 distribution statement, that pins the integer analytic input needed (a Elliott–Halberstam-type hypothesis).
first_step: Check whether Sawin–Shusterman 'On the Chowla and twin primes conjectures over F_q[T]' gives distribution of P-tied polynomials in progressions to modulus degree > deg/2; map to Type I.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

analogues-0031.world: A. Function fields F_q[T] and polynomial rings

title: Chowla over F_q[T] (proved for large q) ↔ parity barrier in ES sieve arguments
connection: ES lower-bound sieves hit the parity barrier; FF Chowla (Sawin–Shusterman, large q) breaks parity in FF. If an FF ES statement follows from FF Chowla, the integer statement needs a Chowla-type input.
why: Clarifies whether parity is the precise barrier for a sieve proof of ES.
first_step: Check whether the FF ES counting function at fixed P can be written with a Möbius/Liouville twist that Chowla controls.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

analogues-0032.world: A. Function fields F_q[T] and polynomial rings

title: Carlitz cyclotomic fields as the FF analogue of Q(ζ_{4C}) in Type II certificates
connection: Type II certificate conditions over Z are splitting conditions in Q(ζ_{4C}). In FF they become splitting in Carlitz cyclotomic fields K_M, which are abelian with Galois group (F_q[T]/M)^*.
why: Clean class field theory in FF makes the certificate covering problem an explicit set-covering in finite abelian groups; any FF covering bound gives a template for Z.
first_step: Express the FF covering trees of FUNCTIONFIELD_ES as covers of (F_q[T]/M)^* by cosets and compute covering numbers.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

analogues-0033.world: A. Function fields F_q[T] and polynomial rings

title: Function-field Chen-type theorem: P + E = (almost prime)·(...) in classes
connection: Chen-type 'almost prime' results are proved in FF with better parameters. The e-slice criterion needs a divisor of P·x-type polynomial in a class; an almost-prime shift result constrains which certificate exists.
why: If FF almost-prime results make ES-type certificate existence automatic, the integer twin would be a Chen-type ES theorem ('p+e has ≤ 2 prime factors with one in class').
first_step: Write the FF e-slice criterion (Lemma 1.3) as 'P·something + e has a divisor ≡ c' and look for an almost-prime formulation.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

analogues-0034.world: A. Function fields F_q[T] and polynomial rings

title: Polynomial ES over Z[T] for P of degree 2: 4/(T² + 1)
connection: Primes of the form T²+1 are ≡ 1 (mod 4) when T even. An identity for 4/(T²+1) over Z[T] with eventually positive denominators would cover them; T²+1 is never a square for T>0, so Mordell–Schinzel's square obstruction does not apply directly.
why: A quadratic-polynomial identity would be a non-linear certificate family; existence/non-existence probes whether the obstruction is genuinely about squares.
first_step: Search for 4/(T²+1) = 1/X + 1/Y + 1/Z with X,Y,Z ∈ Z[T] of degree ≤ 4 (or with T in a fixed class mod M) via linear algebra on coefficients.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

analogues-0035.world: A. Function fields F_q[T] and polynomial rings

title: Polynomial ES at P = T² + T + 1, T⁴ + 1 and other never-square polynomials
connection: Generalizing the T²+1 test: for each irreducible quadratic/quartic f that is never a square and has values ≡ 1 mod 4, ask for a Z[T] identity. Mordell–Schinzel's obstruction is pointwise at square values, which f avoids.
why: A positive find would be a genuine new infinite certificate family for primes of a polynomial shape.
first_step: Run the same coefficient search as for T²+1 on a list of ten such f; note obstructions at fixed T mod M.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

analogues-0036.world: A. Function fields F_q[T] and polynomial rings

title: Integer-valued polynomial ring Int(Z) as denominators
connection: Allow X_i(T) ∈ Int(Z) = {f ∈ Q[T]: f(Z) ⊆ Z} (binomial-coefficient basis). This strictly enlarges the identity world beyond Z[T].
why: Mordell–Schinzel's proof might use integrality of coefficients; if it breaks for Int(Z), new identity families covering harder classes might exist (though T1 at squares should still bite pointwise).
first_step: Check the Mordell–Schinzel proof for where Z[T] coefficients are used; test small binomial-basis ansätze for a square class mod 840.

So the local factor at primes ℓ ∤ 2n carries no arithmetic of n; n enters the singular series only at ℓ | 2n and through the integrality/positivity of reciprocals.
why: Removes a candidate source of 'hard prime' structure: small-prime local densities cannot distinguish hard from easy p; the distinction must come from the p-adic factor, the archimedean window, or global effects.

connection: Type II ES data encode representations by binary forms; over F_q[T] with q odd, binary forms have class groups of imaginary quadratic function fields (Artin). Class numbers are given by L-function values (RH known).

analogues-0051.world: A. Function fields F_q[T] and polynomial rings

title: Positive ES over Z[1/ℓ] for EVERY odd prime ℓ (unit-sum mechanism; checked ℓ < 3000)
connection: Over Z[1/ℓ] the mechanism of other_rings Lemma 3.1 works iff some 1 + ℓ^k has a prime factor ≡ 3 (mod 4). scripts/z52b_analogues_zl.py: every odd prime ℓ < 3000 has such k ≤ 7 (max at ℓ = 2017). A reciprocity argument shows failure for all odd k would force ℓ ≡ 1 (mod 8). (NB: for ℓ with ES(ℓ) known, Z[1/ℓ]-ES is even more trivial by the depth-1 identity of the next item; the unit mechanism matters as an ES-independent proof.)

analogues-0052.world: B. S-integers, number rings, cones, non-commutative rings

title: Depth-1 trivialization: denominators in (1/ℓ)·ℕ make ES trivial whenever ES(ℓ) holds
connection: 4/n = Σ ℓ/x'_i ⇔ 4/(ℓn) = Σ 1/x'_i, and ES(ℓn) follows from ES(ℓ). E.g. ℓ = 3: 4/n = 1/(n/3) + 1/(4n/3) + 1/(4n) for every n. So the 'ℓ-adic depth' hierarchy collapses at depth 1 (k(p) ∈ {0,1}); Prop 3.2's e = 7 identity (depth 3) is not optimal. Likewise ℓ = 2: 4/n = Σ 2/x' ⇔ 2/n = Σ 1/x', trivial.
why: Correction/sharpening of the S-integer picture: the meaningful refinement is not depth but HOW MANY denominators are non-integral (the trivial identity uses two). 'Exactly one non-integral denominator of ℓ-depth 1' is weighted ES with weights (1,1,ℓ), trivial for ℓ ≤ 3 (take z = n) and non-trivial for ℓ ≥ 5.
first_step: Done cheaply: scripts/z52b_analogues_weighted.py finds NO failure of 4/p = 1/x + 1/y + ℓ/z (ℓ ∤ z, z ≤ 3p) for ℓ = 5, 7, 11 and p < 3000. So every single non-unit numerator seems to make ES easy (expected: e.g. 4z − 5p = 3 leaves 3/(pz)). Next: find the uniform identity per ℓ and record the lemma.

analogues-0053.world: B. S-integers, number rings, cones, non-commutative rings

title: Inverting the target prime trivializes ES: positive ES over Z[1/p] for 4/p
connection: In Z[1/p] the unit-sum mechanism applies with ℓ = p itself: if some 1 + p^k has a divisor e ≡ 3 (mod 4) (true for all p < 3000 by the Z[1/ℓ] computation) then 4/p = 1/x + 1/(u p x) + 1/(v p x), x = (p+e)/4. So allowing p-power denominators removes the obstruction; e.g. 4/5 uses e = 3 | 1 + 5.
why: Localizes the difficulty: allowing p-power denominators kills it. (Depth-1 with ℓ = p is circular — it needs ES(p²) — so the unit route is the honest one here.)

title: Trace descent: Galois-sum an O_K solution to get an integer identity with numerator 8
connection: If 4/n = Σ 1/x_i with x_i ∈ O_K (K real quadratic), adding the conjugate equation gives 8/n = Σ Tr(x_i)/N(x_i). When Tr(x_i) | N(x_i) for each i, this is a 3-term unit-fraction representation of 8/n.

analogues-0057.world: B. S-integers, number rings, cones, non-commutative rings

connection: From 4/n = Σ1/x_i and 4/n = Σ 1/x_i' (conjugates), the product (Σ1/x_i)(Σ1/x_i') = 16/n² gives 16/n² as a 9-term sum of 1/(x_i x_j'); pairing diagonal terms 1/N(x_i) gives integer unit fractions.
why: Exhibits a route from a proved world to a k-term integer Egyptian representation of 16/n²; probably weaker than ES but a concrete transfer statement.
first_step: Write the 9 terms and check when the off-diagonal pairs x_i x_j' + x_j x_i' combine into integers; test with the D = 2 identity.

title: Unit-sum mechanism over Z: the only integer e are 1 and 2 — consequence: classes 3 and 2 mod 4 only
connection: Over ℕ, 1/u + 1/v ∈ Z forces e ∈ {1, 2}, giving the classical easy classes. Any p-dependent replacement must produce e = 1/u + 1/v with u, v rational but with x = (n+e)/4 integer — i.e. e may depend on p.
why: Pins down the precise integer statement replacing the universal divisor: 'for every p there is e ≡ 3 mod 4 with e = 1/u+1/v and u·n·x, v·n·x integers' — which is ES itself in e-slice form.
first_step: Write the e-slice form explicitly and check it matches the repo's e-slice / Type I-II classification (ff Lemma 1.3 integer version).

analogues-0072.world: B. S-integers, number rings, cones, non-commutative rings

title: Units of Z[1/2]: 4 becomes a unit and ES is trivial — the dyadic place carries the problem
connection: If 2 ∈ S the numerator 4 is a unit and ES collapses. Together with the Z[1/p] item: the obstruction is spread over the dyadic place and the place p.
why: Suggests a two-place reformulation: ES as a gluing problem between a 2-adic and a p-adic condition with an archimedean constraint.
first_step: Write ES as 'there exist local solutions at 2, p, ∞ with a common global lift of bounded height' and check it against STRONG_APPROX_ES.md.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

analogues-0073.world: B. S-integers, number rings, cones, non-commutative rings

title: ν(p) ≤ 1 trivially: 4/p = 1/(p/3) + 1/(2p) + 1/(2p) — one non-integral denominator always suffices
connection: Define ν(p) = least number of non-integral denominators in a positive S-integer solution. Then ν(p) ≤ 1 for every p via 4/p − 3/p = 1/p = 1/(2p) + 1/(2p). ES ⇔ ν(p) = 0. So the S-integer relaxations collapse completely: any single non-unit numerator suffices.
why: Filter lemma: the entire S-integer/weighted direction gives no intermediate statement between 'trivial' and ES; the only non-trivial content of the S-integer worlds is the unit-sum MECHANISM (e | 1 + η), not the relaxation itself.
first_step: Record as a filter lemma; redirect S-integer effort to finding integer surrogates of η (p-tied 'units').
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

analogues-0074.world: B. S-integers, number rings, cones, non-commutative rings

title: Archimedean crux restated as a 'gap principle' in valuation theory
connection: Cones discrete at all places where they carry sign (ℕ, monic F_q[T], Gaussian sector) give lottery problems; non-discrete cones collapse. Formalize: ES over (R, C) is a finite covering problem iff C ∩ {|x|_v < 1} ≠ ∅ for some sign place v.
why: A precise theorem of this kind would classify all analogue worlds at once and certify that Z is in the hard class.
first_step: State the theorem for Dedekind domains with a cone given by sign conditions at finitely many places; prove the 'collapse' direction from Lemma 3.1.

analogues-0075.world: B. S-integers, number rings, cones, non-commutative rings

title: Imaginary quadratic fields with class number > 1: ES for principal vs non-principal primes
connection: Over O_K with h > 1, a rational prime p ≡ 1 mod 4 may split into non-principal primes; then 4/p has fewer 'divisor' options among principal elements. With a sector cone this is a new hard world.
why: Measures the role of class group in the divisor-in-class lottery; Z has h = 1.
first_step: Take K = Q(√−5), sector cone, test ES for rational p splitting into non-principal primes vs principal ones.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

analogues-0076.world: B. S-integers, number rings, cones, non-commutative rings

title: Positive ES over O_K for n ∈ O_K with Galois-conjugate denominators only
connection: Require the three denominators to form a Galois orbit (K cubic, x, σx, σ²x): 4/n = Tr(1/x). Then ES becomes 'n/4 is the reciprocal of a trace of a reciprocal' — a norm-form equation.
why: Gives a cubic norm-form reformulation for rational n: Tr_{K/Q}(1/x) = 4/n; such equations are amenable to Thue/Schmidt or to equidistribution of units.
first_step: For cyclic cubic K of small conductor, solve Tr(1/x) = 4/p for totally positive x ∈ O_K, p ≤ 10^4.

analogues-0077.world: B. S-integers, number rings, cones, non-commutative rings

title: Integer ES solutions with x = Tr, y·z from norms: 'quadratic orbit' ES
connection: Variant: two denominators conjugate in a real quadratic field (y, ȳ) and one rational x: 4/n − 1/x = Tr(y)/N(y). Then (for solutions where y, z are conjugate quadratic integers) 4/n − 1/x = Tr(y)/N(y): a condition that (numerator, denominator) of 4/n − 1/x arise as (trace, norm) up to scaling — a binary quadratic form condition. (Requiring Tr(y) | N(y) would collapse to the two-term problem, which fails e.g. at n = 5.)
why: Converts ES into representation of numbers by binary quadratic forms with a trace constraint, linking to genus theory and class numbers (repo's CLASS_FORCING).
first_step: Make the equivalence explicit: 1/y + 1/ȳ = (y+ȳ)/(yȳ); classify which (t, N) arise and derive the binary-form condition.

analogues-0078.world: B. S-integers, number rings, cones, non-commutative rings

title: Ring of algebraic integers Z-bar with totally positive cone: ES trivially true?
connection: In the ring of all algebraic integers, every element has square roots etc.; with a totally positive cone, the unit-sum mechanism has infinitely many units, so ES should collapse.
why: A sanity endpoint of the classification (infinite-degree world).
first_step: Note as corollary of Prop 3.3: Z-bar ⊃ Z[√2]; any rational n has a totally positive solution. Record.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

analogues-0079.world: B. S-integers, number rings, cones, non-commutative rings

title: p-adic sign patterns: which quadratic-character patterns (χ(x), χ(y), χ(z)) occur among local solutions
connection: Z_p carries no order, but a sign can be a quadratic character. ES over Z_p with denominators in a quadratic-character cone is a local question solvable by Hensel; relevant only as local data.
why: Local data are inputs to Bright–Loughran's no-BM result and the singular series; the cone version records which sign patterns of x, y, z occur locally.
first_step: Compute, for ℓ ≤ 30, which (χ(x), χ(y), χ(z)) sign patterns occur for local solutions of 4/n with n ≡ 1 mod 4 — compare with global solutions' patterns.

analogues-0080.world: B. S-integers, number rings, cones, non-commutative rings

title: Global sign patterns of ES solutions vs local predictions (Legendre symbols of x, y, z mod small primes)
connection: For each global solution record (x/ℓ), (y/ℓ), (z/ℓ). If some locally allowed pattern never occurs globally at hard primes, that is a hidden global constraint (reciprocity-type).
why: Hidden global constraints are exactly what T1 is; finding more of them maps the obstruction landscape.
first_step: Using existing solution data for p ≤ 10^6, tabulate patterns at ℓ = 3, 5, 7 and test against local frequencies.

analogues-0081.world: B. S-integers, number rings, cones, non-commutative rings

title: Adelic ES: Bright–Loughran no Brauer–Manin obstruction ↔ strong approximation failure
connection: Integral points on the ES surface are not obstructed by Brauer–Manin; ES is therefore an 'existence of integral points beyond BM' question, like Markoff surfaces where strong approximation fails in a structured way.
why: Markoff surfaces have proven 'almost all' strong approximation (Bourgain–Gamburd–Sarnak, W. Chen); an analogous orbit structure on ES surfaces would be a transferable mechanism.
first_step: Check whether the ES affine surfaces have a nontrivial automorphism group acting on integral points (Vieta-like moves); see MARKOFF_ES.md.

analogues-0082.world: B. S-integers, number rings, cones, non-commutative rings

title: Matrix ES over M₂(Z) with the cone of matrices with positive entries
connection: Matrices with positive entries form a multiplicatively closed cone discrete at ∞ (entries ≥ 1). Inverses are rational; ES: (4/n)·I = X⁻¹ + Y⁻¹ + Z⁻¹ with X, Y, Z positive-entry, invertible over Q.
why: This cone links ES to SL₂(N)-type monoids and continued fractions (the repo's SL₂ words form); it might reproduce ES exactly or relax it.
first_step: Check: does a solution with positive-entry X, Y, Z force a solution of ES? Compute small cases n = 5, 13, 17.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

analogues-0083.world: B. S-integers, number rings, cones, non-commutative rings

title: Matrix ES for n·I replaced by a matrix of determinant n
connection: Ask: for every integral M with det M = n (or Hermite normal form), is 4M⁻¹ = X⁻¹ + Y⁻¹ + Z⁻¹ with X, Y, Z positive-definite integral? For M = diag(1, n) it contains ES-like constraints in one coordinate.
why: Gives a family indexed by sublattices of index n; averaging over sublattices might be easier and still imply ES for M = n^{1/k}-free choices.
first_step: Work out k = 2, M = diag(1, p): what does positivity + integrality force on the (2,2) coordinate?
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

analogues-0084.world: B. S-integers, number rings, cones, non-commutative rings

title: ES in Z × Z (product ring) with componentwise positivity: no coupling
connection: In a product ring ES holds iff it holds in each factor. Trivial, but it calibrates: coupling between places is what makes rings like O_K differ from Z × Z.
why: A boundary marker for the cone-classification theorem.
first_step: Note as a one-line lemma in the dictionary.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

analogues-0085.world: B. S-integers, number rings, cones, non-commutative rings

title: Real quadratic fields with N(ε) = +1: other_rings evidence shows coverage, find the proof
connection: For D = 3, 6, 7 (N(ε) = +1) the rational classes were covered numerically. The proof of Prop 3.3 used N(ε) = −1 to get ε^{ℓ+1} ≡ −1; for N(ε) = +1 one needs another route (e.g. ℓ split and ε of even order modulo a prime above ℓ).
why: Completing the classification of real quadratic fields would make 'unit rank ≥ 1 ⇒ ES' a theorem for all real quadratic K.
first_step: For D = 3, find ℓ ≡ 3 mod 4 split in K and a prime 𝔩 | ℓ with ε of even order mod 𝔩 and ε^{j} ≡ −1 mod 𝔩 — then need κ totally positive; test.

analogues-0086.world: B. S-integers, number rings, cones, non-commutative rings

title: ES over the ring of S-integers with S = {∞, 2-adic}? (Z[1/2]) vs S = {∞, 3}: compare collapse mechanisms
connection: Z[1/2]: trivial because 4 is a unit; Z[1/3]: needs e = 7 | 1 + 27. These are two different collapse mechanisms (numerator becomes unit vs universal divisor).
why: Distinguishes two kinds of 'easy' worlds; an integer proof might mimic the second (divisor supply) but never the first.
first_step: List all S-integer rings with |S| = 1 and classify which mechanism applies (done for ℓ < 3000 by the Zsigmondy item).

analogues-0087.world: B. S-integers, number rings, cones, non-commutative rings

title: Eichler orders / quaternion algebras ramified at ∞ and p: ES via ideals of norm p
connection: In the definite quaternion algebra B_{p,∞}, left ideals of norm p correspond to supersingular data; ES-like equations among ideal classes appear in Brandt matrices.
why: Brandt matrices give exact counts of ideal-class relations with Ramanujan bounds; if ES solutions map to Brandt-matrix entries, positivity of counts follows.
first_step: Read bsC_supersingular_transfer.md and check whether any ES count equals a Brandt-matrix entry for small p.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

analogues-0088.world: B. S-integers, number rings, cones, non-commutative rings

title: Totally positive ES for non-rational n ∈ Z[√3]: every class of (O_K/4)^* covered (EVIDENCE)
connection: other_rings found that for D = 3, 6 every class is hit, so positive ES holds for every totally positive n ∈ O_K prime to 2. That is a full ES theorem in a ring with infinite units.
why: Proves ES-for-all-n in a non-trivial ring; checking whether the proof is a finite covering by unit identities gives a template.
first_step: Extract from bs_ff_rings.py output the explicit list of (η, κ) identities covering each class and package as a theorem with proof.

analogues-0089.world: B. S-integers, number rings, cones, non-commutative rings

title: Function-field–number-field bridge: Q(√D) ↔ F_q(T)(√D(T)) real quadratic function fields
connection: Real quadratic function fields (D of even degree with square leading coefficient) have units (Pell polynomial solutions); the unit-sum mechanism applies there too.
why: Shows the unit mechanism is uniform across global fields and identifies Pell-polynomial units as the FF counterpart of η.
first_step: Take q = 3, D = T² + 1, find the fundamental unit (Pell polynomial) and test the mechanism for monic P.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

analogues-0090.world: B. S-integers, number rings, cones, non-commutative rings

title: Gaussian cone ES for Gaussian primes vs ES over Z: is there an injection of solutions?
connection: A solution of ES over Z for p is a solution in the Gaussian cone (real denominators are in the cone). Conversely, from a Gaussian-cone solution for rational p, taking norms or real parts may give integer data.
why: If 'Gaussian cone ES for rational p ⇒ integer ES' via a projection, the Gaussian world would be a strengthening to attack.
first_step: Test: for each Gaussian-cone solution of 4/p (p ≤ 1000) check whether real parts or norms yield an integer ES solution.

analogues-0091.world: B. S-integers, number rings, cones, non-commutative rings

title: Lipschitz/Hurwitz quaternions with integer coefficients ≥ 0 as cone (semiring N[i,j,k])
connection: The semiring of quaternions with non-negative coefficients is multiplicatively closed? (No: i·i = −1 ∉.) Hence a natural non-commutative cone must be designed (e.g. positive real part + norm conditions).
why: Recording a failed cone design avoids wasted searches and clarifies minimal axioms (multiplicative closure is essential for Lemma 3.1).
first_step: List candidate quaternionic cones and check multiplicative closure; keep only valid ones for a search.

analogues-0092.world: B. S-integers, number rings, cones, non-commutative rings

title: ES in rings of integers of CM fields with cone from the maximal real subfield
connection: For a CM field K with totally real K⁺, use denominators in K whose relative norm to K⁺ is totally positive. Units of K⁺ (rank ≥ 1 when [K⁺:Q] ≥ 2) make the unit mechanism available.
why: Another family where infinite units collapse ES; confirms that only Q and imaginary quadratic K (unit rank 0) are hard.
first_step: For Q(ζ_8), test the unit mechanism with units of Q(√2).

analogues-0093.world: B. S-integers, number rings, cones, non-commutative rings

title: Imaginary quadratic fields are the only other unit-rank-0 worlds: Bradford–Ionascu cone is the right twin
connection: Number fields with finite unit group are Q and imaginary quadratic fields. So among number fields the ES-hard worlds (with a sensible cone) are exactly Q and imaginary quadratics.
why: Focuses analogue efforts: Gaussian/Eisenstein cone ES are the only number-field twins, and statements proved for them would be closest to Z.
first_step: State as an Assessment in the cone-classification note; list known results for Gaussian cone ES.

analogues-0094.world: B. S-integers, number rings, cones, non-commutative rings

title: Dual numbers Z[ε]/(ε²): the tangent-space ES
connection: 4/(n + mε) = Σ 1/(x_i + a_i ε) ⇔ ES for n plus the linear condition Σ a_i/x_i² = 4m/n². The a_i are free integers, so the dual-number world asks which ES solutions have a solvable linear tangent condition.
why: Tangent conditions measure how rigid ES solutions are; a 'deformation' world might connect to counting solutions with multiplicities.
first_step: For p ≤ 10^4 and each solution compute gcd conditions for Σ a_i/x_i² = 4m/p² to be solvable for all m.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

analogues-0095.world: B. S-integers, number rings, cones, non-commutative rings

title: Integer consequence of the Z[1/ℓ] world is circular (ES(ℓn) ⇐ ES(ℓ)) — only the unit mechanism gives non-circular content
connection: Clearing ℓ-denominators from a Z[1/ℓ]-solution yields an integer representation of 4ℓ^k/n with ℓ-weighted terms; for the depth-1 identity this is just ES(ℓ)·(1/n). Hence S-integer worlds transfer to Z only through mechanisms not using ES(ℓ) — i.e. the unit-sum mechanism (e | 1 + ℓ^k).
why: Filters out a false lead: 'S-integer ES ⇒ integer Schinzel statement' is empty unless the S-integer proof is unit-driven.
first_step: Record as a filter lemma in the S-integer section; check that no repo memo claims a non-trivial integer consequence of Z[1/3]-ES.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

analogues-0096.world: B. S-integers, number rings, cones, non-commutative rings

title: Ring of formal power series Z[[T]]: ES for 4/(n + T) trivial by Hensel-type lifting?
connection: Over Z[[T]] with 'positivity' of the constant term, 4/(n + T) = Σ 1/X_i requires ES for n at T = 0 plus solvable higher-order equations; higher orders are linear in the corrections.
why: If every ES solution lifts formally, the variety is smooth at integer points along this deformation — a structural fact about the solution variety.
first_step: Check the Jacobian rank of 4xyz − n(xy+yz+zx) at known integer solutions (is the surface smooth there?).
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

analogues-0097.world: B. S-integers, number rings, cones, non-commutative rings

title: ES over a Dedekind domain with infinitely many units but no order: positivity replaced by a norm bound
connection: Replace the cone by 'all |x|_v ≥ 1 at archimedean places' (a norm-bounded set, not multiplicatively closed by inverses). This is the 'height-positivity' world: denominators must have all conjugates ≥ 1.
why: Unlike totally positive, this excludes small units; it may restore lottery behaviour in fields with units, giving hard twins with richer arithmetic.
first_step: In Z[√2], require |x|, |x'| ≥ 1 and search ES for rational p ≤ 10^4; compare with the totally-positive collapse.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

analogues-0098.world: B. S-integers, number rings, cones, non-commutative rings

title: ES over Z[i] for Gaussian primes in the sector cone: does the T1 square obstruction appear at Gaussian squares?
connection: If a Gaussian analogue of certificate lines exists, T1 predicts emptiness at Gaussian squares π² with suitable congruence. Test whether Gaussian squares are the hardest Gaussian-cone cases.
why: A T1 analogue in Z[i] would show T1 is about quadratic reciprocity in general number fields (quartic reciprocity may refine it).
first_step: Classify Gaussian-cone solutions by type and check emptiness of 'line' families at π² for small π.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

analogues-0099.world: B. S-integers, number rings, cones, non-commutative rings

title: Quartic residue symbol (A/p)₄ on certificates: hidden finer obstruction?
connection: For p ≡ 1 (4), the quartic symbol refines (A/p). If certificates' quartic symbols are biased (e.g. never i for some class of p), there may be a finer reciprocity structure, as in the Apollonian quartic obstruction.
why: Quartic reciprocity obstructions appeared in HKRS for Apollonian packings. A quartic bias in ES certificates would be a new invariant.
first_step: Note (cheap test): (A/p) = −1 forces A^{(p−1)/4} = ±i, so only the i vs −i split is informative, and it needs a canonical i (e.g. i ≡ a/b mod p from p = a² + b², a odd, b even). With that normalisation, compute the i/−i split over sign-(−1) words, and the ±1 split over sign-(+1) words, for p ≡ 1 (8) < 10⁶.

analogues-0100.world: B. S-integers, number rings, cones, non-commutative rings

title: Positive ES in Q(√−1) with the cone 'Re > 0 and Im ≥ 0' (half-closed quadrant) vs both-sign cones
connection: Bradford–Ionascu's cone is Re, Im of equal sign; a strict first quadrant is multiplicatively closed only up to 90° sums (it is not closed: i·i). Clarify which quadrant-like sets are closed and which make ES non-trivial.
why: Cone design determines the world; misdesigned cones give trivial or empty problems.
first_step: Check closure of the equal-sign cone (product of two first-quadrant elements can leave the quadrant) — note Bradford–Ionascu's cone may not be multiplicatively closed, and record what they actually require.

analogues-0101.world: B. S-integers, number rings, cones, non-commutative rings

title: Unit fractions generate a DVR (Epstein): structure of R(D) for D = Z[1/S] and O_K
connection: Epstein shows the subring generated by reciprocals of a Euclidean domain is K or a rank-1 DVR. ES asks for specific 3-term representations; the ring R(D) records which 'unit fraction algebra' each world supports.
why: If R(D) ≠ K exactly in the hard worlds (e.g. F_q[T] where R(D) is the DVR at ∞), it gives an algebraic invariant correlating with ES-hardness.
first_step: Compute R(D) for Z, F_q[T], Z[i], Z[√2] from Epstein's theorem and compare with the hard/easy classification.

analogues-0102.world: B. S-integers, number rings, cones, non-commutative rings

title: Egyptian integral domains (Guerrieri–Loper–Oman, Epstein): ES as a 3-term refinement
connection: An Egyptian domain is one where every element of the fraction field is a finite sum of distinct unit fractions. ES is the 'length 3 for numerator 4' refinement. The Egyptian-domain literature classifies which domains have the unrestricted property.
why: Their techniques (e.g. using units or integrality over Egyptian subrings) might yield length bounds, i.e. 'Egyptian length' functions whose Z-value at 4/n is ES.
first_step: Read 'From ancient Egyptian fractions to modern algebra' and Epstein 2303.15685; look for any length-bounded statement.

analogues-0103.world: B. S-integers, number rings, cones, non-commutative rings

title: Egyptian length function ℓ_R(a/b) across domains R
connection: Define ℓ_R(q) = minimal number of unit fractions (with cone) summing to q. ES ⇔ ℓ_ℕ(4/n) ≤ 3. Compare ℓ over Z, F_q[T], O_K: maximal ℓ for numerator-k fractions.
why: A domain-independent invariant enables 'transfer' statements: e.g. ℓ_Z(4/n) ≤ ℓ_{Z[i]}-something.

analogues-0104.world: B. S-integers, number rings, cones, non-commutative rings

title: Tropical/valuative cone over F_q((1/T)): ES 'at ∞' is a leading-coefficient problem
connection: Over the completion F_q((1/T)) with monic cone, ES is the leading-coefficient equation (Lemma 1.1); over R the analogue is just inequality x > n/4. Comparing the completed worlds isolates what is local at the sign place.
why: Shows that in FF the sign place gives a discrete leading-coefficient constraint while over R it gives only an inequality — a structural difference to keep in mind for dictionaries.
first_step: Write both local problems and their solution sets; record as a dictionary entry.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

analogues-0105.world: B. S-integers, number rings, cones, non-commutative rings

title: Weil restriction view: ES over O_K for rational n = system of ES-like equations over Z in [K:Q] variables
connection: Writing x_i = a_i + b_i√D turns the O_K equation into two integer equations (rational and irrational parts) in six variables. Prop 3.3 solutions give an explicit family of integer points on this 6-variable variety.
why: The 6-variable integer variety contains the ES surface (b_i = 0); proved points on it might deform (via an integral curve) toward b_i = 0.
first_step: Write the two equations, then look for curves through the Prop 3.3 points meeting the b = 0 locus.

analogues-0106.world: B. S-integers, number rings, cones, non-commutative rings

title: The numerator set M(p) is divisor-closed, so ES ⇔ M(p) contains a multiple of 4
connection: Let M(p) = {m : m/p is a sum of three unit fractions}. If m/p = Σ 1/x_i and d | m then (m/d)/p = Σ 1/(d x_i), so M(p) is closed under divisors. Hence ES(p) ⇔ 4k ∈ M(p) for some k ≥ 1.
why: Weakens the target from one numerator to an infinite family; the Luca–Pappalardi/Mond–Portier average |M(p)| ≈ (log p)⁴ (up to loglog factors; Σ_{p≤x}A₃(p) ≍ x(log x)³ divided by π(x)) means typical p have many numerators, and one needs just one divisible by 4.
first_step: For p ≤ 10^5 compute M(p) (from all 3-term representations with any numerator) and record which element divisible by 4 appears first; look for a large-m element that is forced (like p + 1 ∈ M(p) always).

analogues-0107.world: C. Numerators m/n, k-term sums, constrained ES

title: Forced elements of M(p): p + 1, p + 2, 2p + ... — which large numerators are always available?
connection: (p+1)/p = 1 + 1/(2p) + 1/(2p) shows p + 1 ∈ M(p); similarly (p+2)/p = 1 + 1/p + 1/p and 3 ∈ M(p). A large forced element divisible by 4 would prove ES via divisor-closure.
why: Any identity m(p)/p = Σ 1/x_i(p) valid for all p with 4 | m(p) proves ES; Mordell–Schinzel-type arguments should forbid polynomial m(p) at square classes, so this pins the obstruction in the m-direction.
first_step: Enumerate polynomial families m(p) = ap + b with uniform identities (b small) and list their m mod 4 for p ≡ 1 mod 4; check whether all forced ones are ≢ 0 mod 4 (T1-type).

analogues-0108.world: C. Numerators m/n, k-term sums, constrained ES

title: All-even ES ⇔ 8/p is a sum of three unit fractions: fails only at p = 17, 241 (p < 2·10^4)
connection: Denominators all even ⇔ 8/p = Σ 1/(x_i/2). In the computation, 'all even' fails only at p = 17 and 241 among 269 primes p ≡ 1 mod 4 below 4000. Schinzel's conjecture for m = 8 predicts finitely many failures.
why: 8/p ⇒ 4/p by divisor-closure, so a proof of the m = 8 statement for p > p₀ would prove ES beyond p₀; m = 8 is an 'over-strengthening' whose exceptions are visible and checkable.
first_step: Done to 2·10^4 (data/z52b/analogues_constraints_20000.txt: still only 17, 241 among 1125 primes). Extend to 10^6 with a faster search and compare with known Schinzel m = 8 data.

title: 'Some denominator ≡ 0 mod 4' fails at exactly the same primes 17, 241 as m = 8
connection: Among p < 4000 the solutions with a denominator divisible by 4 are missing exactly at p = 17 and 241, the same primes where 8/p fails. A structural equivalence (e.g. a bijection of solution types) may lie behind this.

title: Odd-denominator ES is impossible (2-adic): the archetype of a constrained-world local obstruction
connection: If x, y, z are odd, xy + yz + zx is odd and xyz odd, so the reduced fraction has odd numerator, while 4/n (n odd) has numerator 4. So no solution. Likewise exactly one even denominator is impossible by 2-adic valuations (the computation confirms).
why: Gives the template for 'congruence-subgroup denominators' worlds: local obstructions are trivial to detect and separate from genuine lottery failures.
first_step: Generalize: for which multiplicative sets H ⊂ (Z/ℓ^k)^* of allowed denominator classes is there a local obstruction? Tabulate for ℓ ≤ 7.

analogues-0114.world: C. Numerators m/n, k-term sums, constrained ES

title: Denominators ≡ 1 (mod 3) is impossible when 3 ∤ n: a 3-adic obstruction
connection: If x, y, z ≡ 1 mod 3 then 1/x + 1/y + 1/z ≡ 3 ≡ 0 in Z_(3), while 4/n is a 3-adic unit when 3 ∤ n. More generally, with k terms and denominators ≡ 1 mod ℓ, one needs 4/n ≡ k (mod ℓ).
why: Shows that 'number of terms ≡ 0 mod ℓ' interacts with congruence-restricted denominators; a family of worlds where obstructions depend on k mod ℓ.
first_step: Tabulate for ℓ ∈ {3,5,7}, H = subgroup of (Z/ℓ)^*, the classes of n for which ES_H is locally obstructed.

analogues-0115.world: C. Numerators m/n, k-term sums, constrained ES

title: Pairwise coprime denominators: impossible for n ≥ 2
connection: If gcd(x,y) = gcd(y,z) = gcd(x,z) = 1, the fraction (xy+yz+zx)/xyz is already reduced, so xyz = n·t and xy + yz + zx = 4t with t = 1, impossible for positive integers. All solutions need shared factors among denominators.
why: Every solution has a 'gcd skeleton'; the repo's Type I/II parametrisation is exactly the description of that skeleton. A constrained world with exactly one coprime pair is a natural middle case.
first_step: Count, for p < 4000, solutions with exactly one coprime pair vs none (the computation shows 'all pairs share a factor' never fails).

title: Arithmetic-progression denominators x, y, z in AP never occur (p < 4000)
connection: No solution with y − x = z − y appears for any p. Possibly a provable impossibility (or extreme rarity) via the equation 4x(x+d)(x+2d) = p(…)

title: Sierpiński 5/n: the m = 5 twin of ES (verified to 10^18 per Pomerance's notes)
connection: 5/n = 1/x+1/y+1/z is open in exactly the same way: almost-all (Vaughan) and polynomial identities except square classes. Comparing hard classes of m = 4 and m = 5 separates numerator-specific from universal obstructions.

analogues-0120.world: C. Numerators m/n, k-term sums, constrained ES

title: Schinzel's m/n conjecture: table of the largest exception N(m) for m ≤ 30
connection: For each m, compute the n for which m/n is not a 3-term sum. Schinzel conjectures finiteness for each m. The growth of N(m) in m is the 'numerator direction' of the phase diagram.
why: If N(m) grows like exp(c√m) or polynomially, it constrains any uniform method (a method that works for m = 4 should work for all m with a predictable threshold).
first_step: Brute force m ≤ 30, n ≤ 10^5; record N(m) and exception counts; check literature for existing tables (e.g. Guy UPINT D11).

analogues-0121.world: C. Numerators m/n, k-term sums, constrained ES

title: Mordell–Schinzel for general m: are square classes obstructed for every numerator?
connection: For m = 4 square classes mod M admit no polynomial identities. Check whether the same holds for every m (and whether additional obstructed classes appear for composite m such as 8 or 12).
why: A uniform obstruction across m confirms that T1 is about squares, not about 4; extra obstructed classes for some m would be new phenomena.
first_step: Run the identity-coverage search for m = 5..12 modulo 840·k and list uncovered classes; compare with squares.

analogues-0122.world: C. Numerators m/n, k-term sums, constrained ES

title: Numerator ladder 4 | 8 | 16 | …: ES(4·2^j) ⇒ ES(4) and exceptions grow with j
connection: By divisor-closure, 2^{j+2}/p solvable ⇒ 4/p solvable. The exceptional sets E_j for m = 2^{j+2} grow with j; ES ⇔ E_0 = ∅. Data at j = 1 (m = 8): {17, 241} below 4000.
why: Studying how E_j shrinks as j decreases gives a 'descent' picture; a proof that E_{j} ⊆ (explicit finite set) ∪ E_{j+1}... is not obviously helpful, but the E_j structure may reveal which primes are intrinsically hard.
first_step: Compute E_1, E_2 (m = 8, 16) for p < 10^5 and check whether hard ES primes (few solutions, e.g. 5, 13, 17, 193) are in all E_j.

analogues-0123.world: C. Numerators m/n, k-term sums, constrained ES

title: Rav's two-term criterion: ES ⇔ ∃x, two divisors of nx summing to 0 mod (4x−n)
connection: a/b = 1/y + 1/z is solvable iff there are divisors d₁, d₂ of b with a | d₁ + d₂ (Rav 1966). With a/b = (4x−n)/(nx), ES(n) ⇔ ∃ x ∈ (n/4, n/2]-ish and divisors d₁, d₂ | nx with (4x − n) | d₁ + d₂.
why: It turns ES into additive combinatorics of divisor sets modulo m = 4x − n: 'the divisor set D(nx) satisfies D + D ∋ 0 mod m'. Sumset tools (Cauchy–Davenport, Kneser) are native.
first_step: For p < 10⁶ and each x, check whether |D(px) mod m| is large enough that Kneser/Cauchy–Davenport would force 0 ∈ D + D (mod m), and how often that alone certifies.
alt_first_steps: [analogues-0124] Write the exact 2-term criterion and express #ES-solutions(p) as Σ_x (#divisors of (nx)² in a class mod (4x − n)); compare with the repo's Type I/II counts.

[signature-0080] State the criterion precisely for (4x − n)/(nx) and check equivalence with Type I/II divisor forms.

analogues-0124.world: C. Numerators m/n, k-term sums, constrained ES

title: Huang–Vaughan exceptional set asymptotic for a/n = 1/x+1/y → model for ES exceptions in a single slice
connection: Huang–Vaughan prove E_a(N) ~ C(a) N (log log N)^{2^{m−1}−1}/(log N)^{1−1/2^m} for fixed a, via 'delicate analysis of the underlying group structure' ((Z/aZ)^* and subgroups). ES needs a union over slices a = 4x − n with x varying.
why: Their group-structure analysis is exactly the 'divisor in a class' combinatorics; joint control over many a would be a quantitative almost-all ES with structure.
first_step: Read Huang–Vaughan's method and identify whether it extends to 'for some a in a set A(n)' with A depending on n (union bound + correlation).

analogues-0125.world: C. Numerators m/n, k-term sums, constrained ES

title: One numerator-2 term trivializes ES: 4/n = 2/((n+1)/2) + 1/M + 1/M, M = n(n+1)/2
connection: For odd n: 4/n − 4/(n+1) = 4/(n(n+1)) = 2/M = 1/M + 1/M with M = n(n+1)/2. So allowing a single term with numerator 2 (and a repeat) solves every odd n.
why: Boundary marker: the 'weighted ES' world with weight vector (2,1,1) is trivial; difficulty is entirely in the all-ones weight vector.
first_step: Record as a lemma; then explore weight vectors (1,1,1) vs (1,1,2) vs (1,2,3) for distinct denominators.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

analogues-0126.world: C. Numerators m/n, k-term sums, constrained ES

title: Weighted ES: 4/n = a/x + b/y + c/z for fixed weight vectors (a,b,c)
connection: A whole family of ternary problems indexed by (a,b,c). (1,1,2) is trivial (previous item); (1,1,1) is ES. Which weight vectors are 'hard' (lottery) vs 'trivial' (identity covering) vs 'false'?
why: The hard/trivial boundary in weight space exposes what feature of (1,1,1) creates difficulty (e.g. no weight shares a factor with 4).
first_step: Brute-force n ≤ 10^4 for all (a,b,c) with a,b,c ≤ 4 and classify by existence of a finite covering by identities mod 840.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

analogues-0127.world: C. Numerators m/n, k-term sums, constrained ES

title: Signed ES with a size-controlled negative term: 4/n = 1/x + 1/y − 1/z with z ≥ n^{1+δ}
connection: Signed ES is trivial (4/(4k+1) = 1/k − 1/(k(4k+1))). Requiring the negative term to be tiny (z large) interpolates between trivial and ES-like. Find the threshold δ at which signed ES stops being covered by identities.
why: A threshold statement would be a new integer theorem halfway to ES, and the identity families near threshold are candidates to perturb into positive solutions.
first_step: For p ≤ 10^4, compute the maximal z over signed solutions with one negative term; check whether z ≥ p³ is always achievable (via identities).
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

analogues-0128.world: C. Numerators m/n, k-term sums, constrained ES

title: Best underapproximation of 4/n by three unit fractions (Kovač / Nathanson / Chu) — ES ⇔ gap 0
connection: The 'best k-term underapproximation' literature studies max{Σ_{i≤k} 1/x_i ≤ q}. ES ⇔ the 3-term underapproximation of 4/n is exact. Structure theorems for best underapproximations (eventually greedy) might constrain when exactness is possible.
why: If best 3-term underapproximations of 4/n are 'eventually greedy' in a way that forces a particular x, ES reduces to a single e-slice — testable.
first_step: Read Kovač 2406.07218 and Nathanson 2202.00191; compute the best 3-term underapproximation of 4/p for p ≤ 10^4 and check whether greedy first term works.

analogues-0129.world: C. Numerators m/n, k-term sums, constrained ES

title: Odd greedy algorithm (open termination problem) ↔ odd-denominator Egyptian fractions
connection: Every rational with odd denominator is a finite sum of distinct odd unit fractions (Breusch / Stewart, to check), but whether the odd greedy algorithm terminates is a famous open problem. ES with odd denominators is impossible (2-adic), but 4/n with an even number of odd terms (two can suffice, e.g. 4/15 = 1/5 + 1/15) is a natural neighbour.
why: Two open problems about restricted Egyptian expansions; techniques from one (e.g. 2-adic descent) may cross over.
first_step: Check the status of the odd greedy problem and of 'minimal number of odd unit fractions for 4/n' (must be even by parity); compute for n ≤ 1000.

analogues-0130.world: C. Numerators m/n, k-term sums, constrained ES

title: Odd unit fractions for 4/n: parity forces an EVEN number of terms (2 is sometimes enough)
connection: A sum of k odd unit fractions has numerator Σ_i Π_{j≠i} x_j ≡ k (mod 2) over an odd denominator; since 4/n (n odd) has even numerator, k must be even. k = 2 sometimes works (4/15 = 1/5 + 1/15); otherwise k = 4 is the next option.
why: A 4-term odd-denominator ES ('4/n = four odd unit fractions') is a natural open-looking twin; determine whether it is always solvable when the 2-term version fails.
first_step: Compute for odd n ≤ 10^4 whether 4/n is a sum of two, else four, odd unit fractions; look for obstructions mod 8.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

analogues-0131.world: C. Numerators m/n, k-term sums, constrained ES

title: Shifted-prime denominators (Bloom): 4/n with denominators of the form q − 1, q prime
connection: Bloom proved results on unit fractions with shifted prime denominators (density/Ramsey type). The 3-term restriction 4/n = Σ 1/(q_i − 1) is a sparse constrained world.
why: A sparse world where heuristics predict finitely many solutions overall tests the lottery model calibration (expected count ≪ 1 gives failures).
first_step: Compute the expected number of solutions under the lottery model and compare with brute force for n ≤ 10^4.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

analogues-0132.world: C. Numerators m/n, k-term sums, constrained ES

title: Semiprime denominators: 4/p as a sum of three reciprocals of semiprimes
connection: Recent work shows every natural number is a sum of distinct semiprime unit fractions (Shisheng Li). The 3-term version for 4/p is a constrained ES with a natural density of allowed denominators ~ log log x / log x.
why: Probes how ES's solution count scales when denominators are thinned to a density-zero but not too sparse set.
first_step: Brute force for p ≤ 10^4; record failure density; compare with lottery prediction.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

analogues-0133.world: C. Numerators m/n, k-term sums, constrained ES

title: Denominators in short intervals (Croot) ↔ size windows for ES solutions
connection: Croot studied unit fractions with denominators in short intervals [N, N + N^θ]. ES solutions have x ∈ (p/4, 3p/4] and y, z in structured ranges; asking for all three denominators in a short window is a size-constrained world.
why: Size windows are central to the repo's window/slice analysis; Croot's techniques give existence for long sums, hinting at what's needed for three.
first_step: Read Croot math/9904181 to see whether his argument has a 3-term component; compute the window widths of ES solutions for hard primes.

analogues-0134.world: C. Numerators m/n, k-term sums, constrained ES

title: Rado/partition regularity of 1/x + 1/y + 1/z = 4/w
connection: Brown–Rödl-type results transfer Rado's theorem to reciprocal equations. Is 1/x + 1/y + 1/z = 4/w partition regular (monochromatic x, y, z, w in any finite colouring)? The linear counterpart x + y + z = 4w is not regular (no zero subset-sum of coefficients), but reciprocal equations can behave differently.
why: Partition regularity would be a robust 'many solutions' statement for the ES variety across all w, a Ramsey strengthening of 'ES has solutions'.
first_step: Check the reciprocal Rado literature (Brown–Rödl; Gaiser 2306.04029) for 1/x+1/y+1/z = c/w; try 2-colourings by computer for small ranges.
alt_first_steps: [free_opus-0309] Check whether the equation 1/x + 1/y + 1/z = 4/(w) is partition regular in (x,y,z,w) jointly (likely yes by Brown–Rödl transfer); note as distant cousin.

analogues-0135.world: C. Numerators m/n, k-term sums, constrained ES

title: Covering systems ↔ unit fractions (Z.-W. Sun): ES as a statement about AP packings
connection: Sun relates m-covers by residue classes to sums of unit fractions of moduli. Three pairwise disjoint APs with moduli x, y, z have density Σ 1/x_i; ES ⇔ some disjoint triple of APs has density exactly 4/n (disjointness needs at least pairwise gcd > 1, but this is neither automatic — (2,5,10) is an ES triple at n = 5 with gcd(2,5) = 1 — nor sufficient: periods (6,10,14) admit no three pairwise disjoint APs, since that would need three distinct parities).
why: Imports covering-system technology (Hough, Balister–Bollobás–Morris–Sahasrabudhe–Tiba distortion method) into ES via packings.
first_step: Determine for which ES triples disjoint residues exist (a CRT/graph-colouring condition on the gcds) and whether every p has at least one such triple; only then is 'ES ⇔ AP packing' an equivalence.

analogues-0136.world: C. Numerators m/n, k-term sums, constrained ES

title: Elsholtz–Planitzer approximate parametrizations for k ≥ 4 unit fractions
connection: For sums of four and more unit fractions, Elsholtz–Planitzer use approximate parametrizations to count solutions. ES is the k = 3 case where exact parametrizations (Type I/II) exist.
why: Their counting lower bounds for k ≥ 4 may have a pointwise version at specific n; a 4-term pointwise result plus a merging step would be a new route.
first_step: Read arXiv:2012.05984 and 1805.02945; check whether any pointwise (fixed n) 4-term statement is proved.

analogues-0137.world: C. Numerators m/n, k-term sums, constrained ES

title: Four-term ES with distinct denominators is trivial — but four-term with a size cap is not
connection: 4/n as a sum of 4 unit fractions is easy (e.g. via 3/n splitting). With all denominators ≤ C·n (no huge denominators), the 4-term problem becomes a lattice/lottery problem again.
why: Size-capped multi-term ES might be provable for k = 4 with C large while ES (k = 3) remains open, giving a tunable intermediate theorem.
first_step: Compute, for n ≤ 10^4, the least C such that 4/n has a 4-term representation with max denominator ≤ C n; test boundedness.

analogues-0138.world: C. Numerators m/n, k-term sums, constrained ES

title: Distinctness is harmless: the 'distinct' world never fails (p < 4000)
connection: Every p ≡ 1 mod 4 below 4000 has a solution with x, y, z distinct. Folklore says distinctness is WLOG for n > 2.
why: Confirms a reduction used everywhere; worth a one-line lemma (split a repeated term) to remove any doubt.
first_step: Write the splitting lemma: if x = y then 2/x = 1/(x/2)... or use 1/x = 1/(x+1) + 1/(x(x+1)) with care to keep 3 terms; check the literature statement.

areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

analogues-0139.world: C. Numerators m/n, k-term sums, constrained ES

title: A₃(p)-numerator geometry: the set M(p) as lattice points under a hyperbola
connection: m ∈ M(p) iff m/p = Σ 1/x_i; for each Type II parameter set, the achievable m form arithmetic progressions. M(p) is then a union of APs intersected with [1, 3p].
why: If M(p) is a union of many APs with differences coprime to 4, it contains a multiple of 4 — a pigeonhole route to ES via the numerator direction.
first_step: For p ≤ 10^4 compute M(p) and fit it as a union of APs; inspect the differences mod 4.

analogues-0140.world: C. Numerators m/n, k-term sums, constrained ES

title: Egyptian fractions with restricted prime support (Chen–Elsholtz–Jiang; Czenky–McGovern–Plavnik)
connection: Representations of 1 with denominators in S(p_1,…,p_t) (S-units) are studied; ES in Z[1/S] relates. For ES over ℕ with denominators S-smooth except for factors of p, the count is finite and computable.
why: Gives an explicit finite-world version of ES (bounded prime support) where complete enumeration is possible and failure structure can be studied exactly.

title: Riemann–Hurwitz integrality: a surface subgroup of Δ(x,y,z) of index d needs n | d(n − 4)
connection: For an ES solution, a torsion-free normal subgroup of index d in Δ(x,y,z) yields genus g with 2g − 2 = d(1 − 4/n). Hence n must divide d(n − 4); for prime n ≥ 5 this forces n | d.
why: Translates ES into 'Δ(x,y,z) has a finite quotient of order divisible by n with x, y, z element orders' — a group-theoretic existence statement where e.g. PSL₂(F_q) quotients (Macbeath) are classified.
first_step: For small n list ES triples and check whether PSL₂(F_p) is a quotient of Δ(x,y,z) (Macbeath's criterion); see if a uniform choice like PSL₂(F_p) suggests a construction.

analogues-0154.world: D. Geometric, topological and combinatorial host worlds

title: Brieskorn–Pham log canonical thresholds: ES ⇔ 4/n = lct(x^a + y^b + z^c)
connection: For the diagonal singularity x^a + y^b + z^c, lct = min(1, 1/a + 1/b + 1/c). So ES(n) ⇔ 4/n (< 1 for n ≥ 5) is the log canonical threshold of a 3-variable Brieskorn–Pham polynomial.
why: Birational geometry studies the set LCT₃ of 3-dimensional lcts (ACC, accumulation points); ES asks whether all 4/n lie in the Brieskorn–Pham stratum. Other quasi-homogeneous types give natural relaxations.
first_step: Check the known description of LCT for quasi-homogeneous isolated singularities in 3 variables (Arnold's types) and list which rationals arise from each type.

analogues-0155.world: D. Geometric, topological and combinatorial host worlds

title: Quasi-homogeneous relaxations: lct of x^a y + y^b + z^c is (a + b − 1)/(ab) + 1/c
connection: For f = x^a y + y^b + z^c, weights w_y = 1/b, w_x = (b − 1)/(ab), w_z = 1/c give lct = Σ w = (a+b−1)/(ab) + 1/c (if ≤ 1). Each Arnold/Orlik–Wagreich type gives a 'generalized Egyptian' expression for rationals.
why: A family of ES-like problems with a geometric origin; if one type (e.g. chain x^a y + y^b z + z^c) represents every 4/n, it is a provable relaxation and its proof might be adapted.
first_step: Derive the weight-sum formulas for the 7 Orlik–Wagreich-type classes of 3-variable isolated quasi-homogeneous singularities and test which represent 4/p for all p ≤ 10^4.

analogues-0156.world: D. Geometric, topological and combinatorial host worlds

title: Brieskorn links: ES solutions never give integral homology spheres
connection: The link of x^a + y^b + z^c is an integral homology sphere iff a, b, c are pairwise coprime. Pairwise coprime ES solutions are impossible (constraint-world item), so ES links always have non-trivial H₁.
why: Gives a topological invariant (H₁ of the link, related to gcds of the denominators) attached to every solution; the gcd skeleton of Type I/II solutions becomes the torsion of H₁.
first_step: Compute H₁ of Brieskorn links for ES triples of small p and compare with the Type I/II parameters.

analogues-0157.world: D. Geometric, topological and combinatorial host worlds

title: Exact Seifert/pretzel form: ES(n) ⇔ a Seifert space M(0; (x,1),(y,1),(z,1)) with Euler number −4/n (double cover of the pretzel link P(x,y,z))
connection: The Seifert space over S² with unnormalised invariants (x,1),(y,1),(z,1) has rational Euler number e = −(1/x + 1/y + 1/z) and |H₁| = xy + yz + zx. It is the double branched cover of the pretzel link P(x,y,z), with det P = xy + yz + zx. So ES(n) ⇔ some positive pretzel link P(x,y,z) has det = 4xyz/n ⇔ some such Seifert space has e = −4/n.
why: It is an exact translation of the original equation into 3-manifold/knot language. The fields have structure theorems for pretzel knots (sliceness, genus, Heegaard Floer) and for Seifert invariants, with n appearing as the Euler number.
first_step: Tabulate, for n < 200, the pretzel links P(x,y,z) realising ES solutions; check whether Type I/II solution families correspond to natural pretzel families (e.g. one strand dividing another) and whether T1 square classes relate to slice pretzel knots (Greene–Jabuka; det must be a square).

connection: The tree T_{p,q,r} (arms with p, q, r vertices including the centre) has Cartan determinant pqr(1/p+1/q+1/r − 1) (E₈ = T_{2,3,5}: 1; E₆ = T_{2,3,3}: 3). ES ⇔ some T_{x,y,z} has n·det = xyz(4 − n), a hyperbolic lattice of discriminant xyz(n−4)/n.

title: Rectangle tilings: ES ⇔ an n×4 rectangle split into three horizontal strips, each a row of equal squares
