analogues-0169.world: D. Geometric, topological and combinatorial host worlds

title: Spherical / Euclidean / hyperbolic trichotomy as a 'phase diagram' of numerators
connection: 1/x + 1/y + 1/z > 1 (spherical: the infinite family (2,2,r) plus finitely many others), = 1 (Euclidean: (3,3,3),(2,4,4),(2,3,6)), < 1 (hyperbolic). ES with 4/n < 1 sits in the hyperbolic regime; numerators m/n > 1 give the spherical lists.
why: The classification for sums > 1 (one infinite family plus a finite list) is the archetype of an 'Egyptian classification' theorem; ES is the infinite hyperbolic regime where no classification is possible but density is.

connection: A degree-N cover of S² branched over 3 points with all ramification orders x, y, z respectively (uniform data) exists iff Riemann–Hurwitz integrality holds plus combinatorial conditions; for ES triples the data have χ = N(4/n − 1).

connection: Schwarz's list: the hypergeometric equation with exponent differences (λ, μ, ν) has monodromy a triangle group when they are reciprocals of integers; λ + μ + ν < 1 gives hyperbolic monodromy. ES ⇔ some Schwarz triangle with reciprocal angles has angle sum 4π/n.

title: Markov/Hacking–Prokhorov contrast: ES's surface has NO Vieta involution (linear in each variable)
connection: Markov triples a² + b² + c² = 3abc classify degenerations of P² to P(a², b², c²) and their integral points form Vieta-mutation orbits. The ES surface 4xyz = n(xy + yz + zx) is linear in each variable, so x is determined by (y, z): there is no second root and hence no Vieta involution.
why: Records why Markov-type orbit methods (strong approximation via mutation groups) have no direct ES analogue; any group action on ES integral points must come from elsewhere (e.g. Type I/II reparametrizations).

title: xy + yz + zx = N (Borwein–Choi): a symmetric ternary problem solved up to one possible exception (none under GRH)
connection: Borwein–Choi determine the N not of the form xy + yz + zx (x, y, z ≥ 1) — 18 known exceptions plus at most one more unconditionally, the extra one excluded under GRH — via class numbers of Q(√−N). For an ES solution, xy + yz + zx = 4xyz/n (the pretzel determinant).
why: The same symmetric quadratic in x, y, z appears in ES; their class-number method (representations ↔ forms of discriminant −4N) is a proved-twin technique for a closely related equation.

title: The unit mechanism is NOT finite for fixed S: e·κ = 1 + η has infinitely many instances
connection: In e·κ = 1 + η (other_rings Lemma 3.1) only η is an S-unit; e and κ are not, so S-unit-equation finiteness does not apply. E.g. e = 3 divides 1 + 5^{2j+1} for every j. For a fixed S the mechanism therefore offers infinitely many identities, all of the same congruence type.
why: Corrects an over-reach: the reason fixed-S mechanisms cannot prove integer ES is not finiteness but that they are congruence-type (B1) once translated back to Z.

title: Repeated denominators never occur for p ≡ 1 (mod 4): explains 'distinct is WLOG'
connection: The data (499/499 primes) show no solution with x = y or y = z. Proof sketch: x = y gives z = px/(2(2x − p)); gcd(2x − p, x) | p forces 2x − p ∈ {1, p}, and 2x − p = 1 needs x = (p+1)/2 even, i.e. p ≡ 3 (mod 4). Similar for y = z.
why: A clean lemma removing a case and showing the 'repeat world' is empty exactly in the hard class — another archimedean/2-adic coincidence.

why: Square-product solutions correspond to rational points on a double cover of the ES surface (w² = xyz); this connects ES to a K3-like or del Pezzo double cover, where other tools (elliptic fibrations) exist.
first_step: Characterize: xyz = w² on 4xyz = p(xy+yz+zx) — find the parametric families producing squares; see whether failures fit a congruence.

analogues-0264.world: G. Invented worlds, p-dependent fields, integer-side replacement statements

title: Size cap max ≤ p^{3/2}: fails at 359 of 499 primes — most primes need a denominator > p^{3/2}

title: Categorified ES over N[T]: identities with non-negative coefficient polynomials, evaluated at T = 1
connection: If 4/P(T) = Σ 1/X_i(T) with X_i ∈ N[T] and P(1) = n, evaluation at T = 1 gives ES for n and at T = 2, 3, … ES for P(2), P(3), …. So N[T]-solutions are 'categorified' solutions propagating to an infinite family.
why: For a given n, choosing P with P(1) = n freely might make the N[T]-problem easier than ES (more freedom in P), yet it implies ES at n. Conversely Mordell–Schinzel forbids it when P(T) hits square classes at many T.
first_step: For n = 5, 13, 17, search P ∈ N[T] of degree ≤ 2 with P(1) = n and an N[T]-identity of low degree; check what values P(T) take mod 840.

title: ES over Z_(p) (all primes except p inverted, ordering inherited from Q): trivial
connection: Z_(p) ⊂ Q inherits the usual order. Since 4 is invertible in Z_(p) for odd p, 4/p = 1/(p/2) + 1/p + 1/p with positive denominators p/2, p, p ∈ Z_(p). So inverting everything but p trivializes ES — the complementary extreme to Z[1/p].

connection: In FF, NC/degree conditions are degrees of divisors; over Spec Z compactified, positivity + size are Arakelov degrees. ES becomes: a metrized divisor class of degree log(n/4) is a 'sum' of three effective arithmetic divisors with unit-fraction structure.

connection: The N-span of 1 and −ω² (a 60° wedge spanned by two units) is closed under addition; closure under multiplication needs checking ((−ω²)² = ω⁴ = ω, outside the wedge?). Cone design determines whether an Eisenstein twin exists.
why: If no multiplicatively closed discrete cone exists in Z[ω] with full rank, then the Eisenstein world has no faithful ES twin — a structural fact.

connection: Allowing exactly one denominator from a real quadratic O_K (totally positive) while the others are integers. Then 1/α must be rational, so α is rational unless 1/x + 1/y is irrational — impossible. So this world collapses to ES (or to two algebraic denominators).

connection: EXSET_FUNCTION_FIELD 7′ uses monodromy groups of word covers (CFSG ⇒ Alt) to bound large-q exceptional densities by exp(−Ω(n²)). Over Z, the analogue would be a 'Galois group' for the factorization of n + v as tuv − u − v… — no known integer analogue.
why: Integer 'monodromy' could be modelled by Chebotarev in the splitting fields of the polynomial family X·Y·Z − Y − Z − n over Q(n) (Hilbert irreducibility); its Galois group controls the density of n with a word of a given shape.
first_step: Compute the Galois group over Q(n) of the polynomial system defining words of a fixed shape and compare with the FF G_{n,p}.

title: Poisson-shape heuristic validated in FF large q (p_f(n)·e^{−M_g(n)}): test the same model on Z data
connection: The FF large-q densities match an independent-Poisson-shapes model. Over Z, the I3/U exceptional data could be fit by the same model with integer 'shape masses'.
why: If the same model fits Z, it is a strong unified heuristic; if not, the discrepancy is a Z-specific arithmetic effect worth isolating.
first_step: Take the repo's U(n) exceptional data and fit p_f(n)·e^{−M_g(n)} with integer shape masses; compare residuals.

connection: The FF analogue of Mordell's no-covering result is PROVED for q = 9, 27, … (computer-assisted); in contrast F_4 and F_2 have finite coverings. This maps exactly which q behave like Z with respect to coverings.
why: Characterizing q with/without finite coverings (char 2 yes, 3^r no) gives a criterion whose Z-analogue is Mordell; the char-2 exception is the cancellation mechanism.
first_step: Tabulate known covering status for q ∈ {2, 3, 4, 5, 7, 8, 9}; guess the criterion (char 2 ⇔ covering?).

title: Fixed q = 3 resembles Z (EXSET_FUNCTION_FIELD #10): use F_3[T] as the Z simulator
connection: At q = 3, non-square failures vanish at odd n ≤ 15 and are few at even n, with no irreducible failure beyond n = 8 — Z-like behaviour. F_3[T] is the best 'simulator' of Z among FF worlds.
why: Any claimed integer mechanism can be stress-tested in F_3[T] with exact enumeration to large degree, where the analogous statement is checkable.
first_step: Adopt a rule: every proposed ES mechanism gets an F_3[T] translation and a degree ≤ 15 test before Z work.

analogues-0304.world: H. Thin areas filled: finite fields, signed sums, k terms, matrices, repo FF theorems

title: ES mod N: solvable for every N once denominators may share primes with n (no local obstruction)
connection: For every modulus N there are solutions of 4xyz ≡ n(xy + yz + zx) (mod N), but NOT always with x, y, z units: e.g. N = n = 5 forces 5 | xyz. Local solubility in the Bright–Loughran sense allows denominators divisible by primes of n (Type I/II at p).
why: Boundary marker: all content of ES is global; finite-field information enters only through densities (singular series). The 'units-only' local problem is obstructed at primes dividing n — the local shadow of 'p must divide a denominator'.
first_step: Record as lemma; compute the local densities at small primes for the singular series (items in batches B/E).

analogues-0305.world: H. Thin areas filled: finite fields, signed sums, k terms, matrices, repo FF theorems

title: ES over F_q with a cone = an index-2 subgroup (squares): the 'quadratic positivity' finite world
connection: In F_q, require x, y, z to be non-zero squares. Solvability of 4/n = Σ 1/x_i with squares is a question about the diagonal quadric Σ a_i w_i^{−2}… — solvable for q large by Weil; failures only for small q.
why: Small-q failures of 'quadratic positivity' indicate how much a sign-type restriction can obstruct in a finite world — a calibration of T1-like effects at the level of a single prime.
first_step: Brute force for q ≤ 50: for which q and n does 4/n = Σ 1/x_i with x_i nonzero squares have no solution?
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

analogues-0306.world: H. Thin areas filled: finite fields, signed sums, k terms, matrices, repo FF theorems

title: ES modulo p with denominators in an interval [1, H] (Shparlinski-type small solutions)
connection: Count solutions of 4/n ≡ 1/x + 1/y + 1/z (mod p) with 1 ≤ x, y, z ≤ H. For H ≥ p^{1/2+ε} character-sum bounds give many solutions; ES-type statements need H ~ p^{1/3}-ish lifts (the real solutions have x ≈ p/4 though).
why: Determines the minimal box H(p) for modular solvability; integer ES solutions give boxes of size p² for z, so this is a different (stronger) finite question, but its methods (Kloosterman) are those relevant to Type II slices.
first_step: Compute H(p) numerically for p ≤ 2000 and compare with p^{1/3}, p^{1/2}.

analogues-0307.world: H. Thin areas filled: finite fields, signed sums, k terms, matrices, repo FF theorems

title: Signed ES with exactly one negative term and all |denominators| ≤ C·n²: does it always hold?
connection: Signed ES (one minus sign) is trivially solvable with denominators ≍ n² (4/(4k+1) = 1/k − 1/(k(4k+1)), split one more). Bounding all three denominators by C·n² keeps it easy; bounding by n^{3/2} may make it a lottery.
why: A signed analogue with a size cap is a tunable world: its threshold exponent vs the positive ES threshold (> 3/2 from data) compares sign freedom with size freedom.
first_step: For n ≤ 10^4 compute the minimal max-denominator over signed (one negative) 3-term representations of 4/n; compare growth with the positive case.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

analogues-0308.world: H. Thin areas filled: finite fields, signed sums, k terms, matrices, repo FF theorems

title: Signed ES with two negative terms: 4/n = 1/x − 1/y − 1/z — trivial, and what that shows
connection: 1/x − 1/y − 1/z = 4/n with x < n/4: choose x = ⌊n/4⌋ (or nearby) and represent the positive difference by 1/y + 1/z — becomes a 2-term positive problem for the difference, often solvable but not always.
why: Sign patterns (+,+,+), (+,+,−), (+,−,−) form a ladder: (+,+,−) trivial, (+,−,−) reduces to 2-term problems, (+,+,+) is ES. The (+,−,−) case is a natural intermediate.
first_step: For n ≤ 10^4 test (+,−,−) solvability with a bounded first term; list failures.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

analogues-0309.world: H. Thin areas filled: finite fields, signed sums, k terms, matrices, repo FF theorems

title: Signed ES as the 'char-2 shadow': cancellation of equal-size terms ↔ difference of nearly equal unit fractions
connection: In F_2[T], 1/X + 1/(X + δ) has a cancelled leading term; over Z, 1/x − 1/(x + δ) = δ/(x(x+δ)) is small. Signed integer identities in which the negative term is the partner of a positive term mimic F₂ identities.
why: Lifting F₂-proofs to Z would produce signed identities; a 'positivity repair' lemma (replace 1/a − 1/b by positive terms when structure allows) would complete the transfer.
first_step: Take the F₂[T] covering identities (FUNCTIONFIELD_ES §6), substitute T ↦ 2 or T ↦ integer with signs, and see which become signed integer identities for 4/n.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

analogues-0310.world: H. Thin areas filled: finite fields, signed sums, k terms, matrices, repo FF theorems

title: k = 4 positive terms with all denominators ≡ 0 mod 4? ⇔ 16/n as a 4-term sum
connection: Generalizing all-even ⇔ 8/p: 4-term representations with all denominators divisible by 4 ⇔ 16/n is a 4-term sum. Divisor-closure across k-term worlds: (4d)/n with k terms ⇒ 4/n with k terms.
why: A k-term numerator ladder with k = 4 might be provable (more freedom), providing 4-term ES for all n — and a 4 → 3 merging step would be needed.
first_step: Compute exceptions of 16/n as a 4-term sum for n ≤ 10^4.

analogues-0311.world: H. Thin areas filled: finite fields, signed sums, k terms, matrices, repo FF theorems

title: Merging step: from a 4-term solution to a 3-term one (when do two unit fractions sum to a unit fraction?)
connection: 1/a + 1/b = 1/c iff (a − c)(b − c) = c². Given many 4-term solutions of 4/n, ES follows if some pair satisfies this. The density of 'mergeable pairs' among 4-term solutions is a computable statistic.
why: Reduces ES to a statement about 4-term solutions (easier to construct) plus a quadratic coincidence; a 4-term family with a built-in mergeable pair would be a Type I/II family in disguise.
first_step: For n ≤ 2000 enumerate 4-term solutions with bounded denominators and count mergeable pairs; check whether every n has one (it must, since ES holds there).

analogues-0312.world: H. Thin areas filled: finite fields, signed sums, k terms, matrices, repo FF theorems

title: k-term ES with prime denominators except one: Goldbach-flavoured world
connection: 4/n = 1/x + Σ_{i} 1/q_i with q_i primes: sums of reciprocals of distinct primes rarely have small denominators (the denominator is the product). So the world is nearly empty — a rigidity lemma.
why: Rigidity lemmas for prime-reciprocal sums (denominator = product of primes) explain why constrained worlds with prime denominators fail; useful for calibration.
first_step: Prove: Σ 1/q_i over distinct primes q_i (not dividing n) cannot equal 4/n − 1/x unless the q_i divide x·n — then enumerate.

analogues-0313.world: H. Thin areas filled: finite fields, signed sums, k terms, matrices, repo FF theorems

title: Matrix ES with nilpotent perturbations: X = xI + N (unipotent-type) over Z
connection: For X = xI + N with N nilpotent (N² = 0), X⁻¹ = (1/x)I − N/x². Matrix ES with such X reduces to ES plus the linear condition Σ N_i/x_i² = 0 — the dual-number world in matrix form.
why: Connects the dual-number item to matrices: solvable whenever the tangent condition is, so it's a 'first-order' matrix world.
first_step: Record equivalence; test the tangent condition on ES solutions for small p (shared with dual-number item).
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

analogues-0314.world: H. Thin areas filled: finite fields, signed sums, k terms, matrices, repo FF theorems

title: Matrix ES in M_2(Z) with X symmetric positive-definite and det X = x: projective version
connection: For PD integral X with det X = x, (X⁻¹)_{11} = X_{22}/x. Summing (1,1) entries: 4/n = Σ X_i,22/x_i — numerators X_i,22 ≥ 1, so the (1,1)-projection gives a 'numerator-weighted ES'. Matrix ES ⇒ weighted ES with weights X_{22}.
why: Weighted ES with weights ≥ 1 is easier (weights 2 trivialize), so matrix ES is likely easy; this pins how the matrix world relaxes ES.
first_step: Check whether k = 2 matrix ES is trivially solvable via weighted identities (e.g. one matrix contributing weight 2).
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

analogues-0315.world: H. Thin areas filled: finite fields, signed sums, k terms, matrices, repo FF theorems

title: Quaternion ES with norm constraint: N(x) fixed forces x into finitely many points — 'quaternion slices'
connection: In a definite quaternion order, elements of norm m are finite (r₄(m) of them). Requiring 1/x = x̄/N(x) with N(x) | stuff gives finitely many options per norm: quaternion ES is a union of finite slices indexed by norms, like ES's e-slices.
why: The count r₄(m) is a modular form coefficient (Jacobi four squares), so quaternion ES slice counts are modular — a possible source of exact formulas.
first_step: Write the quaternion ES slice count as a sum of r₄-type coefficients; compare to QUATERNION_ES.md.

analogues-0316.world: H. Thin areas filled: finite fields, signed sums, k terms, matrices, repo FF theorems

title: Octonions / Cayley integers: non-associative ES — category check
connection: Unit fractions in a non-associative algebra are still defined (x⁻¹ = x̄/N(x)), and sums make sense, integer scalars still associate, so n·x scaling arguments survive; what may fail are arguments multiplying non-real denominators together (products of three octonions). The world is meaningful but its structure theory is thin.
why: Low value except as a test of which ES arguments use associativity (probably none beyond commutative subalgebras).
first_step: Low priority; note.

analogues-0317.world: H. Thin areas filled: finite fields, signed sums, k terms, matrices, repo FF theorems

title: Gaussian-cone ES for rational p counted by Hecke characters
connection: Solutions in Z[i] with sector constraints correspond to Gaussian integers in angular sectors; counts of Gaussian primes/integers in sectors are given by Hecke Grössencharacters (Kubilius). A sector-count formula for Gaussian-cone ES would use equidistribution of angles.
why: Angular equidistribution is proved (Hecke); if ES's Gaussian twin reduces to 'some solution in a sector', equidistribution of all solutions' angles would prove it for large norm.
first_step: Compute angles of all Z[i] solutions of 4/p (no cone) for p ≤ 1000 and check whether some lies in the cone; test equidistribution.

analogues-0318.world: H. Thin areas filled: finite fields, signed sums, k terms, matrices, repo FF theorems

title: Z[i] without cone: solutions are plentiful; the cone is a 1/4-probability event per solution
connection: If unconstrained Gaussian solutions are many (polylog or more) and angles are equidistributed, the chance that all three denominators land in the cone is ≈ (1/4)³ per solution — so the Gaussian twin is a lottery with known ticket probability.
why: A clean model where the 'lottery' probability is geometric (angles), enabling exact heuristics to compare with the integer lottery.
first_step: Measure the fraction of unconstrained Gaussian solutions with all denominators in the cone for p ≤ 1000.

analogues-0319.world: H. Thin areas filled: finite fields, signed sums, k terms, matrices, repo FF theorems

title: Ultraproduct of the Z[1/ℓ] proofs: uniform k ≤ 7 bound for ℓ < 3000 — is k bounded for all ℓ?
connection: The Z[1/ℓ] mechanism needed k ≤ 7 for all odd primes ℓ < 3000. If k is uniformly bounded, the statement is first-order uniform; if unbounded, the ultraproduct world (nonstandard ℓ) may fail the mechanism with standard k.
why: Uniform boundedness would be a clean elementary theorem; failure would show the mechanism's dependence on ℓ is genuinely arithmetic (Zsigmondy primitive divisors of growing order).
first_step: Extend the search to ℓ < 10^6 and track max k; try to prove k ≤ 3 or so for ℓ ≢ 1 (mod 8).

analogues-0321.world: H. Thin areas filled: finite fields, signed sums, k terms, matrices, repo FF theorems

title: Tropical-at-p world: Type I vs Type II as the two cells of the p-adic tropicalization
connection: At the target prime p, v_p of (x, y, z) must satisfy the tropical equation: min valuation of 4xyz vs of p(xy + yz + zx). The tropical picture alone also allows the cell where all three denominators are divisible by p (locally e.g. x = y = z = 3p/4); globally that cell is excluded only by positivity (4/p = (1/p)Σ1/a_i would need Σ 1/a_i = 4 > 3). So Type I/II completeness = tropical cells + archimedean positivity.
why: Shows which part of the Type I/II split is local and which is archimedean, and suggests analogous splits at ℓ = 2 (the 2-adic cells explain the m = 8 / 4 | denominator observations).
first_step: Write the 2-adic tropical cells and match them to the 2-adic constraint-world data (all even, 4 | denominator).

analogues-0322.world: H. Thin areas filled: finite fields, signed sums, k terms, matrices, repo FF theorems

title: p-adic cone 1 + p^kZ_p: locally OBSTRUCTED, not collapsed
connection: If all denominators lie in 1 + p^kZ_p (k ≥ 1), each 1/x_i is ≡ 1 mod p^k, so the sum is ≡ 3 (mod p^k) and is a p-adic unit; 4/n with p | n has negative valuation. So this cone gives a local obstruction (congruence-subgroup type), not a collapse.
why: Corrects a tempting misapplication of the cone principle: cones of local units impose congruence obstructions; the collapse mechanism needs elements that are small at a sign place.
first_step: Record with the congruence-subgroup obstruction family (batch C items on odd / 1 mod 3 denominators).

analogues-0323.world: H. Thin areas filled: finite fields, signed sums, k terms, matrices, repo FF theorems

title: Adelic interpolation: p-adic solution families at 2 and p glued with archimedean windows
connection: ES at p = existence of a global point; locally at 2, p, ∞ the solution sets are open sets (2-adic patterns, Type I/II at p, size windows at ∞). Strong approximation fails (it's a cubic surface integral-point problem), but measuring the adelic volume of the 'window' gives the expected count.
why: The adelic window volume times the global density should reproduce log²p; mismatch identifies missing local factors.
first_step: Compute the product of local densities at 2, p, ∞ (window) and small primes for the ES integral-point count; compare with Elsholtz–Tao's average.

first_step: Run the existing FF search for q = 3, A ∈ {T², T² + 1, T² + T + 2} for deg P ≤ 10.

connection: In char 3, 4 = 1, so ES_q(4, P) = ES_q(1, P) is trivial (1/P = 1/(P+1) + 1/(P(P+1)) split once more). Constant numerators reduce mod p; only polynomial numerators are faithful.

connection: {n : ¬ES(n)} is Π₁-definable, hence its complement {n : ES(n)} is Diophantine (Σ₁) by MRDP; a polynomial whose positive values are exactly ES-good n exists. Nothing new arithmetically, but gives a 'polynomial certificate world'.

analogues-0329.world: H. Thin areas filled: finite fields, signed sums, k terms, matrices, repo FF theorems

title: ES along thin exponential sequences: Fermat numbers are trivial, 4·3^k + 1 is not
connection: Thin sequences of special form often admit identities: n ≡ 2 (mod 3) is easy (4/n = 1/n + 1/((n+1)/3) + 1/(n(n+1)/3)), so Fermat numbers 2^{2^a} + 1 ≡ 2 (mod 3) are trivial; but n = 4·3^k + 1 ≡ 1 (mod 3) and ≡ 1 (mod 4) is not automatically easy. Systematically listing thin exponential families where ES is automatic vs hard.
why: Exponential families are where power-ladder certificates live; knowing which families are automatically easy narrows hard ones.

analogues-0330.world: H. Thin areas filled: finite fields, signed sums, k terms, matrices, repo FF theorems

title: ES for squares n = p²: always true from ES(p), but certificate lines are empty (T1) — the 'derived' world
connection: ES(p²) follows by scaling a solution for p. Yet no certificate line covers odd squares (T1). So squares are the archetype of 'true but uncertifiable by lines' — solutions come only by inheritance from p.
why: Suggests a general mechanism: hard primes might also be 'inheritance-only' from some related integer (e.g. a solution of 4/(pk) scaled?). Search for inheritance relations ES(m) ⇒ ES(p) with p ∤ m impossible, but p | m possible: ES(p) ⇐ ES(pk) is false direction… check carefully.
first_step: Clarify which inheritance directions exist (ES(d) ⇒ ES(n) for d | n) and whether a p-solution can be 'generated' from solutions at multiples of p by some descent.

title: Gaussian numerator ladder: (1+i)^k/π for k = 1..4 interpolates between 2/n (trivial) and 4/n
connection: In Z[i], 4 = −(1+i)⁴, so the Gaussian-cone ES has numerator (1+i)⁴ up to a unit. The intermediate numerators (1+i)² = 2i and (1+i)³ give worlds 'between 2 and 4' that have no integer counterpart.
why: Locating the first k at which the Gaussian-cone problem becomes hard would show whether difficulty is tied to the full dyadic exponent (v_{(1+i)}(4) = 4) or appears earlier — a dyadic resolution invisible over Z.
first_step: Search for Gaussian primes of norm ≤ 2000 whether (1+i)^k/π (k = 1, 2, 3) is a sum of three cone unit fractions; record failures per k.

title: Dyadic splitting type across imaginary quadratic twins: 2 ramified (Z[i]), inert (Z[ω]), split (Z[(1+√−7)/2])
connection: The numerator 4 factors differently: (1+i)⁴, 2² (inert), (αᾱ)² (split). If ES-type difficulty in cone worlds depends on how 2 splits, the dyadic structure of ES (I3 coordinate 4Z ∪ (8Z − p), m = 8 coincidence) is the integer shadow of that dependence.

title: Sums of reciprocals of small integers modulo p (Bourgain–Garaev / Shparlinski type)
connection: Results show every residue mod p is a sum of a bounded number k of reciprocals 1/x_i (mod p) with x_i ≤ p^ε-type bounds (check exact statements). title: Beatty-restricted denominators: 4/n = Σ 1/⌊k_iθ⌋ for irrational θ
connection: Restricting denominators to a Beatty sequence (density 1/θ) is a 'quasi-random' thinning with equidistribution available (Weyl sums). The world sits between ES (θ = 1) and random thinning.
why: Equidistribution makes the Beatty world analytically tractable on average; if heuristics predict a threshold θ_c beyond which failures appear, it calibrates the ES lottery.

analogues-0335.world: I. Dyadic structure across rings, reciprocal sumsets, thinned denominators, transfer statements

title: Random thinning: keep each integer as a denominator independently with probability ρ — threshold ρ_c(p)
connection: With #ES(p) ≈ c log²p solutions, a random ρ-thinning keeps each solution with probability ρ³; the expected surviving count is c ρ³ log²p, so failures appear when ρ ≲ (log p)^{−2/3}.
why: A purely probabilistic world with an explicit threshold; comparing with the observed failure rates of structured thinnings (norms, Beatty) shows which thinnings are 'random-like'.
first_step: Simulate ρ ∈ {0.5, 0.3, 0.2} on all solutions for p < 2·10^4 and compare failure fractions with the Poisson prediction exp(−ρ³ #ES(p)).

analogues-0336.world: I. Dyadic structure across rings, reciprocal sumsets, thinned denominators, transfer statements

title: Transfer statement A (from F_q[T] density-zero theorem): 'GRH ⇒ #{p ≤ N : ¬ES(p)} ≤ N^{1−δ}'
connection: The FF proof (one-prime identity + RH for Dirichlet L-functions in F_q[T]) suggests the integer statement: under GRH, the ES exceptional set has a power saving. Even a conditional statement of this shape is apparently not in the literature.
why: A clean conditional theorem would be a genuine (if conditional) advance and would quantify what the FF RH step buys over Z.
first_step: Check Elsholtz–Tao and later literature for any GRH-conditional exceptional bound; then try to run the FF argument with GRH-quality Bombieri–Vinogradov over Z.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

analogues-0337.world: I. Dyadic structure across rings, reciprocal sumsets, thinned denominators, transfer statements

title: Transfer statement B (from N(ε) = −1 fields): 'a p-tied integer surrogate η(p) with e | 1 + η(p), e ≡ 3 (mod 4)'
connection: The real-quadratic proof needs a unit η ≡ −1 modulo a prime ℓ ≡ 3 (mod 4). Over Z, candidates for η(p) are p-tied integers (like Pell solutions for Q(√p), 4Cp, p^k); the statement 'for every p some η(p) in a small explicit family has 1 + η(p) divisible by a suitable e' would replace the unit.
why: This is the precise integer target suggested by the cleanest proved twin; it is a divisor-in-class statement over a structured family.
first_step: List small explicit families η(p) and the resulting ES identities; compute which families cover all p < 10^6.

analogues-0338.world: I. Dyadic structure across rings, reciprocal sumsets, thinned denominators, transfer statements

title: Transfer statement C (from F₂/F₄ finite coverings): 'signed covering + positivity repair'
connection: The |A| = 4 FF proofs are finite coverings using char-2 cancellation. Integer statement: a finite set of SIGNED identities covers all p, and for each p one can repair the sign using a second identity — i.e. ES ⇔ a 'repair' lemma for a finite signed covering.
why: Splits ES into a finite (checkable) signed covering and a repair step whose difficulty can be studied separately.
first_step: Construct a finite signed covering of all p ≡ 1 (mod 4) by identities 4/p = 1/x + 1/y − 1/z with z ≫ p; formulate the repair condition explicitly.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

analogues-0339.world: I. Dyadic structure across rings, reciprocal sumsets, thinned denominators, transfer statements

title: Transfer statement D (from Mordell–Schinzel in Z[T]): any proof must be non-uniform in n
connection: Since ES is false over Z[T] (eventual positivity) at square classes, no argument that also works verbatim for 'polynomial n' can prove ES. Proof strategies must use a property of integers that fails for polynomials (e.g. archimedean size of specific values, primality, bounded height search).
why: A meta-filter for proof ideas: test each idea by asking whether it would also 'prove' ES over Z[T].
first_step: Add this filter to the evaluation checklist of later waves (not applied here per brief).

analogues-0340.world: I. Dyadic structure across rings, reciprocal sumsets, thinned denominators, transfer statements

title: Transfer statement E (from the Gaussian twin): ES ⇐ 'Gaussian-cone ES for rational p' + projection
connection: If a projection Z[i]-solutions → Z-solutions existed, the Gaussian twin (with split-prime divisor abundance) would imply ES. The norm-constrained data (40 failures) show norms are not that projection.
why: Identifies a missing map; proving none exists (e.g. by a dimension/degree argument) closes the direction.
first_step: Look for a Galois-equivariant map from Gaussian solutions of 4/p to rational ones (e.g. via real parts of 1/x); test on data.

analogues-0341.world: I. Dyadic structure across rings, reciprocal sumsets, thinned denominators, transfer statements

title: Lifting from mod-p solutions: Hensel/approximation world 'ES over Z/p^kZ with archimedean box'
connection: A solution mod p^k with representatives in the box (p/4, 3p/4] × [1, p²] × [1, p³] and k large enough is an integer solution (the equation is exact once p^k exceeds the size). So ES ⇔ a box-solution modulo a large modulus.
why: Recasts ES as a box problem in a finite ring where character-sum methods apply; the box is tiny relative to the modulus, which is why it's hard.
first_step: Quantify: the box volume vs modulus at which heuristics predict a solution (= log²p expected count); compare with known small-solution theorems.

analogues-0342.world: I. Dyadic structure across rings, reciprocal sumsets, thinned denominators, transfer statements

title: Galois-cohomology world: ES solutions as rational points of a torsor under a torus
connection: The plane X + Y + Z = 4/n in reciprocal coordinates intersects the 'integrality' conditions; integrality of 1/X is a multiplicative condition, so the integral points are points of a torsor under a split torus (G_m³) restricted to a plane — a log-Calabi–Yau setting.
why: Log-CY integral points have a growing theory (Gross–Hacking–Keel mirror symmetry, cluster varieties); ES might be a cluster-type variety whose integral points have canonical bases.
first_step: Check whether the ES surface (or its log-CY compactification) is a cluster variety; compute its boundary divisor and log-canonical class.

analogues-0343.world: I. Dyadic structure across rings, reciprocal sumsets, thinned denominators, transfer statements

title: Hardy field world: ES for n = n(t) a function of a real parameter with eventual positivity
connection: Generalizing Z[T]: n(t) in a Hardy field (e.g. exp-log functions), denominators integer-valued exp-log functions eventually positive. Mordell–Schinzel's obstruction might weaken when exponentials are allowed (power ladders live here).
why: Gives the natural home of 'growing families': identities in exp-log functions of an auxiliary parameter k that cover square classes would have to evade T1 via exponential growth.
first_step: Test whether T1 at odd squares still blocks exp-log identities: does an identity in (k, 2^k) evaluate to certificate lines at squares?

analogues-0344.world: I. Dyadic structure across rings, reciprocal sumsets, thinned denominators, transfer statements

title: ES over Z[√2] with cone 'conjugate ≥ 1' (all embeddings ≥ 1): units excluded, lottery restored?
connection: Elements with all conjugates ≥ 1 form a multiplicatively closed set bounded below by 1 at both places (though dense in [1, ∞) in each embedding) and excluding all non-trivial units. This 'height-positive' cone should behave like ℕ (hard).
why: If computations show ES over this cone fails for some rational p, it is a hard world with richer arithmetic; if it always holds, there is a mechanism beyond units worth extracting.
first_step: Search 4/p = Σ 1/x_i with x_i ∈ Z[√2], x_i, x_i' ≥ 1, for p ≤ 2000, bounded height; compare with integer solution counts.

analogues-0345.world: I. Dyadic structure across rings, reciprocal sumsets, thinned denominators, transfer statements

title: Cone worlds in Z[√2]: compare four cones (ℕ, N[√2], height-positive, totally positive)
connection: A family of four cones in one ring, only partially ordered by inclusion (e.g. √2 ∈ N[√2] is not totally positive), with expected behaviour hard, ?, hard?, easy. Measuring solution counts per cone for rational p gives a direct map of how cone size controls ES.
why: The cleanest single-ring experiment for the cone principle.
first_step: Implement one search with four filters; output solution counts per cone for p ≤ 1000.

analogues-0346.world: I. Dyadic structure across rings, reciprocal sumsets, thinned denominators, transfer statements

title: Max-plus/min-plus degeneration families (Maslov dequantization): ES_h for h → 0
connection: Deform 1/x + 1/y + 1/z = 4/n via x ↦ x^{1/h}-type dequantization; as h → 0 the equation becomes a tropical (max-plus) relation of exponents. Intermediate h give real-analytic families connecting ES to its tropical limit.
why: Mostly geometric intuition (size windows); may help visualize which size patterns are forced.
first_step: Low priority; note.

analogues-0347.world: I. Dyadic structure across rings, reciprocal sumsets, thinned denominators, transfer statements

title: ES for Hurwitz quaternions of prime norm p: does every p have a quaternion solution with commuting denominators?
connection: Commuting quaternion denominators lie in an imaginary quadratic subfield; so quaternion ES with commuting denominators = union over imaginary quadratic orders inside the quaternion order of cone-ES there.
why: Gives a union-of-imaginary-quadratic-twins world: ES over many Gaussian-like rings at once; existence in at least one might be easy.
first_step: For p ≤ 500, search for quaternion solutions with all denominators in a common Z[√−d] ⊂ Hurwitz order.

analogues-0348.world: I. Dyadic structure across rings, reciprocal sumsets, thinned denominators, transfer statements

title: Profinite world: ES over Ẑ is locally solvable, but a 'sign' via an Ẑ^×-character can obstruct it
connection: Without restrictions ES is solvable in Ẑ (allowing non-unit denominators). Imposing a profinite 'sign' such as χ_{−4}(x_i) = 1 (denominators ≡ 1 mod 4) is obstructed: the reciprocal sum is ≡ 3 (mod 4) while 4/n ≡ 0 (mod 4) 2-adically for odd n. The sterile-point program, by contrast, studies which profinite points avoid all CERTIFICATE classes — not solutions.
why: Clarifies that profinite obstructions to certificates (sterile points, T1) are different from local obstructions to solutions (which ES lacks); character-type 'signs' produce the latter.
first_step: Record; connect to FF_STERILE_* and the T1 statement.

analogues-0349.world: I. Dyadic structure across rings, reciprocal sumsets, thinned denominators, transfer statements

title: Sato–Tate-type world: distribution of ES solution 'angles' (x/p, y/p², …) as p varies
connection: Normalized solution coordinates (x/p ∈ (1/4, 3/4], log y/log p, …) may equidistribute w.r.t. a limiting measure as p → ∞, like Sato–Tate angles. Hard primes would be those whose solutions avoid the bulk of the measure.
why: A limiting measure gives a precise heuristic for the probability that no solution falls in the 'admissible region' — the ES lower-tail question.
first_step: For p < 2·10^4 histogram x/p over all solutions and test convergence of the empirical measure.

analogues-0350.world: I. Dyadic structure across rings, reciprocal sumsets, thinned denominators, transfer statements

title: Lens-space/Seifert covering maps as transport between ES(n) and ES(dn)
connection: A d-fold fibre-preserving cover of the Seifert space M(0; (x,1),(y,1),(z,1)) multiplies e(M) by a factor depending on how fibres unwrap; for unwrapping that keeps β_i = 1 one gets ES-type equations for other n.
why: If covers map ES(n') solutions to ES(n) solutions with n' | n or n | n', it is a topological composition law; combined with an inductive scheme it would give ES for products.
first_step: Work out Euler numbers of covers of Seifert spaces with three exceptional fibres (Jankins–Neumann formulas).

analogues-0351.world: I. Dyadic structure across rings, reciprocal sumsets, thinned denominators, transfer statements

title: Category-error check: 'ES in the field of p-adic numbers with absolute value positivity'
connection: Q_p has no ordering, and |x|_p ≥ 1 is not closed under addition; so 'positive' p-adic ES with |·|_p-positivity is ill-defined beyond cones of units (collapse) — record as closed.
why: Avoids repeated reconsideration.
first_step: None (closed).

analogues-0353.world: I. Dyadic structure across rings, reciprocal sumsets, thinned denominators, transfer statements

title: Effective Hilbert-irreducibility world: ES-good p as values outside thin sets of a parameter family
connection: Each Type II family is a rational map from parameters to p; p is ES-good iff it is a value of some family. 'Values of a polynomial map in all primes' is Hilbert-irreducibility territory (value sets of covers). ES ⇔ the union of value sets of countably many covers contains all p ≡ 1 mod 4.
why: Value-set theorems for covers (e.g. Müller, Dèbes) might give density statements with better error terms than sieve methods.
first_step: Formalize Type II families as covers P¹ ← C and look up value-set results for families of covers of growing degree.

analogues-0354.world: I. Dyadic structure across rings, reciprocal sumsets, thinned denominators, transfer statements

title: World of 'n with prescribed factorization of n + 3': p ≡ 2 mod 3 trivial, p + 3 structure controls the x = (p+3)/4 slice
connection: The slice x = (p+3)/4 leaves 3/(px) = 1/y + 1/z, solvable iff px has a divisor ≡ 2 (mod 3) (or similar). So ES on the e = 3 slice is a statement about the prime factors of (p + 3)/4 modulo 3. Similar for e = 7, 11, … (each slice a 'world').
why: Each slice world is a congruence-on-factors world (a Chebotarev statement for p + e); the union over e is ES. Studying slice-world failure densities gives the per-slice ticket probability.
first_step: Compute, for p < 10^6, the failure density of the e-slice for e = 3, 7, 11, 15, 19 and compare with independence predictions.

analogues-0355.world: I. Dyadic structure across rings, reciprocal sumsets, thinned denominators, transfer statements

title: Gaussian twin of the e-slice: e = 1/u + 1/v in the Gaussian cone — are there more universal e?
connection: Over Z only e ∈ {1, 2}. In the Gaussian cone, 1/u + 1/v can be other Gaussian integers (e.g. with u, v conjugate-ish), giving extra universal divisors and possibly covering more classes mod 4Z[i].
why: If the Gaussian cone has a richer universal-e set, its open conjecture may be 'closer to finite covering' than ES — and the extra e's show exactly what Z lacks.
first_step: Enumerate Gaussian e in the cone with e = 1/u + 1/v, u, v in the cone and small norm; classify residues mod 4.

analogues-0356.world: I. Dyadic structure across rings, reciprocal sumsets, thinned denominators, transfer statements

title: FF analogue of hard-prime structure: P with P − 1 'smooth' (many small-degree factors)
connection: Over Z, constrained-world failures cluster at p with smooth p − 1 (601, 1801, 2521). In F_q[T] the analogue is P with P − 1 (or P + c) having many small factors; FF exceptional P's can be checked for this property.
why: If the same 'smooth shift ⇒ hard' pattern appears in FF where proofs exist, the FF proofs explain how such P are still covered — a template for Z.
first_step: From FF exception lists (EXSET_FUNCTION_FIELD data), compute the factorization degree profile of P − 1 for failing vs non-failing P.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

analogues-0357.world: I. Dyadic structure across rings, reciprocal sumsets, thinned denominators, transfer statements

title: Square-class depth: number of moduli M ≤ X with p ≡ square mod M — a T1-depth invariant of p
connection: T1 says certificate lines are empty at squares; a prime p ≡ 1 (mod M) behaves like a square modulo M. The count D(p) = #{M ≤ X : p is a square mod M} (or the largest smooth M with p ≡ 1 mod M) measures how 'square-like' p is.
why: If #ES(p) anti-correlates with D(p), hard primes are 'locally square-like' — a precise version of the smooth-(p − 1) observation and a direct link between hardness and T1.
first_step: Compute D(p) for p < 2·10^4 and correlate with #ES(p) and with constrained-world failures.

analogues-0358.world: I. Dyadic structure across rings, reciprocal sumsets, thinned denominators, transfer statements

title: Sign-twisted FF world: monic denominators but numerator A with leading coefficient c ≠ 1
connection: With A of leading coefficient c, Lemma 1.1 forces lc relations; choosing c a non-square (q odd) twists the 'colour' at ∞ — an FF analogue of changing the numerator's sign class (4 vs −4 or 4 vs 4·non-square).
why: Over Z the analogous twist is numerator −4 (signed) or 4·(−1) — trivial; in FF the twist by non-square c is non-trivial and may model T1's sign layer.
first_step: Run ES_q(cT, P) for q = 3, c = −1 (non-square), deg P ≤ 10; compare with c = 1.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

analogues-0359.world: I. Dyadic structure across rings, reciprocal sumsets, thinned denominators, transfer statements

title: ES with denominators from a lacunary set (powers times small factors): 4/p = Σ 1/(a_i 2^{k_i})
connection: Denominators of the form small·2^k: 4/p − Σ … requires p | some denominator, so at least one denominator is p·(small)·2^k; the problem becomes a 2-adic digit problem for (stuff)/p — likely solvable only for special p (p | 2^k − small).
why: A lacunary world tied to the multiplicative order of 2 mod p: ES-type solvability ⇔ conditions on ord_p(2), an Artin-type problem.
first_step: For p < 5000, test solvability with denominators a·2^k (a ≤ 15) times p^{0,1}; correlate with ord_p(2).
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

analogues-0360.world: I. Dyadic structure across rings, reciprocal sumsets, thinned denominators, transfer statements

title: ES as an integer-programming feasibility problem: divisor enumeration per p; flatness ideas need a convex relaxation
connection: For fixed p, ES is the feasibility of a small polynomial system over Z; after fixing the Type (I/II) and parameters it reduces to divisor enumeration (factorization), so ES is easy per p in practice; Lenstra/Kannan (fixed-dimension LINEAR integer programming) do not directly apply to these quadratic constraints.
why: If a slice can be relaxed to a convex body whose integer points are solutions, Khinchine's flatness theorem (lattice width) could force a point — this needs a genuinely convex formulation, which the quadratic slices lack.
first_step: Formulate one Type II slice as a lattice-width question; compute the width for hard primes and see whether Khinchine's flatness bound could force a point.

analogues-0361.world: I. Dyadic structure across rings, reciprocal sumsets, thinned denominators, transfer statements

title: Union-of-slices world with a 'budget': ES restricted to the first B slices — false for each fixed B, but by how much?
connection: Each fixed set of B slices is a finite covering ⇒ fails on a positive-density set (square classes and more). The density of failures f(B) as B grows measures how fast ES's certificate supply converges.
why: f(B) → 0 is equivalent to Vaughan-type almost-all; its rate is a concrete function to compute and model (e.g. f(B) ≍ exp(−c√B)?).
first_step: Compute f(B) for B ≤ 200 using p < 10^7; fit decay.

analogues-0362.world: I. Dyadic structure across rings, reciprocal sumsets, thinned denominators, transfer statements

title: Catalog: n = p + 2^k (de Polignac / Romanoff / Erdős)
connection: n = p + 2^k (de Polignac / Romanoff / Erdős) ↔ ES as a small-count existence problem. Expected witnesses/n: ≍ Σ_k 1/log n ≍ O(1) (log n terms each 1/log n). Obstruction: covering congruences {0 mod 2, 0 mod 3, 1 mod 4, 3 mod 8, 7 mod 12, 23 mod 24} force n−2^k divisible by a small prime. Status: false infinitely often (an AP of odd failures, Erdős 1950); Romanoff: positive lower density of representables. Mechanism: failure = periodic orbit k ↦ 2^k mod m covered by finitely many moduli; density = Romanoff's L¹ bound on r(n).
why: Canonical O(1)-count failure; ES has no periodic witness parameter, so the covering mechanism has no direct ES analogue — the reason why should be stated as a lemma.
first_step: Write the ES witness set at p as orbit(s) of a map and test whether any finite modulus set can 'cover' it; check whether this reproduces B1 sterility.

title: Catalog: n = p + 2^a + 2^b (Crocker)
connection: n = p + 2^a + 2^b (Crocker) ↔ ES as a small-count existence problem. Expected witnesses/n: ≍ log n. Obstruction: no single-modulus covering; failures come from an explicit sparse family. Status: false infinitely often (Crocker 1971; Pan 2011 gives ≫ x^{1−ε} odd exceptions ≤ x). Mechanism: an explicit sparse family of odd n (check whether it is built from 2^{2^m}−1 and Fermat-number divisibility, as commonly described).
why: Log-count, no covering, still false i.o. — the sharpest warning that 'log² count + no local obstruction' is not enough; ES's count is log² p.
first_step: Read Crocker 1971 (Pacific J. Math.) and isolate the exact structural input; ask whether an ES analogue (p tied to 2^{2^m}) exists among primes.

title: Catalog: odd n = p + 2^a + 2^b + 2^c (Sun's conjecture: every odd n > 8)
connection: odd n = p + 2^a + 2^b + 2^c (Sun's conjecture: every odd n > 8) ↔ ES as a small-count existence problem. Expected witnesses/n: ≍ log² n — same order as ES. Obstruction: none known. Status: open (conjectured by Z.-W. Sun, arXiv:0901.3075). Mechanism: none; numerics only.
why: Exact twin of ES in expected count (log²) with additive instead of multiplicative witnesses; any proof or disproof calibrates ES directly.
first_step: Check whether Crocker's construction extends to three powers (search 'p+2^a+2^b+2^c exceptions'); compute min witness count / log² n up to 10^9.

title: Catalog: Sierpiński numbers k·2^n + 1 (78557)
connection: Sierpiński numbers k·2^n + 1 (78557) ↔ ES as a small-count existence problem. Expected witnesses/n: ≍ Σ_n 1/(n log 2) = ∞ (divergent, log N up to N) but along a periodic orbit. Obstruction: covering set {3,5,7,13,19,37,73}. Status: false for specific k (covering); smallest Sierpiński number still open (78557 conjectured). Mechanism: covering system on n; also partial algebraic factorisation variants (Filaseta et al.).
why: Shows a divergent expected count can still vanish identically when the parameter is periodic mod the covering moduli.
first_step: Formulate an 'ES-Sierpiński' question: a family p(t) of primes candidates for which every ES certificate line is killed mod fixed primes; relate to T1.

title: Catalog: Riesel numbers k·2^n − 1 (509203)
connection: Riesel numbers k·2^n − 1 (509203) ↔ ES as a small-count existence problem. Expected witnesses/n: divergent log, periodic parameter. Obstruction: covering. Status: false for specific k; minimality open. Mechanism: covering.
why: Same mechanism as Sierpiński; included for completeness of the covering family.
first_step: Note: ES certificate families are also 'k·m + 1' shapes (4Cp+1): check whether any covering-type identity is impossible for them by B1.

title: Catalog: Brier numbers (both Sierpiński and Riesel)
connection: Brier numbers (both Sierpiński and Riesel) ↔ ES as a small-count existence problem. Expected witnesses/n: divergent log. Obstruction: simultaneous coverings. Status: exist (explicit large k). Mechanism: two coverings.
why: Simultaneous covering of two linear families is possible — relevant if ES were reduced to two simultaneous divisor conditions.
first_step: Check the size of the smallest known Brier number and the covering moduli used.

title: Catalog: n − 2^k composite for all k (Erdős; e.g. via covering)
connection: n − 2^k composite for all k (Erdős; e.g. via covering) ↔ ES as a small-count existence problem. Expected witnesses/n: O(1). Obstruction: covering. Status: infinitely many such odd n. Mechanism: covering.
why: Dual phrasing of the p + 2^k problem; witness = prime value of a shifted sparse sequence.
first_step: Compare: ES at p asks for a divisor in a class of a p-shifted thin sequence (4Cp+1, C varying) — not a prime value; note the difference in kind.

title: Catalog: n = p + F_k (prime + Fibonacci number)
connection: n = p + F_k (prime + Fibonacci number) ↔ ES as a small-count existence problem. Expected witnesses/n: O(1). Obstruction: covering congruences on the Fibonacci orbit (periodic mod m, Pisano period). Status: check whether: positive proportion represented and an AP of failures known (Wu–Sun style). Mechanism: Pisano periodicity makes covering possible.
why: Any linear-recurrence witness sequence is periodic mod m, enabling coverings; ES witnesses are divisor-type, not recurrence-type.

title: Catalog: Romanoff density for p + 2^k (lower density)
connection: Romanoff density for p + 2^k (lower density) ↔ ES as a small-count existence problem. Expected witnesses/n: O(1). Obstruction: partial covering. Status: positive lower density proved; upper density < 1/2 (van der Corput / Erdős). Mechanism: Cauchy–Schwarz + sieve upper bound for r(n) second moment.
why: Example where second-moment + positive mean gives positive density but not 'almost all'; ES has almost-all, a stronger regime.
first_step: Compute the analogue of Romanoff's second moment Σ R(p)² for ES (count ≍ log² p): already known? compare to Elsholtz–Tao.

title: Goldbach's other conjecture and explicit finite exceptions
connection: OEIS A060003 records odd composites not expressible as a prime plus twice a square, with 5777 and 5993 identified as the known exceptions. It shares F01/F03/F25/F32: a universal arithmetic representation, finite explicit failures, and compact certificates checked by divisor/prime search.

first_step: Build an ES analogue of A060003: for each prime p in increasing order, record the least denominator triple and the minimal search certificate; inspect whether witness-free candidates have a recognizable arithmetic signature.

connection: Linnik–Gallagher: 2n = p + q + 2^{k_1}+…+2^{k_K} ↔ ES as a small-count existence problem. Expected witnesses/n: power (Goldbach part) × polylog. Obstruction: none. connection: n = p + m² (Hardy–Littlewood Conjecture H) ↔ ES as a small-count existence problem. Expected witnesses/n: ≍ √n/log n × singular series. connection: Lemoine–Levy: odd n = p + 2q ↔ ES as a small-count existence problem. Expected witnesses/n: ≍ n / log² n. Obstruction: none. Status: open; verified numerically. Mechanism: circle method for almost all.

why: Prevents investing in 'prove algorithm X always succeeds' routes that are harder than existence.

title: Erdős–Tetali thin bases: random sets A with r_{A,k}(n) ≍ log n for EVERY n — the polylog pointwise regime, solved probabilistically
connection: Erdős–Tetali (1990): for every k there is a basis of order k with Θ(log n) representations of every large n. Same regime as ES (F04: polylog count, F01: every n, F21: pointwise), proved by independence + concentration (Janson/Chernoff) of the random set.
why: The cleanest proof that polylog-many expected witnesses CAN give pointwise existence — when witnesses are independent enough. ES's question becomes: are ES witnesses 'Erdős–Tetali-independent' at each p, and in what quantitative sense?
first_step: Estimate the dependency structure of the ES level events at fixed p (pairwise correlations over (u,B,C)) and compare with the Erdős–Tetali concentration hypotheses (bounded pairwise dependence, expected count ≥ C log n with large C).

first_step: Check whether Erdős–Fuchs (no representation function is c + small error on average) applies to Σ_{n≤N} R(n) to give a lower bound on its fluctuations.

title: Feature: power-size witness reservoir
connection: Dividing-line feature 'power-size witness reservoir'. ES LACKS it (expected witnesses ≍ log² p). To supply it one could: embed ES(p) in a 4-term problem 4/p = Σ_{i≤4} 1/x_i (power count) and prove a 'merging' rule that converts a structured 4-term solution into a 3-term one

title: Feature: free (untied) witness parameter

first_step: List fixed-modulus sub-events of ES (C fixed) and compute the fraction of p ≡ 1 mod 24 solved by C ≤ 10 — how many fixed C are needed empirically?

connection: Zagier: a finite set with two involutions; one has exactly one fixed point ⇒ odd cardinality ⇒ the other has a fixed point = representation. ES: find a finite set S_p (defined by ES-like equations) with an involution whose fixed points are ES certificates and another with a unique fixed point.
why: Parity replaces analysis entirely; it is the only known 'proof from the Book' mechanism for an every-p existence theorem of this flavour.
first_step: Enumerate small finite sets S_p = {(a,b,c,d) ∈ ℕ⁴ : quadratic/cubic ES-like relation = p} with natural windmill-type involutions; compute |S_p| mod 2 for p ≤ 10⁴ and look for sets with provably odd size.

connection: Dividing-line feature 'class-group parametrisation with positivity'. ES LACKS (certificates are not known to biject with a class group or genus). To supply it one could: seek a binary/ternary quadratic form Q_p whose representations of a fixed number correspond to ES solutions; then class number > 0 / genus would force existence

connection: 4/n with restricted denominators (squarefree; x | y | z; x,y,z ≡ 1 mod 4; …) ↔ ES as a small-count existence problem. Expected witnesses/n: ≤ log² n. why: Restricting denominators thins the count — find the restriction at which an ES-type statement provably fails (dividing line inside ES variants).

connection: Erdős–Straus for 4/n with x ≤ y ≤ z and z ≤ n^k bounded exponent ↔ ES as a small-count existence problem. Expected witnesses/n: count depends on k. Obstruction: —. Status: unknown; ES solutions can have z ≍ n² (Type I). Mechanism: —.

title: Between: does Crocker's construction extend to p + 2^a + 2^b + 2^c?
connection: Sun's three-powers conjecture (log² count, same as ES) vs Crocker's two-powers failure (log count). Resolution tells whether log² + no local obstruction can still fail i.o.
why: If a Crocker-type family kills three powers too, the 'log² is safe' heuristic for ES loses its main support; if Crocker provably cannot extend, the reason is a candidate ES lemma.
first_step: Reconstruct Crocker's family; for its members n compute r₃(n) = #{n = p + 2^a + 2^b + 2^c} up to n ≈ 2^64 with Miller–Rabin.

title: Between: Are all exceptions of p + 2^a + 2^b structured (Crocker-type) or are there 'random' ones?
connection: Pan proves ≫ x^{1−ε} exceptions; classify numerically the exceptions ≤ 10^9 by whether they lie in algebraic families.
why: If log-count failures are always structured, then ES (log², and failures provably not AP-structured) gains heuristic support.
first_step: Enumerate odd n ≤ 10^8 not of the form p + 2^a + 2^b; test membership in known families; look at residues mod small primes.

title: Between: Schinzel's N_m growth exponent
connection: Pomerance–Weingartner predict N'_m = exp(m^{1/2+o(1)}); proving any upper bound N_m < ∞ for one m ≥ 4 would be ES-strength.
why: Locates ES (m = 4) on a curve; if exceptions at m = 8..15 follow the Poisson model precisely, the model's prediction 'no exceptions for m = 4' is calibrated.
first_step: Fit observed largest exceptions (PW table: m=8: 241; m=12: 12241; m=15: 20521) against exp(c·m^{1/2}) and against (log p)³/m ≈ const.

title: Between: Why is m = 12 so exceptional in the Pomerance–Weingartner table?
connection: m = 12 has 24 exceptions up to 10^12 vs 9 for m = 10 and 13 for m = 13; the count per m should correlate with an arithmetic singular series (structure of (ℤ/m)^× and −1).
why: An 'ES singular series' S(m, n) that predicts the m-dependence would be the right object to bound below at m = 4.
first_step: Compute heuristic expected counts E_m(p) = Σ_{Type I/II shapes} densities for m = 4..15 and correlate with exception counts.

title: Between: Sums of three cubes: any non-local, non-BM failure?
connection: If some k ≢ ±4 mod 9 provably had no representation, that would be the first integral Hasse failure on a cubic surface without BM — directly ES-relevant.
why: Calibrates the plausibility of ES failing despite no BM.
first_step: Literature check: 'integral points three cubes Hasse principle failure' (Colliot-Thélène–Wittenberg, Siksek).

title: Sporadic exceptions U(n) = {105, 2961, 3985, 25305, 111969, 978145} vs. Ramanujan's 2719
connection: Ramanujan's form had sporadic exceptions explained by a finite computation + GRH. The finite U(n) exception list might be sporadic in the same sense, or the start of a structured family (a reciprocity family as in Apollonian packings).
why: Deciding 'sporadic vs structured' tells whether U(n) is a good proxy target for ES.
first_step: Factor the U(n) exceptions, compute their residues mod 840 and character values (n/ℓ) for ℓ ≤ 50, and extend the U(n) search to 10⁸ if not already done.

title: Between: Smooth-denominator ES

title: Between: ES with a prime denominator
connection: Require one of x, y, z to be prime. Expected count ≈ log² p / log p ≈ log p — a Crocker-scale count inside ES.
why: If ES-with-prime-denominator fails infinitely often in a structured family, the structure is informative; if it holds to 10^9 that is evidence log-count can hold here.

title: Between: ES with the minimal denominator bounded: x ≤ p/4 + p^θ

why: If the minimal x always lies in a short window, ES becomes a bounded search (Π₁ → decidable per p with explicit bound).

title: Between: Explicit (deterministic) thin additive basis with r(n) ≍ log n
connection: Erdős's construction is probabilistic; check whether an explicit construction with r(n) ≍ log n is known (Kolountzakis gave algorithmic constructions; Jain 2024 discusses open aspects).
why: ES = 'a deterministic log²-count system covers every prime'. Whether explicit log-count bases can be certified is the purest derandomisation analogue.
first_step: Check whether explicit/derandomised constructions with r(n) ≍ log n exist (search Kolountzakis 1995; arXiv:2405.08650).

title: Between: Hensley alphabet at critical dimension δ_A = 1/2
connection: Thin-orbit CF problems at exactly the critical exponent have count ≍ polylog — the closest SL₂ analogue of ES₅.

title: ES as an infinite congruence 'covering' of the non-squares; distortion-method analysis
connection: Hough and Balister–Bollobás–Morris–Sahasrabudhe–Tiba bound the uncovered density of covering systems via a distorted-measure sieve. Study the uncovered set of the subsystem with moduli ≤ M within [1, X] as M grows.
why: The distortion method controls the uncovered set precisely for systems with many moduli; ES's system is explicit and its uncovered set is known to contain squares.

title: Feature: two independent witness mechanisms (Type I and Type II)
connection: Dividing-line feature 'two independent witness mechanisms (Type I and Type II)'. ES HAS two (p divides one vs two denominators). To supply it one could: prove they are negatively correlated as failure events (if Type I fails because factors of many 4Cp+1 avoid −1, Type II must succeed) — a 'dichotomy' proof
why: Dichotomy proofs (Siegel-zero dichotomy, Heath-Brown's Artin) convert two weak mechanisms into a pointwise result.
first_step: Compute correlation between R_I(p) and R_II(p) over p ≡ 1 mod 24; negative correlation is a lead.

title: Feature: witness = divisor in a class (multiplicative) rather than prime value (additive)
connection: Dividing-line feature 'witness = divisor in a class (multiplicative) rather than prime value (additive)'. ES HAS multiplicative witnesses; parity barrier is not obviously relevant. To supply it one could: use multiplicative-function machinery (Halász, Matomäki–Radziwiłł) on indicator-type functions of 'has a divisor ≡ −1 mod 4C'
why: Problems with prime-valued witnesses hit the parity barrier; divisor-in-class problems are governed by Stewart-type subgroup criteria instead.
first_step: Express 1[N has a divisor ≡ −1 mod q] in terms of characters of (ℤ/q)^× via the subgroup criterion and check if Halász-type bounds apply when N runs over 4Cp+1, C ≤ X.

title: Feature: exception set closed under a natural operation
connection: Dividing-line feature 'exception set closed under a natural operation'. ES ES exceptions (if any) are closed under nothing obvious; solvable set is closed under multiples. To supply it one could: find an operation T on primes (e.g. p ↦ prime factor of some f(p)) with ES(T(p)) ⇒ ES(p); then descent along T
why: Descent proofs need such operations (Fermat's descent from p | x²+y² to smaller primes).
first_step: Search for identities: 4/p solvable if 4/q solvable for some q | (p + k) with structured k — test numerically which small-q solutions lift.

title: Feature: Linnik-constant bound (smallest witness ≤ n^A)
connection: Dividing-line feature 'Linnik-constant bound (smallest witness ≤ n^A)'. ES UNKNOWN for ES; known witnesses are small in practice. To supply it one could: prove a conditional (GRH) bound on the smallest certificate parameter, turning ES into a finite check per p
why: Least-witness theorems (Linnik, Bach) are among the few pointwise polylog results, though conditional.
first_step: Compute max over p ≤ 10^9 of the minimal Type I parameter a·d (or C) and compare with log² p.

title: Feature: height growth / Baker-type forcing
connection: Dividing-line feature 'height growth / Baker-type forcing'. ES LACKS (no linear forms in logarithms appear). To supply it one could: seek a formulation where nonexistence of an ES certificate forces a very good rational approximation or a small linear form in logs, contradicting Baker
why: Primitive divisors (BHV), Catalan-type results use Baker-type lower bounds to force existence of divisors.
first_step: Ask: if every 4Cp+1 (C ≤ X) has all prime factors in a subgroup H_C avoiding −1, is there an associated multiplicative relation among small primes that Baker could forbid?

title: Feature: Galois-theoretic forcing of divisor classes (cyclotomic/Lucas)
connection: Dividing-line feature 'Galois-theoretic forcing of divisor classes (cyclotomic/Lucas)'. ES LACKS: ES needs divisors ≡ −1 mod 4C of linear forms, which no cyclotomic structure forces. To supply it one could: use Lucas sequences U_n(P,Q) with discriminant D: primitive divisors r of U_n satisfy r ≡ (D/r) mod n, so negative D gives r ≡ −1 mod n for inert r — choose (P,Q) depending on p
why: Zsigmondy/BHV force divisors in classes ±1 mod n; a −1 mod 4C class appears naturally for inert primes.
first_step: Construct for given p a Lucas sequence whose n-th term equals (or divides) 4Cp+1 or a related ES integer; check whether its primitive divisors can be forced inert.

title: Sophie Germain / Aurifeuillean factorisation families extended to primes p of special shape
connection: Repo proved thin families via algebraic factorisations (4X⁴+1) ↔ Aurifeuillean factorisations of Φ_n(x) at special x.
why: Every Aurifeuillean identity gives an infinite family where a p-tied integer factors algebraically; systematically enumerating them could produce more proved thin families.
first_step: List Aurifeuillean identities (Brent's tables) and test each for producing an ES certificate on a polynomial family of n.

title: Feature: self-reducibility to smaller instances
connection: Dividing-line feature 'self-reducibility to smaller instances'. ES HAS ES(n) ⇐ ES(prime factor) (downward), LACKS upward/sideways reductions among primes. To supply it one could: find 'sibling' implications ES(q) ⇒ ES(p) for q related to p (e.g. q | 4p + 1)
why: Inductive proofs need sideways reductions; four-squares uses n ↦ prime factors and composition.

title: Transfer: ES as a Linnik-type problem in the progression 1 mod 4p
connection: For fixed p the auxiliary integers N_C = 4Cp + 1 run through the AP 1 (mod 4p) indexed by C; ES (Type I) asks for an element N_C with a divisor ≡ −1 mod 4C. This is a 'least element of an AP with a factorisation property' question, like Linnik's least prime in an AP.
why: Linnik-type theorems are pointwise in the modulus 4p (power reservoir of AP elements up to (4p)^L) — but the required class mod 4C moves with C, the B2 feature.
first_step: Count, for p ≤ 10^6, the least C with a valid divisor and compare with log² p and with the least prime ≡ 1 mod 4p; check whether 'C ≤ p^ε' always holds.

title: Transfer: trial-count × success-probability profile
connection: Classify thin problems by (#trials, success probability per trial): Goldbach (power, 1/log²), p + 2^k (log, 1/log), ES (C ≤ X gives X trials but success ≈ 1/C-ish ⇒ Σ ≈ log² X).
why: ES has power-many trials but harmonically decaying success: a distinct profile from both 'power reservoir' and 'log trials'. Problems with the same profile and their status would be the right comparison class.
first_step: Find other problems with harmonic success profiles: e.g. 'n has a divisor d ≡ −1 mod k for some k ≤ X' (Stewart-type), and check what's known pointwise.

title: Transfer: Chen-type switching over the C-variable
connection: Sieve the linear sequence N_C = 4Cp + 1 (C ≤ X, p fixed) to make N_C a P₂ = q·r; then ES needs q ≡ −1 mod 4C, equivalently r ≡ −1 mod 4C. Switching principle: count pairs via the other factor.
why: Fixed p, varying C: a one-dimensional linear sieve with level of distribution from Bombieri–Vinogradov-type results for the modulus-varying class condition.
first_step: Write the bilinear form Σ_{C} Σ_{qr = 4Cp+1} 1[q ≡ −1 (4C)] and check which equidistribution input (in q over moduli 4C) is needed.

title: Transfer: Maynard–Tao tuples of C's
connection: Choose C ∈ {C₀h₁, …, C₀h_k} admissible and force many N_{C_i} = 4C_i p + 1 to be almost-prime simultaneously, then use the multiplicative relations between them to force a class −1 factor.
why: Multi-dimensional sieves produce simultaneous structure; ES needs one success among many correlated shifted integers.
first_step: Check whether the N_{C_i} with C_i = C₀h_i (fixed p) form an admissible linear tuple in the variable C₀.

title: Transfer: Type I through binary quadratic forms of discriminant −4d
connection: f | 4a²d + 1 = (2a)²d + 1 means f is primitively represented by a form of discriminant −4d; Type I at (a,d) ⟺ p ≡ −f (mod 4ad) for such f. ES becomes a union of genus/class conditions on p modulo 4ad.
why: Brings class groups and genus theory of Q(√−d) into ES; class-group positivity is a proved-side mechanism.
first_step: For d ≤ 50, compute the set of residues −f mod 4ad realised by represented f, and check how quickly the union over (a,d) covers all classes mod lcm (local covering) vs primes.

title: Transfer: Duke equidistribution for represented values
connection: As d grows, values of forms of discriminant −4d (Heegner-type points) equidistribute (Duke 1988); this might equidistribute the residues −f mod 4ad that Type I offers.
why: Equidistribution in d at fixed p would give many independent chances; pointwise in p requires equidistribution uniform in a small window of d.
first_step: Check the error terms in Duke's theorem vs the window of d needed (d ≤ log^A p).

title: Transfer: Kneser/Olson subset-product theory for gate G4
connection: Stewart's criterion: a fraction fails 2-term representation iff the prime factors of the relevant integer lie in a subgroup H avoiding −1. Kneser/Olson/Davenport-constant bounds describe when subset products must hit −1.
why: ES failure ⟺ for every C, all prime factors of the relevant auxiliary integers lie in subgroups H_C ∌ −1 — a simultaneous confinement over many C.
first_step: Quantify: for random integers N ≡ 1 mod q, the probability of H-confinement ≈ (log N)^{−(1−1/[G:H])}; multiply over independent C to get the heuristic failure rate; compare with data.

title: Transfer: reciprocity across C: simultaneous confinement contradiction
connection: If all prime factors r of N_C lie in H_C ⊂ (ℤ/4C)^× for many C, then quadratic reciprocity links (q/r) for q | C to (N_C/q) = (1/q) = 1. Try to derive a contradiction from many C simultaneously.
why: Exactly how T1 arises at squares; at primes, the reciprocity constraints may be insufficient — finding where they stop is informative.
first_step: Recheck MODP_RECIPROCITY.md and TWISTED_T1.md for the multi-C version.

title: Rosser–Iwaniec semi-linear sieve for 'no divisor ≡ −1 (mod 4C)'
connection: For C = 1, 'N has no divisor ≡ 3 (mod 4)' iff all odd prime factors of N are ≡ 1 (mod 4): a half-dimensional sifted set (Landau–Ramanujan). For general C, ES failure at N requires the prime factors of N to avoid generating −1 in (ℤ/4C)^×.
why: The semi-linear sieve gives sharp upper and lower bounds for such sifted sets; summing over C at fixed p could bound the failure probability.
first_step: For fixed p, compute #{C ≤ X : 4Cp+1 has no divisor ≡ −1 mod 4C} and compare with the semi-linear sieve prediction ∏(1 − 1/ℓ)^{1/2}-type density.

title: Heath-Brown's one-of-three primitive-root theorem
connection: A pointwise family of three candidate bases guarantees that at least one succeeds infinitely often; this is an infinite-family covering result (F34) rather than a single-input universal theorem. It offers a contrasting way to combine several incomplete witness families (F08,F34).
why: ES has many certificate lines each covering thin prime sets; the theorem's finite-family combination strategy is worth testing for analogous line families.
first_step: Identify the exact three-base linear sieve lemma in Heath-Brown and see if ES certificate-line sets have a comparable pairwise independence property.

title: Transfer: AGP-style construction for a disproof (many primes failing simultaneously)
connection: AGP build L with many primes q, q−1 | L. Dually, a counterexample search could build p with p ≡ prescribed residues mod many 4ad simultaneously (CRT) — avoiding all Type I APs up to a bound.
why: Covering-type disproofs fail for ES (failures can't fill an AP), but CRT-constructed 'avoiders' up to a bound X show how many families can be dodged simultaneously; prime in the CRT class then by Linnik.
first_step: Compute the density of residue classes mod lcm{4ad : ad ≤ X} avoiding all Type I/II APs; how fast does it decay with X? (Gives an 'avoidance exponent'.)

title: Transfer: Integral Manin heuristics for the ES fibre
connection: For fixed n the ES equation defines an affine cubic surface; integral-point counting conjectures (Chambert-Loir–Tschinkel; Wilsch, Santens for log Fano) predict (log H)^b growth with a product of local densities as constant.
why: Gives a principled 'singular series' for R(n): ES fails only if the leading constant vanishes (T1?) or by fluctuation.
first_step: Compute the log Kodaira dimension / boundary divisor of the ES fibre and check which integral-point conjectures apply; compare predicted exponent b with the observed log² p.

title: Transfer: hyperbolic lattice-point counting in log-size regions
connection: Type II solutions are integer points on a quadric-type variety in a region whose volume grows only like log² p; equidistribution theorems (Duke–Rudnick–Sarnak, Eskin–McMullen) need power-size regions.
why: Explains in a geometric language why ES sits below the 'counting with error term' regime; points to effective equidistribution in small regions as the needed input.
first_step: Identify an explicit quadric Q and region R_p with #(Q(ℤ) ∩ R_p) = R_II(p); compute vol(R_p).

title: Transfer: Serre thin sets and the image of ES integral points
connection: The set of n with ES solutions is the image of integral points of the ES threefold under the projection to n. Hilbert irreducibility says images of covers are thin; ES asks the image to be everything.
why: Positive statements 'image = everything' are proved for maps with sections (identities) — ES has sections on non-square classes only (Mordell–Schinzel).
first_step: Phrase Mordell–Schinzel as 'no section over the square classes' and ask whether a multisection of growing degree (growing-level identities) exists.

title: Transfer: Halász / Matomäki–Radziwiłł for confinement indicators
connection: The indicator that N has all prime factors in H ⊂ (ℤ/q)^× is multiplicative in N; Halász-type theorems give mean values over short intervals / sequences.
why: Pointwise confinement over the sequence N_C (C ≤ X) is a mean of a multiplicative function along an AP 1 mod 4p — Matomäki–Radziwiłł style results along APs may bound it.
first_step: Check whether MR-type results apply to multiplicative functions along APs with modulus as large as 4p and length X ≈ p^θ.

title: Transfer: Smith's method: ES 'spin' distribution
connection: Koymans–Milovic and Smith control 2-power class group ranks via bilinear 'spin' sums. ES's Type I success for fixed (a,d) is a Jacobi-symbol-type condition on p; the joint distribution over many (a,d) might be a spin system.
why: Smith's method proves 100% results when pointwise criteria lack governing fields — exactly ES's apparent situation.
first_step: Check whether the indicator of 'p solved by (a,d)' can be written via Jacobi symbols (p/q) for q | 4a²d+1 and how they interact for different (a,d).

first_step: Determine whether the ES surface over Q is rational (it is a cubic surface with rational points, so likely rational) and look for curves of genus ≥ 1 in it parametrised modularly.

connection: Zero-sum theory gives sequence lengths forcing a subsequence product equal to 1; ES needs a subproduct (with complement structure) equal to −1 — a 'target' variant of Davenport's constant for (ℤ/4C)^×.
