connection: Romanoff (positive density, O(1) count) vs Vaughan ES (almost all, log² count): they differ essentially in one feature — count size O(1) vs log². ES's position: Growing count upgrades positive density to almost all; does it upgrade almost all to all? (Answer for log count: no — Crocker.)
why: Minimal pairs isolate the feature responsible for crossing the dividing line; each is a precise question about ES.
first_step: None.

title: Universal torsor of the ES surface and its integral points
connection: The ES surface U_n is a (log) del Pezzo/ toric-type surface; universal torsors linearise counting (Salberger, Heath-Brown) ↔ Type I/II parametrisations are torsor coordinates.
why: If the ET parametrisations are exactly the universal torsor, then ES(p) ⟺ an integral point on an affine variety with a free torus action — and the variety might have extra structure (e.g. be a cone over a known variety).
first_step: Compute Pic of a smooth compactification of U_n and compare the ET variables (a,b,c,d,e,f) with Cox ring generators.
alt_first_steps: [dividing-0262] Compute the Picard group/lines of the ES cubic surface over Q̄ and Q, and compare the torsor equations with the Type I variables (a, d, f, …).
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings
alt_titles: [dividing-0262] Feature: universal-torsor parametrisation of the ES surface

title: Feature: singular series bounded below on the target set
connection: Dividing-line feature 'singular series bounded below on the target set'. ES UNKNOWN: an ES local-density product S(p) is not standardly defined; T1 suggests S vanishes on certificate lines at squares. To supply it one could: define S(n) as the Euler product of local solution densities of the ES fibre with positivity region; show S(p) ≫ 1 for primes
why: Every proved pointwise asymptotic (Goldbach-ternary, Waring) needs the singular series bounded below; failures (Conj H at squares) are where it vanishes.
first_step: Compute local densities of 4xyz = n(xy+yz+zx) mod q^k for small q and n = p vs n = m²; check whether the product distinguishes squares.

title: Feature: variance / second moment control
connection: Dividing-line feature 'variance / second moment control'. ES KNOWN on average (Elsholtz–Tao moments). To supply it one could: use the second moment Σ_p R(p)² with Cauchy–Schwarz pointwise in short families (primes in a residue class mod a large modulus)
why: Romanoff-type and almost-all results come from second moments; pointwise needs higher moments or rigidity.
first_step: Read Elsholtz–Tao's moment computations; check whether higher moments (k-th) are computed.

title: Feature: symmetry group of the solution set
connection: Dividing-line feature 'symmetry group of the solution set'. ES HAS only S₃ (permutations) and scaling n ↦ kn. To supply it one could: look for hidden symmetries: Cremona/Geiser involutions of the cubic surface that preserve positivity on some subsets
why: Markoff (Vieta group), Pell (unit group), two squares (involutions) all exploit large symmetry groups.
first_step: Compute birational automorphisms of the ES cubic surface defined over Q (Geiser involutions through rational points) and test whether they map positive integral solutions to integral ones for some pairs.

title: Feature: uniformity in an auxiliary large parameter
connection: Dividing-line feature 'uniformity in an auxiliary large parameter'. ES PARTIAL (PW uniform-in-m Vaughan bound). To supply it one could: introduce an artificial large parameter (m, or modulus Q of restricted classes) where uniform results give pointwise results at a special point
why: Function-field large-q results and PW's uniformity show how an extra parameter can be leveraged.
first_step: Ask: is ES(p) implied by a uniform-in-m statement for m/(kp) with k varying (scaling ES(n) ⇒ ES(kn))?

title: Feature: deterministic witness of fixed algebraic form (identity in p)
connection: Dividing-line feature 'deterministic witness of fixed algebraic form (identity in p)'. ES LACKS at square classes (Mordell–Schinzel). To supply it one could: allow identities in auxiliary forced quantities (two-squares decomposition a, b of p; continued fraction of √p) rather than in p itself
why: Mordell–Schinzel only forbids polynomial identities in n; identities in other p-determined quantities are not covered.
first_step: Run a small symbolic search: rational-function identities 4/(a²+b²) = Σ 1/X_i(a,b) with X_i polynomials (with sign/positivity conditions on regions).

title: Feature: structure of the exceptional set at composite n
connection: Dividing-line feature 'structure of the exceptional set at composite n'. ES ES at composites reduces to prime factors (trivial). To supply it one could: use the fact that U(n)-type variants have sporadic composite failures (105 = 3·5·7, …) to locate which sub-certificate families matter
why: Composite sporadic failures of variants show which certificate families are 'load-bearing'.
first_step: Factor U(n) sporadic list and check whether each prime factor's variant certificates are 'incompatible' under scaling.

title: Feature: multiple disjoint certificate 'regimes' by size (x near p/4 vs x near p)
connection: Dividing-line feature 'multiple disjoint certificate 'regimes' by size (x near p/4 vs x near p)'. ES HAS distinct size regimes (Type I: one denominator divisible by p; Type II: two). To supply it one could: treat regimes as independent experiments and prove an anti-correlation (if small-x regime fails then large-x regime succeeds)
why: Dichotomy arguments need two regimes with complementary failure conditions.
first_step: Compute regime-wise counts for p ≤ 10^7 and their correlation.

title: Feature: p-adic / archimedean transition (local densities at ∞)
connection: Dividing-line feature 'p-adic / archimedean transition (local densities at ∞)'. ES positivity region is bounded (finitely many positive solutions). To supply it one could: view the positive solutions as integral points in a compact region of a non-compact surface; volume of region ~ log² p (matches count)
why: Counting in bounded regions with volume → ∞ slowly is the generic 'small count' regime; proofs require effective equidistribution at log scale.
first_step: Compute the volume of the positivity region in Haar/log measure and compare with R(p) on average.

title: Feature: hereditary consistency across scales (ES(p) solutions at p shape solutions at p·k)
connection: Dividing-line feature 'hereditary consistency across scales (ES(p) solutions at p shape solutions at p·k)'. ES HAS trivial scaling. To supply it one could: seek non-trivial 'lifting' from n = pq to p, i.e. a solution for 4/(pq) which is not a scaled 4/p solution, giving info about p
why: Non-trivial composite information might feed back to primes via descent.
first_step: Count non-scaled solutions of 4/(pq) and test whether their existence correlates with R(p).

title: Feature: fixed-point-free action ⇒ even count
connection: Dividing-line feature 'fixed-point-free action ⇒ even count'. ES UNKNOWN. To supply it one could: if a natural involution on solutions of 4/p has fixed points exactly at special solutions, R(p) parity encodes existence of special solutions
why: Parity-of-count arguments are the cheapest pointwise mechanism (Zagier).
first_step: Compute R(p) mod 2 for ordered/unordered triples and correlate with existence of solutions with x = y or y = z.

title: Feature: strong cancellation in a fixed-target character sum (Rickards–Stange)
connection: Dividing-line feature 'strong cancellation in a fixed-target character sum (Rickards–Stange)'. ES LACKS (fibre size log²). To supply it one could: replace the fibre over p by a larger fibre over a p-dependent family (e.g. all n = p·k, k ≤ K) of size power, then extract p
why: The only proved 'squares + sporadic' theorem uses a long character sum over one target's fibre.
first_step: Count solutions of 4/(pk) over k ≤ K that do NOT come from scaling — is that fibre power-size and does it carry p-information?

title: Meta: build the dividing-line table as a feature matrix and fit a decision tree
connection: Encode each catalog problem by features (count order, obstruction type, witness type, rigidity, reservoir, periodic parameter, symmetry group) and outcome; fit a tiny decision tree and see where ES lands and which feature flips it.
why: A crude but systematic way to read off the dividing line from data; the splits are candidate 'missing features'.
first_step: Export catalog tags from data/z52b/dividing.jsonl to a CSV, hand-correct features, fit sklearn DecisionTreeClassifier with depth ≤ 3.

title: Meta: 'witness profile' taxonomy (trials × success × correlation × structure)
connection: Classify all small-count existence problems by four numbers: log #trials, typical success probability, correlation strength between trials, and presence of algebraic structure. Plot proved/false/open.
why: Moves the dividing-line discussion from anecdotes to a 4-dimensional chart; ES's coordinates can be measured empirically.
first_step: Measure ES's correlation strength between certificate families empirically (pairwise covariance) — the unknown coordinate.

title: Meta: search Guy's UPINT D11 and Erdős problems site for unit-fraction problems with known 'dividing' resolutions
connection: Erdős problems database (erdosproblems.com) lists many unit-fraction problems, some recently resolved; each resolution mechanism is a data point for the dividing line.
why: Recent AI-assisted resolutions are concentrated in abundance regimes; listing which unit-fraction problems remain open sharpens the line.
first_step: Scrape erdosproblems.com tag 'unit fractions' and record status + mechanism for each.

title: Meta: catalogue of 'verified to 10^N, then false' small-count conjectures
connection: Collect conjectures with small expected counts that failed only at large N (Pólya 9·10^8, Mertens, Skewes, Euler sum of powers) and compare their count regimes with ES.
why: All large-first-counterexample examples are oscillation/structure-driven, not count-driven; ES verification to 10^18 is strong evidence against random-type failures but not structural ones.
first_step: Tabulate (expected count at first failure, mechanism) for each; check whether any count-driven conjecture failed beyond 10^9.

title: Meta: Poisson model predicts largest exception for each m — test at m = 4 by 'virtual exceptions'
connection: Under the PW Poisson model P(fail) ≈ exp(−(log p)³/m · κ), compute the expected number of exceptions beyond 10^18 for m = 4: if astronomically small, ES's verification is 'model-complete'.
why: Clarifies what verification to 10^18 means under the best available model.
first_step: Fit κ from m = 8..15 exception data, compute Σ_{p > 10^18} P(fail) for m = 4.

title: Catalog: n = p + k! (prime plus factorial)
connection: n = p + k! (prime plus factorial) ↔ ES as a small-count existence problem. Expected witnesses/n: ≍ (log n/log log n)·(1/log n) → 0. Obstruction: none. Status: density zero of representable n (expected count → 0); not a theorem I verified. Mechanism: count tends to zero.
why: Extreme of the count axis: below O(1) existence fails generically — anchors the bottom of the dividing scale.
first_step: Check whether a density-zero theorem for p + k! is in the literature (search 'sum of a prime and a factorial').

title: Catalog: n = p + x³ (prime plus cube)
connection: n = p + x³ (prime plus cube) ↔ ES as a small-count existence problem. Expected witnesses/n: ≍ n^{1/3}/log n. Obstruction: local mod small primes; algebraic at cubes (n = m³: m³ − x³ factors). Status: open; almost-all expected. Mechanism: —.
why: Same as Conjecture H with cubes: algebraic factorisation at perfect cubes — another 'T1-like' algebraic exceptional family.
first_step: None.

title: Catalog: n = 2^a·3^b + p (prime plus 3-smooth)
connection: n = 2^a·3^b + p (prime plus 3-smooth) ↔ ES as a small-count existence problem. Expected witnesses/n: ≍ log n (#3-smooth ≤ n ≈ log²n/2 log2 log3) × 1/log n ≈ log n. Obstruction: covering possible (periodic orbits of 2^a3^b). Status: unknown to me (check). Mechanism: —.
why: Log-count with periodic two-parameter witnesses; covering may or may not be available in two parameters — informative for the covering mechanism's reach.
first_step: Search for coverings that kill all n − 2^a3^b; compute exceptions ≤ 10^8.

title: Catalog: Every odd n > 1 = p + 2q² (q prime?) / Sun-type mixed sums
connection: Every odd n > 1 = p + 2q² (q prime?) / Sun-type mixed sums ↔ ES as a small-count existence problem. Expected witnesses/n: power/log mixes. Obstruction: various. Status: mostly conjectural (Sun's lists). Mechanism: —.
why: Z.-W. Sun's mixed-sum conjectures supply dozens of small-count problems with numerics; a systematic table of them by count order is a dividing-line dataset.
first_step: Mine arXiv:0901.3075 for conjectures with log or log² expected counts and record their numerical exception lists.

title: Catalog: Erdős: 4/n with x, y, z ≤ C·n²? (size of ES solutions)
connection: Erdős: 4/n with x, y, z ≤ C·n²? (size of ES solutions) ↔ ES as a small-count existence problem. Expected witnesses/n: log² (all solutions have max ≤ n²·const). Obstruction: —. Status: known size bounds (all positive solutions are ≪ n²). Mechanism: elementary.
why: Size bounds make ES a bounded search per n, so 'least witness' questions are well-posed.
first_step: None.

title: Greedy set-cover growth of primes by ES certificate families
connection: Order Type I/II families (by modulus) and compute the minimum number of families needed to cover all primes ≡ 1 mod 24 up to x. Finite coverings are impossible (B1); the growth rate (log x? log² x?) measures 'how infinite' ES's covering is.
why: Compare with covering systems (finite) and with p + 2^k (no covering of the complement). A slow (≈ log x) growth would suggest a structured infinite covering.
first_step: Implement greedy set cover over families with modulus ≤ M for primes ≤ 10^7; plot cover size vs x.

title: AP-avoidance density: CRT classes dodging all Type I families with ad ≤ X
connection: Compute the density δ(X) of residue classes (coprime, ≡ 1 mod 24) that avoid every Type I AP −f mod 4ad with ad ≤ X. ES ⇔ no prime survives all X; the decay rate of δ(X) is the 'covering strength'.
why: If δ(X) decays like exp(−c log² X) it matches Vaughan's exceptional set; slower decay would leave room for many CRT-constructed near-counterexamples.
first_step: Monte Carlo over random large residues, X = 10..2000; fit log δ vs log X.

title: Sieve-limit (parity-type) model for ES
connection: Selberg's parity example shows sieves cannot distinguish primes from integers with λ(n) = −1. Ask for an analogue: a set S with the sieve statistics of primes (level of distribution, local densities) on which every ES certificate family fails — odd squares are such a set for certificate lines (T1).
why: If such a model exists, sieve-only proofs of ES are impossible; if the statistics of primes already exclude it, a sieve route exists.
first_step: Try S = {n : n ≡ 1 mod 24, n = m² or m²·(unit-like)} and generalisations; check which sieve axioms each candidate violates.

title: Kubilius-type probabilistic model of R(p) as a sum of weakly dependent indicators
connection: R(p) = Σ_{families} 1[p ∈ AP(family)]; Kubilius models replace dependence by independence across moduli. The model's prediction for P(R(p) = 0) is exp(−(1+o(1))·E R(p)) if dependence is weak.
why: Formal backbone for the 'log² ⇒ true' heuristic; the dividing line is the dependence structure.
first_step: Fit the empirical distribution of R(p)/E[R(p)] for p ≡ 1 mod 24 and compare to Poisson; repo LOWER_TAIL memos have related data.

title: Turán–Kubilius / Erdős–Kac for the number of certificate families hitting p
connection: If the number of hitting families behaves like ω(n) (Erdős–Kac normal with mean and variance log²-scale), the lower tail would be Gaussian-small, not Poisson-small.
why: Distinguishes two heuristic regimes with very different exceptional-set predictions.
first_step: Compute mean and variance of R(p) in windows; compare variance/mean ratio to 1 (Poisson) vs ≫ 1 (overdispersion).

title: ES as a 'prime covering' dual to Sierpiński: an explicit infinite system that must cover all primes
connection: Sierpiński numbers are k such that a finite covering hits every k·2^n + 1; ES is the claim that an infinite AP system {−f mod 4ad} hits every prime. Both are covering statements, one about a sequence, one about primes.
why: Unifies the failure mechanism of p + 2^k with the success claim of ES: covering theory is the common language.
first_step: Survey: are there theorems that an infinite family of APs with divergent Σ1/modulus and a 'genericity' condition covers all primes (or all integers) except an explicit set?

title: Erdős–Selfridge 'covering with distinct moduli and divergent density' analogue for primes
connection: Known covering results bound minimum modulus (Hough) and handle densities; the ES system has distinct moduli 4ad with multiplicities. Ask for a 'prime covering lemma' with explicit hypotheses.
why: Would give a structural theorem in which ES is an instance — even a conditional one.
first_step: Read Balister–Bollobás–Morris–Sahasrabudhe–Tiba 'distortion method' and see if it bounds uncovered primes for infinite systems.

title: ES certificate as small solution of a congruence: lattice/Thue reformulation with p fixed
connection: For fixed (a, k), Type I asks f | 4a²d+1 with 4ad | p+f: equivalently a pair of congruences in (d, f) — a 2-dim lattice problem modulo p-dependent moduli, solvable by Thue's lemma when moduli and bounds balance.
why: Thue-type pigeonhole proves O(1)-count statements; the obstruction is the divisibility (not congruence) condition f | 4a²d+1.
first_step: Check LONGSHOT_PIGEONHOLE.md and BALANCED_LATTICE.md for this exact form.

title: ES and Romanoff-type 'positive lower density for restricted families' as a stepping stone
connection: Prove: for a fixed finite set of certificate families, the set of primes they solve has positive relative density in the hard classes (trivially true by Dirichlet). The interesting stepping stone is 'density → 1 as family set grows, with an explicit rate' (Vaughan-type).
why: Clarifies which partial results are new vs trivial.
first_step: None; tag as a calibration.

title: Arithmetic statistics of 'ES-failing residue systems' (Cohen–Lenstra style)
connection: Model the subgroups H_C ∌ −1 confining N_C's factors as random subgroups; Cohen–Lenstra-type weights might give the right probabilities for simultaneous confinement.
why: Arithmetic statistics heuristics with correct weights often predict exceptional sets accurately (e.g. Stevenhagen's negative Pell).
first_step: Compute the empirical distribution of the subgroup generated by N_C's prime factors in (ℤ/4C)^× for fixed small C over many p.

title: Stevenhagen-type conjecture for ES: exact density of p solved by families with modulus ≤ M
connection: Stevenhagen predicted the negative-Pell density via a Markov chain on 2-ranks, later proved (Koymans–Pagano). For ES, a Markov-chain model over growing family sets could predict exact densities at finite M.
why: Exact finite-M densities are provable (Chebotarev); comparing them with a model checks the model's dependence structure.
first_step: Compute exact densities of primes solved by families with 4ad ≤ M for M ≤ 200 (finite CRT computation) and fit decay of the unsolved density.
alt_first_steps: [upgrades-0163] Compute empirical densities of failing-at-all-C ≤ K for K = 1..20 and compare with the independence model and with a Rédei-type model.
alt_titles: [upgrades-0163] Rédei/Smith-style exact densities of level-failure profiles

title: Analogy with Lehmer's question for unit fractions: smallest positive value of 4/p − 1/x − 1/y − 1/z
connection: If ES fails at p, the closest approach |4/p − Σ 1/x_i| > 0 is bounded below by 1/(pxyz). Study the 'Egyptian approximation gap' distribution; ES ⇔ gap = 0 is attained.
why: Converts existence into a Diophantine-approximation statement where Baker/geometry-of-numbers tools might bite.
first_step: Compute, for p ≤ 10^5, the minimal positive gap and the number of near-solutions with gap ≤ 1/(p·xyz)·K.

title: Characteristic-p degeneracies of function-field ES (4 = 0 in char 2, 4 = 1 in char 3)
connection: Over F_{2^k}[T], 4/P = 0, so ES asks for three unit fractions summing to 0, which is P-independent and solvable (e.g. 1/T + 1/(T+1) + 1/(T(T+1)) = 0). Over F_{3^k}[T], 4/P = 1/P. These degenerations separate the role of the numerator 4 from the denominator's arithmetic.
why: Cheap sanity variants that test which function-field proofs use the size or arithmetic of the numerator 4 (and the 2-adic slot structure).
first_step: Work out ES over F_{3^k}[T]: is 1/P = 1/X + 1/Y + 1/Z with monic X, Y, Z always solvable, and by what identity?
alt_first_steps: [dividing-0297] Check FUNCTIONFIELD_ES*.md for char 2/3 results; if absent, small brute force over F_2[T], F_3[T].
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings
alt_titles: [dividing-0297] Unit fractions in function fields of characteristic 2/3 as 'bad characteristic' analogues

title: ES over ℤ[1/S] (S-integral ES)
connection: Allow denominators in ℤ[1/S] — i.e. x, y, z rationals with S-unit denominators. For S ∋ 2 or 3 does ES become provable for all p via identities?
why: Moving between integral and rational points one prime at a time locates the integrality obstruction.
first_step: Find the smallest S for which a polynomial identity covers all p ≡ 1 mod 24 with x, y, z ∈ ℤ[1/S] positive.

title: Archimedean variant: 4/p = 1/x + 1/y + 1/z with x, y, z ∈ ℤ allowing one negative denominator
connection: With one negative denominator the problem changes count regime (infinitely many solutions?) and becomes identity-solvable; the dividing line between 'all positive' and 'one negative' measures the positivity cost.
why: Isolates positivity as the obstacle (feature item 'positivity as the whole content').
first_step: Find explicit identities for 4/p = 1/x + 1/y − 1/z valid for all p; check known literature (it is classical that signed versions are easy).
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Expander-free 'thin' structure: ES₅ words as length-3 paths in the Farey graph
connection: ES₅ ⟺ λ(p) ≤ 3: a short path in the Farey/Stern–Brocot graph between specific vertices. Graph distance ≤ 3 problems in growing graphs with no expansion argument.
why: Diameter/short-path existence results in arithmetic graphs (e.g. Cayley graphs of SL₂(ℤ/p)) are proved by expansion only at log diameter, not fixed length.
first_step: See BRAINSTORM/bsA_farey_graph_metric.md.

title: Fixed-length words in SL₂(ℤ): Waring problem for SL₂ / word maps
connection: Every element of SL₂(ℤ/p) is a product of ≤ 3 (or bounded) elements of a given type (Waring for word maps; Larsen–Shalev). ES₅ is a fixed-length word condition in SL₂(ℤ) with integrality.
why: Bounded-width results in finite groups are proved by character theory (Frobenius formula) — a 'thick' count over the group — but ES needs integral lifts.
first_step: Check whether the ES₅ word count over SL₂(ℤ/N) is given by a Frobenius character formula and whether lifting to ℤ is the only gap.

title: Bounded generation of SL₂(ℤ[1/p]) / elementary matrices (Carter–Keller, Vsemirnov)
connection: Bounded generation results (every matrix a product of ≤ N elementary matrices) are pointwise for every element, proved by arithmetic (Dirichlet's theorem) — closest to 'fixed-length word exists for every target'.
why: ES₅ is an existence of a fixed-length word; bounded generation proofs use primes in APs to steer entries.
first_step: Read Vsemirnov / Morgan–Rapinchuk–Sury on bounded generation of SL₂(ℤ[1/p]) and compare the word shape with ES₅'s.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Dirichlet-steering constructions: use primes in APs to steer a certificate
connection: Bounded-generation proofs choose an auxiliary prime q in an AP to make entries coprime/divisible as needed. For ES, choose a prime q ≡ 3 mod 4 dividing a p-tied integer (Obláth: q | p + 1) — steering requires q to divide something specific, not just lie in an AP.
why: Clarifies the gap: steering works when the auxiliary object is free (any prime in an AP), not when it must divide a fixed integer.
first_step: List ES certificate constructions where the auxiliary prime can be chosen freely in an AP (if any exist, they would prove ES).

title: Erdős–Graham problem on 4/n with distinct denominators all ≤ n^{1+ε}?
connection: Bounding the largest denominator changes count; there might be literature on 'Egyptian fractions with small denominators' (Erdős–Graham book) for 4/n specifically.
why: A family where the count is tunable by the size bound.
first_step: Check Erdős–Graham 'Old and new problems' section on unit fractions for size-bounded ES variants.

title: Thick object: the multiplicative group (ℤ/pℤ)^× and its subgroup lattice
connection: ES certificates for p correspond to residues of p modulo many 4ad, but one could also look mod p: x ≡ ? mod p. The set {x : 4x ≡ … mod p} is 'thick' (size p); extraction rule: lift to ℤ with size constraints.
why: Generator-matrix item (thick object × extraction rule): (ℤ/p)^× as thick object with an archimedean extraction rule.
first_step: Write ES Type II as a condition on a residue mod p plus a size bound and check whether the residue set has structure (subgroup/coset).

title: Markoff-surface 'strong approximation' (Bourgain–Gamburd–Sarnak) adapted to U_n
connection: BGS prove the Markoff graph mod p is connected (almost all p) via Vieta moves; the ES surface U_n has a Brauer group ℤ/2 and no BM obstruction. A Vieta-like group action on integer points of U_n would convert existence into 'orbit meets the integral points'.
why: Repo says no analogous action is known — but a *partial* action (e.g. from the 3 'swap' symmetries plus a cremona transformation of the cubic) may exist and nobody computed its orbits.
first_step: Compute the automorphism group of the affine cubic surface U_n over ℚ in Sage (or by hand: it's a 'Cayley-type' cubic with three A1 singularities?); list its elements and check which preserve integrality.
alt_first_steps: [dividing-0306] Check whether the signed ES surface 4xyz = n(xy+yz+zx) has an infinite group of polynomial automorphisms (likely not; record the proof).
[tools-0122] Compute the Cremona/birational automorphisms of the Cayley cubic preserving the ES boundary and build the induced graph on ES solutions mod ℓ for small ℓ.

[tools-0122] Bourgain–Gamburd–Sarnak Markoff mod p strong approximation → ES mod p 'solution graph'

title: Lower bounds for exceptional sets: can one prove ES's exceptional set (if nonempty) is infinite?
connection: For p + 2^k, failures come in APs (infinite). For ES, scaling preserves solvability only downward; an ES counterexample p need not imply others. Ask: does one failing prime force infinitely many failing integers (yes: none — ES(kp) can hold via other factors)?
why: Structure of potential exceptional sets clarifies disproof shapes (single sporadic vs infinite families).
first_step: Prove/disprove: if ES fails at prime p then it fails at p^k (probably false/irrelevant since 4/p^k = (1/p^{k-1})·4/p … check directions).

title: Correlation with Mordell's quadratic-residue classes: strength of 'residual' structure among hard primes
connection: Mordell's classes are exactly p that are squares mod 840 — the T1 shadow. Within these, does R(p) correlate with further quadratic-residue conditions (mod 11, 13, …)?
why: If the hard primes get progressively harder with more QR conditions, T1's shadow is the governing structure; ES failure would need p to be a QR mod 'everything' (impossible for a non-square), suggesting a proof route via 'p non-square ⇒ some character escapes'.
first_step: Compute mean R(p)/log² p for p in hard classes split by (p/11), (p/13), (p/17), (p/19).

title: 'p is not a square' as the only input: character-escape lemma
connection: Since T1 kills certificate lines exactly at squares, and a non-square p is a non-residue modulo some prime ℓ ≤ ℓ(p) (least non-residue-type bound), look for a certificate family that is activated precisely by (p/ℓ) = −1.
why: Turns ES into a least-non-residue problem (pointwise under GRH with polylog ℓ, Burgess unconditionally) if each ℓ has a family activated by (p/ℓ) = −1 that always works.
first_step: For each small prime ℓ, list certificate families whose solvability condition is implied by (p/ℓ) = −1 alone — known to fail? (repo F6 'sign layer is easy'; class layer is the problem). Record where it breaks.

title: Result: CRT avoidance density of ES certificate families decays like exp(−c (ln X)³), c ≈ 0.028
connection: Fraction δ(X) of residues in Mordell's hard classes (prime-like) that avoid every Type I family (p ≡ −f mod 4ad, f | 4a²d+1) and Type II family (p ≡ −e mod 4ab, e | a+b) with ad, ab ≤ X: δ(100) = 7.8e-2, δ(1000) = 1.2e-4, δ(1778) = 9e-6; ln δ/(ln X)³ ≈ 0.025–0.030 stable over X = 56..1778 (2·10⁶ samples).
why: This is exactly the Poisson/independence prediction (expected number of hitting families ~ (log X)³, matching Pomerance–Weingartner's (log p)³/m scaling): ES's certificate families behave like independent events at the level of residues. EVIDENCE only; Chebotarev makes δ(X) the exact density of primes unsolved by families ≤ X.
first_step: Extend to X = 10⁴ with 10⁸ samples (vectorised, memory-bounded) to test whether the exponent 3 persists or creeps.

title: Result: least certificate-family size s(p) has a p-independent distribution (median 22, 99% ≤ ~200) and the CRT model predicts its maximum
connection: For all 179 468 hard-class primes p < 10⁸ the least s = ad (Type I) or ab (Type II) solving p has median 22, 90% quantile 86, 99% quantile 209 — identical to the < 10⁷ sample (22, 85, 187). The max over p < 10⁷ is 1133 (model n·δ(X) = 1 predicts ≈ 1210); over p < 10⁸ it is 2814 at p = 53049049 (model ≈ 1990, next-largest 1467).
why: Quantifies 'how far' one must search per prime and shows the independence model is calibrated on the extreme-value statistic, not only on averages. EVIDENCE only.
first_step: Push to 10⁹ (≈ 1.6·10⁶ hard primes, model predicts max ≈ 3·10³) and check the record-setters for near-square structure (cf. NEAR_SQUARE.md).

title: Prediction: least ES family size grows like exp((ln x / c)^{1/3}) — super-polylog, sub-power
connection: If δ(X) ≈ exp(−c (ln X)³), the largest least-family size among hard primes ≤ x is ≈ exp((ln π_hard(x)/c)^{1/3}) ≈ exp(((ln x)/c)^{1/3}): about 5·10⁴ at x = 10¹⁸. This matches the shape of H4_NOT_POLYLOG.md's proven lower bounds exp((log p)^κ), κ < 1/12 (κ < 1/6 relative to (G)), and suggests κ = 1/3 is the true exponent (for this coordinate).
why: Gives a concrete conjectural Linnik-constant law for ES and an explicit target for the proven-lower-bound programme (raise κ towards 1/3) and for any upper bound (which would be ES-strength).
first_step: Compare with the Salez / Mihnea–Dumitru verification data to 10¹⁸ if family sizes are recorded there; check whether the H4 coordinate and s(p) are comparable.

title: Dividing-line reading of the computation: ES is a 'random covering' with log³ intensity, Crocker's problem a 'random covering' with log intensity
connection: In the residue model, ES's hit intensity grows like (log X)³ (families up to X), so failures become rarer than any power of X; p + 2^a + 2^b has intensity ≈ log n, giving failure probability ≈ n^{−c}, compatible with infinitely many structured failures.
why: Places ES and Crocker's problem on one axis (intensity growth) where ES is comfortably on the 'all n' side, provided independence holds; the open question is only correlation/structure.
first_step: Compute the analogous residue-model intensity for p + 2^a + 2^b + 2^c (expected log²) to complete the axis.

title: Records of least family size: are record-setting primes near squares?
connection: Record primes (830041, 7155121, 7183201, 53049049) are not squares; 830041 = 911² + 120, 7183201 = 2680² + 801. T1 makes certificate lines empty at squares — near-square primes might inherit difficulty.
why: If records concentrate near squares, the T1 shadow governs the tail and the right model is 'random covering conditioned on distance to squares'.
first_step: For hard primes < 10⁸, regress least s(p) on log(distance to nearest square)/log p.

title: Catalog: Primes p with p = x² + y² and x prime (Fouvry–Iwaniec)
connection: Primes p with p = x² + y² and x prime (Fouvry–Iwaniec) ↔ ES as a small-count existence problem. Expected witnesses/n: ≍ √p/log p. Obstruction: none. Status: proved infinitely many (Fouvry–Iwaniec 1997). Mechanism: bilinear forms over Gaussian integers.
why: Thin restriction on a two-squares representation still provable in the family aspect; not pointwise.
first_step: None.

title: Catalog: Gaussian primes in narrow sectors / Hecke Größencharaktere
connection: Gaussian primes in narrow sectors / Hecke Größencharaktere ↔ ES as a small-count existence problem. Expected witnesses/n: power. Obstruction: none. Status: proved for sectors of power width. Mechanism: Hecke L-functions.
why: Angular equidistribution — ES Gaussian liftings would need sector control.
first_step: None.

title: Catalog: Least prime p ≡ 1 mod q with additional splitting (Chebotarev least prime, Lagarias–Odlyzko)
connection: Least prime p ≡ 1 mod q with additional splitting (Chebotarev least prime, Lagarias–Odlyzko) ↔ ES as a small-count existence problem. Expected witnesses/n: power of discriminant. Obstruction: none. Status: proved (bounds ≪ d^{C}). Mechanism: zero-free regions.
why: Least-witness in growing fields; ES's growing-level union is a union of such Chebotarev conditions.
first_step: None.

title: Connection: ES ⟺ Frobenius of p lies in a union of Chebotarev sets of growing level — least-prime-in-Chebotarev theory in reverse
connection: Each certificate family is a Chebotarev condition in Q(ζ_{4ad}) (splitting/residue condition). ES says Frob_p always lands in the union over all levels. Least-prime results answer 'is the first prime in a fixed Chebotarev set small?'; ES asks 'is every prime in the union of growing sets?'.
why: A 'reverse Chebotarev covering' framing makes the dividing feature precise: unions over growing level with total density → 1 at rate exp(−c log³ X).
first_step: Search for theorems of the form 'every prime p lies in some Chebotarev set C_L with L ≤ f(p)' for natural families (e.g. every p splits completely in some field of a family).

title: Connection: 'every prime splits in some member of a family of fields' problems
connection: Examples: every prime p is ≡ 1 mod some small prime ℓ (trivial), every p is a QNR mod some small ℓ (least non-residue), every p splits in some Q(√d) with d small (least QR prime). ES is a non-abelian-free but class-valued version.
why: These 'some member of a family' problems are proved pointwise exactly when the family has a forced member (Burgess / pigeonhole); identifying the forced member is the crux.
first_step: List such problems with their least-witness bounds and check which have unconditional polylog/power bounds.

title: Connection: Erdős–Hall 'every n has a divisor ≡ −1 mod m for some small m'-type statements
connection: Stewart's criterion makes 'n has a divisor ≡ −1 mod m' central. Ask the pointwise question 'for every n ≡ 1 mod 4p…'; the analogous unconditional results for integers in APs are about divisors in residue classes (Erdős–Hall, Hall–Tenenbaum).
why: Divisor-in-class problems for individual integers are typically almost-all; pointwise results need structure (e.g. n has many prime factors).
first_step: Literature check: 'divisors in residue classes Hall Tenenbaum individual integers'.

title: Connection: Erdős's multiplication-table / divisor-in-interval as obstruction to ES Type II sizes
connection: Type II needs e | a+b with 4ab | p+e — divisibility plus size constraints; Ford's multiplication-table theory gives the density of integers with divisors in intervals, which bounds Type II counts.
why: Explains why counts are log-power and not power: integers with structured divisors are rare (Ford's (log)^{−0.086} factor).
first_step: Check Elsholtz–Tao's use of divisor-sum bounds and whether Ford-type exponents appear in ES lower-tail estimates.

title: Connection: sum-product phenomena mod q for 'p ≡ −e mod 4ab, e | a+b'
connection: Type II couples a product (4ab) with a sum (a+b) through divisibility; sum-product estimates force mixed sets to cover residues, but the problem's residue question is trivial locally — the content is integrality and size.
why: Records that sum-product tools address local covering (already free for ES) — a dividing-line non-feature.
first_step: None; note only.

title: Ramsey–ES: a monochromatic solution for every finite colouring (stronger statement)
connection: Croot proved every finite colouring has a monochromatic Egyptian representation of 1. Formulate Ramsey–ES: for every finite colouring of ℕ and every large prime p, is there a monochromatic (x,y,z) with 4/p = 1/x + 1/y + 1/z? If true, it implies ES and may be accessible to Croot-type density arguments (or be false, which is informative).
why: Strengthenings sometimes have better proofs; falsification would show which colourings are 'ES-hard'.
first_step: Test colourings by 2-adic valuation parity, by residue mod 3, and random 2-colourings for p ≤ 10⁴; look for primes with no monochromatic solution.
alt_first_steps: [dividing-0323] None.
refs: arXiv:math/0311421 (Croot, On a coloring conjecture about unit fractions, Ann. Math. 157 (2003))
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings
alt_titles: [dividing-0323] Connection: the 'Ramsey/colouring' version of ES (Erdős–Graham style) is likely easy

title: Connection: ES with 'one denominator a prime power of p' only (x = p^k·u)
connection: Restricting which denominators carry p changes the family set (Type I vs II). Pure Type I or pure Type II counts are each ≍ log³-intensity in the residue model?
why: If one type alone has intensity growing fast enough, ES could in principle be proved within one type; the computation can split intensities by type.
first_step: Modify scripts/z52b_dividing_avoid.py to run Type I only and Type II only; fit exponents separately.

title: Connection: correlation between families measured by survivor statistics
connection: In the residue model, families are independent if δ(X) equals ∏(1 − density of family). Comparing the observed δ(X) with the independent product quantifies correlation exactly (no primes needed).
why: Correlation is the one unknown dividing-line coordinate for ES; this is a direct, cheap measurement.
first_step: Compute ∏_{families ≤ X}(1 − |res|/φ(m)·…) (careful with non-unit residues) vs observed δ(X).

title: Connection: the m/p family in the residue model
connection: Run the same CRT-avoidance computation for m = 5..15 (Type I: f | m a² d + 1, m a d | p + f; Type II: e | a+b, m a b | p + e) and compare δ_m(X) with PW's exception tables.
why: If δ_m(X) predicts the observed largest exceptions for m = 8..15 (e.g. 241 for m = 8), the residue model is validated on cases with actual failures — the strongest available heuristic check for m = 4.
first_step: Parametrise scripts/z52b_dividing_avoid.py by m; note PW's exceptions are for all n, not just primes.

title: Connection: residue model vs actual primes — the only gap is size, not residue
connection: Type I/II parametrisations have no size constraint (Pomerance slides): the residue model is EXACT for each fixed family set. ES ⟺ no prime survives all families; the gap between the model and ES is that X must grow with p (and Chebotarev error terms in level ≈ exp((log p)^{1/3})).
why: Reformulates ES as a uniform Chebotarev/sieve problem at level exp((log p)^{1/3+ε}): far below power level, where Bombieri–Vinogradov-type averages are strong — but needed pointwise for one p.
first_step: Check: is there any pointwise result 'every prime p avoids a sieve of level L = exp((log p)^θ) only if p is in an explicit thin set'? (Least-witness theory for sieves.)

title: Large sieve inequality applied to the exceptional set with the C-form classes as the sifting classes
connection: Classical large sieve: if a set S ⊂ [1, X] avoids ω(q) residue classes mod q for each q ≤ Q, then |S| ≤ (X + Q²)/L with L = Σ_{q ≤ Q} μ²(q) Π_{p|q} ω(p)/(p − ω(p)). For the C-form, S = exceptional set avoids, for each prime a ≡ −1 (mod 4C), the single class r_{C,a} mod a — ω(a) = #{C : 4C | a + 1} = τ((a+1)/4)-ish. So L ≈ Σ_{a ≤ Q} #{C: 4C | a+1}/a ≈ Σ_a τ((a+1)/4)/a ≈ (1/2) log²Q. Hence |exceptions ≤ X| ≪ (X + Q²)/log²Q — with Q = √X: ≪ X/log²X. A quick, elementary exceptional-set bound; weaker than Vaughan but *structurally* it shows the exceptional set has density 0 with a log² saving that mirrors the log²p count.
why: Elementary, and its proof shape (large sieve with ω(a) ~ τ(a+1)) might extend to a *weighted* large sieve giving more; and it exhibits ES's exceptional-set bounds as a special case of sieving by 'divisor-many' classes.
first_step: Verify the computation of L carefully (sum over prime a only, or all a via the full large sieve with multiplicative ω); compare with Vaughan's exp(−c(log N)^{2/3}); check whether larger Q (via Montgomery–Vaughan with Q up to X^{1/2}) or Type II's extra (c,d) classes improve the exponent.

[tools-0255] Recheck which large-sieve inequality the 3/4-exponent note uses and whether Gallagher's larger sieve (prime-power moduli) gives more.
refs: Montgomery, 'The analytic principle of the large sieve' (1978)
Gallagher, A larger sieve, Acta Arith. 18 (1971)

title: Result: ES certificate families are strongly positively correlated (residue model), yet coverage still decays like exp(−c log³ X)
connection: Observed survivor fraction vs product of marginal miss rates (families with s ≤ X): ratio 1.5 at X = 32, 6.5 at X = 100, 4·10² at X = 316, 8.5·10⁵ at X = 1000. Survivors are far more common than independence predicts, but ln δ/(ln X)³ stays ≈ 0.028 while the independent product has ≈ 0.045–0.07.
why: Independence fails badly — the dividing-line 'correlation' coordinate for ES is large — but in a way that only rescales the log³ intensity. This is the empirical form of the T1 shadow: families share quadratic-character conditions. EVIDENCE.
first_step: Identify the correlation source: group families by the quadratic characters their residue sets lie in (χ_{−4d} cosets) and recompute the independence ratio within/between character groups.

title: Result: ES difficulty tracks the least quadratic non-residue n(p) ('pseudosquare-ness')
connection: For hard-class primes < 10⁸ (n(p) ≥ 11 is forced by the classes), corr(log s(p), log n(p)) = 0.42; median least family size is 17, 29, 53, 74 for n(p) in [11,13), [13,20), [20,30), [30,50). But the overall record (s = 2814 at p = 53049049) has n(p) = 17, so n(p) is not the whole story.
why: Primes that look like squares to many small quadratic characters are harder — T1 at actual squares is the limit of this trend. A proof route: 'ES-hardness ≤ function of quadratic-character pattern', with genuine non-squares eventually escaping. EVIDENCE.
first_step: Replace n(p) by the number of primes ℓ ≤ 100 with (p/ℓ) = +1 and by the full character vector; fit s(p) with a regression or tree; look at the residual for the 2814 record.

title: Pseudosquares (Lehmer; Williams–Sorenson) as the native list of ES-hardest primes
connection: T1 kills certificates at odd squares. Primes that are locally square-like (≡ 1 mod 8 and QR modulo all small primes) should be hardest. Lehmer's pseudosquares L_q (least non-square ≡ 1 mod 8 that is a QR mod all primes ≤ q) are tabulated far beyond 10¹⁸. Note 2521 = 2520 + 1, the last I3_𝒞 zero, is ≡ 1 modulo every integer ≤ 10.
why: Pseudosquare tables give an explicit list of the 'most square-like' integers, where an ES failure would be most likely; testing ES/ES₅/I3_𝒞 there is a targeted stress test beyond 10¹⁸.
first_step: Take the known pseudosquares and pseudosquare primes (Sorenson's tables up to ~10²⁵); run the ES certificate search on each; record certificate level and count vs nearby primes.

[fingerprint-0013] Compute U(p)/log²p for the pseudosquare primes up to 10⁸ and compare to random p≡1(840) of the same size; read Lukes–Patterson–Williams on pseudosquares and Schinzel's 1997 bound.

title: Prediction: under GRH the 'sign layer' reaches n(p) ≤ 2 log² p, so if s(p) were a function of n(p) alone ES would follow — the data say it is not alone
connection: Bach's bound makes character patterns of p escape square-like behaviour by ℓ ≈ 2 log² p. If ES-hardness were controlled only by n(p) (plus bounded noise), a GRH-conditional pointwise argument would exist. The observed n(p) = 17 record with s = 2814 shows extra (class-layer) difficulty — consistent with the campaign's 'class, not parity' gap.
why: Separates how much of ES's tail is explained by the sign layer (characters) vs the class layer; quantitative version of FRONTIER's F6/G4 split.
first_step: Quantify: fraction of variance of log s(p) explained by the quadratic-character vector of p modulo ℓ ≤ 100 (linear/tree model).

title: Connection: Type I families carry a quadratic-character condition: Type I at (a,d) needs (d/p) = −1
connection: Elementary: every prime r | f | (2a)²d + 1 has (−d/r) = 1, so the Kronecker character χ = (−4d/·) has χ(f) = 1; p ≡ −f (mod 4d) then gives (−4d/p) = χ(−1) = −1, i.e. (d/p) = −1 for p ≡ 1 mod 4. Hence a Type I solution at (a,d) exists only if d is a non-residue pattern for p, so the least Type I parameter has d ≥ n(p)-type size, and Type I is dead at squares (T1 for Type I).
why: Explains the correlation result (families sharing d share the character condition) and the n(p) trend in one line. Almost certainly the campaign's 'sign layer' (F6) in different notation.
first_step: Check the analogous condition for Type II (e | a+b, 4ab | p+e) and confirm against T1_TEMPLATE.md; then re-run the correlation test within fixed-d groups.

title: Feature: character-sorted family covering — ES as a covering of the 'character cube' {±1}^ℓ
connection: Group certificate families by the quadratic-character pattern they require. ES then needs: for every pattern realised by a prime p (all patterns except 'all +1' for squares), some family compatible with that pattern also hits p's finer class. The coarse layer is a covering of the Boolean cube minus the all-ones corner.
why: Makes T1 (all-ones corner uncovered) and ES (every other corner eventually covered) two parts of one combinatorial statement; the coarse layer may be provable by finite combinatorics.
first_step: Compute, for ℓ ≤ 7 small primes, which corners of {±1}^ℓ are covered by at least one family with s ≤ 1000 (coarse layer), and how the fine layer behaves inside each corner.

title: Catalog: Pseudosquare primality tests (Lukes–Patterson–Williams)
connection: Pseudosquare primality tests (Lukes–Patterson–Williams) ↔ ES as a small-count existence problem. Expected witnesses/n: —. Obstruction: —. Status: proved: primality certified by pseudosquare conditions (under hypotheses). Mechanism: quadratic residuosity patterns.
why: Pseudosquares are where 'looks like a square to all small characters' is quantified; proofs use them as deterministic certificates.
first_step: See pseudosquare connection item.

title: OEIS anchor: U(n) = A192787
connection: Our unordered count U(n) of 4/n = 1/x+1/y+1/z (x≤y≤z) reproduces A192787 term-for-term (n ≤ 30 000 computed); the entry's links/comments are the natural index of prior counting work.

first_step: Read the A192787 entry's references/links and cross-references; record any formula or conjecture not already in FRONTIER.md.

connection: D(n) (x<y<z) matches A073101; D(n)=0 only at n=2 for n ≤ 30 000, i.e. ES with distinct denominators holds 3..30 000.

title: O(n) is odd ⟺ n ≡ 2 (mod 4) for 2 ≤ n ≤ 30 000 (S₃-orbit parity)
connection: Ordered count = #(x=y=z) + 3·#(exactly two equal) + 6·#(distinct), so O(n) ≡ #(all equal) + #(two equal) (mod 2); in range this is odd exactly for n ≡ 2 (mod 4) (the OEIS hit A121262 for 'O mod 2' was an offset artefact of starting at n = 2). Also O(n) ≢ 0 (mod 6) ⟺ n even (in range).
why: Parity of a count via its degenerate (isosceles/equilateral) solutions is the 'involution' template of WINDMILL.md; here the degenerate solutions are fully classified by the isosceles factorisation (see the isosceles-law item), so the parity law should be provable.
first_step: Prove the n ≡ 2 (mod 4) law by counting isosceles solutions via (4x−2n)(4z−n) = 2n² and (4x−n)(4z−2n) = 2n² and the equilateral one (3n/4 integral); then look for a finer involution on U(p) at p ≡ 1 (4) (where there are no degenerate solutions).

title: U(n) never equals 5 (n ≤ 30 000)
connection: The value 5 is the only k ≤ 500 not attained by U(n) for 2 ≤ n ≤ 30 000; at primes ≤ 2·10⁵ the values 5 and 12 are never attained.
why: A gap in the value set is a cheap arithmetic fingerprint; if U(n) ≥ 6 eventually were provable by a structural lower bound it would be a (weak) quantitative ES statement for large n — but likely just small-n accident.
first_step: Extend U(n) to n ≤ 10⁵ and check whether U(n) = 5 ever appears; list all n with U(n) ≤ 8 and test whether they are all ≤ some bound.

title: U(p) ≤ 4 only for p ∈ {2,3,5,13,17}
connection: Among primes ≤ 2·10⁵, U(p) ≤ 4 only at 2,3,5,13,17; for p > 1000 min U(p) is 9 (at 2521), 11, 15, …
why: An explicit lower bound U(p) ≥ c log²p failing only at small p is the kind of statement the BM main-term work (FRONTIER §2.2) predicts; the empirical floor calibrates c.
first_step: Fit min_{p∈[X,2X]} U(p) vs (log X)² for X up to 10⁷ (count program runs in ~1 s per prime at 10⁶).

title: Least prime with U(p) = 6 is 193 (a Type-A failure)
connection: The sequence 'least prime p with U(p)=k' begins 2,5,3,13,–,193,7,97,11,89,19,–,53,…; 193 (López Type-A failure) is the first prime with exactly six solutions.
why: Hard primes for one certificate family show up as the first occurrences of small U-values, i.e. the count sees the same arithmetic.
first_step: Tabulate, for each k ≤ 40, the least p with U(p)=k and check whether these are enriched in p ≡ 1 (24) and in the m/p-failure sets (data/z52b/raw/m*_pr1e5.txt).

title: Record lows of U(p)/log²p are 53, 61, 73, 193, 2521
connection: Scanning primes 50 < p < 2·10⁵, U(p)/log²p sets record lows exactly at 53, 61, 73, 193, 2521 (ratio 0.147 at 2521); no further record up to 2·10⁵.
why: Two of the five records are the Type-A (b=1) failures 193, 2521; the record sequence is a compact 'hardness' fingerprint not in OEIS.
first_step: Extend to 10⁷ with the count program restricted to candidates p ≡ 1 (mod 840) or with large least-QNR (cheap pre-filter), to see if 66529 or other A/R failures become records.

title: 2521 = lcm(1..9) + 1 is the hardest prime ≤ 2·10⁵
connection: 2521 = lcm(1,…,10)+1 minimises U(p)/log²p over primes ≤ 2·10⁵ (U=9); the primes lcm(1..k)+1 = 7, 13, 61, 421, 2521 have ratios 1.85, 0.61, 0.65, 0.44, 0.15 — monotone towards hard.
why: p ≡ 1 mod every small prime power makes every small prime a QR mod p and kills all small-modulus covering identities simultaneously; this is the extremal configuration for Mordell-type coverings.
first_step: Compute U, R, Uv for the next such prime 232 792 561 = lcm(1..19)+1 (≈ 1–2 h with the count program; words sieve to 2.4·10⁸ is cheaper) and test whether it is a (★) or b=1 failure.

title: U(232 792 561) = 276: the lcm(1..19)+1 prime is hard but not extreme
connection: p = lcm(1,…,19)+1 has U = 276, U/log²p = 0.74, U/log³p = 0.039 vs median U/log³p ≈ 0.095 at 10⁷ (below the minimum of 113 random primes at 10⁷); k₁ = 193, k₂ = 83 (k₁/k₂ = 2.3, typical). [An earlier version reported k₁ = 47 < k₂ = 82 — an artefact of a 64-bit overflow in the type classification, fixed after review.]
why: Partially confirms the lcm+1 prediction (hard, ≈ 2.5× below typical) but not 'record-hard'; the Type I/II split is normal, so all-small-primes-split does not starve Type I specifically at this prime.
first_step: Model-guided search for primes ≡ 1 (mod 2520·11·13) ≤ 10¹⁰ with extreme L(1,χ_p); compare their U/log³p with the lcm(1..19)+1 value.
alt_first_steps: [fingerprint-0012] Run z52b_count on 232792561 (needs ~3 GB spf sieve; or patch to factor x by trial division) and check R(p) via the words sieve extended to 2.4·10⁸.
alt_titles: [fingerprint-0012] Prediction: 232 792 561 should be an extreme ES-hard prime

title: U(p) at least-QNR-record primes is only moderately small
connection: At the least p≡1(4) with least QNR q (q=11..47), U(p)/log²p = 0.40,0.37,0.54,0.53,0.36,0.29,0.60,0.53,0.55,0.67,0.61 — below typical (≈1–2) but not record-hard; 2521 (least QNR 11) is far harder (0.15).
why: Shows hardness is not a function of the least QNR alone: p−1 smoothness / p ≡ 1 mod higher prime powers adds a second axis — useful for designing a two-parameter hardness model.
first_step: Regress log U(p) on log L(1,χ_p) and log(σ(p−1)/(p−1)) jointly; check which explains 2521 vs 87481.

title: U(p) residual is driven by L(1,χ_p) (Spearman −0.69)
connection: At ≈9 000 primes p≡1(4) <2·10⁵, the residual of log U(p) (after log p, loglog p) has Spearman ρ = −0.69 with L(1,χ_p) = 2h(p)·log ε_p/√p (real quadratic field Q(√p)); more small QRs ⇒ fewer solutions.
why: Gives a concrete arithmetic 'explanatory variable' for the ES count; the BM main term T(p) = Σ (−uB/p)/φ(4uB) (FRONTIER §2.2) is a weighted sum of the same character, so this is the data face of BM.
first_step: Prove/derive the expected-count heuristic E U(p) ≈ c(log p)² · F(χ_p) with F a finite Euler product, and compare F with our fitted exponent (−0.30).

title: log U(p) ≈ const − 0.30·log L_Q(1,χ_p), saturating at Q ≈ 30
connection: Adding log of the truncated Euler product ∏_{q≤Q}(1−χ_p(q)/q)^{−1} to the (log p, loglog p) regression gives α ≈ −0.30 and R²-gain 0.29 (Q=2), 0.40 (Q=3), 0.47 (Q=7), 0.49 (Q=31), 0.48 (Q=1000).
why: About half the residual variance of log U(p) is explained by the quadratic character of p at primes ≤ 30; this suggests (it does not prove) that much of the count's fluctuation is governed by finitely many local data.
first_step: Fit with separate coefficients per small prime q (2,3,5,7,11,13) to get the local weights; compare to the Elsholtz–Tao local densities.

title: Type II count k₂(p) prefers L(1,χ_{−4p}) large (α ≈ +0.21)
connection: Solutions with two denominators divisible by p (k₂) correlate positively with L(1,χ_{−4p}) = πh(−4p)/(2√p) (ρ=+0.37) and negatively with L(1,χ_p) (α ≈ −0.20); Type I (k₁) sees only χ_p (α ≈ −0.34, χ_{−4p} gain ≈ 0).
why: The two ET types live on different quadratic twists (χ_p vs χ_{−4p} = χ_{−1}χ_p at odd q): a natural 'complementarity' — when one type is starved by its character, the other may be fed.
first_step: Test the complementarity: correlation between k₁ and k₂ residuals; is min(k₁,k₂) ever 0 at p ≡ 1 (4) and if so, is the other large?

title: (★) count R(p) correlates with h(−4p) (α ≈ +0.38, R²-gain 0.20)
connection: The c=1 Type-II line R(p) = #{4uBC−u−B=p} fits log R ≈ … + 0.38 log L_Q(1,χ_{−4p}) (gain 0.20) and only −0.17 on χ_p (gain 0.09).
why: R(p) is the campaign's central count; a class-number dependence suggests an exact or approximate formula in terms of h(−4p)/Hurwitz numbers (theta-series origin), cf. KUDLA_ES.md.
first_step: Fit log R(p) on log L(1,χ_{dp}) for twists d ∈ {−4,−8,−3,−20,…} jointly (class numbers themselves scale like √p, R like log²p, so only L-values/Euler products can enter); identify the minimal twist set.

title: U(p) uncorrelated with a_p of non-CM elliptic curves
connection: Spearman of U(p)-residual with a_p(11a1)/2√p is +0.004, with a_p(37a1)/2√p −0.005, with |a_p(32a1)|/2√p +0.007, with Ramanujan τ(p)/p^{5.5} +0.006 (n≈9 000).
why: Null result: no detectable dependence on these Hecke eigenvalues, so a naive 'ES count tracks a fixed non-CM form' fingerprint is not supported; the detected dependence is through quadratic characters/L-values.
first_step: Repeat with weight-2 newforms of level 4·d for d | 840 and with weight-3/2 forms (Shimura lifts) where class numbers do appear.

title: a_p(32a1) mod 8 is just (2/p)
connection: The strong correlation of U(p) with a_p(y²=x³−x) mod 8 (ρ=+0.55) is identical to that with (2/p) (ρ=−0.55): for this CM curve a_p mod 8 encodes p mod 8.
why: Records a spurious-looking modular-form 'match' and its trivial explanation (guard against false fingerprints).
first_step: None needed; use as a sanity check whenever a CM form correlates.

title: (7/p) anomaly: U(p) does not see the character at 7
connection: Residual Spearman of U(p) with (2/p), (3/p), (5/p) is −0.55, −0.31, −0.28 but with (7/p) only −0.013, although Mordell's classes p ≡ 3,5,6 (mod 7) are covered by identities.
why: Suggests the mod-7 identity contributes O(1) solutions while 2,3,5 contribute families ∝ log p; identifies which local primes matter for the count — relevant to any weighted covering.
first_step: Split U(p) by p mod 7 class and by whether the mod-7 identity solution exists; check whether the 7-family has bounded size.

title: U(p) vs least QNR: ρ = −0.66
connection: Residual of U(p) correlates −0.66 with the least quadratic non-residue of p and +0.46 with #QNR among primes ≤ 29.
why: Least-QNR is Burgess/Vinogradov territory; a proof that U(p) ≥ 1 using 'some small prime is a QNR' (Linnik–Vinogradov n₂(p) ≪ p^{1/(4√e)+ε}) is exactly the Type-I mechanism.
first_step: Write the Type-I count as a sum over QNRs and check numerically that its main term scales with #QNR ≤ log p.

title: Least primitive root vs U: ρ = −0.57 (proxy check)
connection: The least primitive root g(p) is a QNR, so g(p) ≥ least QNR; its correlation is weaker than least QNR (−0.66).
why: Proxy relationship; recorded to avoid double-counting in multi-feature models.
first_step: Partial correlation of U with g(p) given least QNR.
alt_first_steps: [fingerprint-0023] Partial correlation of U with ord_p(2)/(p−1) controlling for (2/p) and least QNR.
alt_titles: [fingerprint-0023] U(p) vs least primitive root: ρ = −0.57

title: U(p) vs τ(p−1) and σ(p−1)/(p−1): ρ ≈ −0.53
connection: More divisors of p−1 ⇒ fewer ES solutions (ρ(τ(p−1)) = −0.53, ρ(σ(p−1)/(p−1)) = −0.53, ρ(φ(p−1)/(p−1)) = +0.42).
why: Smooth p−1 means p ≡ 1 modulo many small numbers — the Mordell-class obstruction; links ES hardness to the Erdős–Pomerance world of smooth shifted primes.
first_step: Test whether τ(p−1) remains significant after controlling for L(1,χ_p) (partial correlation).

title: U(p) vs τ((p+3)/4): ρ = +0.59
connection: U(p) residual correlates +0.59 with τ((p+3)/4) and +0.48 with τ(p+3), but only +0.12 with τ(4p+1), +0.12 with τ(p+4), +0.05 with τ(p+12).
why: x = (p+3)/4 is the smallest admissible first denominator; solutions with x=(p+3)/4 come from divisors of (p+3)/4-related numbers; a single shift explains a large share of variance.
first_step: Count solutions by x−⌈p/4⌉ ∈ {0,1,2,…} and measure what fraction of U(p) comes from the first few x; relate to divisors of p+3, p+7, …

title: Real quadratic regulator log ε_p anticorrelates with U(p) (ρ = −0.44)
connection: log ε_p and log ε_p/√p correlate −0.44 / −0.51 with U(p)-residual; h(p) alone ≈ 0 (−0.04); CF period of √p −0.27.
why: By the class number formula, 2h(p)R/√p = L(1,χ_p) (R = log ε_p): the regulator carries the L-value since h(p)=1 mostly; a direct ES ↔ fundamental unit link is the CF/Pell side of the CF-length forms of ES (ES₅).
first_step: Correlate the five-slice / λ(p) ≤ 3 certificate counts with the CF period of √p and with the regulator.

title: h(−3p) correlates positively with U(p) (ρ=+0.46)
connection: U(p) residual vs h(−3p) (imaginary quadratic field Q(√−3p)) ρ = +0.46; vs h(−4p) only +0.08 (raw) / +0.14 (normalised).
why: χ_{−3p}(q) = (−3/q)(p/q): another twist; ES identities with denominator 3 (p ≡ 2 mod 3 classes) suggest the −3 twist is natural.
first_step: Fit log U on all of log L(1,χ_{dp}) for d ∈ {1,−1,−3,−4,−8,5,−20,…} jointly and identify the minimal set.

title: Uv(p) (U-certificates) ~ U(p): ρ = +0.64; R(p) only +0.24
connection: The ES count U(p) correlates +0.64 with the U-certificate word count Uv(p), +0.46 with I3(p), +0.32 with W(p) but only +0.24 with the (★) count R(p).
why: R(p) is a thin slice with its own character (χ_{−4p}); Uv tracks the whole count. Useful when choosing which certificate family to attack for a lower bound proportional to U(p).
first_step: Compute what fraction of each p's ES solutions correspond to (★), U, I3 words via the explicit maps; check whether the fraction is stable.

title: minz(p) is always a multiple of p (p ≤ 2·10⁵)
connection: For every prime p ≤ 2·10⁵ the least possible largest denominator minz(p) ≡ 0 (mod p) (OEIS-style constant-zero transform).
why: If provable it pins the optimal solution's structure: the largest denominator always carries p; could give an extremal-solution parametrisation and a minimal-height bound.
first_step: Try to prove: in any solution of 4/p with largest denominator z, if p ∤ z then z ≥ … > some solution with p | z; else find a counterexample for composite-free p beyond 2·10⁵.

title: minz(p)/p sequence: 1,1,2,2,3,4,6,3,6,8,8,10,… (not in OEIS)
connection: floor(minz(p)/p) at primes; at p≡1(4): 2,4,6,8,10,4,14,9,10,8,28,7,…; minz(p)/p correlates −0.42 with τ(4p+1) and −0.31 with R(p).
why: The cofactor of p in the optimal denominator is a 'height' of the cheapest certificate; small values relate to (★) with small C (divisors of 4Cp+1).
first_step: Identify minz(p)/p with the least C such that 4Cp+1 has a divisor ≡ −1 (mod 4C) or similar; test equality over our range.

title: Height growth: max_{p≤X} minz(p)/p
connection: Record values of minz(p) occur at 2,3,5,7,11,13,17,23,29,31,37,53,… (nearly every prime early on); record minz(p)/p would measure the worst certificate height.
why: An upper bound minz(p) ≤ p^{1+θ} for all p is equivalent to ES with a height bound; empirical θ guides which 'bounded C' statement to aim for.
first_step: Compute max_{p ≤ X} log(minz(p)/p)/log p for X up to 10⁷ and fit.

title: n ∤ minlcm(n) ⟺ 4 | n
connection: The least common denominator of a solution of 4/n is divisible by n except exactly when 4 | n (data n ≤ 30 000; OEIS A008586 match for the exception positions).
why: Trivial direction: 4|n gives 4/n = 1/(n/4)·… with smaller lcm; but the converse (n | lcm for 4 ∤ n) is a clean lemma ensuring p-adic content of every solution.
first_step: Prove: if 4 ∤ n then every solution's lcm is divisible by n (consider v_q of both sides for q^a ∥ n).

title: minlcm(p)/p at primes not in OEIS; correlates +0.23 with least QNR
connection: The least common denominator over solutions, divided by p, behaves like a cost: larger when small primes are QRs (ρ=+0.23 with least QNR, +0.20 with L(1,χ_p)).
why: Smallest common denominator = smallest N with 4N/p a sum of three divisors of N (Egyptian-fraction 'practical number' view) — links ES to practical numbers / Erdős–Graham denominators.
first_step: Check: is minlcm(p)/p always a practical number? Compute and compare to OEIS A005153.

title: Mordell classes: x = (n+3)/4 fails only for n ≡ 1 (mod 24)
why: The sequence (not in OEIS) is the failure set of the single simplest identity family; its intersection with R-zeros and Type-A failures shows which hard primes the 'greedy' family catches.
first_step: Characterise: n with no solution with x=(n+3)/4 ⟺ 12/(n(n+3)) not a sum of two unit fractions ⟺ no divisor pair condition; derive the density and compare to count 373 ≤ 30 000.

title: Greedy-failure composites: 49, 169, 361, 553, … (squares and products)
connection: The composite members of the x=(n+3)/4 failure set include many odd squares ≡ 1 (24) (49, 169, 361, 961, 1369, …) but not all (25 is certified: 4/25 = 1/7 + 1/70 + 1/350 with 7 = (25+3)/4), and non-squares like 553 = 7·79, 721, 793, 889.
why: Squares are over-represented (a T1-like effect for a single identity family) but not uniformly obstructed; non-square composite failures show the obstruction is not only quadratic.
first_step: List non-square composite members ≤ 10⁵ and check whether each factors into primes that are themselves failures (multiplicativity test).

title: U(n) records at 2,3,6,8,10,12,15,24,30,40,48,60,… vs highly composite numbers
connection: Record positions of U(n) (not in OEIS) are dominated by smooth numbers but are not A002182 (15, 30, 40 appear; 36 does not).
why: Records of a divisor-sum-like count should track the extremal order of a specific divisor function; identifying it gives the right 'max U(n) ≍ ?' growth.
first_step: Compare record positions with records of Σ_{d|n} τ(d)², τ(n)τ(n+1)…; fit max_{n≤X} U(n) vs exp(c log X/log log X).

title: Easy primes: U(p) records eventually all ≡ −1 (mod 840)
why: Mirror of the hard primes (≡ 1 mod 840): ES-easiest primes are ≡ −1 modulo highly composite numbers (5039 = 7! − 1 = 2·2520 − 1). The count is a function of p's position relative to smooth numbers.
first_step: Note 55439 = 2·27720 − 1 and 5039 = 2·2520 − 1 are records; test the next candidates 2·lcm(1..k) − 1 and lcm(1..k) − 1 when prime; OEIS search of the record list gave no match.
alt_first_steps: [fingerprint-0037] Check if record primes satisfy p+1 = smooth with record τ(p+1); OEIS search of the record list (no match).

title: U(p) mod m is equidistributed (small bias at U ≡ 1 mod 6)
connection: For p≡1(4) >100 (n=8 843), U(p) mod 2,3,4,8 are flat within noise; U(p) ≡ 1 (mod 6) is 1361 vs ≈1490 expected (≈3.5σ low).
why: No parity constraint ⇒ no simple involution explains U(p); the mod-6 dip may be a counting artefact (e.g. solutions with y=z).
first_step: Separate solutions with repeated denominators (x=y or y=z) and recount mod 6.

title: k₁(n), k₂(n) are new sequences
connection: Number of solutions of 4/n with exactly one (k₁) / two (k₂) denominators divisible by n: k₁ = 0,2,0,1,5,5,0,5,6,6,9,…; k₂ = 1,1,1,1,2,2,2,1,4,3,…; neither in OEIS.
why: At primes these are ET Type I/Type II counts; separate sequences make it possible for others to find formulas.
first_step: Submit both (with k₃ ≡ 0 for n>1, a trivial lemma) to OEIS after independent verification.

title: k₂(p) ≥ 1 for every prime p ≤ 2·10⁵
connection: Every prime ≤ 2·10⁵ has a solution with exactly two denominators divisible by p (Type II); min k₂(p) over p ≡ 1 (4) > 1000 is small but nonzero.
why: ET note Type II is the 'easier to count' type; empirical universality of Type II alone is the statement many campaign lines target.
first_step: Record the minimum k₂(p) per dyadic range and list primes with k₂(p) = 1.

title: k₁(p) can be small while k₂(p) is not — or vice versa?
connection: k₁ and k₂ have residual correlation driven by different characters; tabulating the joint distribution of (k₁(p), k₂(p)) shows whether simultaneous smallness is rarer than independence predicts.
why: Anti-correlation of the types' local obstructions would be the cleanest heuristic for 'one type always works'.
first_step: Compute Spearman(k₁ residual, k₂ residual) and the count of p with both below their 5% quantiles vs 0.25% expected.

title: nx(n): number of distinct first denominators
connection: nx(n) = #{x : some solution has this smallest denominator}: 1,2,2,1,3,3,4,3,4,3,6,2,… (not in OEIS); at primes correlates like U (ρ=−0.65 with L(1,χ_p)).
why: nx is the 'first-step branching' of the greedy tree; lower bounds on nx(p) are ES; it is the quantity a sieve over x controls.
first_step: Fit nx(p) vs log p (likely ≍ log p, not log²p) and check whether nx(p) ≥ 1 has a shorter proof form (one-shift divisibility).

title: maxx(p) − p/4 (largest smallest-denominator)
connection: The largest possible smallest denominator maxx(p) has maxx − p/4 weakly tied to least QNR (ρ=−0.19); maxx(p) ≤ 3p/4 always; the sequence is not in OEIS.
why: Measures how 'balanced' the most balanced solution can be (BALANCED_LATTICE.md); balanced solutions are rare and relate to the cubic surface's real-point distribution.
first_step: Plot (maxx(p) − p/4)/p; compare with the balanced-solution census in BALANCED_LATTICE.md.

title: U(p) at p ≡ 1 (24) vs p ≡ 1 (840) distributions
connection: Spearman of residual U(p) with 1[p≡1 mod 24] is −0.62, with '840-square class' −0.38, with 1[p≡1 mod 840] −0.15 (rare event).
why: Quantifies how much of hardness is the classical Mordell residue structure — a reference point for any proof that treats 'bad residue classes' separately.
first_step: Compute mean U(p)/log²p per class mod 840 (the six square classes 1,121,169,289,361,529) and rank them.

title: Mordell's six square classes mod 840 are exactly the six ES-hardest classes by count, in the order 1, 121, 361, 169, 529, 289
why: Quantitative refinement of Mordell's theorem: the classes with no polynomial identity are also the classes with the fewest solutions on average, and the ordering inside them (1 hardest, 289 least hard) is a new fingerprint to explain (by 3-, 5-, 7-adic depth: 1 ≡ square of 1 mod everything).
first_step: Explain the order by which of 3, 5, 7 divide p − 1 (class 1: all three; 121 ≡ 1 mod 3,5 and 2 mod 7; 361 ≡ 1 mod 3,8 and 1 mod 5, 4 mod 7; 289 ≡ 4 mod 5, 2 mod 7) and extend to classes mod 9240.
alt_first_steps: [fingerprint-0045] Group primes ≤ 2·10⁵ by class mod 840 and by class mod 9240 = 840·11, compute mean and min of U(p)/log²p.
alt_titles: [fingerprint-0045] Which square class mod 840 is hardest?

title: U(p) vs smoothness of p−1: ρ(P⁺(p−1) exponent) = +0.40
connection: log P⁺(p−1)/log p correlates +0.40 with U(p) residual: smooth p−1 ⇒ hard.
why: Smooth shifted primes have positive density for P⁺(p−1) ≤ p^{0.2961} (Baker–Harman, cited in FORCED_WINDOW.md); ES-hard primes may be concentrated there, which is a thin set amenable to separate treatment.
first_step: Estimate density of 'ES-hard' (ratio below 0.3) among primes with P⁺(p−1) ≤ p^{1/3} vs others.

title: Hard primes are p ≡ 1 mod a large smooth modulus — compare with Carmichael/Korselt primes
connection: 2521, 1201, 3361, 20521, 21841, 4201, 14401, 9601 all have p−1 divisible by 2⁴·3·5² or 2⁴·3·5·7 etc.; these are exactly the primes used to build Carmichael numbers (Erdős construction, p−1 | L).
why: Shared extremal structure (p−1 | L for smooth L) — tools for counting such primes (AGP, Erdős) could count ES-hard candidates.
first_step: Test: are ES-hard primes over-represented among prime factors of Carmichael numbers ≤ 10¹²? (Pinch's tables).

title: Hardest 30 primes ≤ 2·10⁵ by U/log² are all ≡ 1 (mod 24)
why: Confirms Mordell's classical reduction quantitatively and shows the hard set inside 1 (mod 24) is further structured by mod-5/7/9/16 conditions.
first_step: Compute the hard list's distribution mod 5, 7, 9, 16, 25 vs all p ≡ 1 (24) to measure each prime power's contribution.

title: Campaign hard-prime lists are not in OEIS
why: No hidden classical identity (e.g. 'primes p with property X of p−1') explains them — or OEIS lacks it; submission would expose them to outside pattern-finders.
first_step: Submit the R-zero list with a definition and b-file to OEIS; also add I3 zeros (114 terms) and U failures.

title: 5/n and 6/n: no 3-term failure (primes ≤ 10⁵, all n ≤ 4000)
connection: U₅(p), U₆(p) ≥ 1 for all primes 3..10⁵ and all n ≤ 4000 (6/n trivially follows from 3/n except tiny n).
why: Sierpiński's 5/n is the nearest sibling of ES; joint fingerprints (U₄(p), U₅(p)) can show whether the same primes are hard for both.
first_step: Compute Spearman(U₄(p)/log²p, U₅(p)/log²p) at p ≤ 10⁵ and list primes hard for both.
refs: arXiv:2511.16817 (Pomerance–Weingartner, Exceptions to the Erdős–Straus–Schinzel conjecture)

title: 7/n fails only at n = 2 (≤ 10⁵ primes, n ≤ 4000)
connection: Consistent with PW (no 7/n exception in [3, 10¹³]); 7/p counts at primes are small (U₇(p) = 0,1,2,3,2,8,4,…).
why: 7/n is the smallest numerator where the local (mod-m) obstruction picture differs from 4 and 5; any ES method that is numerator-uniform must also handle 7.
first_step: Fit U₇(p) vs log²p and check whether the hardest 7/p primes coincide with the hardest 4/p primes.
refs: arXiv:2511.16817 (Pomerance–Weingartner, Exceptions to the Erdős–Straus–Schinzel conjecture)

title: '3-divisible ES': 12/p fails at 22 primes ≤ 10⁵, last 12 241
why: Contains the Type-A failures 193 and 2521 and the R-zero 577: the '3-divisible' sub-problem is hard on the same primes — a sub-ES whose failure set is a fingerprint of global hardness.
first_step: Extend 12/p to 10⁷ (fast: x ∈ (p/12, p/4]) to test finiteness; check whether 66529, 409, 5569 eventually appear (they do not ≤ 10⁵ except as listed).
refs: arXiv:2511.16817 (Pomerance–Weingartner, Exceptions to the Erdős–Straus–Schinzel conjecture)
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: '4-divisible ES': 16/p last failure ≤ 10⁵ is 83449 — an R-zero
connection: 16/p failures (38 primes ≤ 10⁵) include 193, 577, 1201, 2521, 3361, 3169, 4801, 33601, 36529, 78721 and end at 83449, which is also a (★) failure.
why: Two independent hardness tests pick out the same large prime 83449: suggests a shared 2-adic obstruction (p ≡ 1 mod 16? 83449 mod 16 = 9) worth isolating.
first_step: Compute v₂(p−1), p mod 16/32/64 for all 16/p failures and for the 14 R-zeros; test whether 2-adic depth predicts both.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: '5-divisible ES': 20/p fails at 63 primes ≤ 10⁵, last 90001
connection: No ES solution with 5 | x, y, z at 63 primes ≤ 10⁵, including 1201, 2521, 4201, 4801, 8761, 21841, 24481 (ES-hard) — the last at 90001 = 9·10⁴+1.
why: The 5-divisible failure set mirrors primes ≡ 1 (mod 5^a·…) — a local obstruction at 5 that compounds global hardness.
first_step: Tabulate p mod 25 and mod 125 for 20/p failures vs random primes.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Divisibility-strengthened ES_k ladder (k | x,y,z): last failures 241, 12241, 83449, 90001, ≥97777, 92401, …
why: PW prove n_m ≥ exp(m^{1/3+o(1)}), so ES_k fails infinitely far out as k grows but each ES_k plausibly has finitely many failures — a quantitative family 'between' ES and false statements, useful to calibrate any method's strength (a method proving ES_k for k=3 would be stronger than ES).
first_step: Pick the smallest k (k=2, 'even ES') and try to push the census to 10¹⁰ with a dedicated sieve; check whether the 8/n exceptions really stop at 241.
refs: arXiv:2511.16817 (Pomerance–Weingartner, Exceptions to the Erdős–Straus–Schinzel conjecture)
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Failure sets are monotone under divisibility of the numerator (sanity + structure)
connection: If m | m′ then fail(m) ⊆ fail(m′) (multiply all denominators of an m′/n representation by m′/m to get one of m/n); verified on all m ≤ 48, p ≤ 10⁵. 'Primitive' failures (not explained by a divisor d ≥ 5 of m) number 0,0,1,6,4,8,3,22,10,8,25,32,17,45,…
why: ES is the bottom of a divisibility lattice of Schinzel problems; primitive failure counts strip out inherited obstructions and are the right 'new difficulty' per numerator.
first_step: Submit primitive-failure counts to OEIS; examine whether primitive failures of 4k concentrate on primes hard for 4/p.
refs: arXiv:2511.16817 (Pomerance–Weingartner, Exceptions to the Erdős–Straus–Schinzel conjecture)

title: Hardness index H(p) = #{m ≤ 48 : m/p fails} correlates with U(p)/log²p (ρ = −0.43)
why: A single prime-level 'obstruction profile' across numerators: if hardness were a local (Euler-product) phenomenon, H(p) should be predictable from p mod small numbers — a cheap test of locality.
first_step: Regress H(p) on Legendre symbols (q/p) for q ≤ 30 and on p mod 8,9,16,25; report R².

title: R-zeros and Type-A failures across numerators: 193 fails 19 numerators, 577 13, 2521 11, 3361 11, 409 7, 9601 5, 5569 4, 66529 3, 23929 0
connection: Among m ∈ [5,48], the campaign's hard primes fail many m/p; but 23929 (an R-zero) fails none — R-failure is not 'globally hard'.
why: Separates certificate-line hardness ((★) zeros) from intrinsic ES hardness — useful to decide which hard primes are artefacts of a chosen line.
first_step: For each of the 14 R-zeros compute U(p)/log²p and H(p) to rank 'intrinsic' vs 'line-specific' hardness.

title: PW numerics reproduced: for every m ∈ [20,48] some prime in (m², 2m²) fails m/p
connection: Counts of failing primes in (m², 2m²): m=20:6, 21:5, 22:5, 23:5, 24:13, …, 48:70 — consistent with PW's reported numerics for m ≥ 20.
why: Independent confirmation of a 2025 literature claim with our engine; and the counts per m give an empirical density to compare with PW's probabilistic model.
first_step: Compare the counts with PW's predicted number (their Elsholtz–Tao-style density) in (m², 2m²).
refs: arXiv:2511.16817 (Pomerance–Weingartner, Exceptions to the Erdős–Straus–Schinzel conjecture)

title: Prime numerators have far fewer failures than composite ones
why: Composite m inherit failures from divisors (monotonicity) but also have fewer 'cheap' identities; the prime-m sequence measures the bare Schinzel difficulty.
first_step: Fit #failures(m) for prime m vs m (power law?) and compare with PW's exp(m^{1/3}) lower bound for n_m.
refs: arXiv:2511.16817 (Pomerance–Weingartner, Exceptions to the Erdős–Straus–Schinzel conjecture)

title: 9/n fails exactly at {2,5,11,19} (≤ 10⁵ primes, n ≤ 4000)
connection: Tiny, apparently complete exception set for 9/n; 9 = 3² so 9/n relates to 3/n-type identities.
why: Small complete exception lists are the most 'fingerprintable'; no OEIS hit for {2,5,11,19} beyond spurious ones.
first_step: Prove completeness of {2,5,11,19} for 9/n by covering congruences (expected possible since 9/n has many identities) — a warm-up for the ES covering obstruction.

title: 10/n fails at {2,3,7,11,43,61,67,181}; 11/n at {2,3,4,37}; 13/n at {2,3,4,5,7,14,53,61,67,79,211,281}
connection: Complete-looking small exception lists (n ≤ 4000 all, primes ≤ 10⁵), none in OEIS; composite exceptions occur (4 for 11 and 13, 14 for 13).
why: Each list is a finite certificate target; the presence of composite exceptions (4, 14) shows the reduction-to-primes fails for m ≠ 4, unlike ES.
first_step: Explain 13/14 and 11/4 failures (why multiplicativity breaks) and check whether any composite n > 100 fails m/n for m ≤ 13.

title: 15/p failure set contains three of the 30 hardest ES primes (4201, 12601, 20521)
connection: 15/p fails at 25 primes ≤ 10⁵ ending 1103,1171,1367,4201,6301,12601,16831,20521; 4201, 12601, 20521 are top-30 hard for 4/p though 15 is not a multiple of 4.
why: Cross-numerator coincidence not explained by divisibility monotonicity; suggests a shared local cause (p ≡ 1 mod 120 or 840?).
first_step: Compute p mod 840 for 15/p failures and test enrichment of p ≡ 1 (mod 120).

title: m/p failures are enriched in primes adjacent to 5-smooth numbers
connection: For m=12, 15 of 22 failures have p−1 or p+1 5-smooth (only 182 such primes ≤ 10⁵ in total); m=20: 27/63; m=24: 39/146 — OEIS returns spurious A219669 ('primes neighboring a 5-smooth number') for m=45.
why: Primes next to smooth numbers are ≡ ±1 modulo many small numbers simultaneously — the Mordell-class mechanism; a quantitative version is a 'smooth-neighbour' hardness law.
first_step: Compute failure rate among 5-smooth-neighbour primes vs others for each m; extend to 7-smooth.

title: Last-failure sequence by numerator m (7..48) is not in OEIS
why: These are lower bounds for Schinzel's n_m (true values may be larger beyond 10⁵); a curated table would let PW-type theory be compared with data.
