connection: Record a multiplicative scale factor and a congruence correction along each matrix or continued-fraction move.
why: The cocycle may reveal telescoping products that enforce integrality after a whole word.
first_step: Compute the scale cocycle for three verified moves and search short loops with unit total correction.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Escape to the cusp
connection: Interpret unusually large minimal denominators as possible degeneration of an associated lattice basis.
why: This can distinguish missing certificates from certificates hidden in highly anisotropic regions.
first_step: For difficult bounded instances, compute successive minima of a relevant small lattice and compare them with denominator imbalance.

title: Adelic height bookkeeping
connection: Combine real denominator size with p-adic valuation penalties in a single explicitly defined height.
why: A balanced height might reveal a descent invisible to the archimedean maximum alone.
first_step: Define a height on one rational parametrization and calculate its change under two exact transformations.

title: Arithmetic tori from norm-one units
connection: Use norm-one units to move along a norm-equation slice while preserving its right-hand side.
why: The remaining question becomes whether the orbit reaches the positivity and congruence region needed for ES.
first_step: For a small real quadratic norm equation, compute unit-orbit residues modulo the required modulus.

title: p-adic dynamics of parameter maps
connection: Iterate an exact rational parameter transformation over residue rings and inspect attracting or periodic classes.
why: Stable modular behavior could support iterative congruence repair before real positivity is addressed.
first_step: For a verified map, enumerate its defined orbits modulo 3² and 3³ and compare lifting patterns.

title: Convex relaxations of bounded searches
connection: Relax selected bilinear constraints using valid convex envelopes inside a finite parameter box.
why: The relaxation can prune impossible boxes or reveal promising corners, without supplying integer witnesses by itself.
first_step: Apply McCormick envelopes to one bounded auxiliary equation and compare feasible boxes with exact enumeration.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Reciprocal convexity bounds
connection: Use convexity of 1/t to derive necessary bounds on denominator sums and imbalance within a chosen search region.
why: These bounds are elementary and can reduce search without risking false sufficiency claims.
first_step: Derive Jensen and tangent-line bounds for ordered x≤y≤z satisfying the reciprocal sum.

title: Harmonic–arithmetic mean constraints
connection: Relate denominator spread to the fixed reciprocal sum through mean inequalities.
why: Quantitative spread bounds can distinguish balanced and highly skewed certificate families.
first_step: Derive the sharp lower bound on x+y+z over positive real solutions and inspect the integer gap for small p.

title: Stationary points of certificate cost
connection: Minimize smooth proxies such as log(xyz) on the real ES surface under specified denominator ordering and bounds.
why: Critical points indicate where an integer search should concentrate, not where integer solutions must exist.
first_step: Use Lagrange multipliers for one bounded cost and compare its minimizers with actual small certificates.

title: Curvature-adapted sampling
connection: Sample near the real solution surface with density adjusted to local curvature and rounding sensitivity.
why: This may propose integer candidates more efficiently than sampling a rectangular box.
first_step: Compute the Hessian of z=pxy/(4xy−p(x+y)) and compare two bounded sampling schemes.

title: Transport between neighboring prime surfaces
connection: Map real points on the p surface to nearby points on the p′ surface and measure the exact integer rounding defect.
why: The defect may suggest a correction identity linking nearby instances.
first_step: Scale a known triple by p′/p, round two coordinates, and factor the exact residual for the third.

title: Optimal transport of divisor-residue measures
connection: Compare residue distributions from two auxiliary parameters using a cost based on allowed residue moves.
why: A low-cost transport plan might identify concrete transformations connecting complementary families.
first_step: For a small modulus, solve a finite transport problem between two divisor-residue histograms and inspect its dominant edges.

title: Finite Fourier uncertainty
connection: Relate concentration of a divisor-residue distribution to concentration of its Fourier transform.
why: A distribution supported on too few residues must carry detectable spectral structure in a finite group.
first_step: Compute support and Fourier support for exact small examples and identify the characters responsible for concentration.

title: Harmonic analysis beyond the unit group
connection: Use the full multiplicative residue monoid when auxiliary factors are not units, rather than forcing a group model.
why: A monoid representation can retain valuation strata that ordinary character expansions omit.
first_step: Construct multiplication operators on residues modulo 12 and decompose their invariant subspaces.

title: SAT encodings of bounded denominator search
connection: Encode the cleared ES equation and positivity bounds as a Boolean circuit with explicit carries.
why: A satisfying assignment is an exactly checkable finite witness, and the encoding may expose reusable logical constraints.
first_step: Build a tiny bounded instance for p=13 and compare decoded models with direct enumeration.

title: SMT over mixed integer structures
connection: Combine integer arithmetic, divisibility, and bit-vector residue constraints in a bounded solver model.
why: Different theories may cooperate better than one large expanded polynomial equation.
first_step: Model one auxiliary divisor family with explicit finite bounds and compare integer-only with mixed-theory formulations.

title: Quantifier elimination for fixed ansatzes
connection: Use real or Presburger quantifier elimination only on subproblems whose language genuinely fits those methods.
why: Exact parameter-region descriptions could simplify one family without pretending general nonlinear integer arithmetic is decidable.
first_step: Choose a linear-congruence ansatz and eliminate one bounded parameter using a Presburger tool.

title: Counterexample-guided identity synthesis
connection: Alternate proposing symbolic denominator formulas with finding primes or parameter values violating their claimed domain.
why: Counterexamples refine the synthesis grammar while every accepted identity requires symbolic verification.
first_step: Run a small CEGIS loop over affine numerator and denominator templates restricted to one residue class.

title: Syntax-guided parametrizations
connection: Define a grammar of gcd, floor, product, and reciprocal operations and search short candidate certificate programs.
why: A restricted grammar makes discovery auditable and encourages explicit formulas rather than opaque predictions.
first_step: Enumerate expressions of depth at most three and test exact identities on a training set before symbolic checking.

title: Equality saturation for rational identities
connection: Store equivalent rational expressions in an e-graph and extract forms with simpler integrality conditions.
why: Equivalent formulas can have very different arithmetic usability even when their real values agree.
first_step: Build an e-graph from a few verified reciprocal identities and score expressions by denominator-factor complexity.

title: Abstract interpretation of parameters
connection: Propagate intervals, congruence classes, and sign information through a candidate denominator program.
why: A sound abstract domain can prove that many inputs produce positive integers without enumerating them.
first_step: Implement transfer rules for addition, multiplication, and exact division on interval-congruence pairs.

title: Constraint propagation on factor domains
connection: Maintain finite domains for factor residues and remove choices that cannot participate in a valid complementary pair.
why: Arc consistency can sharply reduce bounded search while preserving every actual solution.
first_step: Apply AC-3 to a three-variable factor-residue model and compare remaining domains with exhaustive solutions.

title: Modular conflict learning
connection: When a parameter box fails for a provable modular reason, store that reason as a reusable nogood.
why: Learned conflicts can apply across many primes sharing the same local labels.
first_step: Extract one sound modular conflict clause from a failed bounded search and test its reuse on other instances.

title: Proof complexity of bounded failures
connection: Compare lengths of machine-checkable unsatisfiability proofs for different bounded ES encodings.
why: Short proofs may reveal elementary exclusions worth expressing as human lemmas.
first_step: For several deliberately too-small boxes, compare proof sizes under direct and factorized encodings.

title: Proof-carrying witness search
connection: Make each search result carry the integer arithmetic needed to verify positivity and the cleared identity independently.
why: This decouples experimental algorithms from trust in their implementation.
first_step: Specify a compact witness record and a verifier using only exact integer operations.

title: Independent arithmetic verification
connection: Check generated triples by two algebraically distinct routes: cleared products and reduced rational sums.
why: Independent formulations can catch implementation errors or malformed records.
first_step: Write a small verifier specification and test it against deliberately corrupted triples.

title: Trusted-kernel pipelines
connection: Route heuristic discoveries into a tiny theorem-checking kernel rather than trusting the search or symbolic algebra package.
why: The proof obligation stays explicit even when discovery uses complicated tools.
first_step: Choose one elementary family and separate its discovery script from a minimal proof of the resulting identity and divisibility conditions.

title: Grammar compression of certificates
connection: Compress a finite certificate database using shared identity templates and parameter substitutions.
why: A short grammar can reveal repeated constructions hidden among many individual triples.
first_step: Cluster exact triples by common rational-expression templates and compare compressed description lengths.

title: Algorithmic simplicity of difficult instances
connection: Compare the shortest known certificate-generating program with the smallest numerical certificate.
why: A huge denominator might still have a simple recurrence description, suggesting a different notion of difficulty.
first_step: For a small set of large-height examples, search short recurrences generating their denominator triples.

title: Minimum-description-length family selection
connection: Balance the coverage of a formula against the complexity of its exceptional-case conditions.
why: This discourages overfitting while keeping every mathematically valid family available.
first_step: Encode formula syntax and residue exceptions with an explicit code, then compare several portfolios on held-out primes.

title: Levin-style program search
connection: Dovetail candidate certificate programs with budgets depending on program length.
why: This gives a systematic discovery baseline and highlights the cost of the chosen expression language.
first_step: Enumerate a tiny arithmetic-program language and allocate execution steps by a prefix-code weight.

title: Fair interleaving of infinite families
connection: Run countably many valid parameter searches in a schedule that eventually explores every finite parameter tuple.
why: Fairness prevents one expensive family from starving other methods, without guaranteeing ES itself.
first_step: Specify a diagonal schedule over family index and parameter height and prove every finite tuple is reached.

title: Stopping bounds for ordered triples
connection: Exploit x≤y≤z to derive finite search bounds for fixed p before discussing algorithmic completeness.
why: A correct finite bound distinguishes exhaustive verification from an arbitrary cutoff.
first_step: Derive p/4<x≤3p/4 and the resulting bound on y from the positive residual, then implement a bounded enumeration plan.

title: Total-search complexity questions
connection: Ask what complexity classification would follow if ES witnesses had a specified polynomial bit-length bound.
why: The conditional formulation separates existence from efficient verification and avoids assuming ES is already a total search theorem.
first_step: Write the witness relation and identify exactly which unproved size and existence statements are needed for a TFNP-style classification.

title: Parameterized complexity by factor count
connection: Treat the number of distinct auxiliary prime factors or modulus structure as an algorithmic parameter.
why: Subset-product search may be tractable in a parameter even when the integer itself is large.
first_step: Derive running-time bounds for residue selection in terms of factor count and group invariant factors.

title: Treewidth of arithmetic factor graphs
connection: Measure the width of a factor graph after separating valuations, carries, and residues.
why: Small treewidth would support exact dynamic programming for that bounded encoding.
first_step: Construct three alternative factor graphs for the same tiny instance and compare elimination widths.

title: Meet-in-the-middle divisor selection
connection: Split prime-power factors into two groups and match complementary target residues.
why: This is an exact algorithmic alternative to enumerating every divisor when modular inverses are handled correctly.
first_step: Implement the split for unit factors of a small auxiliary integer and handle nonunits in separate valuation strata.

title: FFT convolution on cyclic residue coordinates
connection: Use discrete-log coordinates in a cyclic unit group to turn divisor-selection convolution into cyclic convolution.
why: Fast convolution can count residue witnesses exactly with suitable integer reconstruction.
first_step: For a small prime modulus, compare direct dynamic programming with an exact convolution implementation.

title: Bitset propagation of attainable residues
connection: Represent reachable residues by bitsets and update them under each allowed factor power.
why: Bit-parallel operations can make large bounded surveys cheaper without changing the mathematics.
first_step: Benchmark bitset and set-based reachability for moduli below 1000 using the same factorizations.

title: Decision diagrams for factor subsets
connection: Compress repeated residual subproblems using zero-suppressed decision diagrams or related shared DAGs.
why: Many distinct divisors can share the same remaining residue problem.
first_step: Build a small decision diagram for target-residue divisor selection and compare its node count with the number of divisors.

title: Dominance pruning of partial certificates
connection: Define a sound partial-order dominance relation between search states with identical arithmetic obligations.
why: A dominated state can be removed only when every completion has a no-more-expensive counterpart.
first_step: Prove one dominance rule based on equal residue state and remaining factor inventory, then measure pruning.

title: Modular fingerprints for duplicate detection
connection: Use several modular reductions to cheaply reject unequal symbolic or numerical certificates before exact comparison.
why: Fingerprints accelerate deduplication while exact fallback prevents collisions from becoming false identities.
first_step: Design a hash-plus-exact-check pipeline for canonical denominator triples and rational identity expressions.

title: Arithmetic-circuit complexity
connection: Compare expanded polynomial identities with compact straight-line arithmetic circuits.
why: A low-complexity circuit may expose composition structure that expansion obscures.
first_step: Represent three candidate families as circuits and count multiplication gates after common-subexpression elimination.

title: Straight-line certificates for huge denominators
connection: Store denominators by exact arithmetic programs when their decimal expansions are unwieldy.
why: Compact descriptions can make recurrent or compositional families practical, provided equality is still verified exactly.
first_step: Encode a small recurrence family as straight-line programs and compare evaluation and verification costs.

title: Modular interpolation of identities
connection: Recover candidate polynomial coefficients from evaluations modulo several primes and reconstruct rational coefficients.
why: This can make symbolic discovery cheaper, followed by exact identity checking.
first_step: Recover a known low-degree numerator identity from modular samples as a pipeline sanity check.

title: Sparse interpolation of parameter relations
connection: Exploit a small expected monomial support when reconstructing relations among certificate parameters.
why: Sparse reconstruction may discover concise algebraic constraints missed by dense fitting.
first_step: Use a low-degree monomial dictionary on a sample of exact certificates and validate any recovered relation symbolically.

title: Polynomial identity testing with deterministic closure
connection: Use randomized evaluations to reject false formulas quickly, then perform exact symbolic verification on survivors.
why: Random testing is a filter, never the final proof of an identity.
first_step: Generate a batch of candidate identities, filter at random integer points, and expand only the survivors.

title: Small-root lattice attacks on residual equations
connection: Check whether a chosen ES parametrization yields a modular polynomial with a genuinely small unknown suitable for lattice small-root methods.
why: Cryptanalytic techniques are relevant only when explicit size inequalities are met.
first_step: Derive one univariate modular residual and check whether a Coppersmith theorem covers its degree, modulus, and root bound.

title: Approximate common divisors as hints
connection: Explore cases where several auxiliary values are near multiples of an unknown useful factor.
why: Shared approximate divisibility might reveal a factor-selection strategy if the error model is justified.
first_step: Construct exact small examples from known certificates and test whether the useful factor is recoverable from the proposed hints.

title: Hidden-number-style parameter recovery
connection: Treat partial information about modular products as a lattice recovery problem for an auxiliary parameter.
why: The analogy is meaningful only when the available information matches an explicit hidden-number instance.
first_step: Write a toy recovery problem with exact known high bits and compare its recovered parameters with valid certificates.

title: Partial factor bits from congruence constraints
connection: Use the required residue of a useful divisor as partial information in a factorization problem.
why: A residue class supplies genuine bits of structure, though it may be far too weak for existing algorithms.
first_step: For small auxiliary integers, measure how much the target congruence shrinks the divisor search and check partial-factor recovery literature.

title: Smooth-order factorization steering
connection: Choose auxiliary parameters whose likely useful factors have smooth multiplicative-group order, then test a p−1-style factoring strategy.
why: This is a construction-and-search heuristic, not a claim that such factors always exist.
first_step: For C≤100, compare certificate usefulness of factors found cheaply by a small smooth-order budget.

title: Elliptic-curve factorization as a probe
connection: Use small factoring budgets to sample auxiliary factors and ask whether easily found factors already yield many certificates.
why: This measures whether complete factorization is unnecessary for exploratory coverage.
first_step: Apply equal small ECM budgets to a bounded list of auxiliary values and verify all certificates obtained from partial factorizations.

title: Batch gcd across parameter values
connection: Compute shared factors among many p-tied auxiliary integers using gcd relations and batch techniques.
why: Shared factors can be extracted without factoring every value separately.
first_step: For fixed p and bounded C, derive pairwise gcd restrictions and compare batch extraction with individual trial division.

title: Product and remainder trees
connection: Use product trees to test many candidate divisors against many auxiliary values efficiently.
why: This supports broad experiments and may reveal unexpectedly reusable factors.
first_step: Design a memory-bounded remainder-tree pass for a small family of auxiliary values and target divisors.

title: Factor-base relations for certificate search
connection: Collect auxiliary values smooth over a chosen factor base and record their residue-selection structure.
why: This borrows a relation-collection viewpoint without assuming factorization-style linear algebra directly solves ES.
first_step: Build a tiny factor-base relation matrix and determine what additional condition turns a relation into an actual target divisor.

title: Discrete-log coordinates with multiplicity constraints
connection: Use discrete logs only to linearize residues, retaining the bounded exponent ranges of actual divisors.
why: Solving the unrestricted linear congruence alone would create nonexistent divisors; bounded coefficients are essential.
first_step: Compare bounded and unrestricted exponent solutions in a small cyclic unit group and quantify spurious solutions.

title: Factoring-free gcd certificates
connection: Search for constructions where a useful divisor is produced as a gcd of two explicit expressions.
why: A gcd can supply a verified factor without requiring complete factorization.
first_step: Try short polynomial gcd expressions in p and C and retain only cases where the gcd provably has the target residue.

title: Certified prime selection for experiments
connection: Separate primality verification of test inputs from ES witness verification so arithmetic strata remain trustworthy.
why: Misclassified inputs could distort experiments about prime-only behavior.
first_step: Specify a test-data format carrying primality evidence or a reproducible deterministic primality procedure alongside each p.

title: Las Vegas certificate discovery
connection: Allow random candidate generation but accept outputs only after deterministic exact verification.
why: Randomness then affects runtime rather than the correctness of reported witnesses.
first_step: Design a randomized parameter sampler with explicit timeouts and an independent certificate checker.

title: Small-bias parameter schedules
connection: Replace unrestricted random residues with a small explicitly generated sample space and measure which character tests it fools.
why: A derandomized schedule may preserve relevant coverage statistics if the test class is identified.
first_step: Construct a tiny small-bias distribution for a selected finite group and compare its character averages with those of uniform sampling.

title: Perfect-hash-style family isolation
connection: Use hash partitions to isolate one witness among many candidate factors, simplifying a bounded search subproblem.
why: Isolation can aid algorithm design, while an exact check prevents the hash mechanism from inventing witnesses.
first_step: Apply a small family of residue hashes to known multi-witness instances and measure isolation rates.

title: Memory-bounded parallel parameter search
connection: Split the auxiliary domain into deterministic chunks with no shared giant divisor table.
why: A streaming design enables much broader evidence collection without uncontrolled Cartesian-product allocations.
first_step: Specify chunk sizes, per-worker memory caps, and an exact merge key for a bounded search prototype.

title: Cache keys as mathematical assumptions
connection: Key cached computations by the full parametrization, modulus, positivity convention, and search bounds.
why: This prevents results from one mathematical model being silently reused in a different one.
first_step: Audit a toy search cache and construct two deliberately incompatible configurations that must not share entries.

title: Permutation-equivariant certificate models
connection: Train predictors on unordered denominator triples using features invariant under all six coordinate permutations.
why: Respecting exact symmetry can reduce spurious distinctions in learned family structure.
first_step: Compare a symmetric feature model with a raw-coordinate baseline on canonicalized bounded certificates.

title: Factor-graph neural heuristics
connection: Use a graph model whose nodes represent prime factors, residues, and valuation slots to rank partial assignments.
why: The architecture mirrors actual arithmetic constraints, while final outputs still require exact verification.
first_step: Train only on tiny exhaustively solved factor-selection instances and test ranking quality on larger held-out ones.

title: Learning the next family to try
connection: Predict which exact certificate family should be attempted first from cheap features of p.
why: A learned selector accelerates search without becoming part of the correctness argument.
first_step: Compare a small classifier with a fixed family order using measured total arithmetic operations.

title: Decision trees as conjecture extractors
connection: Fit shallow trees using residue and character features, then translate each leaf into a proposed arithmetic lemma.
why: A transparent leaf condition is a concrete object for proof or counterexample search.
first_step: Fit a depth-three tree for one family's success and exhaustively test each leaf condition in a larger range.

title: Symbolic regression of witness costs
connection: Fit simple formulas for least auxiliary size using arithmetic features rather than raw prime magnitude alone.
why: The goal is a testable growth conjecture or selector, not numerical evidence of universal existence.
first_step: Restrict symbolic regression to a small grammar and validate predictions on a disjoint prime range.

title: Rational-function recognition in families
connection: Group certificates by a discrete template label and attempt exact rational interpolation of their parameters as functions of p.
why: Recovered formulas can be verified symbolically and their integrality domains derived.
first_step: For one visually coherent cluster, interpolate low-degree rational functions from exact data and test unused points.

title: Counterfactual feature interventions
connection: Alter one arithmetic feature in synthetic parameter data while holding the exact algebraic model fixed where possible.
why: This helps distinguish genuine mechanisms from correlated labels in observational prime data.
first_step: Within one residue-compatible family, vary a single auxiliary prime factor and measure the resulting target-residue change.

title: Active learning at family boundaries
connection: Choose new examples near the boundary where a simple family selector changes its prediction.
why: Boundary cases may expose missing congruence hypotheses more quickly than uniform sampling.
first_step: Train a shallow selector, query its most ambiguous bounded inputs, and inspect the exact divisibility reasons for each outcome.

title: Uncertainty-guided experiment allocation
connection: Allocate computation to prime strata where count models disagree rather than only to predicted hardest cases.
why: Disagreement can expose model misspecification and broaden the exploratory dataset.
first_step: Compare two simple count models and search a balanced sample of their largest disagreement cases.

title: Calibration of success predictions
connection: Measure whether predicted success probabilities for a fixed search budget match observed frequencies.
why: Well-calibrated uncertainty is useful for scheduling, but cannot turn a probability estimate into a proof.
first_step: Build reliability curves on held-out primes and separate calibration by small-residue strata.

title: Out-of-distribution prime tests
connection: Train only on one range or residue stratum and evaluate on genuinely new arithmetic regimes.
why: This detects selectors that memorize local density patterns rather than generalizable mechanisms.
first_step: Hold out an entire congruence class and a larger magnitude range, reporting both separately.

title: Explaining count outliers
connection: For primes with unexpectedly few witnesses, decompose the prediction error into factorization, local-density, and family-overlap features.
why: An explanation may suggest a targeted new identity instead of merely another statistical model.
first_step: Select ten low-count outliers and compare each feature against matched primes of similar size.

title: Matched prime pairs
connection: Pair primes with nearly identical cheap arithmetic features but very different least witness costs.
why: Contrasts can isolate information missing from a proposed selector.
first_step: Match on residues modulo a small modulus and several character labels, then inspect auxiliary factorizations of the largest-cost contrasts.

title: Biclustering families and primes
connection: Find blocks of the incidence matrix where a group of families succeeds on a specific group of primes.
why: Blocks may correspond to hidden arithmetic regimes with complementary constructions.
first_step: Run a simple exact or heuristic biclustering on a bounded incidence matrix and characterize blocks by residue features.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Nonnegative latent mechanisms
connection: Factor a nonnegative count matrix into a few latent family and prime components, then seek arithmetic interpretations.
why: Unlike a proof, the factorization only suggests which mechanisms might be shared.
first_step: Fit ranks two through five and inspect whether components align with known gcd or character labels.

title: Embeddings of matrix words
connection: Learn or hand-design representations that place equivalent or easily transformable matrix words near each other.
why: A useful representation could guide discovery of short exact rewrite sequences.
first_step: Compare embeddings based on modular actions with raw word edit distance on verified equivalent words.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Motifs in proof graphs
connection: Mine repeated small subgraphs in graphs of exact algebraic derivations.
why: Recurring proof fragments may become reusable lemmas or identity-generation macros.
first_step: Encode ten elementary derivations as operation DAGs and identify repeated three-operation motifs.

title: Invariant discovery with counterexamples
connection: Search low-degree expressions constant under verified certificate transformations, rejecting candidates on fresh exact examples.
why: A discovered invariant can organize orbit structure and explain why some moves fail to connect families.
first_step: Solve linear equations for quadratic invariants of one transformation and check survivors symbolically.

title: Language-model analogy proposals with algebraic gates
connection: Use a language model only to propose cross-domain encodings, then require a written map and a checked toy instance.
why: The algebraic gate separates a useful analogy from merely similar terminology.
first_step: Prompt for five encodings of the same residual factor equation and discard only those lacking a well-defined map.

title: Semantic retrieval of equivalent equations
connection: Search literature by algebraic shape and alternate terminology rather than only by the phrase Erdős–Straus.
why: Relevant results may use norm equations, reciprocal partitions, or restricted divisor sums under different names.
first_step: Form five precise search queries from the equation (ay−b)(az−b)=b² and inspect the returned definitions.

title: Citation-graph bridges
connection: Trace papers that connect two relevant areas, such as restricted divisor problems and finite-group zero-sum theory.
why: Bridge papers may supply a transferable lemma not indexed under Egyptian fractions.
first_step: Search for a paper using both topic vocabularies, verify it exists, and inspect its cited technical tools.

title: A dictionary of incompatible conventions
connection: Translate denominator ordering, primitive conditions, and sign conventions across candidate papers before comparing results.
why: Apparent contradictions or missed equivalences can come from different definitions.
first_step: Build a one-page convention table for three verified sources once located, including exact theorem hypotheses.

title: Lean formalization of one family
connection: Formalize one elementary rational identity together with its positivity and divisibility hypotheses.
why: A small verified example establishes the shape of proof obligations without trying to formalize the whole campaign.
first_step: Choose the simplest directly checked family and locate the Lean lemmas needed for rational field simplification.

title: Positivity proof certificates
connection: Attach explicit positive-factor decompositions to every symbolic denominator expression.
why: An algebraically correct identity can still fail as an ES construction if denominators are nonpositive.
first_step: For three candidate formulas, rewrite each denominator into products or sums whose signs follow from stated hypotheses.

title: Integer–rational coercion discipline
connection: Treat exact division as a separate proved step before moving a parametrization from integers to rational identities.
why: This prevents silent truncation or unjustified integrality in machine and human proofs.
first_step: Write a typed proof outline for one formula, marking every use of integer divisibility and rational coercion.

title: A library of divisibility transport lemmas
connection: Collect reusable lemmas carrying divisibility through substitutions, gcd cancellation, and complementary factors.
why: These small facts recur across many distinct constructions and can reduce proof friction.
first_step: Formalize or precisely state five transport lemmas needed by the residual factor-pair equivalence.

title: Certified completeness of finite enumeration
connection: Prove the ordered-denominator bounds used by an exhaustive verifier and connect them to its loop limits.
why: A witness checker proves individual successes; a completeness proof also validates bounded absence claims.
first_step: Write a proof outline linking x and y inequalities to each loop endpoint of a toy exhaustive search.

title: Formal translation between word and fraction certificates
connection: Specify both sides of one short matrix-word equivalence and prove the conversion including sign and congruence conditions.
why: A checked bridge would allow discovery in one language and validation in another.
first_step: Select a length-two or length-three word and manually derive the forward and reverse formulas before formalizing.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Parametric proof objects
connection: Represent an infinite family by a polynomial identity proof plus a separate modular integrality proof.
why: This makes the difference between many tested examples and a genuine family theorem explicit.
first_step: Define a record containing symbolic denominators, domain hypotheses, the identity, and integrality certificates.

title: Replayable symbolic proof traces
connection: Export each algebraic simplification as a sequence of exact transformations rather than only a final yes/no answer.
why: A small checker can replay discovery-tool output independently.
first_step: For one rational identity, record clearing denominators, ring normalization, and hypothesis use as separate trace steps.

title: Extracting certificate algorithms from proofs
connection: Given a constructive family theorem, extract the parameter-to-denominator function with its domain test.
why: The extracted algorithm connects proof structure to measurable search behavior.
first_step: Take one hand-proved family and write its domain predicate and witness constructor as separate pure functions.

title: Property-based arithmetic testing
connection: Generate structured random inputs satisfying a family's hypotheses rather than arbitrary integers.
why: This efficiently catches transcription errors while remaining only a development check.
first_step: Design generators for divisibility-compatible parameters and test the cleared identity and positivity separately.

title: Metamorphic tests from scaling
connection: Use exact transformations such as scaling a valid triple along with n to generate consistency checks.
why: If 4/n=Σ1/x, scaling all four quantities by a positive integer preserves the identity.
first_step: Specify a test transforming a valid witness at n into one at kn and verify all fields update consistently.

title: Mutation testing for certificate checkers
connection: Deliberately change signs, residues, denominator values, and domain assumptions to test whether a verifier rejects false claims.
why: A checker that accepts corrupted data cannot support trustworthy experiments.
first_step: Create one mutation per required condition and confirm that each is rejected for a mathematical reason.

title: Croot-related exact-sum techniques
connection: Investigate whether methods in work associated with Croot on Egyptian fractions contain a tunable exact-sum or smooth-denominator ingredient.
why: A method for assembling reciprocal sums might have a restricted three-term component, but this is only a literature lead.
first_step: Check which Croot papers prove exact reciprocal-sum statements and extract the precise flexibility in numerator, length, and denominator support.

title: Erdős–Graham coloring methods
connection: Ask whether techniques around the Erdős–Graham Egyptian-fraction problem suggest a useful partition of denominator candidates.
why: Coloring or density arguments might inspire family selection even if their conclusions involve many terms.
first_step: Locate a verified statement and proof source, then check whether any intermediate lemma controls a fixed small number of terms.

title: Bloom-related density increments
connection: Investigate whether work associated with Bloom on unit-fraction problems offers a density-increment mechanism adaptable to structured divisor sets.
why: The potentially transferable object is a lemma about reciprocal mass, not an assumed three-term theorem.
first_step: Find the relevant paper, verify its hypotheses, and compare its denominator set with divisors of a p-tied integer.

title: Sylvester-style product recurrences
connection: Check how classical product recurrences for Egyptian fractions encode divisibility, then ask whether alternative initial conditions yield three-term terminal states.
why: Product recurrences provide exact rational identities whose length and congruences can be tracked.
first_step: Locate a reliable source for the recurrence, derive it independently, and test modified initial parameters symbolically.

title: Engel expansions as intermediate representations
connection: Compare multiplicative-denominator Engel expansions of 4/p with ordinary unit-fraction decompositions and possible regroupings.
why: Nested denominator structure may make some exact merges easier to describe.
first_step: Compute short Engel expansions for small primes and test adjacent-term merges into a single unit fraction.

title: Lüroth-style digit systems
connection: Check whether a rational expansion with consecutive-product denominators can be converted into a useful three-term ES ansatz.
why: The digit system offers a different exact decomposition grammar, not an automatic short representation.
first_step: Verify the precise Lüroth expansion formula and test finite rational examples for algebraically valid regroupings.

title: Ostrowski numeration of parameter choices
connection: Use continued-fraction-based numeration to encode auxiliary integers relative to p and a chosen modulus.
why: The digits may align with Euclidean recurrences and make congruence repair more local.
first_step: For one rational rotation, write several successful auxiliary values in Ostrowski coordinates and compare their digit patterns.

title: Odd-denominator greedy variants
connection: Compare a greedy rule restricted to odd denominators with unrestricted greedy search on related residual fractions.
why: Restrictions can expose parity mechanisms even if they make termination harder.
first_step: Define a precise odd-denominator choice rule and compute its first three residuals on a bounded set of admissible rational inputs.

title: Primary-source identity genealogy
connection: Trace an elementary ES identity backward through citations to learn which substitutions and failed variants accompanied it.
why: Historical derivations may reveal nearby constructions omitted from modern summaries.
first_step: Choose one commonly reproduced identity, locate its earliest accessible source, and record the original parameter restrictions.

title: 8/n and k/n siblings: Kahn–Kalai threshold across the numerator k
connection: Varying the numerator k (k/n = 1/x+1/y+1/z) changes the expected solution count; Schinzel–Sierpiński-type problems are open for each k ≥ 4.
why: A threshold picture across k (where 'almost all' becomes 'all') calibrates ES's position.
first_step: Compute failure counts of k/n for k = 4..12, n ≤ 10^6 (excluding trivial obstructions) and fit expected-count vs failure-rate curves.

title: Two-term and four-term boundary cases
connection: Compare the rigid two-term equation and more flexible four-term constructions with the three-term target.
why: A controlled bridge might identify the exact extra degree of freedom that must be eliminated.
first_step: Start from an explicit four-term identity and solve the exact condition under which two terms merge to one.

title: Distinct-denominator variants
connection: Separate certificates with repeated denominators from those with three distinct denominators and compare their construction mechanisms.
why: Repeated terms form special algebraic slices that might seed perturbative identities.
first_step: Classify the x=y and y=z cases exactly, then search one-parameter deformations preserving integrality.

title: Primitive-to-scaled transfer
connection: Track how primitive denominator shapes generate certificates for composite n and which shapes first appear at prime n.
why: This may reveal composition laws without confusing the easy scaling direction with a converse.
first_step: Canonicalize triples by their common gcd and map the resulting primitive shapes to the reduced fraction they represent.

title: Beyond polynomial parametrizations
connection: Explore rational, recurrent, floor-based, and piecewise arithmetic witness formulas as genuinely different representation classes.
why: A limitation of one formula class need not rule out another, and each class has explicit verification obligations.
first_step: Write one toy certificate rule in each representation class and list exactly how its identity and domain would be proved.

title: A precise question for an outside specialist
connection: Translate one ES subproblem into the native language of a finite-group, algorithmic-number-theory, or dynamics expert.
why: A sharply bounded lemma is more actionable than asking someone to solve the whole conjecture.
first_step: Draft a one-page question about bounded subset products hitting a specified residue, with a small worked ES example and no claim of equivalence beyond the derived map.

title: Function-field comparison laboratory
connection: Replace integers by Fq[T] in a precisely stated reciprocal equation and compare divisor-selection mechanisms in odd characteristic.
why: Polynomial degree and explicit factorization make a controlled analogue, while positivity has no direct counterpart.
first_step: Write the analogue over F3[T], enumerate monic inputs of degree at most three, and record which integer-side conditions need replacement.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Characteristic sensitivity of the numerator
connection: Separate characteristics dividing four from those where four is invertible before importing finite-field analogies.
why: In characteristic two the numerator vanishes, so an unqualified transfer would be mathematically misleading.
first_step: Compare the cleared equation in characteristics 2,3,5 and explicitly label degenerate components.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Degree profiles versus denominator heights
connection: Classify polynomial certificates by the three denominator degrees and compare them with logarithmic integer heights.
why: Degree balance can expose cancellation regimes that are difficult to see in numerical size data.
first_step: Enumerate degree profiles in a small odd-characteristic model and derive the leading-coefficient cancellation conditions.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Specialization with integrality audits
connection: Investigate when a polynomial or rational-function identity remains an integral positive certificate after substituting an integer.
why: An identity specializes automatically where defined, but integrality and positivity require separate hypotheses.
first_step: Take one symbolic identity and derive all denominator divisibility and sign conditions after T→m.

title: Polynomial continued fractions
connection: Compare short continued fractions over Fq[T] with the integer word formulations, retaining coefficient degree and unit information.
why: The Euclidean algorithm survives, but ordering and parity constraints change substantially.
first_step: Compute length-three expansions over F5[T] and identify which coefficient conditions correspond to the integer formulation.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Separable and inseparable parametrizations
connection: Check whether a function-field construction relies on derivatives or Frobenius powers that have no direct integer analogue.
why: Separating these mechanisms can identify the genuinely transferable algebraic part.
first_step: For a candidate polynomial parametrization, compute its derivative and determine whether its parameter map is separable.

title: Resultants as specialization filters
connection: Use resultants to detect when specialized auxiliary factors acquire common divisors or lose coprimality.
why: The resultant supplies an explicit finite arithmetic obstruction to naive factor independence.
first_step: Compute the resultant of two polynomial denominator factors and derive which primes can divide both specializations.

title: Norm descent over polynomial rings
connection: Compare norm-equation certificate slices over integers and over a polynomial ring with a quadratic extension.
why: The parallel can isolate the role of units, ideal classes, and signs in the two settings.
first_step: Work out one quadratic norm equation over F5[T] and compare its factorization steps with the corresponding integer equation.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: S-unit support restrictions
connection: Fix a small set of allowed denominator primes and translate the reciprocal equation into an S-unit-type relation.
why: Restricted support gives a sharply defined subproblem whose solutions can be explored exactly.
first_step: For S={2,3,5,p}, enumerate bounded exponent triples and write the resulting multiplicative relations.

title: Boundary divisors and integral points
connection: Compactify a rational parametrization and identify which boundary components correspond to zero, infinite, or nonintegral denominators.
why: The boundary may explain why rational abundance does not directly imply useful integer points.
first_step: For one explicit chart, homogenize its equation and label every boundary component by its arithmetic meaning.

title: Logarithmic geometry of denominator exclusions
connection: Treat denominator vanishing loci as a marked divisor and compare charts respecting that divisor.
why: A log-geometric description may organize which coordinate changes preserve the relevant open set.
first_step: Write the marked boundary for two birational charts and compute how each boundary factor transforms.

title: Fibrations with arithmetic sections
connection: View a chosen auxiliary parameter as the base of a fibration and look for sections that are integral on specified congruence classes.
why: A section supplies a family; its arithmetic domain can be analyzed independently of generic rational solvability.
first_step: For a simple conic fibration, find one rational section and derive its integer-specialization conditions.

title: Torsor coordinates for gcd removal
connection: Introduce auxiliary variables to encode pairwise coprimality and factor allocation, seeking a torsor-like parametrization.
why: Such coordinates may separate multiplicative structure from the main additive equation.
first_step: Starting from a gcd-stratified triple, write all auxiliary factors and prove the reconstruction map is exact on one stratum.

title: Cox-ring-inspired monomial bookkeeping
connection: Ask whether divisor classes on a simple compactification suggest a useful multigrading of parameter monomials.
why: A multigrading can explain which substitutions preserve the equation and boundary conditions.
first_step: For a basic rational surface chart, assign formal divisor degrees to denominator factors and check homogeneity of the cleared relation.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Real components and positivity chambers
connection: Partition the real auxiliary variety by signs of all denominator factors and analyze each chamber separately.
why: Only certain chambers yield positive unit fractions; chamber transitions may suggest controlled transformations.
first_step: For a two-parameter rational family, draw the zero sets of denominator factors and label every positive chamber.

title: Finite covers that expose square conditions
connection: Pass to a cover adjoining the square root of a discriminant and examine whether the lifted equation becomes simpler.
why: The cover records an exact arithmetic condition rather than assuming every base point lifts.
first_step: Construct the discriminant double cover of a quadratic slice and write its rational-point map back to certificates.

title: Galois actions on factor-allocation types
connection: Study how algebraic conjugation permutes possible factors in a norm-based parametrization.
why: Invariant allocations may descend to rational or integer expressions that are not obvious in split coordinates.
first_step: For one quadratic-field slice, list conjugate factor assignments and compute their invariant products and traces.

title: Genus-two slices as stress tests
connection: Impose a simple additional relation and check whether a higher-genus curve appears with a few explicit certificate points.
why: Such slices can reveal which constraints make a family too rigid while still providing concrete finite examples.
first_step: Try a cubic relation between two denominators, compute the curve genus, and inspect the known points without assuming completeness.

title: Rational curves through known certificates
connection: Use a known rational point as the base of a line or low-degree curve construction on the ES surface.
why: A curve through a witness may generate a new family, with integrality conditions available for explicit calculation.
first_step: Intersect lines through a small known triple with the surface and solve for the remaining intersections.

title: Infinitesimal deformations and exact correction
connection: Compute tangent directions at a certificate, then ask which directions extend to rational curves with controllable denominators.
why: Tangent data can propose families, but exact substitution is required beyond first order.
first_step: Linearize the cleared equation at one small triple and test two tangent directions with quadratic correction terms.

title: Bad reduction of parametrization charts
connection: Identify primes where a symbolic chart or its inverse loses rank or acquires extra components.
why: Those primes may require a different chart and can explain irregular local behavior.
first_step: Compute Jacobian minors and denominator factors for one chart, then list small primes dividing their fixed coefficients.

title: Enumerating low-degree curves on the surface
connection: Search directly for lines or conics contained in a chosen compactification rather than guessing denominator formulas individually.
why: Coefficient equations turn the family search into a finite symbolic problem at each degree.
first_step: Substitute a general affine line with rational coefficients and solve the resulting coefficient equations.

title: Theta series of congruence lattices
connection: When a certificate subproblem becomes a positive-definite quadratic representation with residue restrictions, encode its counts by a theta series.
why: Theta coefficients are exact representation counts for that specific subproblem; the reduction must be proved first.
first_step: Find one quadratic slice with explicit congruences and compute its first few representation counts directly.

title: Indefinite quadratic-form orbits
connection: Study indefinite quadratic slices using reduction and automorphisms rather than finite ellipsoid enumeration.
why: Infinite orbits may generate recurrent witnesses, with positivity handled along the orbit.
first_step: For one binary indefinite form arising from a slice, compute a fundamental automorphism and its residues modulo 8.

title: Modular congruences for representation counts
connection: Check whether a theta-encoded certificate count has coefficient congruences that force nonvanishing in a useful subsequence.
why: A nonzero residue of an integer count would certify positivity, but the modular-form identification needs verification.
first_step: For a proved quadratic reduction, test coefficient residues modulo a small prime and check the relevant modular-form literature.

title: Half-integral-weight correspondence leads
connection: Investigate whether a ternary quadratic certificate slice produces a theta series amenable to half-integral-weight tools.
why: The possible connection is through exact representation counts, not a presumed automorphic proof of ES.
first_step: Identify the quadratic form, verify the theta-series hypotheses, and check whether a Shimura-type correspondence addresses its coefficients.

title: Theta-quotient expansions as identity catalogs
connection: Inspect explicit q-expansions of a campaign-relevant theta quotient for coefficient identities suggesting arithmetic parametrizations.
why: Formal series relations may point to new exact constructions if the coefficient interpretation is established.
first_step: Derive a short q-expansion from the defining product or sum and check each coefficient interpretation independently.

title: Eisenstein and cusp contribution separation
connection: For a valid modular count, separate an explicit main contribution from the cusp contribution before assessing positivity.
why: The decomposition could reveal the exact estimate needed for one slice, without assuming it is available.
first_step: Locate the modular space for a concrete theta series and determine whether its Eisenstein projection can be computed at low level.

title: Complex multiplication specializations
connection: Look for special quadratic parameters where norm or theta expressions simplify through extra algebraic symmetry.
why: Special values might yield isolated constructive families rather than uniform coverage.
first_step: Choose a small discriminant, compute the associated norm expressions, and test whether the ES congruences simplify.

title: Brandt-matrix residue dynamics
connection: Investigate whether quaternion-order data associated with a certificate formulation admit finite matrices whose paths encode useful norm relations.
why: An explicit path interpretation could provide exact combinatorial operations on arithmetic objects.
first_step: For one small definite quaternion order, check available definitions of Brandt matrices and derive what a matrix entry counts before linking it to ES.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Spinor-genus diagnostics on quadratic slices
connection: Check whether local representation conditions for a selected quadratic form split into globally different arithmetic classes.
why: The goal is to understand that slice's representation pattern, not to infer an obstruction for ES as a whole.
first_step: Compute small representation data for a concrete ternary form and check literature on its genus and spinor genus.

title: Local-to-global comparison in a fixed slice
connection: Compare exact integer representations with solvability modulo increasing moduli for one explicitly derived quadratic subproblem.
why: A discrepancy identifies what extra arithmetic data the slice requires while leaving other families untouched.
first_step: For a small form and target range, enumerate representations and modular solutions with a common documented bound.

title: Automorphic periods as counting interpretations
connection: Ask whether an already established lattice or quaternion count can be expressed as a period with arithmetic coefficient meaning.
why: A period formula would connect geometric symmetry to exact counts, but requires a concrete identity rather than analogy alone.
first_step: Write the finite count explicitly and search for an existing period formula matching its group, stabilizer, and congruence level.

title: p-adic variation of modular counts
connection: If a valid modular family of representation counts exists, compare its coefficients as an auxiliary weight or level varies p-adically.
why: Variation may reveal congruence relations useful for selecting a family, not universal nonvanishing by itself.
first_step: Choose one verified modular family and check whether its coefficient congruences fit a known p-adic interpolation framework.

title: Mahler equations for recursive selectors
connection: Check whether a digit-recursive certificate selector has a generating function satisfying a functional equation involving z and z^b.
why: A functional equation could certify a recursive pattern if the selector recursion is proved first.
first_step: For a toy digit-based family, derive the coefficient recursion and test the resulting Mahler-type equation formally.

title: Local zeta functions of certificate congruences
connection: Count solutions of a fixed auxiliary polynomial system modulo powers of a prime and package the counts in a generating function.
why: The local zeta data may reveal stable lifting patterns and singular branches.
first_step: For a small odd prime q, count solutions modulo q and q² in a bounded-dimensional model and separate singular from nonsingular classes.

title: p-adic integrals for valuation distributions
connection: Express a local valuation histogram as an integral over residue classes and compare it with direct enumeration.
why: This provides a compact language for how divisibility conditions interact across powers of one prime.
first_step: For one auxiliary polynomial, compute the proportions with valuation 0,1,2 modulo a sufficiently high prime power.

title: Motivic comparison as a bookkeeping lead
connection: Ask whether several auxiliary varieties share a common geometric decomposition that explains repeated finite-field count formulas.
why: A decomposition could transfer exact counting identities, but any motivic interpretation remains to be checked.
first_step: Compute point counts of two related charts over several small odd fields and seek an explicit cut-and-paste decomposition.

title: Newton polygons for valuation branches
connection: Apply Newton-polygon analysis to a one-variable polynomial arising after fixing auxiliary parameters.
why: The slopes can constrain valuations of possible roots and guide which congruence lifts deserve attention.
first_step: For a quadratic or cubic residual polynomial, draw its Newton polygon at a small prime and compare predicted root valuations with exact examples.

title: Finite-field incidence bounds
connection: Represent a reduced certificate relation as incidences between points and curves over a finite field.
why: Incidence geometry can estimate modular witness abundance, with integer lifting kept as a separate problem.
first_step: For the residual factor equation modulo q, identify the point and curve sets and count incidences directly for small q.

title: Sum–product over residue rings
connection: Explore additive and multiplicative expansion in Z/mZ while stratifying by ideals and zero divisors.
why: Composite moduli are intrinsic to many certificate conditions, so field-only models may omit essential structure.
first_step: For m=12,20,24, compute sumsets and product sets of actual attainable residue sets within each gcd stratum.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Reciprocal additive energy modulo q
connection: Study additive relations among inverses of a structured denominator set in a finite field.
why: This is a direct modular analogue of the reciprocal sum and can identify concentration or additive structure.
first_step: Choose an odd prime q not dividing p; compute the additive energy of inverses of a short nonzero interval in Fq and compare its three-fold sums with 4/p modulo q.

title: Major-arc structure of reciprocal phases
connection: Analyze exponential sums over candidate denominators with phases tied to the exact reciprocal equation after clearing a common modulus.
why: Major arcs may identify rational resonances that correspond to useful congruence families.
first_step: Derive a finite Fourier expression for a common-denominator three-sum count and identify its largest frequency contributions.

title: Circle-method toy models with three terms
connection: Build a smoothed, bounded model of the three-denominator equation and explicitly separate the exact count from its analytic approximation.
why: A toy model can reveal which variable ranges supply enough averaging without claiming the full method works.
first_step: Write the orthogonality integral for a bounded integer version of the cleared equation and inspect its diagonal and singular contributions.

title: Delta-symbol decompositions of the residual
connection: Check whether an exact delta expansion can separate multiplicative variables in the cleared ES equation.
why: Separation could expose new bilinear structures, but convergence and range conditions must be verified.
first_step: Write the finite integer residual and compare exact delta-symbol formulas with its size and variable ranges.

title: Determinant-method maps of certificate concentration
connection: Use low-degree polynomial relations to describe where bounded certificates cluster on the surface.
why: A concentration theorem or experiment could suggest missing parametrizations rather than serve as a reason to discard a route.
first_step: Fit low-degree curves to a bounded set of exact points and check containment symbolically before consulting determinant-method estimates.

title: Inverse descriptions of bounded failure
connection: Ask what common structure is forced when many explicitly chosen certificate mechanisms all fail for one input.
why: An inverse statement could turn a failure pattern into the hypothesis of a different constructive family.
first_step: For three exact families, combine their failure congruences and derive the simplest remaining arithmetic condition without treating it as a global obstruction.

title: Dual certificates for relaxed parameter cones
connection: Use linear-programming duality to explain infeasibility of a specific linear relaxation of an auxiliary family.
why: A short dual identity can suggest which constraint must change, while remaining strictly local to that ansatz.
first_step: For one small infeasible linearized instance, compute a rational Farkas certificate and interpret each multiplier arithmetically.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Lemma barter across communities
connection: Package one arithmetic lemma and one potentially useful external theorem hypothesis as a two-way translation task for specialists.
why: The exchange can expose a missing hypothesis or a tractable substitute without asking for a verdict on ES.
first_step: Draft separate finite-group and quadratic-form versions of one concrete subproblem, each with a worked example and an explicit desired conclusion.

title: Backward construction from a desired last step
connection: Start with the final exact integrality or positivity lemma a certificate proof would need, then solve backward for parameter choices satisfying it.
why: Backward search can produce identities that forward enumeration misses, with every reverse step checked algebraically.
first_step: Choose a target congruence for a complementary divisor, substitute it into the residual equation, and solve for one remaining auxiliary parameter.

title: Transfer-matrix / partition-function view of the ES certificate set
connection: The set of e-slices e ≡ −p (mod 4) with −1 ∈ {ab⁻¹ mod e : ab | N} ↔ a 1-D statistical-mechanics chain whose 'spins' are the prime factors of N and whose Boltzmann weight is the indicator of the product landing in −1 mod e.
why: Positivity of a partition function (Z > 0) is exactly ES(p); stat-mech has tools (Lee–Yang zeros, cluster expansions) for proving positivity/non-vanishing that number theory does not routinely use.
first_step: Write Z_p(β) = Σ_e Σ_{ab|N} exp(−β·dist(ab⁻¹, −1 mod e)) and numerically locate its complex-β zeros for p ≤ 10⁵; check whether zeros avoid the real axis uniformly (Lee–Yang-type) and whether the pattern differs at odd squares.

title: Ising model on the modular-hyperbola graph of N
connection: The modular hyperbola xy ≡ −1 (mod e) restricted to divisors of N ↔ an Ising/Potts model whose ground-state energy is 0 iff the e-slice is non-empty.
why: Ground-state problems on frustrated graphs are where spin-glass theory produces sharp phase diagrams; ES asks for 'no frustration' at every p.
first_step: Build the graph (vertices = divisors of N, edges = pairs with ab⁻¹ ≡ −1 mod e) for a few hundred p, compute frustration index vs log p, look for a universal scaling law.

title: Random matrix statistics of the ES solution-count sequence f(p)
connection: f(p) (number of 4/p solutions) ↔ eigenvalue-count statistics; ask whether the normalized fluctuations of f(p)/log²p follow a known RMT law (GUE/GOE/Poisson) or a Selberg-class law.
why: If f(p) behaves like a 'spectral count' of some operator, then a lower bound f(p) ≥ 1 could be a spectral gap statement instead of a sieve statement.
first_step: Compute f(p) for primes up to 10⁷ (repo has data), fit the distribution of f(p)/E[f] and its two-point correlation along primes; compare to Poisson and to divisor-function moments (Deshouillers–Dress–Tenenbaum arcsine law).
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Arcsine law for divisors applied to 4Cp+1
connection: Deshouillers–Dress–Tenenbaum: divisors of a typical n are arcsine-distributed on the log scale ↔ ES needs a divisor of 4Cp+1 in a specific residue class −1 mod 4C, for SOME C.
why: Averaging over C (not over p) is a legitimate thick object at a fixed p; the arcsine law tells where divisors cluster, suggesting which C-range to aim at.
first_step: Search 'arcsine law divisors residue class' and check whether a residue-class-restricted DDT theorem exists (Tenenbaum's work on divisors in APs); then test numerically on 4Cp+1, C ≤ p, for fixed p.

title: Quantum-chaos / Berry–Tabor view of the e-slice as an integrable billiard
connection: The levels x = (quantity with p in it) of an integrable system have Poisson statistics (Berry–Tabor); the ES certificate x values for fixed p might be modelled by a 2-torus billiard's level set.
why: Poisson statistics would make f(p) ~ Poisson(log²p) with P(f=0) = exp(−c log²p), which is the heuristic ES already relies on; a rigorous Berry–Tabor-type theorem for a suitable flow would be a 'new input'.
first_step: Read Marklof's survey on Berry–Tabor for values of quadratic forms; check whether the e-slice set {(a,b): ab | N, ab⁻¹ ≡ −1 mod e} can be stated as values of a binary form at lattice points.

title: Integrable lattice model whose conserved quantity is 4/n − 1/x − 1/y − 1/z
connection: Discrete integrable maps (QRT maps, Painlevé discretizations) preserve rational invariants; ask whether U_n: 4xyz = n(xy+yz+zx) is the level set of a QRT-type invariant whose dynamics move integer points.
why: Markoff-type surfaces have Vieta involutions generating all integer points; U_n is a cubic surface too, and an integrable birational map might generate solutions from a seed.
first_step: Check whether U_n admits a non-trivial birational automorphism group of infinite order (compute via Magma/Sage: automorphisms of the cubic surface 4xyz = n(xy+yz+zx) preserving the integral structure); see if the Vieta-style 'flip in one variable' is well-defined for this equation.

title: Bethe-ansatz-like counting of ES solutions via a quantum many-body spectrum
connection: Solutions of 4/n = 1/x+1/y+1/z ↔ Bethe roots of a 3-particle system where total 'momentum' 4/n is shared; completeness of Bethe ansatz = existence of a root configuration.
why: Completeness theorems for Bethe ansatz are existence statements proved for every n (e.g. XXX chain for all lengths), by algebraic rigidity — one of the two mechanisms (R) the campaign identified as able to give pointwise results.
first_step: Search 'Bethe ansatz Egyptian fractions' and 'Bethe equations unit fractions'; otherwise try to write the Bethe equations of a 3-magnon sector of a chain of length n and compare with the unit-fraction structure.

title: Physics of Egyptian fractions: resistor networks (parallel resistances add reciprocally)
connection: Parallel resistors: 1/R = Σ 1/R_i ↔ ES: can resistance p/4 be made from three integer resistors in parallel.

connection: Unit-fraction sums appear in lens/mirror equations; 4/n = 1/x+1/y+1/z is three cascaded optical elements with integer focal lengths. Integer-focal-length lens combinatorics (Gaussian lens formula over ℤ) is a tiny literature.

title: Sandpile/abelian-network identity element and divisors of 4Cp+1
connection: Chip-firing on the cycle graph ℤ/e with e ≡ −p mod 4 has a group structure (sandpile group ≅ ℤ/e); the e-slice condition −1 ∈ {ab⁻¹} is membership of −1 in a subset-product set inside this group.
