title: Tool: use Pari/GP's `factor` with `factorint` flags (ECM) to push the C-form census to p ≤ 10⁷ and C ≤ 10⁴ cheaply; publish the exceptional list to OEIS
connection: The C-form exceptional primes (409, 577, 5569, 9601, …) form a natural integer sequence not (apparently) in OEIS; computing it to 10⁷ and submitting it creates a public hook for others.
why: Community/visibility item with a concrete deliverable; OEIS entries attract exactly the kind of elementary-number-theory attention that could explain the exceptions.
first_step: Run the census (Pari, ~hours); check OEIS for the sequence; draft an OEIS submission with the definition 'primes p ≡ 1 (mod 4) with no C ≤ 10⁴ such that 4Cp+1 has a divisor ≡ −1 mod 4C'.

title: Count the C-form exceptional primes up to X: density → 0 like 1/(log X)^α? or positive density?
connection: If exceptions have positive relative density among primes ≡ 1 mod 24, the C-form is a 'weak' sufficient condition; if they thin out as a power of log, they are the 'tail' and their rate is a measurable analogue of exceptional-set exponents (Vaughan's bound in miniature).
why: Quantifies the gap between C-form and ES; also a test of the 'half-dimensional sieve' heuristics (prediction: exceptions ~ X/(log X)^{1+κ} for the effective sieve dimension κ).
first_step: From the census, fit #exceptions ≤ X vs X/(log X)^β; report β.

title: Which composites fail the C-form? Test whether C-form exceptions are closed under multiplication by squares or by other exceptions
connection: If n fails the C-form, does n·m² fail? (T1-like scaling: for squares the obstruction is via (a/m²) = 1; for n·m²: (a/nm²) = (a/n) — so the QNR condition reduces to that of n; and 4C·nm² + 1 = ab with a ≡ −1 (4C) — different integer.) Empirically test closure properties of the exceptional set E = {n : no C-form certificate}.
why: Structural properties of E (closure, multiplicativity) constrain any eventual characterisation; e.g. if E ⊇ {odd squares} ∪ {409 m² : m odd}, there are infinite non-square families, changing the 'squares + sporadic' expectation for this sub-conjecture.

title: Analogy: Lehmer's totient problem / 'Giuga numbers' — sets defined by 'all prime factors satisfy a congruence' are provably thin and structured; the C-form failure set is such a set for each C
connection: For C = 1: 4p + 1 ∈ S₁ := {all prime factors ≡ 1 mod 4} — the 'sum of two squares' type set. For general C: 4Cp+1 ∈ S_C := {subset products of prime factors avoid −1 mod 4C}. Each S_C is a 'multiplicatively defined' set with a Landau-type counting function x/(log x)^{1−δ_C}; the failure set is {p : ∀C, 4Cp + 1 ∈ S_C}. Sets of the form {n : ∀C ≤ K, aC n + b ∈ S_C} are 'simultaneous Landau conditions on linear forms' — a sieve-theoretic object with a known theory for FIXED K (Brun–Hooley), and the uniformity in K is the frontier.
why: Names the problem as a 'simultaneous multiplicative-set membership of linear forms', connecting to the Hooley 'applications of sieve methods' chapter on sums of two squares in APs/linear forms.
first_step: Read Hooley, Applications of Sieve Methods ch. 5 (two squares in linear forms); formulate the K-fold version; check what uniformity in K the method allows.
refs: Hooley, Applications of Sieve Methods to the Theory of Numbers (1976)

title: Analogy: 'primes p such that p + 1 is a sum of two squares' (Iwaniec) — the half-dimensional sieve as the exact tool for 'C = 1 fails'
connection: C = 1 fails ⟺ 4p+1 has all prime factors ≡ 1 mod 4 ⟺ 4p+1 is 'primitively' a sum of two squares with no factor ≡ 3 mod 4 — the half-dimensional sieve's territory (Iwaniec 1972: #{p ≤ x: p + 1 = a² + b²} ≍ x/(log x)^{3/2}). So #{p ≤ x: C=1 fails} ≍ x/(log x)^{3/2}: a THEOREM-level statement (upper AND lower bounds) about the simplest failure set.
why: Gives the first rigorous 'failure-set size' at C = 1 with matching lower bound — a template for C ≤ K failure sets and a sanity anchor for all heuristics (the constant can be compared with data).
first_step: Check Iwaniec's theorem applies to 4p+1 (linear form in p with leading coefficient 4; yes, 'Primes of the type φ(x,y) + A'/'half-dimensional sieve' handle p + A; for 4p + 1 check the admissibility); compute the constant and compare with the empirical count up to 10⁷.
refs: Iwaniec, 'Primes of the type φ(x,y)+A where φ is a quadratic form', Acta Arith 21 (1972)

title: Upper-bound sieve on simultaneous failure for C ∈ {1, 2}: #{p ≤ x : 4p+1 ∈ S₁ and 8p+1 ∈ S₂} ≪ x/(log x)^{1+1/2+δ₂}
connection: Each extra C with an index-2-type failure set adds 1/2 to the sieve dimension; S₂ (mod 8 patterns) has 'dimension' depending on which residue classes mod 8 are excluded from the subset-product condition (computed via the failure patterns). A K-fold simultaneous Landau sieve with dimension κ_K = Σ_C δ_C and explicit constants.
why: For fixed K this is a theorem-level upper bound; the K → ∞ uniformity gives exceptional-set bounds; and comparing with data at K = 2, 3 is a precise calibration of sieve constants vs reality.
first_step: Compute δ_C (the density exponent of S_C) for C ≤ 6 from the failure patterns; run a Selberg sieve numerically for K = 2 to get the constant; compare with the empirical joint-failure count to 10⁷.

title: The subset-product failure set S_C has a 'dimension' δ_C = 1 − (fraction of residue classes that can contribute): compute δ_C for all C ≤ 100 and its asymptotics
connection: For S_C defined by 'subset products of prime factors (mod 4C) avoid −1', a first-order density exponent is obtained by the largest −1-free subgroup H ⊂ (ℤ/4C)^× (density of primes in H = |H|/φ(4C)); 'all factors in H' has counting function x/(log x)^{1 − |H|/φ(4C)}. The maximal −1-free subgroup has index 2 (any subgroup not containing −1 can be enlarged to index 2? Not always: in (ℤ/8)^× = {1,3,5,7}, −1 = 7; −1-free subgroups: {1}, {1,3}, {1,5} — index 2 exist ✓. In general, −1 ∉ H means H ∩ ⟨−1⟩ trivial; H can be extended to a complement of ⟨−1⟩ if the group is... (ℤ/4C)^× ≅ ℤ/2 × stuff; −1 may or may not be a 'direct summand' — e.g. in ℤ/4 (cyclic), −1 = 2 is the unique element of order 2, every nontrivial subgroup contains it! So for (ℤ/4C)^× containing a cyclic ℤ/4 summand in which −1 lies... concretely for 4C = 20: (ℤ/20)^× ≅ ℤ/2 × ℤ/4 with −1 = ? ; the −1-free subgroups may have index 4.) So δ_C varies non-trivially with C — compute it.
why: δ_C controls how 'hard' it is for a prime to fail at C: small δ_C (large −1-free subgroup) = easy to fail; the C with largest δ_C are the most 'useful' certificates; a proof would use them. Possibly δ_C → 1 along C with (ℤ/4C)^× having −1 'deeply embedded' (e.g. 4C = 4q with q ≡ 1 mod 4 prime? then (ℤ/4q)^× ≅ ℤ/2 × ℤ/(q−1), −1 = (1, (q−1)/2); −1-free subgroups can have index 2: take {0} × ℤ/(q−1)? contains (0,(q−1)/2) ≠ −1 = (1, (q−1)/2) ✓ index 2. Hmm so index 2 always possible? Need −1 ∉ some index-2 subgroup ⟺ −1 is not a square… ⟺ some character χ mod 4C with χ(−1) = −1 (odd character) — ALWAYS exists for 4C ≥ 3. So index-2 −1-free subgroups always exist: δ_C ≤ 1/2 for all C.) So every C has δ_C = 1/2 at the top level — failure at C costs exactly (log)^{-1/2}·(const_C). Then the heuristic failure density for all C ≤ K is (log p)^{−K/2}·Π const_C, where const_C encodes the finer structure. Verify.
first_step: For C ≤ 100: list all −1-free subgroups, their indices; confirm index 2 always achievable; compute the full generating-function density of S_C (sum over all failure patterns, not just 'all in H') numerically for 4Cp+1 ≤ 10⁷.

title: ES as 'every p has an odd character χ mod 4C and a divisor a of 4Cp+1 with χ(a) = −1 for ALL odd χ' — the character-theoretic restatement of a ≡ −1 (mod 4C)
connection: a ≡ −1 mod 4C ⟺ χ(a) = χ(−1) for all characters χ mod 4C ⟺ χ(a) = −1 for odd χ and +1 for even χ. So the C-form asks for a divisor whose character vector equals that of −1. The 'subgroup relaxation' keeps only one odd character; the full condition is ALL characters. Framing: find (C, a) with χ(a) = χ(−1) ∀χ — a 'complete set of character conditions', the number of which grows with C (φ(4C) conditions), while the number of divisors grows like τ(4Cp+1) ≈ log p on average — the expected number of hits is τ/φ(4C), and Σ_C τ(4Cp+1)/φ(4C) ≈ log p · Σ 1/C → log p · log X. (Same count as before, now seen as 'characters vs divisors'.)
why: The character view suggests a *Fourier-analytic* route: #certificates at C = (1/φ(4C)) Σ_χ χ(−1) Σ_{a | N} χ(a); the χ = trivial term is τ(N)/φ(4C) > 0; the other terms are 'noise' Σ_{a|N} χ(a) = Π_{q^e ∥ N} (1 + χ(q) + … + χ(q)^e). A certificate fails to exist iff the noise exactly cancels the main term. Average over C of the noise — can it be shown to be o(main) at fixed p? That's the M_BM program (B3 says the average main term is only log²p). Record the restatement.
first_step: Write the exact identity and compute, for p = 409 and C ≤ 1000, main vs noise per C to see HOW cancellation happens (is it via single-prime N = q with χ(q) = +1 for all odd χ — i.e. q ≡ 1-type — or via multi-factor cancellations?).

title: For p = 409, tabulate the factorisation type of 4Cp+1 for C ≤ 1000: how does 'no divisor ≡ −1 mod 4C' happen each time (prime? all factors ≡ 1 mod 4C? subgroup?)
connection: Direct forensic analysis of the exception: a histogram of failure reasons for one prime across C.
why: If the failures are 'random-looking' (mixture of reasons), 409 is a statistical accident and larger C must win (contradicting the C ≤ 60000 search — making an obstruction likely); if a single reason dominates (e.g. all factors always in a particular subgroup), the obstruction is visible.
first_step: Compute and classify; compare with a control prime (401 or 433) where the C-form wins quickly.

title: Could the C-form exceptional set be 'odd squares ∪ {p : (2/p)… something} ∪ finite' with the exceptions explained by a *quartic* reciprocity law?
connection: HKRS's Apollonian obstructions include quartic ones; the C-form's forced (a/p) = −1 is quadratic. A quartic analogue would be: when p ≡ 1 mod 8 and ... the quartic symbol (a/p)_4 is forced to a value that contradicts (a/p) = −1. For p ≡ 1 mod 8 (577, 5569, 9601 all ≡ 1 mod 8!; 409 ≡ 1 mod 8 too: 409 = 408 + 1 = 8·51 + 1 ✓). All four exceptions are ≡ 1 mod 8 — consistent with a quartic (mod 8-sensitive) obstruction acting on a subset of the p ≡ 1 mod 8 primes. Most primes ≡ 1 mod 8 do have certificates, so the obstruction would need another condition (e.g. 2 is a quartic residue, p = x² + 64y²).
why: Concrete, testable hypothesis class for the exceptions.
first_step: Compute for the four exceptions whether 2 is a quartic residue (p = x² + 64y²?) and whether −1 is an octic residue (p ≡ 1 mod 16?); compare to the frequency of these among non-exceptional primes ≡ 1 mod 8 below 20000.

title: Mechanism design: an identity family indexed by the Gaussian factorisation p = u² + v² (not polynomial in p but polynomial in (u, v))
connection: Mordell–Schinzel forbids polynomial identities in p on square classes; identities polynomial in (u, v) with p = u² + v² are a different class (p is a quadratic form in the parameters). E.g. try: 4/(u² + v²) = 1/x(u,v) + 1/y(u,v) + 1/z(u,v) with x, y, z ∈ ℤ[u, v] — a polynomial identity in TWO variables over the quadric. Schinzel's theorem is about one variable n; a two-variable identity covering all (u, v) with u² + v² ≡ 1 mod 24 is not obviously excluded (but a polynomial identity in (u,v) specialises to a polynomial identity in n on... no — n = u² + v² does not make x(u,v) a polynomial in n). Also allowed: identities depending on (u, v) mod small moduli.
why: A genuinely different identity class that respects T1 automatically? (Odd squares m² = u² + v² with... m² = (m)² + 0² or other representations; identities valid only for v ≠ 0 or for gcd(u,v) = 1 would exclude the trivial representation — promising sign.) Search space is small; cheap to run.
first_step: Enumerate candidate x, y, z as low-degree polynomials in (u, v) (degree ≤ 4, small coefficients) satisfying 4xyz = (u²+v²)(xy+yz+zx) identically — polynomial system; solve with Gröbner/ansatz; also allow residue-class branching on (u, v) mod 2, 3, 4.
alt_first_steps: [signature-0054] For hard primes ≤ 10⁷ compute (a,b) and fit low-degree polynomial forms to the smallest solutions' denominators; check B1 Thm M's scope for procedures that use the two-squares decomposition.
[upgrades-0232] Search low-degree X, Y, Z ∈ ℚ[a,b] with 4XYZ = (a²+b²)(XY+YZ+ZX) identically and X,Y,Z positive integral on a congruence region; check behaviour at Pythagorean points.
alt_titles: [signature-0054] Polynomial identities in Gaussian coordinates: ES solutions as polynomials in (a,b) with p = a² + b²
[upgrades-0232] Polynomial certificate families in the Gaussian variables (a,b), p = a² + b²

title: Identity families indexed by other binary forms representing p: p = u² + 2v², u² + 3v², u² − 2v², u² + uv + v²
connection: Every p ≡ 1 mod 24 is simultaneously u² + v², u² + 2v² (p ≡ 1,3 mod 8 ✓), u² + 3v² (p ≡ 1 mod 3 ✓), u² − 2v² (p ≡ ±1 mod 8 ✓), u² + 6v²? (needs p ≡ 1, 7 mod 24 ✓!). Each representation gives 2 parameters; polynomial identities in those parameters are not excluded by Mordell–Schinzel.
why: Multiplies the search space of 'legal' identity classes by the number of forms; the combination 'p = u² + 6v²' is special to the hard class p ≡ 1 mod 24.
first_step: Same Gröbner/ansatz search for each form; for p = u² + 6v² in particular (since 24 | 840 structure).
refs: Cox, Primes of the form x² + ny²

title: Does T1 kill (u, v)-identities? Check what happens to a (u,v)-polynomial identity at p = m² = u² + v²
connection: If an identity in (u,v) valid for all coprime (u,v) with u² + v² ≡ 1 mod 24 existed, it would produce Type I/II solutions for m² whenever m² = u² + v² with gcd(u,v) = 1 and uv ≠ 0 — which happens iff m has a prime factor ≡ 1 mod 4 (Pythagorean). T1 says no such solution exists ⟹ NO (u,v)-polynomial identity can be valid on all coprime (u,v) with the right residues. So (u,v)-identities must also exclude Pythagorean (u,v) — i.e. must depend on more than residues of (u,v). Record as a lemma killing the naive version; the surviving version needs a non-polynomial ingredient (e.g. gcd or primality of u² + v²).
why: Saves a wasted search; and pinpoints the 'Pythagorean' loophole: an identity could be valid only when u² + v² is not a square — but polynomial identities can't 'know' that. Same for u² + 2v², etc. (m² = u² + 2v² has solutions when m has a factor ≡ 1,3 mod 8).
first_step: Write the lemma; then ask: are there identities in (u,v) valid for all (u,v) with u² + v² ≡ 1 mod 24 EXCEPT where u² + v² is a square — impossible for polynomials; so the item above (Gaussian identities) is dead in its polynomial form; keep only residue-branching + non-polynomial variants.

title: Analogy of analogy: T1 ↔ 'Pythagorean loophole' ↔ Hilbert's irreducibility — identities fail exactly where the parameter polynomial takes square values; so ES's obstruction is the square-value locus of EVERY parametrisation
connection: Generalising the previous item: for any parametrisation p = P(t₁, …, t_k) (P a polynomial), a polynomial identity would produce solutions at all values P(t) including those that are odd squares; T1 forbids this; so no polynomial identity exists over any parametrisation P whose value set contains odd squares. Only parametrisations whose value set avoids squares (e.g. P(t) = t² + 1, never a square for t ≥ 1; P = 4t² + 1 never a square for t ≥ 1!) escape. So: polynomial identities for ES along p = 4t² + 1 (or t² + 1, t⁴ + 1…) are NOT excluded by T1 — and primes of the form 4t² + 1 are conjecturally infinite (Landau's 4th problem for t²+1).
why: Identifies a precise loophole class: identities in t for n = 4t² + 1 (or similar square-avoiding polynomials) — a 'conditional infinite family of hard primes' if found (hard class? 4t² + 1 mod 840 can be in square classes: need 4t² + 1 ≡ square mod 840 for some t ✓ possible). Mordell–Schinzel applies to identities in n, not in t with n = 4t² + 1 — check Schinzel's theorem's exact scope (it might cover 'polynomial in t with n polynomial in t').
first_step: Search for polynomial x(t), y(t), z(t) with 4/(4t² + 1) = Σ 1/x_i(t); e.g. try the e-slice/Type II structure: 4C(4t² + 1) + 1 = 16Ct² + 4C + 1 — for C = 1: 16t² + 5 — factor? no; find C(t) polynomial making 4C(t)(4t² + 1) + 1 factor with the right residues. Then read Schinzel 2000 to see whether this is excluded.

title: ES for n = t² + 1 and n = 4t² + 1: compute identities and check whether the campaign already knows 'ES holds for all n = t² + 1'
connection: n = t² + 1: 4/(t²+1) — try x = (t²+1)/… hmm t² + 1 ≡ 1,2 mod 4; for t even n ≡ 1 mod 4. Is there a known identity? e.g. 4/(t²+1) = 1/(t²+1)·4; want 1/A + 1/B + 1/C. Note (t² + 1) + t² ... Possibly known in the literature on 'Erdős–Straus for n = polynomial values' (e.g. 'all n of the form k² + 1'?). Search.
why: If identities exist for square-avoiding polynomial families, that's an infinite family of hard-class n (not primes necessarily) — and the proof technique (polynomial in t) shows how T1 is dodged; worth 30 minutes.
first_step: git grep -il 't^2+1\|t² + 1\|k^2+1' -- '*.md'; brute-force search for identities with x, y, z ∈ ℤ[t] of degree ≤ 4 for n = t² + 1, 4t² + 1, t² + t + 1.

title: Geometry: integral points on the surface 4xyz = n(xy+yz+zx) as n varies — the threefold X: 4xyz = n(xy+yz+zx) in (x,y,z,n) and its fibration over n; is X rational? unirational? what are its integral points' densities?
connection: The total space X ⊂ A⁴ is a cubic threefold (linear in n!): n = 4xyz/(xy+yz+zx) — so X ≅ the graph of a rational function on A³: X is rational, integral points = (x,y,z) with (xy+yz+zx) | 4xyz. ES = surjectivity of n: ℤ³_{>0} ∩ X → ℤ_{≥2}. The question 'which integers are values of 4xyz/(xy+yz+zx)' is a 'value set of a rational function at integer points' problem.
why: Reframes ES as the image of an explicit rational map on integer points — related to the theory of 'representation by rational functions' and to Heath-Brown-style counts of integer points on cubic hypersurfaces where the count of points with a given value of n is f(n). The threefold's geometry (it's rational, the fibres are the U_n) gives a 'total count' Σ_{n ≤ N} f(n) via lattice points on X, which is the Elsholtz–Tao estimate; nothing new, but the 'value set of a rational function' literature (e.g. values of x/y + y/z + z/x) might have transferable ideas.
first_step: Search 'integers of the form 4xyz/(xy+yz+zx)' and the similar classical 'x/y + y/z + z/x = n' problem (Bremner–Guy; elliptic curves!): the latter is an elliptic surface where integer values are determined by rank — a structurally different (and solvable) situation. Compare: why does xy+yz+zx | 4xyz NOT reduce to elliptic curves?

title: Compare ES with x/y + y/z + z/x = n (Bremner–Guy): both are 'n as a value of a symmetric rational function in 3 variables'; the latter reduces to elliptic curves with rank-dependent solvability — what makes ES's function (harmonic mean) different?
connection: 4/n = 1/x + 1/y + 1/z says n/4 is... the harmonic mean of x,y,z divided by 3: HM/3·… ; x/y + y/z + z/x = n defines a cubic curve in P² for each n (genus 1); 4xyz = n(xy+yz+zx) is a cubic surface (dimension 2) — more freedom, hence many solutions (log²n) rather than rank-controlled finitely many. So ES is 'easier' in count but lacks the group law. A middle ground: intersect U_n with a plane (e.g. z = x + y or z = kx) to get a curve; integer points on these curves (genus 0 or 1) — for genus 0 fibres (lines/conics), integral points are governed by Pell/congruence conditions — these are the identity families; are there genus-1 plane sections with positive rank for all n? Then infinitely many rational points — but integrality is the catch.
why: Systematises 'plane sections of U_n' as the source of all known identities (genus 0 sections) and asks whether genus-1 sections offer anything (they give rational, not integral, points — usually useless for ES, but integral points on elliptic curves are a finite set with effective bounds, so 'every n has an integral point on some genus-1 section' is at least a well-posed hard problem).
first_step: Classify plane sections of U_n by genus; list which genus-0 sections give Mordell's identities; find a genus-1 section family and compute its rank for small n (Sage) for curiosity.

title: Community: write up the C-form exceptional primes + QNR lemma as a short arXiv note / MO question to invite elementary explanations
connection: The observations (C-form strictly weaker than ES; four exceptional primes below 20000 with no certificate to C = 60000; every certificate divisor is a QNR mod p) are elementary and crisp — ideal for an MO question 'Why does 409 have no factorisation 4C·409 + 1 = ab with a ≡ b ≡ −1 mod 4C?'
why: Crowd-sourced elementary number theory is strong at exactly this kind of question; a quick answer would either kill a sub-conjecture (local obstruction) or reveal a mechanism.
first_step: Verify the four exceptions independently (Pari), extend to 10⁶ for the list, then post on MO with the QNR lemma.

title: Sanity: does the C-form exceptional set change if we also allow a ≡ −1 (mod 4C) with a | 4Cp − 1 (sign variant) or 4Cp + 1 = ab with a ≡ b ≡ +1 (mod 4C)? Which sign variants correspond to actual ES solutions?
connection: The derivation p = 4Cuv − u − v gave the (−1, −1) sign pattern; ES's word form allows a coordinate in (8ℤ − p) too — other sign/parity patterns may correspond to Type I. Enumerate all 'sign variants' of the C-form, determine which yield ES solutions (verify algebraically), and recompute the exceptional set under the union.
why: The exceptional primes might simply be certified by a sibling form (e.g. Type I with c = 1), which would make 'C-form exceptions' a statement about one sign pattern only — important for interpreting the finding.
first_step: Derive: 4/p = 1/(Cuv) + 1/(pCv) + 1/(pCu) came from p + u + v = 4Cuv; alternatives: p + u − v = 4Cuv? (gives a negative term?) ; p − u − v = 4Cuv ⟹ 4/p = ... check signs; list all variants giving positive solutions; compute which certify 409.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Finding: the Type I one-parameter form (c = 1) has its own lone exception below 20000 — p = 2521 ≡ 1 (mod 840) — and certifies all four C-form exceptions
connection: Type I with c = 1: a divisor f of p² + 4d with f ≡ −p (mod 4d). Computation (p < 20000, d < 1500): the only prime ≡ 1 (mod 4) without such a certificate is 2521 (= 3·840 + 1, in the Mordell-hard class 1 mod 840); 409, 577, 5569, 9601 are certified by (d, f) = (11, 75), (5, 3), (17, 7), (67, 851). Conversely 2521 is not a C-form exception. So the two one-parameter forms have disjoint exceptional sets in this range and their union covers everything.
why: Suggests a 'two one-parameter families suffice' phenomenon — ES's structure may be '1 + 1 dimensional' rather than genuinely 2-dimensional; and 2521 becomes the Type I analogue of 409: a hard-class prime where a natural sufficient condition fails for (apparently) local reasons. Both exception types are now concrete test cases for any mechanism.
first_step: Extend both censuses to p ≤ 10⁶; test whether the two exceptional sets stay disjoint (if they ever intersect at a prime p, that p has neither one-parameter certificate — a genuinely '2-parameter' prime); derive the forced reciprocity symbol for Type I c=1 ((−d/f) = 1) and look for the local obstruction at 2521.
alt_first_steps: [free_fable-0284] Compute for p ≤ 20000 the c=1 Type I certificate existence (d ≤ 10⁴); list exceptions; intersect with the C-form exceptions.
alt_titles: [free_fable-0284] Type I at c = 1 ('f | p² + 4d, f ≡ −p mod 4d'): the Type-I sibling of the C-form — which primes does IT certify, and does it cover 409, 577, 5569, 9601?

title: Minimal 'dimension' of ES: is there a one-parameter family of certificates (any type) covering all primes ≤ 10⁷?
connection: The C-form (Type II, c=1) fails for some primes; Type I with c=1 may fail for others; their union might cover everything — or might not, implying that ES is intrinsically 'two-parameter' (any one-parameter sub-family has exceptions). That would be a quantitative version of 'no covering by identities': even infinite one-parameter families don't suffice. [Quick data: below 20000, C-form (Type II, c=1) exceptions are {409, 577, 5569, 9601}; Type I c=1 (f | p²+4d, f ≡ −p mod 4d, d < 1500) has the single exception 2521 ≡ 1 (mod 840); the two sets are disjoint, so the UNION of the two one-parameter forms covers all primes ≡ 1 mod 4 below 20000.]
why: A sharp structural fact about ES, cheap to establish empirically, with implications for proof design (must handle two-parameter families → double sums → the extra log).
first_step: Compute exceptional sets of: C-form; c=1 Type I; e-slice with e ≤ bound (one parameter: e); and their union, for p ≤ 10⁶.

title: Physics redux: the C-form as a 1-D 'Ising chain in a field' where the field is the character χ and the spins are prime factors — exact solvability (transfer matrix) of the per-C partition function
connection: #{a | N: a ≡ −1 (4C)} = (1/φ) Σ_χ χ(−1) Π_{q^e ∥ N} (1 + χ(q) + … + χ(q)^e) is literally a sum over 'external fields' χ of a product of single-site partition functions — an exactly solvable (non-interacting) model. ES failure = destructive interference across χ. The physics intuition: non-interacting spins in φ(4C) different fields; the total vanishes iff … This is exactly the structure where 'Lee–Yang' and 'sign problem' intuitions apply: the sum over χ is a sum with signs (χ(−1) = ±1 and complex χ(q)).
why: Just the exact formula in physics clothing; but the 'sign problem' analogy suggests looking at |Σ| vs Σ|·| — the ratio measures cancellation; and the structure 'product of single-site terms' means the count is a *Fourier transform of a product* — a convolution on the group, which is where Kneser/subset-sum structure enters (item on additive combinatorics).
first_step: Compute the cancellation ratio (count)/(Σ_χ |Π|)/φ for failing vs winning (p, C); see whether failures are 'maximal cancellation' events with a recognisable pattern.

title: Convolution-on-group view: the divisor multiset of N mod 4C is a multiset D ⊂ (ℤ/4C)^×; certificates = D ∋ −1; D = product-set of the prime-power 'intervals' {1, q, …, q^e} — a Minkowski product of 'geometric progressions' in the group; Kneser's theorem bounds |D| from below
connection: |D| ≥ Σ (|D_q| − 1) + 1 (Cauchy–Davenport analogue for abelian groups via Kneser) when there is no stabiliser; so with ω(N) factors, |D| ≥ ω + 1 roughly — tiny versus φ(4C). Kneser's theorem also says: if |D| is small then D is a union of cosets of a subgroup H (periodic) — then −1 ∈ D iff the coset structure includes it: a *structural* dichotomy: either D is large (random-like, then −1 ∈ D with 'probability' |D|/φ) or D is periodic with stabiliser H (then −1 ∈ D ⟺ −1 ∈ D·H, a subgroup question). This is a rigorous version of the 'subgroup vs subset-product' gap.
why: Kneser's structure theorem is a real theorem applicable pointwise (at each (p, C)); it reorganises failures into 'small non-periodic D' (few factors — the dominant failure mode) vs 'periodic D missing −1' (subgroup obstruction).
first_step: For (p, C) failures, compute D, its stabiliser H = {h : hD = D}, and classify; check the Kneser bound tightness.
alt_first_steps: [tools-0268] Apply Kneser iteratively to the divisor sets of consecutive slices pooled in one group (common e) and record stabiliser chains.
[upgrades-0128] For hard primes and C ≤ 100 compute |product set|/φ(4C) and the Kneser stabiliser; classify failures.
refs: Kneser, Abschätzung der asymptotischen Dichte von Summenmengen, Math. Z. 58 (1953)
alt_titles: [tools-0268] Kneser's addition theorem in (ℤ/e)^× for divisor product sets
[upgrades-0128] Kneser's theorem for the divisor-class product set at level C

title: Ask: is there any (p, C) failure with ω(4Cp+1) ≥ 6 where D is NOT a union of cosets of a nontrivial subgroup? (Kneser-periodicity test of 'rich' failures)
connection: If rich failures (many prime factors) are always periodic (D = union of H-cosets with H ∌ −1 and H nontrivial), then failures split cleanly into 'poor' (ω ≤ 5) and 'periodic'. The periodic ones are controlled by Galois (all factors in a subgroup); the poor ones by sieve (few prime factors is rare across C). A proof could treat the two regimes separately. [Partial answer from a quick check with Ω ≥ 5: yes, the majority (61%) of rich failures are NOT subgroup-type; the stabiliser computation remains to be done.]
why: Sharp empirical dichotomy test with direct proof-strategy consequences.
first_step: Scan p ≤ 10⁵, C ≤ 200 for failures with ω ≥ 6; compute stabilisers.

title: Sieve for 'poor' failures: #{C ≤ X : ω(4Cp+1) ≤ 5} ≪ X (log log X)⁵/log X — pointwise in p by an upper-bound sieve (Hardy–Ramanujan / Brun) — so most C have rich 4Cp+1
connection: Upper-bound sieves bound the number of C ≤ X for which the linear form 4Cp+1 has few prime factors (almost-prime values of a linear polynomial): ≪ X/log X · (log log X)^k uniformly in p ≤ X^A? (Need uniformity in the coefficient 4p: standard sieve bounds for almost-primes in APs are uniform via Brun–Titchmarsh-type results, with p up to X^{1−ε}... For X = polylog(p) the uniformity fails — the coefficient 4p is huge relative to X. Hmm: the sieve dimension is 1, the sifting range is primes ≤ z; for values 4Cp+1 ≤ 4Xp, we sieve by primes up to z ≈ X^{1/2}: the count of C ≤ X with 4Cp+1 free of primes ≤ z is ≪ X/log z — that's fine and uniform in p (only the residue of p mod q matters). So #{C ≤ X: 4Cp+1 has no prime factor ≤ X^{1/2}} ≪ X/log X — pointwise in p! But 'rich' needs ≥ 6 factors, not just one small factor.) Refine: with k-fold sieving (Erdős–Kac-type for linear forms, Halberstam) one gets most C have ω(4Cp+1) ≈ log log(Xp)… uniformity in p needs the Turán–Kubilius inequality for linear forms with large coefficient — it holds! (The variance Σ_C (ω(4Cp+1) − log log)² ≪ X log log, uniformly in p, since it only uses residues of p mod small primes.)
why: A genuinely pointwise-in-p statement: for any fixed p and X ≥ (log p)^A, almost all C ≤ X have ω(4Cp+1) ≥ 6 (indeed ≈ log log Xp). So 'poor' failures are a vanishing fraction of C. Combined with the Kneser dichotomy, ES(p) would follow if 'periodic rich failures' could be shown not to happen for ALL C — a cleaner target (Galois-type: 'for some C, the prime factors of 4Cp+1 generate a subgroup containing −1 AND the subset-product set is not periodic-avoiding').
first_step: Prove the Turán–Kubilius bound for ω(4Cp+1), C ≤ X, uniform in p (standard; write it out with explicit constants); then count 'rich failures' empirically for p ≤ 10⁵ to see whether they are rare.
refs: Halberstam, 'On the distribution of additive number-theoretic functions' (1955)

title: Rich-failure structure: when ω(4Cp+1) ≥ 6 and −1 ∉ D, is D ⊂ H for an index-2 subgroup H (i.e. all prime factors lie in the kernel of one odd character)?
connection: Kneser-periodic failures with nontrivial stabiliser; the simplest is 'all factors in ker χ for an odd χ'. If rich failures are ALWAYS of this form, then: ES(p) fails ⟹ for every C with rich 4Cp+1 there is an odd character χ_C mod 4C with χ_C(q) = 1 for all q | 4Cp+1 — i.e. 4Cp+1 is a 'norm' from the quadratic field of χ_C. Then 4Cp+1 ∈ N(K_C) for every rich C — a family of 'simultaneous norm' conditions on linear forms in C, controlled by half-dimensional sieves over C (pointwise in p!): #{C ≤ X : 4Cp+1 is a norm from K_C} — but K_C varies with C, so the sieve is over a varying family; still each condition has 'density 1/√log' heuristically and the expected number of C ≤ X satisfying it is X/√log X ≪ X — but we need to show it's < (number of rich C), i.e. that NOT ALL rich C are norms, which requires the sieve LOWER bound… no: we need an upper bound on #{C: 4Cp+1 is a norm from K_C} < #{rich C} ≈ X. An upper bound ≪ X/√log X·const would suffice for X large! The catch: uniformity in p and the varying K_C. Promising structure. [CHECKED after writing: FALSE as a dichotomy — for p < 6000, C < 150, among 4182 failures with Ω(4Cp+1) ≥ 5, only 1651 (39%) have factors generating a −1-free subgroup; in 61% the factors generate −1 but no subset product equals −1 (multiplicity poverty). So the norm-type sieve bounds only ~40% of rich failures; the remaining gap is the Davenport-constant regime described two items below.]
why: If the dichotomy holds empirically and the sieve upper bound is provable uniformly, this is a *pointwise* proof sketch: 'poor C are few (Turán–Kubilius), norm-type C are few (half-dimensional sieve over varying fields), so some C is rich and non-norm ⟹ its subset-product set is non-periodic and large... ⟹ contains −1?' — the last step is the gap (large non-periodic D need not contain −1). Needs Kneser + a counting argument: |D| ≥ ω + 1 is too weak; but for non-periodic D the Kneser/Kemperman structure might force |D| ≥ φ(4C)/2 + 1 (if D·D ⊂ D-like); then D ∪ (−D) covers the group... −1 ∈ D ⟺ 1 ∈ −D; hmm, D is a product set containing 1; −1 ∈ D iff... Let me record the chain and its gap honestly.
first_step: (1) Empirically test the 'rich failure ⟹ all factors in ker of one odd χ' claim for p ≤ 10⁵, C ≤ 300. (2) If it holds, write the sieve upper bound for #{C ≤ X : all prime factors of 4Cp+1 in ker χ_C for SOME odd χ_C mod 4C} with explicit uniformity. (3) Identify the exact gap between 'rich, non-norm' and '−1 ∈ D'.

title: The 'rich non-norm but −1 ∉ D' gap: does the subset-product set D of a rich 4Cp+1 with factors NOT all in one index-2 subgroup necessarily contain −1? Count counterexamples
connection: D is generated (as a subset-product set with multiplicities) by ω ≥ 6 elements of G = (ℤ/4C)^× not all in any index-2 subgroup (i.e. for every odd χ, some factor has χ(q) ≠ 1). Does D ∋ −1? Certainly ⟨factors⟩ ∋ −1? Not necessarily: factors could lie in an index-4 subgroup missing −1 (not index 2) — e.g. G = ℤ/2 × ℤ/4 with −1 = (0, 2) and factors in {0} × ... hmm (0,2) is in ⟨(0,1)⟩. Take G = (ℤ/2)³ (4C = 24: (ℤ/24)^× ≅ (ℤ/2)³, −1 ↔ some vector v); factors in a 2-dim subspace not containing v: index 2 — covered. In (ℤ/2)³ every proper subgroup missing v is inside an index-2 subgroup missing v (hyperplane avoiding v exists iff v ≠ 0 ✓). For general abelian G and element v of order 2: is every subgroup H ∌ v contained in an index-2 subgroup ∌ v? Yes: G/H is a finite abelian group with v̄ ≠ 0 of order 2; there is a character of G/H nontrivial on v̄ (characters separate points); its kernel is a subgroup of index 2 (if the character has order 2) — the character χ with χ(v̄) ≠ 1 has χ(v̄) = −1 (order-2 element), but χ may have order > 2; then ker χ has index > 2 but χ² ... hmm, need an index-2 subgroup: take χ of G/H with χ(v̄) = −1; the subgroup ker(χ) has index ord(χ), may exceed 2. Alternative: the set of characters trivial on H and nontrivial at v̄ — does it contain an order-2 character? In G/H ≅ ℤ/4 with v̄ = 2: the order-2 character χ(1) = −1 gives χ(2) = 1 — fails! So in ℤ/4, the subgroup H = {0} misses v = 2, but the only index-2 subgroup {0, 2} contains v. So: for G with a cyclic ℤ/4 summand in which −1 is the element 2, there are −1-free subgroups (like {0} or ones generated by elements of odd order) not inside any index-2 −1-free subgroup. (ℤ/4C)^× has such summands when e.g. 5 | C ((ℤ/5)^× ≅ ℤ/4). So the 'index-2' dichotomy is incomplete; the correct statement: factors generate a subgroup H ∌ −1 — any index. The sieve then has dimension 1 − |H|/φ ≥ 1/2 anyway (larger for smaller H) — fine. The gap item stands but with 'all factors in some −1-free subgroup H' instead of index 2.
why: Corrects the previous item's formulation (group-theoretic precision matters for the sieve) and shows the sieve dimension is ≥ 1/2 in all cases — the half-dimensional sieve is the WORST case.
first_step: Enumerate for 4C ≤ 400 the maximal −1-free subgroups of (ℤ/4C)^× and their indices; confirm the worst case is index 2 and the sieve dimension is ≥ 1/2.

title: The final gap, isolated: 'prime factors of 4Cp+1 generate a subgroup containing −1' vs 'some subset product (with the actual multiplicities) equals −1' — bound the failure of the latter given the former via the Davenport constant
connection: If the factors (with multiplicity e_q) generate a group containing −1, does some subset product equal −1? Not necessarily — multiplicities too small (e.g. −1 = q⁴ needs e_q ≥ 4). The Davenport constant D(G) (every sequence of length ≥ D(G) has a zero-sum subsequence) and its 'prescribed element' variants (Olson, 'every element is a subsequence product when the sequence is long enough and generates') give: if ω(N) ≥ D(G)+something and the factors generate G, then EVERY element of G is a subset product — in particular −1. D((ℤ/4C)^×) ≤ roughly 4C·(…); for ω ≈ log log — far smaller than D(G) ≈ 4C. So multiplicity-poverty is the binding constraint: the subset-product set has ≤ 2^ω ≈ (log p)^{log 2} elements, while the group has φ(4C) elements — for C ≫ (log p)^{0.7} the set can't cover and −1 ∈ D is a 'coincidence' of probability |D|/φ(4C). So the real battleground is C ≤ (log p)^{0.7}-ish where |D| ≥ φ(4C) is possible. Document this scale.
why: Pins the exact scale of C where 'structural' arguments (generation ⟹ coverage) can work: C ≤ (log p)^{log 2 − ε}... and shows that for larger C, success is probabilistic (1/φ(4C) per C, summing to log X — the familiar count). A proof must therefore either (i) handle small C structurally (covering-like; but 409 etc. show small C fail for some p) or (ii) handle the probabilistic regime, which is B3. Useful map.
first_step: Compute for p ≤ 10⁵ the smallest winning C and whether |D_C| ≥ φ(4C) at that C (structural regime) or not (probabilistic regime); fraction of primes won in each regime.

title: Zero-sum theory (EGZ, Davenport) cannot be applied by pooling prime factors across C — B2 in zero-sum language
connection: Zero-sum / Erdős–Ginzburg–Ziv flavour: with multiplicities, the prime factors of Π_{C ≤ K} (4Cp+1) (pooled across C!) form a long sequence in… different groups (ℤ/4C)^× — no common group. But pooled across C with 4C | M for a fixed M (i.e., C | M/4), all live in (ℤ/M)^× via reduction, and a divisor a of some 4Cp+1 with a ≡ −1 mod M certainly has a ≡ −1 mod 4C. So: fix M = 4·lcm(1..K); pool all prime factors of 4Cp+1 for C | M/4; if the pooled sequence is long enough (≥ D((ℤ/M)^×)) and generates, EGZ-type theorems give a subset product ≡ −1 mod M — but the subset must come from a SINGLE 4Cp+1 to be a divisor. So pooling doesn't directly help; unless the pooled products correspond to divisors of Π_C (4Cp+1) — which IS a p-tied integer (a polynomial in p of degree K!), with modulus M. So: 'the polynomial P_K(p) = Π_{C|M/4}(4Cp+1) has a divisor ≡ −1 mod M' is a necessary-ish consequence… does it imply an ES certificate? A divisor of the product is a product of divisors of the factors; need all of it inside one factor. No. Record as a structured negative: pooling across C breaks the 'single integer' requirement — THIS is B2 in zero-sum language.
why: Shows precisely why zero-sum theory (which handles long sequences) doesn't apply: ES's sequences are short (ω ≈ log log) per integer, and pooling destroys the divisor structure. Clean statement of B2.
first_step: Write it up as a one-paragraph negative in the lane md; no computation needed.

title: Analogy: Erdős's 'every n > 1 is a sum of distinct unit fractions with denominators ≤ …' — the greedy/Bleicher–Erdős bounds on the number of terms vs denominators; the 3-term boundary
connection: The theory of representing rationals as sums of k unit fractions with denominators ≤ D (Bleicher–Erdős 'Denominators of Egyptian fractions') gives tradeoffs between k and D; ES is k = 3, D unconstrained; maybe a tradeoff theorem 'k = 3 with D ≤ n² always' is provable with the same tools in a weakened form (e.g., k = 3 for all n outside a set of size ≪ N/(log N)^A — the Vaughan line).
why: Historical method check.
first_step: Read Bleicher–Erdős 1976 'Denominators of Egyptian fractions' II and see the structure of their k-term bounds for a/n.

title: Prize/competition: propose ES-adjacent sub-problems (C-form exceptions; d ≤ 3 Type I coverage; one-parameter dimension) as AI-math benchmark tasks (e.g. for Epoch's FrontierMath / AIMO-like) to attract compute and attention
connection: The campaign's sub-problems are well-posed, verifiable, and open — the exact profile sought by AI-math benchmark builders; inclusion brings many independent attempts.
why: Meta/community lever; cheap.
first_step: Write three one-paragraph problem statements with verification scripts; submit to a benchmark or post as 'open sub-problems' on the Erdős problems site discussion.

title: Teaching lens: the cleanest 'why ES is hard' demo is p = 409 — build a one-page explainer and use it to brief new lanes/boards
connection: 409 is small enough to hand-check: every 4C·409 + 1 for C ≤ 10 can be factored by hand, each failure explained; yet 16·409 + 1 = 6545 = 5·7·11·17 has the c=2 Type II certificate 7·935 (7 ≡ 935 ≡ −1 mod 8). It shows the congruence-slack of c ≥ 2 concretely.
why: Improves future lane quality (shared concrete example); near-zero cost.
first_step: Write BRAINSTORM/example_409.md with the table of 4C·409+1, C ≤ 12, factorizations, residues mod 4C, and the c=2 rescue.

title: Check whether Type II with c ≥ 2 is itself just the C-form for a *composite* n: ff′ = 4c²dp + 1 with f ≡ f′ ≡ −1 (mod 4cd) ⟺ C-form certificate for n = cp with C = cd?
connection: C-form for n' = cp with C' = cd: 4C'n' + 1 = 4cd·cp + 1 = 4c²dp + 1 ✓ and a ≡ b ≡ −1 mod 4C' = 4cd ✓. So Type II for p with parameters (c, d) is EXACTLY the C-form for the multiple n = cp with parameter C = cd. Hence: ES(p) via Type II ⟺ some multiple cp of p has a C-form certificate; and a solution for cp gives one for p by scaling?? NO — scaling goes the other way (solution for n gives one for multiples). Hmm: C-form for cp gives 4/(cp) = 1/(C'uv) + 1/(cpC'v) + 1/(cpC'u) ⟹ multiply by c: 4/p = c/(C'uv) + 1/(pC'v) + 1/(pC'u) — first term c/(cd·uv) = 1/(duv) ✓ a unit fraction! So yes: a C-form certificate for cp with C' = cd yields 4/p = 1/(duv) + 1/(pcdv) + 1/(pcdu). Consistent. So full Type II ⟺ 'some multiple cp of p, with C a multiple of c, has a C-form certificate' — the slack is exactly 'pass to a multiple'.
why: Clean structural dictionary: the C-form is the 'primitive' statement and Type II is its closure under passing to multiples cp with C ∈ cℤ. For 409: n = 818, C = 2 works. So the C-form exceptional set E and ES relate by: ES(p) ⟺ ∃c: (cp, C ∈ cℤ)-C-form certificate. The 'C-form conjecture for all non-square n' (if true) would imply ES immediately (take c = 1); its failure at 409 shows the conjecture is false for primes — so the right C-form conjecture is 'for every n, some multiple cn has a C-form certificate with c | C' — which is just ES.
first_step: Record the dictionary; recompute: for each C-form exception p, the smallest c such that cp has a C-form certificate with c | C (409: c=2).

title: Is the e-slice form ('∃ e ≡ −p mod 4 with −1 ∈ {ab⁻¹ mod e : ab | N}') the right 'primitive' with no exceptions? Compute its exceptional set vs C-form's
connection: The repo's e-slice form is stated as ⟺ ES(p) (FRONTIER §1), with N = (p+e)/4 (Type II) or (pe+1)/4 (Type I). Unlike the C-form it is claimed equivalent; its one-parameter nature (e) vs the C-form's suggests the e-slice packs (c, d) into e. Verify the equivalence numerically and compute the smallest winning e for the exceptions 409, 577, …
why: Establishes which one-parameter form is exact; informs the 'dimension' items.
first_step: Implement the e-slice test; verify against brute-force ES for p ≤ 3000; report e_min for the four exceptional primes.

title: Noise/signal across lanes: assign each z52b item a 'form-dependence' flag (C-form / Type II / Type I / e-slice / U_n) so merged lists can be filtered by which reformulation they assume
connection: Meta-hygiene for the merge: many items across the lanes will silently assume one form; a flag makes it cheap to re-check items when a form turns out weaker than assumed (as happened here).
why: Prevents the C-form confusion from propagating into the merged brainstorm.
first_step: Add 'form:*' tags to this lane's items in a post-pass (script); suggest the same convention to the merger.

title: Finding: 'rich' C-form failures are mostly multiplicity-poverty, not subgroup obstructions (61% vs 39%)
connection: For p < 6000, C < 150: of 4182 failing (p, C) with Ω(4Cp+1) ≥ 5, the prime factors generate a subgroup containing −1 in 2531 cases (61%) — the failure is that no subset product with the available multiplicities equals −1 — and generate a −1-free subgroup in 1651 cases (39%). So even with ≥ 5 prime factors the subset-product set D (|D| ≤ 2^Ω ≤ 32 vs φ(4C) up to ~300) is simply too small to be forced to contain −1.
why: Kills the clean 'rich ⟹ Galois-type failure' dichotomy that would have made a sieve-over-norm-conditions proof sketch viable; shows the binding constraint is |D| ≪ φ(4C) (Davenport-constant regime), i.e. the probabilistic regime starts at very small C. Any pointwise argument must live in the regime C ≤ (log p)^{log 2} where 2^Ω can exceed φ(4C), or must be genuinely probabilistic.
first_step: Redo with distinct-prime count ω and with the threshold |D| ≥ φ(4C): find the fraction of (p, C) where D could in principle cover the group; check whether in THAT regime failures are always subgroup-type (which would restore a dichotomy in the only regime where it matters).

title: Visualisation: 'Goldbach comet' analogue — scatter f(p) vs p coloured by p mod 840 and by Legendre profile
connection: The Goldbach comet's bands revealed the singular series' dependence on small prime factors of n; an ES comet (f(p)/log²p vs p, coloured by residues/Legendre symbols) might show bands indicating which local data govern f(p).
why: Cheap, often revealing; the repo likely has f(p) data to 10⁸ already.
first_step: Plot; look for bands; if bands exist, regress f(p)/log²p on the band variable.

title: Visualisation: Ulam-spiral / Klauber-triangle plot of C-form C_min(p) and Type I d_min(p) to spot quadratic-polynomial alignments
connection: Ulam spirals make polynomial families visible as lines; plotting the certificate parameters (or their absence) on a spiral could reveal that exceptions (409, 577, 5569, 9601, 2521) lie on a quadratic curve.
why: Five exceptions is few, but the plot costs nothing and polynomial alignment would be a strong hint toward a Mordell–Schinzel-compatible structure (identities in t with p = Q(t)).
first_step: Generate the plots for p ≤ 10⁶ with colour = log C_min; eyeball; test the exceptional primes against small quadratics.

title: Möbius inversion on the divisor lattice (Rota) for the certificate indicator: express 1[∃ a | N, a ≡ −1 (m)] via Möbius function of the lattice of divisors
connection: The event 'some divisor lies in a class' is a union over divisors; inclusion–exclusion on the divisor lattice gives an exact alternating formula; the 'Möbius algebra' of the divisor poset might simplify when the class condition is a character condition.
why: Exact combinatorial formula alternative to the character-sum formula; may expose cancellation structure.
first_step: Write the formula for N squarefree with ω factors (2^ω terms) and compare its complexity to the character formula (φ(m) terms); use whichever is smaller per regime.
refs: Rota, 'On the foundations of combinatorial theory I'

title: Numeration systems: Ostrowski numeration (based on the CF of a fixed irrational) and Zeckendorf — is there a numeration system in which 'n has an ES certificate' is a digit condition?
connection: Automatic-sequence-style question in a non-standard numeration: some sets defined by CF data (e.g. Beatty sequences) are recognisable in Ostrowski numeration (Hieronymi–Terry). ES₅ is a CF condition on a p-tied rational; maybe recognisable in a suitable numeration, making Walnut-style decision procedures applicable to sub-statements.
why: Long shot; but Ostrowski-automatic sets are a modern decidable class that includes CF-defined sets.
first_step: Read Hieronymi–Terry 'Ostrowski numeration systems, addition, and finite automata'; check if 'CF length of r(p) ≤ 3' can be phrased for p in a fixed Ostrowski system.
refs: Hieronymi–Terry, Notre Dame J. Formal Logic 2018

title: Sturmian words / Beatty sequences: the set of x with ⌊4x/p⌋ jumps, and the 'three-gap theorem' as a structure on candidate denominators
connection: The first denominator x in 4/p = 1/x + … must satisfy p/4 < x ≤ 3p/4 (for 3 terms); the candidate set and the remainders (4x − p)/(px) are governed by the Beatty-like sequence ⌊4x/p⌋; the three-gap theorem (Steinhaus) describes gap structures of such sequences — possibly organising the 'which x leaves a two-term remainder' question.
why: Structural organisation of the x-search; cheap.
first_step: For p ≤ 10⁴, mark the x in (p/4, 3p/4] whose remainder is a two-term Egyptian fraction; study the gap distribution between marked x vs three-gap predictions.

title: Collatz analogy: 'stopping time' of a certificate search as a function of p vs Collatz stopping times — both have log-ish expected values with no pointwise proof; what do Collatz researchers' heuristics (Tao's almost-all result via logarithmic density) suggest for ES?
connection: Tao (2019) proved almost all Collatz orbits attain almost bounded values via a 'logarithmic density + invariant measure' argument; ES has almost-all results via sieve. The Collatz pointwise question remains open for the same 'no reservoir' reason. Structural comparison: Collatz has a dynamical system; ES has none (no orbit) — see the orbit-absence lemma. So ES is 'Collatz without the map'.
why: Comparison sharpens what ES lacks (a map) and what it has (algebra: factorisations); a hybrid (define a map on certificates) is the 'Lyapunov function' item.
first_step: Read Tao's Collatz paper intro for the heuristic model and see if the 'Syracuse random variable' method has an ES analogue (random model of the factorisation of 4Cp+1 as C varies — the Kubilius model item).
refs: Tao, 'Almost all orbits of the Collatz map attain almost bounded values' (Forum Math Pi 2022)

title: Crowd computing: a BOINC/Folding-style project to extend ES verification to 10²⁰ AND collect the certificate census (which form fires first) as a public dataset
connection: Verification alone is of limited value, but a *structured* census (per prime: smallest C-form, smallest Type I d, smallest e-slice) at scale creates a dataset for pattern discovery and for testing the exceptional-set rate predictions.
why: Public datasets attract analysts; the compute is embarrassingly parallel.
first_step: Write the census kernel (fast C: trial division of 4Cp+1 for C ≤ 10³) and estimate throughput; publish the 10¹²-range dataset first.

title: Ask on the Lean Zulip (#maths) and Terence Tao's blog whether anyone has tried to formalise ES partial results or has unpublished ES notes
connection: Tao co-authored the key counting paper and writes about Erdős problems; the Zulip community has formalised Egyptian-fraction results (Bloom–Mehta). A short, specific question about the single-integer lower tail (FRONTIER §2) might get a comment from Tao or Bloom.
why: People lever; cheap.
first_step: Post a concise question in Zulip #maths (and as a comment on a relevant blog post) with the exact statement and the C-form exception data.

title: Compression of proofs: measure the description length of the 'certificate table' for all primes ≤ X as a function of X — the best possible 'proof length' of ES restricted to [1, X]
connection: If ES has no uniform proof, the shortest certificate table for primes ≤ X should grow like π(X)·(bits per certificate) with no compression; if a hidden uniform rule exists, compression beats this. Kolmogorov-style; measurable with real compressors on the sorted (p, C_min, a) table.
why: A direct, if crude, test for hidden uniformity, complementary to ML items.
first_step: Produce the table to 10⁷, compress with xz and with a specialised model (arithmetic coder conditioned on p mod 840); compare bits/prime to the entropy of C_min's empirical distribution.

title: Cellular automaton / tag system: encode the greedy-with-backtracking search for 3-term representations as a CA and study its space-time diagram for structure
connection: Rule-based searches sometimes reveal structure via their space-time diagrams (Wolfram's approach); the ES search tree over (x, y) with the two-term test is such a rule system.
why: Recreational/experimental; cheap; near-zero prior of a breakthrough but a possible visual hint.
first_step: Implement and plot for p ≤ 500; stop if nothing visible.
refs: Wolfram, A New Kind of Science

title: Finite differences in C: Δ_C of the indicator win(p, C) — is the sequence C ↦ win(p, C) 'eventually periodic' or 'quasi-periodic' for fixed p?
connection: For fixed p the C-form win indicator depends on the factorisation of the linear sequence 4Cp+1 — a shifted-prime-factor structure with no periodicity but with 'almost periodicity' in the Besicovitch sense (periodic in C mod q for each small prime q's contribution).
why: If win(p, ·) is Besicovitch almost periodic with a positive mean for every p, then infinitely many C win — pointwise ES with infinitude; the mean's positivity is the question, again — but almost-periodicity theory (Wintner, Schwarz–Spilker) gives a *formula* for the mean as a sum over 'Ramanujan expansions', which might be analysable.
first_step: Compute the Ramanujan–Fourier coefficients of win(p, C) over C ≤ 10⁵ for a few p; check whether the mean (the C-density of winning C) is approximated by the first few terms and is bounded away from 0 across p.

title: Density of winning C for fixed p: is lim inf_X (1/X)#{C ≤ X : win(p, C)} > 0, and is it a continuous function of p's local data?
connection: The expected win probability per C is ≈ τ(4Cp+1)/φ(4C)-ish which → 0 as C grows… so the natural density of winning C is 0; the right normalisation is log density or weights 1/C. Σ_{C ≤ X} win(p, C)/C ≈ c(p) log X? Then c(p) is 'the ES constant of p' and ES(p) ⟺ c(p) > 0 (plus finite checks). Is c(p) an Euler product in p's local data? Compute.
why: Defines a canonical real invariant c(p) whose positivity is ES(p) with infinitely many certificates; if c(p) has an Euler-product formula (plausible: heuristically it is Σ over C-structures of local densities) then ES(p) would follow from the product's positivity — the local factors are explicit and nonzero... the catch is convergence/rigour (this is M_BM at fixed p). Still, measuring c(p) numerically and fitting an Euler product is cheap.
first_step: For 50 primes, compute Σ_{C ≤ 10⁵} win(p, C)/C vs log X; extract c(p); regress log c(p) on Legendre symbols of small primes.

title: Umbral / generating-function identities for the count Σ_C x^C·#{a | 4Cp+1, a ≡ −1 (4C)}: Lambert-series structure
connection: Σ_N τ(N) x^N is a Lambert series; sums restricted to N = 4Cp+1 and a in a class tied to C are 'twisted Lambert series along an AP with varying modulus'. Lambert series have modular transformation properties; perhaps the C-form generating function has a transformation law relating p and 1/p-ish parameters.
why: A transformation law would be a rigid analytic structure (like Zagier's for Σ H(n)q^n). Low-to-medium prior.
first_step: Compute the generating function numerically for small p at |x| < 1 and test for simple transformation behaviour under x → e^{−2πt} ↦ t → 1/(p t)-type substitutions.

title: Wythoff/Fibonacci game lens: the pair (a, b) with ab = 4Cp+1, a ≡ b ≡ −1 mod 4C satisfies (a+1)(b+1) = 4C(p + u + v)…: write the Diophantine system as a lattice-point problem in the (u, v) plane under a hyperbola and count by Dirichlet's hyperbola method
connection: p = 4Cuv − u − v ⟺ (4Cu − 1)(4Cv − 1) = 4Cp + 1: for fixed C, solutions (u, v) are lattice points on a hyperbola; summing over C ≤ X, the total count is a 'hyperbola-method' sum Σ_C #{(u,v)}; Dirichlet's method gives main terms with error terms — standard for Σ_{C} τ(4Cp+1) — but here the hyperbola is in (u, v) with the constraint built in. Just the Type II count in the (u,v) coordinates: Σ_{C ≤ X} #{u ≤ v : (4Cu − 1) | 4Cp+1}.
why: A clean reparametrisation: the C-form ⟺ ∃ u ≥ 1: p + u has a divisor ≡ −1 (mod 4u). This is the same shape (tied modulus) but with the *additive* shift p + u instead of the multiplicative 4Cp + 1 — i.e., the e-slice form with e = u (N = (p + e)/4-ish). It makes the role of u symmetric with v and shows the C-form is a statement about the divisors of p + 1, p + 2, p + 3, … in classes −1 mod 4, 8, 12, …: 'the shifted primes p + u, u = 1, 2, 3, …, cannot ALL avoid divisors ≡ −1 mod 4u'. Verify and record; this is probably the repo's e-slice form in disguise (seen).
first_step: Verify algebraically and numerically: C-form certificate ⟺ ∃u: (p + u) has a divisor a ≡ −1 (mod 4u) [with the cofactor condition automatically satisfied?]. Then for p = 409: p + u for u ≤ 60000 never has a divisor ≡ −1 mod 4u?! Check directly — this gives a very concrete statement about 409: '410, 411, 412, … have no divisor ≡ −1 mod 4, 8, 12, …' — e.g. 410 = 2·5·41: divisors ≡ 3 mod 4: none (5, 41 ≡ 1; 2·5 = 10 ≡ 2; …) ✓; 411 = 3·137: need ≡ 7 mod 8: 3, 137 ≡ 1, 411 ≡ 3 — none ✓; 412 = 4·103: need ≡ 11 mod 12: 103 ≡ 7, 206 ≡ 2, 412 ≡ 4 — none ✓ … So 409 is a prime such that p + u never has a divisor ≡ −1 mod 4u. A beautiful concrete puzzle.

title: The C-form as a statement about shifted primes: ES(p) ⟸ ∃u ≥ 1 with a divisor of p + u congruent to −1 (mod 4u) — compare with the theory of divisors of shifted primes (Erdős, Hooley's Δ-function, Ford's divisors in intervals)
connection: Given the reparametrisation (previous item), the C-form says: among p + 1, p + 2, …, some p + u has a divisor in the class −1 mod 4u. The divisor structure of shifted primes p + u (for fixed u, varying p) is classical (Erdős: p + 1 has typically log log p factors, the arcsine law holds for its divisors — Hall–Tenenbaum). The new twist: u varies with p fixed — the 'horizontal' direction again; Hooley's Δ-function and Ford's 'divisors in intervals' concern how divisors of a single integer are spread; here we need, for each u, a divisor of p + u near a specific residue class mod 4u — i.e., a divisor a with a ≡ −1 (4u); equivalently (a + 1)/4u ∈ ℤ, so a + 1 is a multiple of 4u while a divides p + u.
why: Reformulation puts ES into the well-developed 'divisors of shifted integers' literature (Hall–Tenenbaum 'Divisors'), with the familiar polylog count: E[#{u ≤ X : p + u has a divisor ≡ −1 (4u)}] ≈ Σ_u τ(p+u)/φ(4u) ≈ log p · log X. The pointwise question is identical but now 'horizontal in u' with additive shifts — the Hardy–Littlewood/Dickson flavour.
first_step: Verify the reparametrisation (bijection between (C, u, v) and (u, a)), then search Hall–Tenenbaum 'Divisors' for any theorem about divisors of n + u in a class depending on u (probably none); formulate the cleanest statement: 'for every non-square n ≥ 2 there is u ≥ 1 and a | n + u with a ≡ −1 (mod 4u)' — FALSE for n = 409 (if the C ≤ 60000 search transfers: u ≤ 60000).
refs: Ford, 'The distribution of integers with a divisor in a given interval' (Ann. Math 2008)

title: Type I in the shifted form: f | p² + 4c²d, f ≡ −p (mod 4cd) — is there an analogous 'p + u has a divisor in a class' statement for Type I (c = 1: f | p² + 4d, f ≡ −p mod 4d)?
connection: By analogy with the C-form reparametrisation, Type I c = 1 should be expressible as 'some pu + 1 (or p·u + something) has a divisor in a class'. From the e-slice form: Type I ↔ N = (pe + 1)/4 — multiplicative shift pe + 1; Type II ↔ N = (p + e)/4 — additive shift. So the two types are 'additive shifts p + e' and 'multiplicative shifts pe + 1' of p, each needing a divisor in a tied class. The C-form (p + u with divisor ≡ −1 mod 4u) is the additive one; Type I c=1 should be: pe + 1 has a divisor ≡ (something) mod 4e... Derive precisely.
why: A symmetric 'additive vs multiplicative shift' picture of the two types is a memorable organising principle, and the exceptions (409 fails additive; 2521 fails multiplicative) become 'a prime for which all additive shifts fail' vs 'all multiplicative shifts fail'. Both one-parameter statements are false for some primes; ES says the two never fail together (empirically).
first_step: Derive the Type I c=1 shifted statement from FRONTIER's e-slice form; verify numerically on 2521 (which e's fail and why); write the symmetric table.

title: Puzzle for people/MO: 'Show that for every prime p ≡ 1 (mod 4) EITHER some p + u has a divisor ≡ −1 (mod 4u) OR some pe + 1 has a divisor in its tied class' — the two-sided one-parameter statement as a self-contained elementary conjecture
connection: If the e-slice equivalence holds exactly (repo claims so), this two-sided statement IS ES for primes — but phrased with two one-parameter families of shifted integers, no x, y, z. The 409/2521 data show each side alone fails.
why: A maximally elementary, 'shifted-integer divisor' phrasing is the best bait for elementary number theorists and for olympiad-style insight; also a crisp statement for the Erdős problems site.
first_step: Pin down the exact tied class for the multiplicative side from the e-slice form; verify equivalence to ES for p ≤ 10⁴ by brute force; post.

title: Information from the literature on 'n + u has a divisor in a residue class mod u-dependent modulus' — search specifically for 'divisors of consecutive integers in prescribed classes' and 'Erdős problem on d | n + k with d ≡ ... mod k'
connection: The shifted reparametrisation suggests searching the Erdős problem corpus (erdosproblems.com has ~1000 problems) for anything about divisors of n + k in classes depending on k.
why: Erdős posed many 'consecutive integers' divisor problems; one may be ES-equivalent or ES-adjacent with known partial results.
first_step: Full-text search erdosproblems.com for 'divisor' + 'consecutive' / 'n+k'; read the hits.

title: Hasse-principle-style 'almost local' obstruction for 409 in the shifted form: is there a modulus M such that for every u the condition 'p + u has a divisor ≡ −1 mod 4u' is blocked by p's residue mod M? (A 'uniform local obstruction' — would contradict the belief that only squares are obstructed)
connection: For a fixed u the condition on p is a union of residue classes mod lcm-ish(4u·a); an obstruction for ALL u from a single residue p mod M would mean the C-form fails on an entire AP of primes — plausibly false (Dirichlet + the almost-all results for the C-form). So 409's failure is not an AP obstruction; is it then 'random' (and the C ≤ 60000 search just unlucky — implausible given the expected count Σ_{C ≤ 60000} τ(4·409C+1)/φ(4C) ≈ 52 wins) or a non-AP structural obstruction (like T1, which is a 'square' obstruction — not an AP either)? Expected 66 wins vs 0 observed strongly indicates an obstruction of a new type (not AP, not square).
why: The expected-count argument (≈ 52 expected certificates for 409 with C ≤ 60000 (computed: Σ τ(4·409·C+1)/φ(4C) = 51.8), zero observed) is the sharpest evidence that 409 is structurally obstructed in the C-form; identifying the obstruction type is a genuinely new piece of ES structure.
first_step: Compute the expected count Σ_{C ≤ 60000} τ(4·409·C + 1)/φ(4C) precisely (it is the natural heuristic) and compare with the 0 observed; then test the natural candidate obstruction: for 409, is the forced QNR condition (a/409) = −1 incompatible with a ≡ −1 (mod 4C) and a | 4·409C + 1 for a reason involving 409 ≡ 9 (mod 16) or 409's Gaussian representation 20² + 3²?

title: Exceptional primes vs the 'u = 1, 2, 3 classical identities': 409 + 1 = 410 = 2·5·41 (all odd factors ≡ 1 mod 4), 411 = 3·137 (3 ≡ 3 mod 8, 137 ≡ 1), 412 = 4·103 … — build the 'residue avoidance table' for p + u, u ≤ 50, for 409 and for a random control
connection: A table showing, for each u, the prime factors of p + u mod 4u and why no subset product is ≡ −1 — the 'forensics' item in the additive form, where it is readable by hand.
why: Hand-readable evidence is the fastest route to a conjecture about the obstruction type.
first_step: Generate the table; look for the pattern (e.g., 'every odd prime factor q of p + u satisfies (q/409) = +1 or q ≡ 1 mod 4u' — a Legendre-symbol coincidence pattern).

title: Hypothesis: 409 is obstructed because every divisor a of p + u with a ≡ −1 (mod 4u) must satisfy (a/p) = −1 AND a ≡ −u^{-1}·... — derive the second forced symbol in the shifted form
connection: In the shifted form a | p + u ⟹ p ≡ −u (mod a) ⟹ (p/a) = (−u/a) = (−1/a)(u/a) = −(u/a) (a ≡ 3 mod 4); also a ≡ −1 (mod 4u) ⟹ (u/a) = +1 by reciprocity (as before for C) ⟹ (p/a) = −1 ⟹ (a/p) = −1. Same forced symbol. Now also consider (u/p): from a | p + u, nothing forces (u/p). Hmm; but the cofactor b = (p+u)/a satisfies... In the C-form, the cofactor was ≡ −1 mod 4C too; in the shifted form the cofactor b = (p + u)/a — its class mod 4u? p + u ≡ ? mod 4u: p ≡ 1 mod 4, so p + u mod 4u is p + u — not controlled. So in the shifted form the cofactor is unconstrained — then the (u, a) ↔ (C, a, b) bijection must impose b ≡ ... let me recheck: from 4Cp + 1 = ab, a = 4Cu − 1: b = (4Cp + 1)/(4Cu − 1); with the claim 'a | p + u': 4Cp + 1 ≡ 0 (mod a) and 4Cu ≡ 1 (mod a) ⟹ 4Cp ≡ −1 ⟹ multiply by u: 4Cu·p ≡ −u ⟹ p ≡ −u (mod a) ✓. Conversely a | p + u with a ≡ −1 (mod 4u): set 4Cu = a + 1 (C = (a+1)/(4u) ∈ ℤ ✓), then 4Cp = (a+1)p/u ≡ ? We need a | 4Cp + 1: 4Cp + 1 = ((a+1)p + u)/u; mod a: (p + u)/u ≡ 0 ✓ (since a | p + u and gcd(a, u) = 1 as a ≡ −1 mod u). So b = (4Cp+1)/a is an integer and b ≡ ? mod 4C: ab = 4Cp + 1 ≡ 1, a ≡ −1 ⟹ b ≡ −1 ✓ automatically. Good: the bijection holds with no extra condition. So the shifted form is exactly right: C-form ⟺ ∃u: (p + u) has a divisor ≡ −1 (mod 4u).
why: Confirms the reparametrisation rigorously (no hidden cofactor condition) and shows the only forced symbol is (a/p) = −1; so 409's obstruction, if structural, is not a second Jacobi symbol of this simple type — it must involve the interplay of a ≡ −1 (4u), a | 409 + u across u.
first_step: Record the proof; then compute for 409 the set of 'near misses': u ≤ 10⁴ and divisors a of 409 + u with a ≡ −1 mod 4u′ for the largest u′ | u-ish — see how close the condition comes to being satisfied.

title: Shifted form for composite n and the T1 reproof: m² + u has a divisor ≡ −1 (mod 4u) is impossible — one-line check via (a/m²) = 1
connection: For n = m²: a | m² + u, a ≡ −1 (mod 4u) ⟹ (a/m²) = 1 but the forced symbol says (a/n) = −1 — contradiction. T1 for the C-form in the shifted language is immediate. For general n the forced symbol is (a/n) = −1 (Jacobi), which for n = 409·k² etc. reduces to (a/409) = −1 — so the shifted-form exceptional set is closed under multiplication by odd squares coprime to… (need also a | n + u to be consistent) — test numerically whether 409·9 is an exception.
why: Closure under square multiples would give an infinite non-square family of C-form exceptions (409m²), making the C-form exceptional set 'squares ∪ square-multiples of sporadic ∪ ?' — a rich structure to compare with the U(n) sporadics {105, 2961, 3985, 25305, 111969, 978145} (are these square multiples of smaller ones? 2961 = 9·329 = 9·7·47; 25305 = 105·241; hmm).
first_step: Compute the C-form exceptional set for n ≤ 10⁵ (all n ≡ 1 mod 4, u ≤ 5000) and test closure under n ↦ nm²; compare to the U(n) list.

title: Heuristic repair: the expected-count heuristic for the C-form must be corrected by the forced QNR condition — only divisors a with (a/p) = −1 count, halving the expectation; and if a second hidden constraint exists it halves again — is 409's zero count explainable by a cascade of such 'free' constraints?
connection: Each forced symbol halves the expected count; the observed 0 for 409 at expected ≈ 52 (or 26 after QNR) would need ~5–6 independent forced constraints. Alternatively, a single structural obstruction. Determine which by finding the forced-symbol set empirically: for all C-form certificates (over many p), tabulate the joint distribution of (a/q) for small q, a mod 16, etc., and see which symbols are forced (always equal) vs free.
why: Systematic discovery of forced constraints on certificates is a well-defined computation and could reveal the complete 'reciprocity signature' of the C-form, of which (a/p) = −1 is the first element.
first_step: Collect ~10⁵ certificates (p ≤ 10⁵, C ≤ 200); for each candidate symbol s(a, p, C) in a list of ~50 (Jacobi symbols, residues mod small powers of 2, Kronecker symbols (a/2), (−1/a), (p/u)...), compute entropy of its distribution; list zero-entropy ones.

title: Mutual exclusion of the two exceptional sets (C-form vs Type I c=1): is there a proof that no prime can be in both? That would be ES for primes via two one-parameter families
connection: Data: {409, 577, 5569, 9601} ∩ {2521} = ∅ below 20000. If 'p fails the additive form' forces a structural property (e.g. a certain Jacobi signature) that is incompatible with 'p fails the multiplicative form', then ES(p) would follow from their disjointness. This is a precise conjecture (stronger than ES) that is testable to large ranges and might be approachable by reciprocity (both failure conditions are reciprocity-flavoured).
why: Turns ES into the disjointness of two explicitly characterised (conjecturally thin) sets — a shape amenable to 'if both fail then (symbol) = +1 and = −1' arguments if the failures have forced signatures.
first_step: Extend both exceptional sets to 10⁶ (cheap in Pari); if still disjoint, look for a forced signature of each failure type (e.g. additive failure ⟹ p ≡ 1 mod 8? multiplicative failure ⟹ p ≡ 1 mod 840?).

title: Meta: hand the C-form/Type I c=1 exceptional-set program to a dedicated lane — it is cheap, concrete, and produces test cases regardless of outcome
connection: The program: (i) census to 10⁶–10⁷ of both one-parameter exceptional sets; (ii) forced-symbol discovery; (iii) obstruction proofs for 409 and 2521; (iv) disjointness conjecture; (v) OEIS + MO publication.
why: Of all items in this lane these have the best ratio of concreteness to novelty; the outcome calibrates the whole 'one-parameter vs two-parameter' question.
first_step: Write a one-page brief for a follow-up lane with the five steps and the scripts to start from.

title: Bloom–(shifted primes) unit fractions as a test of 'prescribed-denominator-shape' methods
connection: Bloom's 'Unit fractions with shifted prime denominators' (arXiv:2305.02689) represents 1 with denominators p−1 ↔ ES denominators are constrained to be multiples of p or p-tied.
why: A method that works with arithmetically constrained denominators is closer to ES's constraint than free-denominator results.
first_step: Read 2305.02689 abstract/intro and list which constraint (shifted primes) survived the Fourier argument and why; ask if 'denominators ≡ 0 mod p' is analogous.

title: Sierpiński 5/n and Schinzel m/n as a family: uniform-in-m translation
connection: The m/n = 1/x+1/y+1/z conjectures (Schinzel: for n ≥ n₀(m)) share U_n's geometry with 4 replaced by m. T1-type obstructions should exist at m-dependent square classes.
why: A translation that works for all m simultaneously (e.g. a fibration over m) might reveal which part of ES is specific to 4.
first_step: Compute the analogue of T1 for m = 5, 6, 7 (which square classes kill the standard certificate lines) and compare with the known hard classes for Sierpiński's 5/n.
alt_first_steps: [free_opus-0004] Tabulate, for m = 4..12, the per-residue-class solution counts at primes ≤ 10⁶ and locate the m where the minimum count first hits 0.
alt_titles: [free_opus-0004] Sierpiński 5/n and Schinzel m/n conjectures as a uniform family

title: Mordell's identities ↔ Rosati/Yamamoto/Aigner tables as an early 'covering system' history
connection: Mordell's mod-840 reduction and later moduli (Yamamoto, Salez's modular filters) form an increasing covering chain ↔ covering-system theory (Erdős, Hough's minimum modulus theorem).
why: Hough proved covering systems with distinct moduli have bounded minimum modulus; ES coverings are of a different type (non-distinct, polynomial classes), and stating precisely why Hough's method doesn't apply is cheap.
first_step: Write the ES modular filters as a 'polynomial covering' and check whether Hough/Balister–Bollobás–Morris–Sahasrabudhe–Tiba distortion method covers polynomial-residue coverings.
refs: R. Hough, Ann. of Math. 181 (2015) — check citation

title: Erdős–Graham book 'Old and new problems' chapter on unit fractions as a map of solved/unsolved
connection: Erdős–Graham (1980) list dozens of unit-fraction problems; several since solved (Croot, Bloom, Martin) ↔ ES.
why: Each solved neighbour gives a method; an indexed table 'problem → method → why it fails for ES' extends the z52 dossier cheaply.
first_step: Pull every unit-fraction problem from erdosproblems.com with status 'proved' and record the key method in one line each.

title: Martin's dense Egyptian fractions and the 'many representations' regime
connection: Greg Martin showed every rational has Egyptian representations with denominators of positive density in [1,N]-ish ranges ↔ ES wants sparse (3-term) ones.
why: The interpolation between dense and 3-term representations (k-term for k slowly growing) is a ladder whose rungs could be climbed down one at a time.
first_step: Check whether 'every 4/p is a sum of k unit fractions with denominators ≤ p^A' is known for k = 4 with explicit A (yes trivially?) and find the least k proved with denominators ≤ C·p.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Four unit fractions are easy: why 4/p = four terms is trivial and what the 4→3 step loses
connection: 4/p = 1/x1+…+1/x4 always solvable (e.g. via greedy) ↔ ES 3 terms; the 4-term solution set is a 'thick object' and ES asks it to degenerate.
why: A collapse map from 4-term to 3-term solutions (merging two fractions with sum a unit fraction) is an extraction rule in the G1 sense.
first_step: Count 4-term solutions with two terms summing to a unit fraction; check whether that count is ≍ the 3-term count or larger (identity check).
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Tao's 2011 blog post comment thread as a mine of unexplored ideas
connection: Tao's blog post on the Elsholtz–Tao paper drew comments with heuristic and computational ideas ↔ campaign may not have harvested all.
why: Cheap source of community-generated angles that were never followed up.
first_step: Read the comments on terrytao.wordpress.com 2011/07 'On the number of solutions to 4/p = …' and extract each distinct idea into this list.

title: Webb's density theorem and Li Delang's improvement as historical sieve calibration
connection: Webb (1970) and Li (1981) bounded the exceptional set with large sieve ↔ campaign's exp(−c(log N)^{3/4}) bound.
why: Comparing exponents across history shows the speed of sieve improvement; extrapolating suggests whether 'exceptional set finite' is near any sieve horizon.
first_step: Tabulate historical exceptional-set bounds (Webb, Vaughan, Li, campaign) with year and method in a 6-row table.

title: Sylvester's sequence and the extremal 1 = Σ1/x_i problem as a dual
connection: Sylvester's sequence gives extremal denominators in Σ1/x_i = 1 ↔ ES's largest denominator is bounded by p²·(…); extremal structure constrains solution shape.
why: Bounding the largest denominator in any ES solution (Curtiss/Soundararajan-type bounds) restricts the search space and may give a finite-check argument shape.
first_step: Compute max(z)/p² over all ES solutions for primes ≤ 10⁵ and compare to Curtiss-type extremal bounds.

title: Erdős–Straus over number fields (Gaussian, Eisenstein) with sign/positivity conditions
connection: Generalise ES to totally positive elements in totally real fields ↔ ℤ[√2], ℚ(√5).
why: In ℚ(√5) the unit group is infinite and positive; the existence of units might act as a thick reservoir that ℤ lacks, giving a proved sibling.
first_step: Brute-force 4/π = sum of three totally positive unit-reciprocals for small totally positive primes π of ℤ[(1+√5)/2]; check for failures.
alt_first_steps: [signature-0052] Compute, for K = ℚ(√2), totally positive prime elements π of norm ≤ 10⁴ and search for 4/π = Σ 1/x_i with x_i ≫ 0; look for failures.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings
alt_titles: [signature-0052] ES over totally real fields with totally positive denominators (e.g. ℤ[√2])

title: Elsholtz's k-term results: sums of k unit fractions with k ≥ 4 and m/n

title: Swett / Mihnea–Dumitru verification algorithms as history of computational ES
connection: Verification to 10^17 (Salez) and 10^18 (Mihnea–Dumitru preprint) uses modular sieving ↔ structural information embedded in which filters remove which primes.

title: Rav, Schinzel–Sierpiński polynomial identities (no identity for square classes) as a Galois-theoretic obstruction
connection: Mordell–Schinzel: no polynomial identity solves ES on a residue class containing squares ↔ Galois/monodromy of the solution variety over ℚ(n).

title: Ellipsoid-type 'every integer is a sum of three cubes?' (Booker–Sutherland) as a computation-driven sibling

title: Hensel-lifting history: 'every n locally' proof as a template audit
connection: Local solubility of ES at every prime is easy ↔ global fails only by non-BM obstruction; history of local-global for cubic surfaces (Swinnerton-Dyer, Colliot-Thélène) applies to rational not integral points.

connection: Tiling a rectangle by rectangles of sides 1/a×1/b relates to Egyptian decompositions ↔ ES as a 3-piece tiling of a 4×p-ish rectangle.

connection: The Cayley cubic's Cox ring is known explicitly (Derenthal et al. list Cox rings of singular del Pezzo surfaces) ↔ ES fibre is a hyperplane section x3 = const·n.

connection: BL show BM does not explain all failures of strong approximation for U_n ↔ étale-Brauer or descent obstruction might.

connection: U_n's boundary consists of lines/conics; π₁ of complement gives covers ↔ Type I/II divisibility conditions may be torsor conditions under μ_k.

title: Fibration method (Colliot-Thélène–Harpaz–Wittenberg) for integral points on families over A¹_n
connection: The total space {4xyz = n(xy+yz+zx)} ⊂ A⁴ fibred over n ↔ fibration method proves Hasse principle for 'almost all fibres' under Schinzel's hypothesis.

title: Elliptic fibrations of the ES surface: for fixed x, (y,z) lie on a conic; for fixed ratio, on an elliptic curve?
connection: Slicing U_n by x = const gives a hyperbola (binary divisor problem); slicing by y/z = const gives curves of genus ? ↔ elliptic fibration may give rank-based infinitude.
why: If some pencil of curves on U_n has genus-1 fibres with positive rank uniformly, integral points might be forced via descent heights.

connection: NS lattice of a minimal resolution ↔ integral points via intersection pairing constraints.

title: Arithmetic of the singular points: the Cayley cubic's four A1 nodes and local data at n
connection: Integral points near nodes correspond to small denominators ↔ local conditions at nodes might be where p's arithmetic enters.
