title: Reduction mod p of the ES surface at n = p: counting F_p-points with constraints
connection: U_p mod p degenerates (n ≡ 0) ↔ solutions for 4/p have p | some denominator; the mod-p geometry of the degenerate fibre controls Type I/II.
why: The degenerate fibre xyz = 0 mod p structure is exactly Type I vs Type II split; higher p-adic structure might give Hensel-type existence.
first_step: Write the p-adic Newton polygon / blow-up of U_n at n = 0 and see whether ES(p) is a statement about ℤ_p-points of a model plus a global condition.

title: Hecke eigenvalues at p as a certificate source (trace formula identity)
connection: R(p) = trace of some Hecke-like operator? If R(p) = Σ over a set of a_f(p) with f in a fixed space, Deligne's bound would control it.
why: A finite-dimensional space would give R(p) = main + O(p^{1/2-ish}·dim) error — but main is log², so need dim growth; still worth seeing if R(p) has any modular generating function.

title: Theta series of the ES 'certificate lattice' and its Eisenstein/cusp split
connection: Repo has theta quotients ↔ Siegel–Weil: the Eisenstein part is the genus average; the cusp part is the fluctuation.
why: For ternary forms the cusp part at prime index is bounded by Duke's subconvexity; for ES-type objects identifying the 'weight' and 'level' tells whether subconvexity could ever beat the main term.
first_step: Write R(p) as Fourier coefficient of a (possibly mock / indefinite) theta series; identify weight and level growth.

title: Mock modular / indefinite theta (Zwegers) for the two-sign hyperbola count
connection: Counts of lattice points in hyperbolic regions with sign conditions are coefficients of indefinite theta series. Zwegers completes these to non-holomorphic modular objects. ES₅ counts points on XY = tp+1 in a cone with a character.
why: Indefinite theta series are the natural home of 'divisor counts with sign' (e.g. Hecke's indefinite theta, Andrews–Dyson–Hickerson). Size log²n is consistent with mock objects of weight 1 (σ₀-type).
first_step: Write Σ_n N₋(n) qⁿ as an indefinite theta series of signature (1,1) or (2,2) with a character; check the Zwegers/Vignéras convergence conditions.

title: Appell–Lerch sums: Σ_{u,B≥1} q^{4CuB−u−B} as a Lambert-type series
connection: Σ_{u,B≥1} q^{auB−u−B} = Σ_u q^{−u} q^{(au−1)}/(1−q^{au−1}) is a Lambert/Appell–Lerch series ↔ R(p) is the q^p coefficient of Σ_C of these.
why: Lambert series coefficients are divisor sums; Appell–Lerch sums have modular completions which yield exact formulas for coefficients in some cases.
first_step: Compute the series F(q) = Σ_{C≥1} Σ_{u≥1} q^{4Cu−u−1}/(1−q^{4Cu−1})-type expansion and check against R(n) to 10⁴.

title: Rademacher-type exact formula for a mock modular generating function of R(n)
connection: If Σ R(n) q^n (or a twist) were mock modular, Bringmann–Ono-style exact formulas give coefficients as convergent Kloosterman–Bessel series.
why: Exact formulas with positive main term and explicitly bounded tails are how partition-function positivity facts are proved pointwise.
first_step: Check growth: R(n) is polylog, inconsistent with the exponential growth of weight-<0 mock forms; so look for weight-1 or weight-0 objects (logarithmic growth plausible for weight 1 Eisenstein-like). Test whether n ↦ M₀(n) matches a weight-1 Eisenstein coefficient shape.

title: Weight-1 forms and Kronecker characters: M_BM as a sum of class numbers
connection: M_BM(p) = Σ (1 − χ_{−4uB}(p))/φ(4uB) is an average of characters ↔ L(1,χ) and class numbers of ℚ(√−uB·p)?
why: Swapping sum order may give M_BM(p) as a weighted sum of L-values attached to p; class-number lower bounds (Siegel, Goldfeld) are pointwise.
first_step: Rewrite T(p) = Σ (−uB/p)/φ(4uB) by grouping by m = uB: Σ_m (−m/p)·g(m) with g(m) = #{splittings}/φ(4m); compare with L(1, (−·/p))-weighted sums.

title: Goldfeld–Gross–Zagier effective class numbers as a pointwise lower-bound precedent
connection: GGZ gave an effective lower bound h(−D) ≫ log D via an elliptic curve of rank 3 ↔ ES needs a pointwise polylog lower bound.
why: One of the very few pointwise lower bounds of logarithmic size in number theory; obtained via an auxiliary L-function with high-order zero. Could ES's count be forced positive by an auxiliary object with forced vanishing?
first_step: Write the abstract structure: positivity of a quantity via an auxiliary L-function's central vanishing; ask what L-function would encode R(p).

title: Class number of ℚ(√−p) and ES: correlation test
connection: h(−4p) controls representations of p by binary forms of discriminant −4p ↔ ES solutions involve binary forms 4uB·…
why: If R(p) correlates with h(−4p) or h(4p)·log ε_p, a class-number formula identity might lurk.

title: Real quadratic fields ℚ(√p): fundamental unit, continued fraction of √p and ES
connection: ES₅ uses continued-fraction length ≤ 3 of something tied to p ↔ the CF of √p (period, palindromes) encodes ℚ(√p) arithmetic.
why: If certificate CFs relate to the CF expansion of √p or (√p+1)/2, the infinite unit group could be a thick reservoir.

title: Tropicalisation of the ES equation and valuations at p
connection: Tropical variety of 4xyz = n(xy+yz+zx) under p-adic valuation ↔ which valuation patterns (v_p(x),v_p(y),v_p(z)) are allowed (Type I/II).
why: Tropical geometry classifies degenerations; may reveal hidden Type III-ish patterns for composite n and their absence for primes.

title: Toric degenerations and Ehrhart counting of ES solutions in boxes
connection: Counting lattice points in polytopes defined by Type II inequalities ↔ Ehrhart quasi-polynomials.
why: The (★) count over a cut-off region is a lattice-point count in a hyperbolic region; Ehrhart theory with dilation p might give exact periodic formulas for partial counts.

title: Additive combinatorics: sum-product phenomena in (ℤ/p)^× and ES Type I
connection: Type I: f | p²+4c²d, f ≡ −p mod 4cd ↔ product sets {ab⁻¹ : ab | N} hitting −1 mod e.
why: Sum-product/Bourgain–Glibichuk–Konyagin: product sets of moderate size in (ℤ/q)^× cover everything; e-slice form needs the divisor-ratio set mod e to contain −1.

title: Olson's theorem / Erdős–Ginzburg–Ziv for products of divisors

title: Lattice-point counting in −Γ₁(c) with fixed upper-right entry p (Kloosterman/Kuznetsov for Γ₁(c))

title: Thue's lemma / pigeonhole for x ≡ ay mod p with small x, y and ES
connection: Thue: for any a there exist |x|,|y| ≤ √p with x ≡ ay (mod p) ↔ ES Type II pair form p ≡ −(u+B) mod 4uB.

connection: Representations of 4p or p by norm forms of real quadratic fields always exist when the class group is trivial ↔ ES certificates as norms.

title: Class field theory: ES(p) ⇐ p splits completely in some field K_p of bounded degree?
connection: If ES(p) held whenever p splits in a fixed field K, Chebotarev would give density; ES needs every p, so need a family of fields covering all splitting types.

title: Non-congruence classes: polynomial identities valid on Chebotarev classes of non-abelian fields (e.g. 2 a quartic residue)
connection: Mordell–Schinzel rule out polynomial identities on square classes (congruence classes). Classes like 'p = x² + 64y²' (2 is a quartic residue) are Chebotarev classes of non-abelian fields and are not unions of congruence classes, so identities with p-dependent algebraic parameters (e.g. involving x, y with p = x² + 64y²) could cover them.
why: The repo has NONCONG_LIFTS. Native class-field-theory classes give an infinite supply of new 'families' whose parameters are norms (x,y), sidestepping the congruence-class formulation of B1.
first_step: Search for ES identities in parameters (x, y) with p = x² + y² (or x² + 64y²) of bounded degree, e.g. x = f(a,b) with p = a² + b², by polynomial ansatz + solve; test coverage of the hard class.

connection: If R(p) = trace of Frobenius on some motive (minus main term), Weil bounds give pointwise control ↔ but R(p) is integral-point count, not F_p count.

title: Siegel's lemma with congruence conditions: a small solution of a linear system tied to p
connection: Siegel's lemma guarantees small integer solutions of underdetermined linear systems ↔ ES Type II linear in C for fixed (u,B).
why: For fixed u, the condition (4uC−1) | p+u is linear in a hidden quotient: p + u = k(4uC − 1); i.e. p = 4uCk − u − k: symmetric bilinear in (C,k)! Siegel can't force bilinear, but the structure is a 'multiplicative Siegel lemma'.

connection: Statistical mechanics: count of certificates = zero-temperature limit of a partition function over the trial set 𝓡 with energy = 'distance from divisibility' ↔ R(p).
why: Smooth relaxations (finite β) are analytically tractable (sums of exponentials of residues) and could be bounded below; the question is whether a β-interpolation lower bound survives β → ∞.

connection: Random multiplicative function models (Harper) ↔ T(p) with Legendre symbol replaced by Steinhaus/Rademacher multiplicative f.
why: Harper's 'better than square-root cancellation' for random multiplicative sums suggests T(p) behaves better than worst case; quantifies M_BM lower bound tightness.
first_step: Simulate T_f = Σ f(u)f(B)·(−1-twist)/φ(4uB) for random multiplicative f and compare distribution to empirical T(p).

title: Brownian / random-walk model for the greedy remainder chain
connection: Successive remainders in Egyptian expansions as a Markov chain ↔ probability the chain hits numerator 1 at step 2.
why: Gives a heuristic per-p probability that simple algorithms succeed; separates algorithmic from existential difficulty.
first_step: Simulate the 'first-term then remainder' chain over all first terms x ∈ [p/4, 3p/4] and record the success probability distribution per p.

title: Entropy/information-theoretic view: bits of p needed to specify a certificate
connection: A certificate (u,B,C) has ~3 log log p bits beyond p ↔ information about p revealed by existence of a certificate.
why: If certificate existence for p were 'hard information', compression arguments (Kolmogorov) could say something; at least clarifies that certificates are tiny relative to p.
first_step: Compute the empirical entropy of the minimal certificate (u,C) distribution conditioned on p mod small moduli; does p mod 840·k predict it?

title: Kolmogorov complexity argument: a counterexample p would be 'simple'?
connection: Incompressibility method: if every p ≤ X of high complexity has a certificate, counterexamples must be low-complexity ↔ disproof search direction.
why: Adversarial searches already target structured p; formalising 'low complexity' (short description) to prioritise searches is a meta improvement.
first_step: Rank candidate primes by description length (e.g. p = a·b^k + c with small a,b,c) and search ES hardness there first.

title: Ergodic theory of multiplicative semigroups: Furstenberg ×2×3 and certificates as orbit points
connection: Furstenberg's ×2×3 rigidity ↔ the multiplicative semigroup of divisors of p-tied integers acting on (ℤ/4C)^×.
why: Rigidity theorems give pointwise density of orbits (every infinite ×2×3-invariant closed set is everything); a finite analogue (Bourgain–Lindenstrauss–Michel–Venkatesh effective) gives 'orbits of 2,3 in (ℤ/q)^× are dense'.
first_step: Check BLMV/Bourgain effective ×a×b results: does {2^i 3^j mod q} hit −1 for all q with small exponents? Then ask if 4Cp+1-divisors contain a fixed multiplicative structure.

title: Mixing of the map p ↦ (p mod 4uC−1) as u,C vary: equidistribution of residues of a single integer
connection: Residues of a fixed p modulo a growing family of moduli ↔ ES needs p ≡ −u mod (4uC−1) for some pair; this is 'one integer vs many moduli' — Erdős–Turán type discrepancy.
why: Discrepancy of {p/m} for m in a structured set is a classic (Vinogradov-type) problem; known results (e.g. on p mod m for m ≤ √p) might give existence in some ranges.
first_step: Measure discrepancy of fractional parts {(p+u)/(4uC−1)} over the trial set and compare with random; the ES event is the fractional part being exactly 0.

title: Billiards / circle rotation: p mod m for consecutive m as a rotation-like sequence
connection: p mod m for m near √p behaves like a quadratic sequence (Dirichlet divisor problem) ↔ ES divisibility events are zeros of p mod (4uC − 1).
why: Near m ≈ √p, p mod m follows parabolic arcs; divisors appear at structured places. Could the ES moduli family hit such arcs?
first_step: Plot (m, (p+u) mod m) for moduli m = 4uC−1 near √p and look for parabolic patterns permitting a forced zero.

title: Quantum unique ergodicity analogy: certificates as 'mass' of a p-dependent state
connection: QUE for Hecke eigenforms gives pointwise equidistribution in the eigenvalue aspect ↔ ES certificate counts as 'mass in a small set'.
why: QUE is pointwise in the spectral parameter (Lindenstrauss, Soundararajan); a QUE-type statement for a p-indexed family would give pointwise counts, but the target set must be fixed-size.
first_step: Find whether R(p)/M(p) can be written as ⟨φ_p, 1_A φ_p⟩ for some natural p-family of states φ_p and fixed set A.

title: Thermodynamic formalism for Egyptian fraction expansions (Engel/Sylvester series dynamics)
connection: Engel expansions and Sylvester series have ergodic theory (Rényi) ↔ 3-term Egyptian representations as short orbits.
why: Known metric theory of Engel/Sylvester digits could supply heuristic densities for 'expansions of length 3'.
first_step: Compute the Engel/Sylvester (greedy) expansion of 4/p and its length distribution over primes; correlate with ES difficulty.

title: Phase transition in random Egyptian-fraction CSPs (k-term with bounded denominators)
connection: Random CSP satisfiability thresholds ↔ ES as satisfiability of a sparse constraint system indexed by p.
why: If ES-like random instances undergo a sharp transition at 'expected solutions ≈ 1', ES sits at expected ≈ log² p — deep in the satisfiable phase; how deep quantifies safety margin.
first_step: Define random analogues: replace p by random integers in a residue class and compute the fraction with zero solutions as function of bound on denominators.

title: Extreme value theory for max over p ≤ X of (minimal certificate size)
connection: Gumbel/Fréchet laws for maxima of iid ↔ max_p min-certificate as function of X.
why: If the max grows like (log X)^a with EVT-consistent fluctuations, extrapolate beyond 10¹⁸; deviations flag structure.
first_step: From repo census data, extract record-setting primes for 'least u in I3 word' and fit EVT growth.

title: Records sequence of hardest primes as an OEIS-style object
connection: Sequence of primes p where min certificate size exceeds all previous ↔ OEIS has such records for ES? (check).
why: Records concentrate structure (adversarial primes); their pattern (residues, factorisations of p±small) suggests failure mechanisms.
first_step: Search OEIS for 'Erdos-Straus' sequences; compute records for 'smallest x in 4/p = 1/x+…' and submit/compare.

title: Fokker–Planck / diffusion model of log R(p) along p
connection: log R(p) as a stochastic process in p ↔ smooth main term plus noise.
why: Autocorrelation of R across nearby primes (p, p+840k) shows whether difficulty is local in residue or random.
first_step: Compute autocorrelation of R(p)/M(p) between primes in the same class mod 840 with lag k.

title: Maximum entropy model for certificate distribution given residue constraints
connection: MaxEnt with constraints p mod q for q ≤ Q ↔ best prediction of R(p) from local data.
why: The gap between MaxEnt prediction and actual R(p) is the 'global' part; if it's small, ES difficulty is local-plus-noise.
first_step: Fit log R(p) ~ Σ_q β_q·1[p ≡ a mod q] by regularised regression and report R² vs Q.

title: Boltzmann sampling of certificates for very large p (10^100)
connection: Analytic combinatorics Boltzmann samplers ↔ draw random (u,C) weighted by 1/(4uC−1) and test divisibility.
why: Monte Carlo estimates of R(p) at astronomical p (where full enumeration is impossible) test whether the main term persists; finds adversarial p faster.
first_step: Implement weighted sampling over (u,C) for p ~ 10^50 random primes ≡ 1 mod 840 and estimate hits per 10⁹ samples vs M(p) prediction.

title: Harmonic-mean interpretation: p/4·3 is the harmonic mean of x,y,z
connection: 4/p = 1/x+1/y+1/z ⟺ harmonic mean H(x,y,z) = 3p/4 ↔ means inequalities (H ≤ G ≤ A) give box constraints.
why: Box constraints from mean inequalities are already used; the 'harmonic mean of three integers equals 3p/4' phrasing might connect to integer means literature.
first_step: Search 'integers with prescribed harmonic mean' literature for existence theorems.

title: Crystallography / Bravais lattices: 1/x+1/y+1/z as Miller-index relation
connection: Miller-index plane equations x/a + y/b + z/c = 1 ↔ the plane through (x,0,0),(0,y,0),(0,0,z) contains the point (p/4,p/4,p/4) ⟺ 1/x+1/y+1/z = 4/p.
why: Geometric reformulation: ES(p) ⟺ some lattice plane with positive integer axis intercepts passes through (p/4)(1,1,1). Lattice-plane counting (geometry of numbers) might apply.
first_step: Use this: count lattice planes through q = (p/4)(1,1,1) with integer intercepts; relate to primitive vectors (1/x,1/y,1/z) scaled — check if this is a known equivalence to ET.

title: Intercept form: ES as a plane through the diagonal point — projective dual
connection: Dual: points (1/x,1/y,1/z) of the plane X+Y+Z = 4/p with unit-fraction coordinates ↔ rational points on a plane with all coordinates reciprocals of integers.
why: Duality may bring Schmidt subspace theorem-type tools (points of small height on planes with coordinates of special form).
first_step: Record the dual formulation and check whether Schmidt-subspace-type results bound the number of solutions in a way that conflicts with zero (no: they give upper bounds) — note as calibration.

title: Mechanical analogy: springs in series (compliance adds) and integer stiffness
connection: Springs in series: 1/k = Σ 1/k_i ↔ same algebra as resistors; equivalent reformulation.
why: Duplicate of resistor item in algebra but different community (mechanics puzzles); keep as outreach variant.
first_step: Combine with resistor outreach note (no separate work).

title: Kinetic theory of the 'trial division' process: occupancy problem
connection: Balls-in-bins: each trial modulus m 'catches' p if p ≡ r_m mod m ↔ ES is non-empty-catch.
why: Occupancy problems with heterogeneous bin probabilities have sharp zero-probability estimates (Poisson clumping heuristic, Aldous).
first_step: Apply Aldous' Poisson clumping heuristic to ES with clumps = shared-factor moduli; compute adjusted zero probability.

title: Chen–Stein Poisson approximation for the ES certificate count
connection: Stein's method bounds total-variation distance of a count to Poisson; if R(p) were approximately Poisson(μ) with μ ≍ log²p, P(R=0) ≈ e^{−μ}.
why: Gives a quantitative heuristic and identifies which dependencies (shared prime factors) break Poisson behaviour.
first_step: Compute the Arratia–Goldstein–Gordon b1,b2,b3 terms for the ES certificate events at p ≤ 10^6 on data.

title: Second moment method over primes in short intervals: positive proportion with R(p) ≥ 1 in every interval
connection: Paley–Zygmund on R over primes in [X, X+H] ↔ ES almost-all in short intervals.
why: Repo has interval results; second moment at H = (log X)^A would be a new 'every short interval contains many ES primes' result (weak but new form).
first_step: Check repo's (D)30 interval result range of H; compute what second moment would need for H = (log X)^A.

title: Dynamics on the space of lattices: ES certificates as cusp excursions of a p-indexed orbit
connection: Orbits of diagonal flows on SL₃(ℝ)/SL₃(ℤ) visiting the cusp correspond to small vectors ↔ ES certificates are small vectors in p-dependent lattices.
why: Cusp excursions are governed by Diophantine properties; Littlewood-type pointwise statements are hard but some (Einsiedler–Katok–Lindenstrauss) give measure results.
first_step: Write a 3D lattice Λ_p such that a vector in a specified small cone ⟹ certificate; examine whether the a-orbit of Λ_p is known to enter the cusp region.

title: Littlewood conjecture analogy: inf n‖nα‖‖nβ‖ = 0 vs ES certificates as simultaneous small values
connection: Both ask for simultaneous small values of products of distances ↔ ES Type II p ≡ −(u+B) mod 4uB is a multiplicative Diophantine approximation condition.
why: Littlewood is open too, with measure-zero exceptional set (EKL) — a parallel of 'almost all' ES results; methods might transfer in either direction.
first_step: Write ES Type II as a product-of-distances condition and compare its structure with Littlewood's.

title: Bohr sets / Bohr neighbourhoods of p: certificates as elements of a Bohr set
connection: Bohr set B(Γ,ε) = {x : ‖γx‖ < ε} ↔ ES certificates require p/m near −u/m exactly (ε = 0).
why: Additive-combinatorics machinery on Bohr sets gives structure for 'approximate' ES; exact would need ε < 1/m.
first_step: Compute, per p, the approximate certificate count with tolerance ε = k/m for k ≤ K and check if exact count ≈ approximate/(2K+1).

title: Annealed vs quenched averages for certificate counts
connection: Disordered systems: quenched average E[log Z] vs annealed log E[Z] ↔ log R(p) average vs log of average.
why: A large gap indicates rare-event dominance (some p with huge counts, e.g. via Linnik), which affects lower-tail heuristics.
first_step: Compute E[log(1+R(p))] vs log E[R(p)] over primes in dyadic ranges up to 10⁸.

title: Zeta-function regularisation of Σ_{u,C} 1/(4uC−1) as continuum main term
connection: Main term M₀ ~ (3/(2π²)) log² p from Σ 1/φ(4uB) ↔ Epstein-type zeta functions; regularised values give constant terms.
why: Exact secondary terms (log p and constant) sharpen the empirical comparison and the zero-probability model.
first_step: Derive the full asymptotic M₀(p) = a log²p + b log p + c + o(1) via Mellin transform; check against computed values.

title: Chaotic dynamics: the 'Egyptian map' T(a/b) = a/b − 1/⌈b/a⌉ and its periodic structure mod p
connection: Iterating the greedy step on all a/p, a ∈ (ℤ/p)^× defines a map on residues ↔ ES asks about orbits of length ≤ 3 from a = 4 through rescaled fractions.
why: Graph structure of this map on F_p (functional graph) could have computable statistics (tree sizes) related to ES.
first_step: Build the functional graph of the greedy-remainder map on fractions with denominator dividing p·k for small k; compute statistics.

title: Hydrodynamic limit of certificate count as p → ∞ along residue classes
connection: Limit shape of the set of successful (log u/log p, log C/log p) ↔ the main-term density.
why: A limit shape theorem (empirical measure of certificates converges) for almost all p is plausibly provable and would describe where certificates live.
first_step: Plot the empirical measure of (log u, log C)/log p for successful pairs over many p; compare with 1/(uC) density prediction.

title: Benjamini–Schramm / local limit of the 'divisor graph' around p
connection: Local weak limits of graphs ↔ the neighbourhood structure of p in the ES certificate graph.
why: Too abstract unless a concrete graph emerges; keep as curiosity.
first_step: Define graph: vertices = primes ≤ X, edge p~q if they share a certificate modulus; compute degree distribution.

title: Quantum algorithm: Grover search for certificates and complexity of certification
connection: Grover gives √ speedup for unstructured search ↔ ES certificate search space ~ p log p trials, polylog winners.
why: Not a proof route; clarifies computational complexity of finding a certificate (classical best ~ ?).
first_step: Determine the best classical algorithm complexity for finding one ES solution for a given p (repo/verification code) and record whether it's polylog-time heuristically.

title: Shor-type period finding: ES certificate as a hidden-subgroup instance?
connection: HSP over (ℤ/N)^× ↔ ES gate: subgroup generated by divisor classes containing −1.
why: Curiosity mapping; might reveal that certificate-finding reduces to factoring 4Cp+1 (which it does) — so ES search ∈ BQP-easy given factoring.
first_step: Write explicit reduction: ES(p) certificate search ≤ factoring of numbers 4Cp+1 for C ≤ polylog — then note quantum polynomial time.

title: Coppersmith small-root method: find (d, d′) with dd′ = 4Cp+1, d ≡ −1 mod 4C as a small root of a bivariate polynomial
connection: Writing d = 4Ck − 1 makes the condition (4Ck−1)·d′ = 4Cp+1, a bivariate polynomial with a small root (k, d′). Coppersmith/Howgrave-Graham finds small roots when they exist below a size bound.
why: This is the crypto-native 'factoring with a hint' toolbox. A lattice whose reduced basis has a short vector exactly when a certificate exists would be an existence criterion of a new kind (a Minkowski bound).
first_step: Build the Howgrave-Graham lattice for fixed small C and p ~ 10¹²; check whether the reduced-basis norm predicts certificate existence (compare with ground truth).

title: Factoring with hints: ES as 'find a factor of 4Cp+1 in a residue class' (Coppersmith known-MSB/LSB attacks)
connection: Coppersmith factors N given half the bits of a factor; ES wants a factor of N_C = 4Cp+1 ≡ −1 mod 4C — i.e. the low bits (mod 4C) of the factor are known.
why: Known-LSB factoring (factors in a prescribed class mod M with M ≥ N^{1/4}) is polynomial time via lattices; ES's modulus 4C is tiny relative to N^{1/4}, but summing over C gives many tries.
first_step: Quantify: for which C is 4C ≥ (4Cp+1)^{1/4}? (C ≥ p^{1/3}) — then Coppersmith decides existence of a factor ≡ −1 mod 4C exactly; check whether the large-C range alone has certificates often (data).

title: CRT-construction of adversarial p evading all small certificates (Chinese remainder adversary)
connection: Choose p mod Π(4uC−1) avoiding −u for all small (u,C) ↔ B1 barrier; the smallest such p as function of the menu bound.
why: Gives the 'cost' of evading menu of size B; growth rate of the minimal evader vs actual certificate sizes calibrates how big the menu must be at p.
first_step: Compute minimal prime p ≡ 1 mod 840 avoiding all (u,C) with 4uC−1 ≤ B for B = 10..200 via CRT + sieve; plot log p vs B.

title: Proof complexity: does ES for p ≤ N have short resolution/cutting-plane certificates?
connection: Each ES(p) has a polynomial-size certificate (x,y,z) ↔ 'ES for all p ≤ N' has a certificate of size N·polylog; the question is whether a uniform short proof exists — Π₁ statements and bounded arithmetic.
why: Bounded arithmetic (S¹₂, IΔ₀) characterisations: if ES were provable in IΔ₀+Ω₁, there would be polynomial-time witnessing — certificate finding in poly(log p) time. This turns a proof-theoretic question into an algorithmic one.
first_step: Read Buss witnessing theorem; formulate 'ES provable in S¹₂ ⟹ poly(log p)-time certificate algorithm'. Test: is there a heuristic poly(log p) algorithm for certificates (yes, try small C)? Is it provably correct?

title: Witnessing theorem contrapositive: if certificate-finding is hard (e.g. needs factoring), ES is not provable in weak arithmetic
connection: Divisor-form certificates need factoring 4Cp+1 ↔ if every certificate search needs factoring, ES ∉ provable in S¹₂ (under crypto assumptions).
why: Gives a meta-theorem: proofs must use non-constructive or strong tools; clarifies why elementary attempts fail.
first_step: Check whether ES certificates can be found without factoring (e.g. via the Type I trial form, which needs only divisibility tests, poly-time per trial). If yes, the obstruction vanishes.

title: Two-squares in PPA (Zagier windmill) ↔ ES in PPA? A search-problem formulation of windmills
connection: Finding x²+y² = p is in PPA via the Zagier involution (and is known poly-time via Cornacchia) ↔ ES windmill involutions would put ES-search in PPA.
why: If ES-search were PPA-hard or PPA-complete under a natural encoding, that would mean ES's proof must be a parity argument — direct guidance.
first_step: Check the literature on 'Fermat two squares' complexity class membership (e.g. Goldberg–?); attempt to write an ES windmill as a PPA instance (a graph of degree ≤ 2 with p-dependent vertices).

title: Pigeonhole (PPP) certificate: injectively map a set of size > N into a set of size N
connection: PPP problems: pigeonhole collisions ↔ ES certificates from a collision in a map from (thick set) to (smaller set) where collisions are certificates.
why: Thue's lemma is a PPP-style argument; ES via a collision would be a G1 'collision' column cell.
first_step: Look for a map from a set of size ≍ p (e.g. residues a mod p) to a set of size < p whose collisions yield (u,B,C) — test candidates on small p.

title: Program synthesis: search for a short program f(p) → (x,y,z) correct for all p ≤ 10⁸
connection: Program synthesis (e.g. enumerative, stochastic superoptimisation, LLM-guided) ↔ a uniform algorithm with provable termination would be ES.
why: Any synthesised program with a bounded loop is a finite menu (B1, must fail i.o. under Dickson); but unbounded-loop programs with simple invariants could suggest a proof structure.
first_step: Run a DSL search (loops over small parameter, modular tests) for programs certifying all primes ≤ 10⁶ with minimal description length; inspect top programs for invariants.

title: Termination analysis tools (ranking functions) applied to an ES search loop
connection: Software verification proves loop termination via ranking functions ↔ ES ⟺ 'for c := 1,2,… test certificate(p,c)' terminates for all p.
why: Automated termination provers (AProVE, Ultimate) fail on number theory, but the framing exposes what invariant is needed: a ranking function = a quantity decreasing until success.
first_step: Write the search loop in C and run a termination analyser to see what it asks for (expect failure; record the missing invariant).

title: Automata: is the set of p (in base b) with a certificate of size ≤ B a regular language? (Büchi/Cobham)
connection: Sets defined by finitely many congruence conditions are b-automatic ↔ finite menus give automatic sets; ES (all primes) is not automatic but the complement of a finite menu is.
why: Cobham's theorem: automatic in two multiplicatively independent bases ⟹ ultimately periodic. Menus are periodic; any 'digital' certificate rule (digit-carry algorithms, B1 hatch) gives automatic sets in one base only — a way to classify digit-based ideas.
first_step: Take a digit-carry ES rule (repo E2 hatch) and compute its automaton; check whether its success set is periodic (then B1) or genuinely base-dependent.

title: Walnut theorem prover for automatic-sequence statements about ES menus
connection: Walnut (Shallit) decides first-order statements about automatic sequences ↔ menu-coverage statements are automatic.
why: Fast way to prove/disprove finite-menu coverings rigorously (although B1 says they fail on primes, Walnut can check for structured n like 4^s + k families).
first_step: Encode the repo's 4^s + k family proofs in Walnut (base 4 automatic) as a test, then try open 4^s + 297 or 15·2^s + 1 families.

title: Lattice attacks on 'hidden number problem' as a model for finding u with p ≡ −u mod (4uC−1)
connection: HNP: recover hidden α from approximations of α·t mod q ↔ ES conditions as simultaneous approximations.
why: Cryptanalysis has fine-tuned lattice dimensions/bounds for such problems; reuse could design efficient certificate finders for huge p.
first_step: Write ES Type II as approximations of p/(4uC−1) to integers; try a BKZ-based search for certificates at p ~ 10^40 and compare yield with brute force.

title: ECM-style randomised factoring of 4Cp+1 tuned to divisors ≡ −1 mod 4C
connection: ECM finds small factors; ES only needs some divisor in a class ↔ certificate search at astronomical p.
why: Engineering: lets adversarial searches reach p ~ 10^100 cheaply (only smooth parts needed).
first_step: Implement: for C ≤ 10⁴, pull small factors of 4Cp+1 by trial division/ECM and test subproducts for class −1 mod 4C; measure success rate at p ~ 10^100.

title: Index calculus analogy: smooth relations and linear algebra over (ℤ/4C)^×
connection: Index calculus finds discrete logs by collecting smooth relations ↔ ES gate: express −1 as a product of factor-base primes' classes, with the factor base = small primes dividing p-tied integers.
why: Linear algebra over exponent vectors mod the group exponent makes 'is −1 in the generated subgroup' decidable; collecting relations across many C might show the subgroup is always everything.
first_step: For hard p, collect smooth parts of 4Cp+1 for C ≤ 10³; for each C compute the subgroup generated mod 4C; record when it's proper.

title: Lattice of exponent vectors: ES certificate as short vector in a relation lattice
connection: Repo gon_lll_relation_lattice ↔ relation lattices among divisor classes.
why: Already explored in repo; listing for coverage. New angle: use LLL to find a subproduct with prescribed class AND size constraint simultaneously.
first_step: Read BRAINSTORM/gon_lll_relation_lattice.md; check whether the size constraint (d < √N) was included in the lattice.

title: Model checking / BDDs for residue-class coverage up to large modulus
connection: Binary decision diagrams represent huge residue-class sets compactly ↔ the uncovered set after modular filters.
why: Exact representation of the uncovered set mod M (M huge) enables precise density of residual primes and structure detection.
first_step: Represent uncovered residues mod 840·Π small primes as a BDD over CRT digits; measure size growth.

title: ILP / MIP solvers on the ES Diophantine equation with bounds
connection: Integer programming with nonlinear constraints ↔ certificate search; branch-and-bound gives infeasibility certificates for bounded boxes.
why: Infeasibility certificates (dual bounds) for 'no certificate in box' are mechanical proofs of local non-existence; could expose structure in hard primes.
first_step: Formulate 4xyz = p(xy+yz+zx) with x ≤ y ≤ z bounds in a MINLP solver (SCIP) for p=409 restricted to Type II (★) and inspect the infeasibility proof.

title: Cryptographic hardness assumption: 'ES-certificate search is hard' as a one-way function candidate
connection: If certificates were hard to find but easy to verify, p ↦ certificate is a NP-search; crypto reductions require average-case hardness ↔ ES almost-all results suggest easy on average.
why: Fun meta: certificate search is easy heuristically (small C works), so ES gives no OWF; that easiness itself is evidence of a uniform algorithm.
first_step: Quantify: over primes ≤ 10⁹, distribution of the work (number of trials) to find the first certificate; if max work is polylog, conjecture a 'polylog search time' strengthening.

title: Strengthened conjecture: first certificate found within O(log² p) trials in a canonical order
connection: Stronger statement 'ES with an explicit search bound' ↔ like Linnik's constant or least-prime-in-AP bounds.
why: Stronger, more rigid conjectures are sometimes easier to attack (induction/structure) or to refute (giving insight). Also gives a cheap computational target.
first_step: Fix canonical order on (u,C) by 4uC−1; compute max over p ≤ 10⁹ of the index of first success / log² p.
