title: Multiplication-table divisor distribution
connection: Multiplication tables share F10, F15, F21: ES needs a divisor in a specific congruence class of a tied integer.
why: Fine-scale divisor distribution could improve over generic divisor-count estimates.
first_step: For the forms 4Cp+1, tabulate divisors by residue class and interval for a bounded sample of primes, then compare with known multiplication-table bounds.

title: Character-sum cancellation and genus terms
connection: Character-sum counting shares F04, F20, F21; real characters can dominate while non-real characters cancel on average.
why: An explicit formula for the exceptional character contribution may yield a sharper pointwise criterion.
first_step: Re-derive the count's character expansion and isolate the Kronecker-character term for p≡1 mod 4.

title: Chebotarev and splitting-sensitive Diophantine families
connection: Splitting problems share F06, F29, F36; Chebotarev controls average prime classes but not necessarily a witness for every prime.
why: Separating the distribution-of-primes issue from the per-prime construction can focus the ES reduction.
first_step: List which ES identity families require p split in Q(i), and check whether a compositum's Frobenius classes encode them.

title: Quadratic reciprocity obstructions in parametrised identities
connection: Reciprocity-limited parametrisations share F08, F09, F29: a natural family fails on a quadratic-residue locus.
why: Alternative reciprocity symbols or multiple parameters may cover complementary loci.
first_step: For each known ES family, record its Legendre-symbol condition and test whether two families have complementary failure sets.

title: Covering congruences in prime representation problems
connection: Finite congruence coverings share F03, F29, F34 and build a union of identity families over residue classes.
why: Covering-system optimization might reveal a broader set of usable identities, even if finite coverage is impossible.
first_step: Encode existing ES identity conditions as residue-class sets modulo a common modulus and search for minimal complementary covers.

title: Infinite covering systems by parametrised families
connection: Infinite covering problems share F03w, F30, F34 and replace one finite certificate with infinitely many thin families.
why: A structured infinite cover could accommodate the square-class failures of current finite templates.
first_step: Sort known ES families by prime density and overlap; formulate a criterion under which their union covers all primes.

title: Finite certificate impossibility and polynomial values
connection: Bounded-certificate failures share F09, F35, F36 and show that fixed algebraic templates can miss infinitely many inputs.
why: The obstruction can help identify what additional parameter dependence a successful ES argument must exploit.
first_step: Read the proof of the conditional no-finite-scheme result and list precisely which assumptions fail for infinite or adaptive schemes.

title: Prime gaps and thin algebraic sequences
connection: Thin-family problems share F30, F34, F36 and balance infinitely many explicit cases against no density guarantee.
why: Prime-producing subsequences may be organized via sieve estimates even when proving primality of each parameter sequence is unavailable.
first_step: For a known ES-valid sequence, count primes in its values or identify a guaranteed prime subsequence using established results.

title: Random covering and coupon-collector heuristics
connection: Random covering models share F03, F24, F34; many thin identity families may collectively cover each prime class.
why: A quantitative overlap heuristic can prioritize families with complementary local behavior.
first_step: Estimate coverage probabilities from the actual residue conditions of known ES identities, not independent random assumptions.

title: Poisson heuristics for rare representation counts
connection: Rare-count problems share F04, F24, F37 and model the number of representations as a random variable with fluctuations.
why: A calibrated lower-tail model can identify whether the observed witness abundance is enough to make failures implausible.
first_step: Estimate the mean and variance of the prime witness count from data and compare against a Poisson model stratified by p mod 8.

title: Large deviations for arithmetic representation counts
connection: Representation-count problems share F04, F21, F24 and require a lower-tail bound rather than just a mean estimate.
why: A large-deviation inequality might show that zero representations are too rare to occur at prime inputs.
first_step: Check independence or dependency hypotheses for the ES representation indicators and compute a second-moment lower-tail bound.

title: Linnik-type maximal fluctuations of representation functions
connection: Arithmetic representation functions share F04, F21, F37: average sizes can coexist with exceptional large spikes.
why: Upper fluctuation results warn against replacing a pointwise lower bound with an average or typical estimate.
first_step: Read the maximal-order bound for the relevant divisor sum and derive what it says about ES witness-count fluctuations.

title: Computational proof certificates for Diophantine existence
connection: Certificate problems share F23, F32, F35: a compact witness is easy to verify even when finding one universally is hard.
why: A verifiable finite certificate could support modular reductions or proof-carrying searches over residue classes.
first_step: Design a checker for a residue-class identity certificate and verify its proof obligations independently of the generator.

title: Formal verification of exhaustive congruence arguments
connection: Finite congruence proofs share F03, F23, F32 and can be checked by small proof certificates.
why: A machine-checked database of identities could safely expand the current congruence toolkit and detect missed classes.
first_step: Encode the standard ES Mordell identities and their residue coverage in a proof assistant or a short independently audited checker.

title: SAT/SMT certified search for finite identity menus covering residue classes
connection: SAT solvers settled Boolean Pythagorean triples, Schur number 5 and Keller's conjecture in dim 7 with certified proofs; ES identity families mod M form a finite covering problem per modulus (B1 says no finite menu covers all, but menus can be optimised).
why: SAT/ILP can find minimal identity menus and certify which residue classes mod M are uncoverable by identities of bounded degree — sharp data for B1-type statements.
first_step: Encode 'polynomial identity families with coefficients ≤ K cover class r mod M' as SAT/ILP for M = 840·k and certify the uncovered set.
alt_first_steps: [signature-0402] Generate bounded-coefficient bilinear/trilinear identities for ES and SAT-search for residue coverage beyond known families.
refs: Heule–Kullmann–Marek, Solving and verifying the Boolean Pythagorean triples problem via cube-and-conquer, SAT 2016
Brakensiek–Heule–Mackey–Narváez, The resolution of Keller's conjecture, arXiv:1910.03740
alt_titles: [signature-0402] SAT/SMT search for Diophantine identity families

title: Continued fractions and bounded-length Diophantine representations
connection: Bounded continued-fraction problems share F16, F17, F32 and encode integers through short recurrences.
why: Short-CF classification may produce new finite families of ES certificates or expose the exact exceptional parameter set.
first_step: Translate the ES₅ formulation into continuants and search for a theorem bounding the omitted length-three cases.

title: Theta series and coefficient nonvanishing
connection: Theta-series problems share F19, F31, F32: arithmetic representations become coefficients of modular generating functions.
why: Coefficient formulas may isolate congruence obstructions or positivity contributions invisible in the original equation.
first_step: Inspect the ES theta-quotient identity and compare it with modular-form coefficient nonvanishing criteria at prime indices.

title: Modular forms and nonvanishing of Fourier coefficients
connection: Coefficient-nonvanishing problems share F19, F20, F36; analytic average nonvanishing may fall short of every prime coefficient.
why: Methods proving nonzero coefficients in specified progressions could give a pointwise route for ES's generating function.
first_step: Identify the modular object, its Eisenstein/cusp decomposition, and available nonvanishing theorems for the relevant prime subsequence.

title: Quaternion orders and representation of primes
connection: Quaternionic representation problems share F29, F31, F36 and encode prime splitting through lattice or order structure.
why: The Gaussian/quaternion reformulation may give a geometric parametrisation of the hard split-prime classes.
first_step: Write the ES quadratic-form reformulation explicitly and compare its lattice with norm representations in a quaternion order.

title: Additive combinatorics of reciprocal residues
connection: Reciprocal residue sets share F10, F22, F33, where modular inverses combine additively to hit a target residue.
why: Sumset expansion could show that allowed denominator residues cannot avoid all ES target configurations.
first_step: For a prime modulus, compute restricted reciprocal sumsets from the ES denominator conditions and test known sum-product expansion bounds.

title: Graph connectivity of Diophantine representations
connection: Representation graphs share F14, F38, F39: vertices are solutions and local transformations connect them.
why: If each nonempty fibre has a canonical connected component, induction or descent might extend from a set of seeds.
first_step: Construct the ES witness graph under coordinate swaps and Vieta moves for small primes, then determine whether graph invariants suggest a general connectivity lemma.

title: Orbit counting under S3 symmetry
connection: Symmetric representation problems share F14, F38, F04; orbit-stabilizer corrections affect the count of witnesses.
why: Correctly separating generic and degenerate orbits may improve exact counting and parity deductions.
first_step: Compute stabilizers of ES triples and derive an orbit-count identity for R(p), including repeated-coordinate cases.

title: Branching processes for solution-tree growth
connection: Solution-tree problems share F24, F38, F39 and model repeated involutive moves as branching orbits.
why: Tree growth statistics could predict the number of distinct witnesses generated from a seed, while exposing cycles.
first_step: Determine whether the ES transformation graph is locally tree-like at bounded height and calculate its first-return probabilities.

title: Universal Diophantine statements with multiplicative closure
connection: Universal representation problems share F01, F02, F06; multiplicative closure reduces the domain to primes plus local cases.
why: The reduction template may identify a clean prime-only theorem and prevent wasted effort on composite inputs.
first_step: Formalize the ES multiple-closure map and compare it with closure reductions in other universal Diophantine representation problems.

title: Local solubility without integral global points
connection: Local-global counterexamples share F06, F07, F27 and test whether local conditions suffice under positivity and integrality.
why: A catalogue of mechanisms helps distinguish a hidden obstruction from a genuinely hard global construction.
first_step: Compare ES with integral conic and norm-form examples having solutions at every completion but no integral point.

title: Positivity in additive Diophantine equations
connection: Positive-variable problems share F27, F33, F01, while signed solutions can be plentiful and structurally misleading.
why: Positivity-aware methods may yield monotone bounds and compact search regions absent from the signed equation.
first_step: List all sign-sensitive inequalities in the ES parametrisations and test whether they define a convex feasible region for one denominator.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Almost-all versus every-input representation theorems
connection: Universal-versus-almost-all problems share F01, F05, F21 and make exceptional inputs the central issue.
why: Methods that eliminate exceptions in neighboring representation problems may indicate what additional arithmetic input ES lacks.
first_step: Compare the proof architecture of an almost-all theorem with a pointwise theorem for a nearby fixed-term representation problem.

title: Branching of prime representations by quadratic forms
connection: Quadratic-form representation problems share F29, F31, F36 and encode prime classes through splitting and lattice points.
why: Representation by several related forms might give complementary prime classes analogous to a family-cover strategy.
first_step: List the quadratic forms in ES reformulations and compare their represented prime classes via genus characters.

title: Genus theory and one-sided representation counts
connection: Genus-theory problems share F20, F29, F31 and can explain main terms while leaving a pointwise positive count unsettled.
why: Explicit genus-character decompositions may indicate whether the ES main term is forced or merely expected.
first_step: Decompose the ES count into genus characters and compare the local densities with the predicted main term for each prime class.

title: Residue-class divisor sums and real-character bias
connection: Divisor sums share F10, F20, F37; exceptional real characters can create one-sided fluctuations.
why: Understanding bias helps avoid a false expectation that generic cancellation forces every class to receive a divisor.
first_step: Compute the real-character contribution to the ES divisor count separately and see when it can dominate the error terms.

title: Exceptional primes for parametrised reciprocal identities
connection: Sparse algebraic failure sets share F08w, F25, F30, where a construction works except at explicit exceptional inputs.
why: A classification of failure sets may show that multiple parametrisations leave only a manageable intersection.
first_step: For each ES identity family, factor the obstruction polynomial and compare its prime roots with the failures of sister statements.

title: Prime gaps inside thin congruence-defined families
connection: Thin-family and congruence problems share F03w, F30, F36; families may contain infinitely many primes without positive density.
why: Effective lower bounds for primes in a union of thin families could underpin an infinite-cover construction.
first_step: Check whether any known ES parameter sequences are polynomial or recurrence sequences with established prime-counting theorems.

title: Adelic methods for integral points in families
connection: Arithmetic families share F06, F07, F13, F20; local densities may vary with the parameter and influence global integral points.
why: Uniform adelic analysis could identify parameter classes with systematically stronger integral-point counts.
first_step: Compute local densities of ES surface points at primes dividing 2p and compare with the global expected count across p residue classes.

title: Certificate-length bounds and NP-style arithmetic witnesses
connection: Small-witness problems share F32, F01, F23: every positive instance has a short certificate even if universal existence is open.
why: Uniform certificate bounds can make exhaustive search on reduced instances feasible and enable proof-carrying transformations.
first_step: Derive an explicit bound on the minimal ES denominator from known constructions and test whether it is polynomial in p with effective constants.

title: Sawin–Shusterman Chowla and twin primes over 𝔽_q[T] for function-field ES
connection: Sawin–Shusterman prove Chowla and twin-prime-type results over 𝔽_q[T] for fixed q large relative to characteristic data, via étale cohomology bounds; function-field ES certificates are divisor events of shifted polynomials (p(T)+e(T)).
why: Provides fixed-q (not just large-q-limit) tools; could prove function-field analogues of the pointwise ES lower tail.
first_step: Write the function-field Type II count at fixed prime polynomial P(T) of degree n and check whether Sawin–Shusterman's short-interval estimates cover the slice family.
alt_first_steps: [signature-0426] Write the ES count over F_q[T] at fixed prime polynomial P as a point count of a variety V_P/F_q and check whether its top cohomology is controllable (dimension, irreducibility).
refs: Sawin–Shusterman, On the Chowla and twin primes conjectures over F_q[T], Ann. Math. 196 (2022), arXiv:1808.04001
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings
alt_titles: [signature-0426] Sawin–Shusterman: twin primes and Chowla over F_q[T] (q large) by étale cohomology — the geometric pointwise route

title: Zhi-Wei Sun's family of refined-Lagrange conjectures with explicit finite exception lists
connection: Sun posed dozens of 'every n is … with constraint …' conjectures, each with finite explicit exceptions; several were proved (ternary forms, quaternions, spinor theory). Shares F01, F25, F23.
why: A large catalogue of solved siblings sharing the 'finite explicit exceptions' feature (like U(n)) with documented proof techniques.
first_step: Scan Sun's survey of conjectures on refinements of Lagrange's four-square theorem; list proved ones and their tools.
refs: Z.-W. Sun, Refining Lagrange's four-square theorem, J. Number Theory 175 (2017) 167–190

title: Andrews–Dyson–Hickerson precedent: a q-series whose coefficients are almost always 0 but unbounded
connection: ADH showed σ(q) has coefficients that are almost always zero yet take every integer infinitely often, via Hecke characters of Q(√6) and an indefinite form. The ES count is the opposite (expected ≍ log²n, never 0 conjecturally), but it is also an indefinite-form coefficient.
why: ADH is the template for exactly computing an indefinite-theta coefficient as a Hecke-character sum over ideals. That would make N₋(p) a sum over ideals of norm p in a quadratic field, i.e. a closed formula.
first_step: Try to express the χ-signed word count Σ_w χ(w) at prime p as a sum over ideals in some real quadratic field (ADH method); test numerically.
alt_first_steps: [signature-0429] Write D_t⁻ − D_t⁺ as a sum over x² − y² type forms (split indefinite theta) and look for an ADH-style real-quadratic twist with the same coefficients.
refs: Andrews–Dyson–Hickerson, Partitions and indefinite quadratic forms (Invent. 1988)
alt_titles: [signature-0429] Andrews–Dyson–Hickerson: σ(q) coefficients almost always 0 yet unbounded, via indefinite theta / Hecke characters of ℚ(√6)

title: Zwegers/Appell–Lerch: Kronecker's θ(x²)/θ(x)²-type quotients as Appell–Lerch sums with completions
connection: Quotients of Jacobi theta functions in the elliptic variable are Appell–Lerch sums (Kronecker's identity); Zwegers' completion makes them harmonic Maass–Jacobi forms. ES's (K1′) normal form is such a quotient (F19).
why: Bringmann–Ono-style methods give exact formulas/asymptotics for coefficients of mock objects; a sign-definite exact formula at prime indices would be ES-relevant.
first_step: Match (K1′) of METAPLECTIC_ES with Zwegers' μ(u,v;τ) and compute its completion; check whether the nonholomorphic part is supported on squares (T1).

title: Strong symmetric genus spectrum (May–Zimmerman: every value occurs) as a ∀g∃G sibling via triangle groups
connection: May–Zimmerman: there is a group of every strong symmetric genus. Proofs use explicit group families acting with triangle signatures; Riemann–Hurwitz ties genus to 1/x + 1/y + 1/z (see triangle-orbifold item). Shares F01, F12.
why: A solved ∀∃ statement whose witness lives in the same unit-fraction equation (via Riemann–Hurwitz) — possibly a source of explicit families (x,y,z) with constrained 1/x+1/y+1/z.
first_step: Read May–Zimmerman's construction and check which signatures (x,y,z) and areas arise; see if area (p−4)/p is ever forced.

title: Hurwitz 84(g−1) / the spectrum of 1 − 1/x − 1/y − 1/z: gaps near 0 vs ES's values (n−4)/n
connection: The set {1 − 1/x − 1/y − 1/z} has the minimum positive value 1/42 and a well-studied accumulation structure (Hurwitz). ES asks whether every (n−4)/n belongs to {1 − Σ1/x_i} (n ≥ 5).
why: The order structure of the triangle-group 'area spectrum' (it is well-ordered with known limit points) is classical; ES is a membership question for an explicit sequence in it.
first_step: Compute the area spectrum up to denominator 10⁶ and its intersection with {(n−4)/n}; visualise where the hard n sit in the spectrum.

title: Salez's modular filters (verification to 10¹⁷) as an explicit infinite covering family
connection: Salez found new modular equations (identity families) and used them as sieving filters to verify ES to 10¹⁷ (F23, F03, F34).
why: The filters are a concrete enumerated set of 'lines'; their combined density deficit as a function of the number of filters is an explicit covering-rate curve to compare with the Poisson model.
first_step: Extract Salez's filter list and compute the density of primes left uncovered by the first k filters for k up to 10³; fit the decay rate.

title: Mihnea & Bogdan (arXiv 2509.00128, 2025): ES verified to 10¹⁸ with solution-count data f(p) — data for signature calibration
connection: The paper extends verification to 10¹⁸ and evaluates the solution-counting function f(p) (F23, F04); check what count statistics are reported.
why: Independent count data to calibrate the log²p model against an outside source.
first_step: Compare their reported count statistics with M_BM(p) predictions at matching heights.

title: Lagrange's four squares: closure (Euler identity) + prime case by pigeonhole and descent — template for F02
connection: Four squares reduces to primes by a composition identity; the prime case is done by finding a multiple mp represented (pigeonhole) and descending m to 1. ES reduces to primes by trivial closure; the prime case has no descent.
why: An ES descent ('from a solution of a structured 4/(mp)-type equation produce one with smaller m') would be a Lagrange-type proof.
first_step: Search for an operation turning ES-type data at mp (e.g. a solution where m divides two of the denominators) into data at m'p with m' < m.

title: Davenport–Lewis–Schinzel / Cassels–Pfister: polynomial-identity theorems for sums of squares ↔ Mordell–Schinzel for ES
connection: Davenport–Lewis–Schinzel: if f ∈ ℤ[t] and f(n) is a sum of two squares for every n, then f is a sum of two squares of polynomials; Cassels–Pfister: a polynomial that is a sum of k squares of rational functions is a sum of k squares of polynomials. These are the sums-of-squares analogues of 'no polynomial identity covers the square classes' (F09).
why: Shows how polynomial-identity impossibility is proved by valuation/specialisation arguments; could give a uniform proof of F09 and its extensions (identities in two parameters, Gaussian coordinates).
first_step: Re-prove Mordell–Schinzel's ES statement by a Cassels–Pfister-style specialisation at a square point and see what extra hypotheses would allow identities in (a,b) with p = a² + b².

title: Feature flip F13 (cubic → quadric): 4/n = 1/x + 1/y is a hyperbola — fully solved by divisors
connection: The 2-term equation is a split conic; its solvability is a divisor-in-class condition and fails on a positive-density set. ES adds one variable and becomes a cubic surface with hyperbola fibres (F15).
why: Exactly measures what the extra dimension buys: from a single divisor condition (fails often) to a union over the fibre parameter (fails maybe never).
first_step: Compute the density of primes failing the 2-term condition for 4/p − 1/x as x ranges over the first K admissible values; plot the decay in K.

title: Feature flip F14: weighted equation 4/p = 1/x + 1/y + 2/z is trivial — symmetry/unit numerators are load-bearing
connection: Trivial: x = y = z = p gives 1/p + 1/p + 2/p = 4/p. Also for p ≡ 1 (mod 4), x = (p+3)/4 leaves 12/(p(p+3)) = 3/N with N = p(p+3)/4, and 3/N = 1/N + 2/N. Breaking the unit-numerator symmetry kills the problem.
why: Confirms the difficulty sits in the symmetric unit-numerator structure (F12, F14) — any proof must use that all numerators are 1.
first_step: List all weightings (a,b,c) with a+b+c small for which a/x + b/y + c/z = 4/p is trivially solvable; the first non-trivial weighting is a sub-problem ladder.

title: Feature flip F18: SL₂(ℤ) → SL₂(ℤ[i]) / Bianchi groups — Gaussian words for p ≡ 1 mod 4
connection: ES's SL₂ form asks for [[a,p],[c,d]] with congruence conditions. Over ℤ[i], p = ππ̄ splits; a Gaussian SL₂ version could split the problem into two conjugate halves.
why: Hard primes split in ℤ[i] (F29); a formulation where the splitting is visible could separate T1-type obstructions (which concern rational squares) from the generic case.
first_step: Write the SL₂(ℤ[i]) analogue with entry π and conditions mod (1+i)^k c; check whether norm maps produce ES matrices.

title: Feature flip F22: problems with the parity barrier broken by an extra algebraic structure (Friedlander–Iwaniec x² + y⁴, Heath-Brown x³ + 2y³)
connection: Thin-sequence prime counts became possible when the sequence had bilinear structure (Type II sums). ES's (★) word 4uBC − u − B is bilinear in (u,B) at fixed C.
why: If the ES lower-bound problem can be phrased as a sieve problem over a thin bilinear set, Friedlander–Iwaniec-type Type II estimates are the relevant input — on average over p at least.
first_step: Formulate 'p with R(p) = 0' as a sieve problem and check whether Type II information over (u,B) is available in the FI sense.
refs: J. Friedlander, H. Iwaniec, The polynomial X² + Y⁴ captures its primes, Ann. of Math. 148 (1998) 945–1040
D. R. Heath-Brown, Primes represented by x³ + 2y³, Acta Math. 186 (2001) 1–84

title: Feature flip F24: sub-problems where the heuristic predicts infinitely many failures (single lines) — calibrate the union
connection: Each single ES line (e.g. (★) at a fixed level C) is expected to fail infinitely often (e.g. whenever 4Cp+1 is prime — infinitely often under Dickson/Schinzel); (★) overall fails at 14 primes ≤ 10¹⁰; ES itself is verified to 10¹⁸.
why: The transition 'infinitely many failures → finitely many → none' along the union is a measurable phase diagram; its rate is the key heuristic input.
first_step: Plot, for unions of the first k lines (ordered by density), the count of failures ≤ X for X = 10⁶..10⁹; fit failure counts ~ X·exp(−c k).

title: Feature flip F38: Markoff (quadratic in each variable ⇒ Vieta group) vs ES (multilinear ⇒ no Vieta) — what symmetry group does the ES cubic have?
connection: The ES surface 4xyz = n(xy+yz+zx) is multilinear; its automorphisms include S₃ and Cremona-type maps (x ↦ 1/x turns it into a plane 1/x+1/y+1/z linear in reciprocals!). In reciprocal coordinates X = 1/x it is the plane X + Y + Z = 4/n.
why: The integral-points problem is 'points of the plane X+Y+Z = 4/n with all coordinates unit fractions' — the symmetry group of the problem is the affine group of that plane preserving the unit-fraction lattice condition; a new angle on F38/F39.
first_step: Determine the group of birational automorphisms of the ES surface over ℚ that preserve positivity and integrality for infinitely many n.

title: Feature flip F39: Stern–Brocot / Calkin–Wilf trees enumerate every rational exactly once — is there a tree enumerating ES words with p at a bounded depth?
connection: Universality of a tree enumeration is trivial for rationals; ES's word forest (F39) has connectivity results. A tree in which every prime appears within bounded depth would prove ES₅-type statements.
why: Gives a combinatorial reformulation: bounded-depth covering in an explicit tree (like λ(p) ≤ 3 in the Euclid tree).
first_step: Compute the depth of each hard prime in the Stern–Brocot-type tree generated by the ES₅ moves; check bounded depth up to 10⁸.

title: Montgomery–Vaughan power-saving exceptional set for ES or (★)
connection: MV proved E_Goldbach(N) ≪ N^{1−δ} by large sieve + zero density + Siegel-zero analysis; ES has only E(N) ≪ N exp(−c(log N)^{3/4}) and 3/4 is sharp for CRT sieves (EXCEPTIONAL_KARY3).
why: A power-saving exceptional set would need exactly the non-CRT input the campaign identified (residue-dense large sieve); MV is a model of how that input looked for Goldbach.
first_step: Read MV §§3–6 and identify the step that becomes 'large sieve over moduli 4uB with p in the variable'; check whether the ES analogue of their Siegel-zero case analysis is available.
alt_first_steps: [signature-0447] Write the heuristic exceptional-set size predicted by the Poisson model (∑_n exp(−M(n))) and compare with N^{1−δ}: is a power saving even heuristically true for ES?
refs: H. L. Montgomery, R. C. Vaughan, The exceptional set in Goldbach's problem, Acta Arith. 27 (1975) 353–370
alt_titles: [signature-0447] Feature flip F40: Goldbach's exceptional set has a power saving (Montgomery–Vaughan) — why ES's is stuck at exp(−c(log)^{3/4})

title: Heuristic exceptional-set size for ES and for (★) alone: Σ_n exp(−M(n)) vs. proved bounds
connection: Under the Poisson model with mean M(n) ≍ log²n the expected number of failures ≤ N is Σ exp(−c log²n) < ∞, while for single lines it diverges. Shares F24, F05, F40.
why: Quantifies the 'distance' between the proved exceptional bound (N exp(−c(log N)^{3/4})) and the heuristic truth (O(1)).
first_step: Compute Σ_{n≤N} exp(−M_BM(n)) numerically for N = 10⁸ with the measured zero-law constant; compare with observed (★) failure counts.

title: Positive-proportion pointwise lower bound: R(p) ≥ c·log²p for a positive proportion of primes (second-moment / Paley–Zygmund)
connection: From first and second moments of R(p) over p ≤ X, Paley–Zygmund gives R(p) ≥ ½E[R] on a positive proportion (F05w, F04).
why: A clean, likely provable intermediate theorem with the right order of magnitude — the 'Romanoff' rung of ES.
first_step: Check whether the second moment Σ_{p≤X} R(p)² ≪ X log⁴X is available (ET-type divisor-sum bounds) and write the Paley–Zygmund deduction.

title: Smallest-solution size statistics: max denominator of the best ES solution vs. p^θ
connection: ES witnesses have size ≤ poly(p) (F32). The distribution of the minimal possible max-denominator (or minimal level C) over hard primes is an observable comparable to 'least witness' problems (least nonresidue ≪ log² p under GRH, least prime in AP). Note (★) has no level at all for 14 primes ≤ 10¹⁰, so the level statistic needs the union with other lines.
why: If the least witness is always ≤ (log p)^A (in level coordinates) a bounded-search proof shape becomes plausible — B1 says no fixed bound works, but a log-power bound is untouched by B1.
first_step: For hard primes ≤ 10⁹ record the minimal C with R_C(p) > 0 and minimal max(x,y,z)/p; fit against log p.

title: Feature flip F03: n ≡ 0, 2, 3 mod 4 and non-square classes mod 840 are covered by identities — what if the hard classes were non-squares?
connection: Mordell's identities cover every class except the six square classes mod 840 (F03, F08, F09). The squares are exactly the classes no polynomial family can reach — the reciprocity obstruction is the reason.
why: Problems with a finite congruence covering of ALL classes are solved by identities; ES's residual set is forced to be the squares by reciprocity — the same reason as in Apollonian packings (HKRS).
first_step: For moduli M = 840·ℓ (ℓ ≤ 50), confirm the set of uncovered classes stays 'squares mod M' and record the minimal identity degree needed per class.

title: Feature flip F31: Gauss's three-squares count r₃(n) ~ class number — a lattice count with a class-number main term
connection: r₃(n) = 12h(−4n)-type formulas give pointwise lower bounds via Siegel. If any ES count is (even partially) a class number, Siegel-type lower bounds apply (ineffectively).
why: Search for a lattice/genus formulation where an ES sub-count equals a class number or a sum of class numbers of discriminants tied to p.
first_step: Compute R(p) and Σ_{small D} h(−Dp) for hard primes ≤ 10⁶ and regress; any exact relation would be striking.

title: Feature flip F11 downward: 3/n = 1/x + 1/y fails for p ≡ 1 mod 3 — the 'numerator = terms + 1' ladder starts with a genuine obstruction
connection: 3/p as two unit fractions requires a divisor condition that fails for primes p ≡ 1 mod 3 (local-type obstruction), while 4/p in three terms has no local obstruction. m/n in m−1 terms: m = 3 fails, m = 4 is ES.
why: Shows ES is the first rung where the obstruction disappears; the reason (one extra free parameter) is quantifiable.
first_step: Verify the 3/p criterion and check m = 4 with 2 terms (4/p = 1/x + 1/y ⟺ p ≡ 3 mod 4) to complete the small ladder table.

title: Feature flip F28: Type III-like solutions for composite n (neither type, e.g. 4/9 = 1/4 + 1/6 + 1/36) — the T1-free channel at squares
connection: For n = m², Type I/II vanish (T1) but ES(m²) holds via solutions not of Type I/II (e.g. 4/9 = 1/4 + 1/6 + 1/36). Mixed-type solutions are the channel T1 does not see.
why: Understanding how ES survives at squares (via factor m) clarifies why primes cannot use that channel and what a 'prime analogue' would be.
first_step: Classify all ES solutions of 4/m² for odd m ≤ 101 by gcd pattern with m; check whether every one is a scaled solution of 4/d for d | m, d < m².

title: Feature flip F36: problems where GRH IS known to give the pointwise result (least nonresidue, Artin, Ramanujan's form) — common structure
connection: Check whether in each GRH-success case (least nonresidue, Ramanujan's form x²+y²+10z², …) a single L-function or bounded family controls the event at the given n; caveat: Hooley's GRH proof of Artin uses infinitely many Kummer-field zeta functions and gives a density, so the criterion needs refinement. ES's event needs a family of size ≍ p of characters χ_{−4uB} at once.
why: Gives a structural criterion: count how many L-functions must be simultaneously controlled; ES needs too many for GRH-type explicit formulas.
first_step: For each GRH-success sibling, record the number of L-functions and the conductor range used; tabulate vs ES.

title: Feature flip F37: problems where a two-sided asymptotic for the pointwise count IS true (r₄(n) = 8σ*(n))
connection: Exact formulas (Jacobi) give two-sided control; ES provably has no two-sided polylog asymptotic (Linnik-type large values).
why: Confirms that ES requires a one-sided method; methods built on exact formulas (Jacobi-type) cannot be complete for ES.
first_step: List the exact formulae known for ES-like counts (theta-quotient normal form) and identify which term carries the Linnik large values.

title: Feature flip F27 (cone): 4/n = 1/x + 1/y + 1/z with x,y,z ∈ ℤ_{≠0} and at most one negative — count grows polynomially
connection: Allowing one negative denominator turns the problem into an indefinite one; check whether the solution count then grows like n^δ (it stays finite unless 4/n is a unit fraction). The positive cone cuts it down to polylog.
why: Counting solutions in sub-cones (e.g. one denominator 'barely negative') interpolates between trivial and ES; a continuity/sign-change argument across the cone boundary could be a route.
first_step: Count signed solutions with |negative denominator| ≤ p^θ for hard p and see how the count decays as θ → 0.

title: Pratt-certificate analogy: recursive ES certificates via factors of p-tied integers
connection: Pratt certificates for primality recurse on factors of p − 1. ES witnesses are divisors of p-tied integers (F10). A recursive scheme: a witness for p from 'witness-like data' for prime factors of 4Cp+1.
why: Recursive certificate structures sometimes reveal inductive proofs (as for Pratt: every prime has a short certificate, by induction).
first_step: For hard primes, record which prime factors q of 4Cp+1 'produce' the class −1 (q ≡ −1 mod 4C or products) and whether q's own ES data predict it.

title: Additive energy of {1/x} and three-fold sums: Bourgain-type sum-product for reciprocals of integers ≤ N
connection: How many rationals of height ≤ H lie in {1/x + 1/y + 1/z}? Counting 3-fold reciprocal sums is a sum-product/energy question (F33).
why: A lower bound showing the 3-fold reciprocal sumset hits a large fraction of rationals a/n with small numerator would be a density version of ES-type statements.
first_step: Compute |{1/x+1/y+1/z : x,y,z ≤ N}| ∩ {4/n} for N up to 10⁴ and the energy of the reciprocal set.

title: Graph-theoretic reformulation: bipartite 'divisor graph' between levels C and primes p; (★) ⟺ no isolated prime vertex
connection: Make a bipartite graph with an edge (C, p) when R_C(p) > 0 ((★) divisor form at level C). (★)(p) ⟺ p has degree ≥ 1 — false at 14 primes ≤ 10¹⁰, so an ES version must add edges from other lines (e.g. the b = 1 line). Degree distribution ≍ Poisson(log²p) heuristically.
why: Graph tools (expansion, Hall-type conditions, random-graph thresholds for isolated vertices) give a different language for the lower tail (F04, F24).
first_step: Compute the bipartite graph for p ≤ 10⁷, C ≤ 10³; check the isolated-vertex threshold vs. random bipartite graphs with the same degree sequence.

title: Sierpiński/Riesel numbers: k·2^n + 1 composite for all n via covering — a 'shifted integer always composite' phenomenon
connection: Covering congruences force k·2^n + 1 to be composite for all n. ES needs p-tied integers 4Cp + 1 to be composite WITH a divisor in a class; a covering forcing compositeness is a step in the right direction for a fixed p.
why: If for each hard p a covering-type argument forced some 4Cp + 1 (C ≤ K) to have a SMALL prime factor q ≡ −1 mod 4C·…, a witness might follow (small prime factor in the right class ⇒ witness when cofactor class matches).
first_step: For hard primes, find small primes q with q | 4Cp + 1 and q ≡ −1 (mod 4C) for some C < q (i.e. C ≡ −(4p)⁻¹ mod q with the class condition); count such (q, C) pairs with q ≤ log²p.

title: Small-prime-factor witnesses: q | 4Cp + 1 with q ≡ −1 (mod 4C) is itself a witness (d = q)
connection: If a prime q ≡ −1 (mod 4C) divides 4Cp + 1 then the cofactor is ≡ −1 too (product ≡ 1), so d = q is a (★) witness. For each prime q and each C with 4C | q + 1, q | 4Cp + 1 is a single congruence on p mod q.
why: So the set of p witnessed by (q, C) is one residue class mod q; (★)(p) for a hard prime p ⟸ p lies in some class {p ≡ −(4C)⁻¹ mod q : 4C | q+1} — an infinite covering by single residue classes (F34). These are (★) witnesses, so the covering misses the 14 (★)-failures ≤ 10¹⁰; for ES it must be combined with other lines. Note q ≥ 4C − 1, so q ≈ C scale.
first_step: For each hard prime p ≤ 10⁸, find the least prime q such that some C with 4C | q + 1 satisfies q | 4Cp + 1; study the distribution of that q.

title: Maynard–Tao multidimensional sieve over the (c,d) certificate grid
connection: Maynard–Tao weights (Σλ_{d1..dk})² detect many simultaneous 'prime/structured' events among k linear forms; the ES Type I certificate grid offers many linear-in-(c,d) objects at fixed p (e.g. moduli 4cd, values p²+4c²d).
why: MT weights produce 'at least m of k events happen' from first-moment data only — the shape we want for 'at least one certificate fires' — and here the average is over (c,d) at a single fixed p.
first_step: Write the k-tuple of events E_j = '4c_jd_j·(stuff) has a divisor ≡ −p mod 4c_jd_j' for an admissible family of (c_j,d_j) = (c0+jh, d0) and compute the MT ratio Σ_j S_j / S_0 numerically at p ~ 10^6.
refs: Maynard, Small gaps between primes, Ann. Math. 181 (2015)

title: Maynard 'dense clusters of primes in subsets' for certificate families
connection: Maynard (Compositio 2016) shows any positive-density subset of admissible linear forms contains many simultaneously prime values; ES certificates are indexed by a dense set of linear forms in the C-parameter (4Cp+1, Cp+...).
why: Gives a combinatorial robustness: we need not control which certificate fires, only that a dense sub-family of forms is admissible at p.
first_step: Check whether the family {4Cp+1 : C ≤ X} with the divisor-in-class event can be recast as primality of auxiliary linear forms f = (4Cp+1)/d for d in a fixed finite set; test admissibility mod small primes.
refs: Maynard, Dense clusters of primes in subsets, Compositio Math. 152 (2016)

title: Zhang / Polymath8 smooth-moduli level of distribution with modulus 4C smooth
connection: Zhang and Polymath8a get primes equidistributed in APs to smooth moduli beyond x^{1/2}; in ES Type I the tied modulus 4C (or 4cd) is free to be chosen smooth.
why: Choosing C among smooth numbers gives well-factorable moduli, which is exactly where beyond-1/2 equidistribution (dispersion + Kloosterman) is available.
first_step: Restrict the ES Type I/II search to C that are y-smooth (y = log^2 p) and measure on data whether R(p) restricted to smooth C keeps the log^2 p main term (p ≤ 10^7).
refs: Zhang, Bounded gaps between primes, Ann. Math. 179 (2014)
Polymath, Variants of the Selberg sieve…, Res. Math. Sci. 1 (2014)

title: Maynard 'Primes in APs to large moduli I–III' with p-dependent residue class
connection: Maynard (2020) extends Bombieri–Vinogradov-type results to moduli up to x^{3/5} for fixed residue classes and (part III) to uniform residue classes; ES needs divisors of p-tied integers in classes −p mod 4C that move with p.
why: Part III's uniformity in the residue class is exactly the feature a p-dependent class needs.
first_step: Read Maynard 'Primes in arithmetic progressions to large moduli III: uniform residue classes' and write the ES Type II count Σ_e #{ab | (p+e)/4 : a ≡ −b mod e} as a sum over moduli with residue a(p); identify which theorem shape is needed.
refs: Maynard, Primes in arithmetic progressions to large moduli I, arXiv:2006.06572

title: Lichtman beyond-square-root Goldbach/AP methods for tied moduli
connection: Lichtman (2023) improves level of distribution for primes in APs with well-factorable weights to x^{0.617…} and uses it for Goldbach-type counts; ES Type I/II counts are linear-sieve-like sums over moduli 4C.
why: Any improvement in the level for the ES counting function shrinks the exceptional set exponent (repo's E(N) ≪ N exp(−c(log N)^{3/4})).
first_step: Check whether Lichtman's well-factorable weights can be placed on the C-variable (4C | modulus) in the repo's exceptional-set argument (paper/es-threequarter-note.tex).
refs: Lichtman, Primes in arithmetic progressions to large moduli and Goldbach beyond the square-root barrier, arXiv:2309.08522

title: Fouvry–Radziwiłł level of distribution of unbalanced convolutions
connection: Fouvry–Radziwiłł show α*β with one short factor has level of distribution beyond 1/2 for all residue classes; ES divisor counts 1_{ab|N} are convolutions with one short divisor.
why: ES certificates typically use a small divisor a and a large cofactor — the unbalanced regime FR handle.
first_step: Express the Type II e-slice count as Σ_{a small} Σ_{b} 1_{ab = N} with class conditions and check whether FR's theorem (moduli to x^{1/2+δ}) applies when averaging over p in the exceptional-set argument.
refs: Fouvry–Radziwiłł, Level of distribution of unbalanced convolutions, arXiv:1811.08672

title: Guth–Maynard large values of Dirichlet polynomials → short-interval exceptional sets
connection: Guth–Maynard (2024) improve zero-density (Ingham 12/5 → 30/13) via large-values estimates; ES exceptional-set bounds pass through prime counts in short intervals/APs.
why: Zero-density improvements translate to shorter intervals where almost all ES-good primes are detected; could sharpen E(N) or the size of windows where every prime is covered.
first_step: Locate in the repo's exceptional-set notes which zero-density exponent is used and recompute the window exponent with A = 30/13.
refs: Guth–Maynard, New large value estimates for Dirichlet polynomials, arXiv:2405.20552

title: Matomäki–Radziwiłł at fixed p along the C-progression
connection: MR show bounded multiplicative functions have the same mean in almost all short intervals as in long ones; the integers 4Cp+1 (C varying) form an AP of modulus 4p at fixed p.
why: A short-AP version (Klurman–Mangerel–Teräväinen) could show divisor-class statistics of 4Cp+1 in short C-windows match long averages for one fixed p — pointwise in p, average over C.
first_step: Check whether Klurman–Mangerel–Teräväinen 'multiplicative functions in short arithmetic progressions' covers modulus q = 4p with interval length X = p^{θ}; compute what θ the ES Type I count needs.
refs: Matomäki–Radziwiłł, Multiplicative functions in short intervals, Ann. Math. 183 (2016), arXiv:1501.04585

title: Tao entropy decrement in the C-variable at fixed p
connection: Tao's entropy decrement (log-Chowla two-point, Erdős discrepancy) shows that at most scales the residues of n mod small primes behave independently of the random variable studied; here the random variable is C ↦ 4Cp+1 with p fixed.
why: It converts correlations into averages with a free prime shift — and at fixed p the average over C is legitimate (no averaging over p).
first_step: Formulate: random C ≤ X, X_C = (divisibility pattern of 4Cp+1 by primes ≤ H); compute the empirical mutual information I(X_C ; C mod ℓ) for p = a hard prime from DISPROOF_AVENUES.md.
alt_first_steps: [upgrades-0122] Compute the empirical entropy of the joint pattern (D_C(p) > 0)_{C ∈ [K, 2K]} for fixed p across dyadic K and check whether it saturates the independent-model entropy.
refs: Tao, The logarithmically averaged Chowla and Elliott conjectures for two-point correlations, arXiv:1509.05422
alt_titles: [upgrades-0122] Entropy decrement across levels

title: Helfgott–Radziwiłł expansion of divisibility graphs
connection: Helfgott–Radziwiłł (2021) prove expansion of graphs on integers where n ~ n+p if p | n (prime p in a range), improving log-Chowla; ES witnesses are divisibility relations d | N with N in a p-tied family.
why: A divisibility-graph expander on {4Cp+1 : C ≤ X} could transport 'some witness' along edges, the kind of local-to-global step ES lacks.
first_step: Build the graph on C ≤ 10^5 (fixed p) with edges C ~ C' if a common prime ℓ ≤ H divides both 4Cp+1 and 4C'p+1 and compute its spectral gap.
refs: Helfgott–Radziwiłł, Expansion, divisibility and parity, arXiv:2103.06853

title: Pilatte two-point log-Chowla improvement via graph spectra
connection: Pilatte (2023) gets (log X)^{−c} savings for two-point log Chowla using spectral bounds for random-like graphs on integers; same graph-on-divisibility template as Helfgott–Radziwiłł.
why: Quantitative spectral inputs are what a fixed-p C-average argument would need.
first_step: Read Pilatte's graph construction and check whether its vertex set can be replaced by an AP {4Cp+1}.
refs: Pilatte, Improved bounds for the two-point logarithmic Chowla conjecture, arXiv:2310.19357

title: Matomäki–Radziwiłł–Tao higher uniformity in short intervals
connection: MRT (Annals 2023) prove Gowers/nilsequence uniformity of bounded multiplicative functions in almost all short intervals; ES counts are correlations of multiplicative-type indicator functions along affine forms in C.
why: Uniformity norms control linear-form correlations — e.g. Σ_C 1_{d | 4Cp+1}·1_{class}.
first_step: Write the C-average of the Type I indicator as a correlation of multiplicative functions along linear forms in C and identify which Gowers norm controls it.
refs: Matomäki–Radziwiłł–Tao–Teräväinen–Ziegler, Higher uniformity of bounded multiplicative functions in short intervals on average, arXiv:2007.15644

title: Linear correlations of restricted divisor functions (Matthiesen-type) with p as a coefficient
connection: Matthiesen proved asymptotics for Σ_t Π_i f(L_i(t)) for divisor-type f via the Green–Tao machinery. R(p) is Σ_C of a restricted divisor function of the linear form 4pC + 1; with more structure (several levels) it becomes a correlation.
why: Gives asymptotics with uniformity questions in the coefficient p — the precise point to check.
first_step: Matthiesen, 'Linear correlations of multiplicative functions', Proc. LMS 121 (2020), arXiv:1606.04482 — verified: fixed linear forms only, coefficients may NOT grow with the range; so the needed input is a uniform-in-coefficients version — state it precisely and look for partial results (e.g. for τ-type functions via Kloosterman methods).
alt_first_steps: [tools-0013] Check whether 'number of divisors ≡ −1 mod q' restricted divisor functions satisfy Matthiesen's hypotheses (they are not multiplicative but are sums over characters mod q of multiplicative functions).
refs: arXiv:math/0404188 (Green-Tao, primes contain arbitrarily long APs)
Matthiesen, Linear correlations of multiplicative functions, arXiv:1606.04482
alt_titles: [tools-0013] Matthiesen: linear correlations of divisor-type functions

title: Green–Sawhney 'primes of the form p²+nq²' bilinear technique for p²+4c²d
connection: Green–Sawhney (2024) count primes of the form p² + nq² with p,q prime using Type I/II bilinear sieve on a binary quadratic form; ES Type I concerns divisors of p² + 4c²d, values of the same form shape.
why: Their Type II information on x² + n y² over thin variables is closely aligned with ES's quadratic value p² + 4c²d at fixed p.
first_step: Read Green–Sawhney's Type II estimate and check whether it gives equidistribution of divisors of p² + 4c²d in residue classes mod 4cd when c,d range over boxes at fixed p.
refs: Green–Sawhney, Primes of the form p^2 + nq^2, arXiv:2410.04189

title: Friedlander–Iwaniec asymptotic sieve (x²+y⁴) for thin certificate families
connection: FI breaks parity for primes x²+y⁴ via bilinear forms on a thin quadratic sequence; ES Type I with d a square gives p² + (2cy)², sums of two squares.
why: Restricting to d = y² makes the Type I object a Gaussian norm, where FI-type bilinear technology is designed to work.
first_step: Compute, for p ≤ 10^7, the fraction of primes with an ES Type I certificate having d a perfect square, and whether it stays bounded below.
refs: Friedlander–Iwaniec, The polynomial X^2+Y^4 captures its primes, Ann. Math. 148 (1998)
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Heath-Brown x³+2y³ cubic parity breaking analogue for norm-form certificates
connection: Heath-Brown's primes of the form x³+2y³ use a Type II estimate on a cubic norm form; ES certificates can be written as divisors of norms from Q(√−d) at fixed p.
why: A norm-form viewpoint replaces 'divisor in residue class' by 'ideal in ray class', where parity-breaking for norm forms exists.
first_step: Write the Type I certificate as: an ideal 𝔞 | (p + 2c√−d) with N𝔞 ≡ −p mod 4cd, i.e. a ray-class condition, and list the ray class field.
refs: Heath-Brown, Primes represented by x^3+2y^3, Acta Math. 186 (2001)

title: Maynard 'primes represented by incomplete norm forms' for ES norm forms
connection: Maynard (Forum Pi 2020) counts primes as norms N(a1ω1+…+akωk) with missing coordinates, using a sieve beyond classical parity; ES Type I divisor event is a norm-divisibility event in quadratic fields.
why: Incomplete-norm-form technology handles thin sets of algebraic integers, relevant to certificates where only a few coordinates vary (c,d at fixed p).
first_step: Check whether 'N𝔞 for 𝔞 | (p+2c√−d)' with c,d in boxes is an incomplete-norm-form set in Maynard's sense.
refs: Maynard, Primes represented by incomplete norm forms, arXiv:1507.05080

title: Maynard primes with restricted digits → thin sets with Fourier control
connection: Maynard (Invent. 2019) counts primes with a missing decimal digit by strong Fourier bounds on the thin digit set; the set of ES-hard residue patterns (Mordell classes mod 840 and deeper digit-like conditions mod 4C) is a digit-like thin set.
why: Template for proving that a thin, Fourier-structured set of p's must intersect the ES-good set.
first_step: Compute the Fourier transform (mod M = 840·k) of the indicator of 'not covered by identities of modulus ≤ M' and compare its L1 norm with Maynard's digit-set bounds.
refs: Maynard, Primes with restricted digits, Invent. Math. 217 (2019), arXiv:1604.01041

title: Merikoski largest prime factor of n²+1 → ES Type I values p²+4c²d
connection: Merikoski (JEMS 2023) shows P⁺(n²+1) > n^{1.279} using Deshouillers–Iwaniec Kloosterman bounds on divisors of n²+1 in ranges; ES Type I needs a divisor of p²+4c²d in a specific class and range.
why: His divisor-in-range distribution for quadratic values is the closest existing tool to 'a divisor of a quadratic value lies in a prescribed window'.
first_step: Re-derive Merikoski's Type I/II information for the polynomial X² + 4c²d (X = p fixed, c varying) and record the admissible divisor ranges.
refs: Merikoski, Largest prime factor of n^2+1, arXiv:1908.08816

title: de la Bretèche–Drappeau level of distribution of quadratic polynomials
connection: de la Bretèche–Drappeau (JEMS 2020) prove level of distribution beyond 1 for #{n ≤ x : q | n² + D} averaged over q; ES Type I is 'f | p² + 4c²d with f ≡ −p (mod 4cd)'.
why: Exactly the object (divisors of a quadratic value) with level > 1 — needed when f is larger than the square root.
first_step: Check whether their result allows a residue condition f ≡ a (mod 4cd) on the modulus f itself, and whether the polynomial variable can be c (with p fixed).
refs: de la Bretèche–Drappeau, Niveau de répartition des polynômes quadratiques et crible majorant pour les entiers friables, JEMS 22 (2020)

title: Duke–Friedlander–Iwaniec / Tóth equidistribution of roots of quadratic congruences with modulus condition
connection: Roots ν/f of ν² ≡ −D (mod f) equidistribute (DFI 1995 primes, Tóth composite); ES Type I asks that p be such a root (p² ≡ −4c²d mod f) while f ≡ −p mod 4cd — a joint condition on root and modulus.
why: Joint equidistribution of (root mod f, f mod m) pairs is a natural theorem to aim for and would give averaged Type I counts in new ranges.
first_step: Compute empirically, for D = 4c²d fixed small and f ≤ 10^6, the joint distribution of (ν/f, f mod 4cd) and check for correlation.
refs: Duke–Friedlander–Iwaniec, Equidistribution of roots of a quadratic congruence to prime moduli, Ann. Math. 141 (1995)

title: Dunn–Kerr–Shparlinski–Zaharescu bilinear forms with modular square roots
connection: DKSZ bound bilinear sums Σ α_m β_n e(h√(mn)/q) over modular square roots; ES Type I at fixed f involves √(−4c²d) mod f, bilinear in (c, d).
why: Bilinear square-root sums are exactly what appears when one Fourier-expands the Type I condition in c and d.
first_step: Fourier-expand 1_{p² ≡ −4c²d (mod f)} and isolate the bilinear square-root sum; compare with DKSZ hypotheses.
refs: Dunn–Kerr–Shparlinski–Zaharescu, Bilinear forms in Weyl sums for modular square roots and applications, arXiv:1908.10143

title: Bettin–Chandee trilinear forms with Kloosterman fractions
connection: Bettin–Chandee bound Σ α_m β_n ν_a e(a·m̄/n); ES exponential sums carry e(h·\overline{4c}/p) or e(h·p̄/4c) fractions with three free variables (h, c, d).
why: Trilinear structure matches the three ES certificate parameters.
first_step: Write the Type I/II indicator's Fourier expansion, identify the trilinear Kloosterman-fraction sum, and check BC's ranges.
refs: Bettin–Chandee, Trilinear forms with Kloosterman fractions, arXiv:1502.00769

title: Fouvry–Kowalski–Michel trace functions over primes for ES residue indicators
connection: FKM show algebraic trace functions K(n) mod q have Σ_{p≤x} K(p) = o(π(x)) for x ≥ q^{3/4+ε}; ES conditions like '(−p mod 4C) ∈ some set' are trace-function-type functions of p.
why: Gives equidistribution of primes p against arbitrary algebraic weights — e.g. the set of p for which a given finite menu fails mod q.
first_step: Check whether the 'menu failure' indicator mod a prime q (FIXED_MODULUS_SHOTS.md) is a bounded-conductor trace function and apply FKM to get prime densities.
refs: Fouvry–Kowalski–Michel, Algebraic trace functions over the primes, Duke Math. J. 163 (2014)

title: Polymath8 Type III / Deligne estimates for τ3-like ES counts
connection: Polymath8a's Type III estimates use Deligne's RH for correlations of hyper-Kloosterman sums to put τ3 in APs beyond 1/2; ES Type II solution counts are restricted triple-divisor counts (three denominators).
why: τ3-in-APs technology is the natural input for counting ES solutions in APs of n.
first_step: Write f(n) restricted to a fixed residue class of n as a τ3-type sum and test what level of distribution in n the ET average proof needs.
refs: Polymath, New equidistribution estimates of Zhang type, Algebra & Number Theory 8 (2014)

title: Irving / Liu–Shparlinski–Zhang divisor function in APs to smooth or prime-power moduli
connection: Irving (2015) and Liu–Shparlinski–Zhang get τ(n) equidistributed in APs to smooth / prime-power moduli beyond 2/3; ES's tied modulus 4C can be chosen a power of 2 times smooth.
why: Choosing 4C = 2^k is a legitimate ES sub-family (TWO_POWER_LADDER) and prime-power moduli have extra equidistribution.
first_step: Compare TWO_POWER_LADDER.md counts with the divisor-in-AP-to-2^k asymptotic; check which range of k the LSZ theorem covers.
refs: Irving, The divisor function in arithmetic progressions to smooth moduli, IMRN 2015
Liu–Shparlinski–Zhang, Divisor problem in arithmetic progressions modulo a prime power, Adv. Math. (2018)

title: Granville–Koukoulopoulos–Matomäki 'when the sieve works'
connection: GKM (Duke 2015) characterise when sifted sets by a set of primes have the expected density; the 'divisors avoid a coset structure' condition in ES is a sifted-set condition on prime factors of 4Cp+1.
why: Precise conditions for sieve heuristics to be correct are what a pointwise lower-tail claim needs.
first_step: Check whether the sifting set 'primes ℓ whose class mod 4C lies in a subgroup H not containing −1' satisfies GKM hypotheses uniformly in C.
refs: Granville–Koukoulopoulos–Matomäki, When the sieve works, Duke Math. J. 164 (2015)

title: Ford–Maynard theory of prime-producing sieves
connection: Ford–Maynard analyse which sieve-theoretic information (Type I/II ranges) can and cannot produce primes, extending the parity problem; ES is a 'one witness among polylog' problem with a parity-like barrier.
why: A formal limit theory for sieve information could make the campaign's B-barriers precise or show a gap.
first_step: Check whether Ford–Maynard's framework (arXiv 2024) includes sequences where the target is 'has a divisor in a class' rather than 'is prime'.
refs: Ford–Maynard, On the theory of prime producing sieves, arXiv:2407.14368

title: Erdős primitive-set / Lichtman: ES-covered n as a set of multiples
connection: Since a solution for n gives one for every multiple of n, the set of n covered by any fixed family of identities is a set of multiples ℳ(B) of a primitive set B; Lichtman (2022) proved the Erdős primitive set conjecture Σ 1/(b log b) ≤ Σ_p 1/(p log p).
why: Sets-of-multiples theory (Besicovitch, Erdős, Hall) quantifies how much a family covers and how the uncovered set (divisor-closed) can look.
first_step: For the repo's identity menus up to modulus M, compute the primitive generator set B among primes ≤ 10^7 and the density of ℳ(B); test whether Σ_{b∈B} 1/(b log b) tracks the uncovered density.
refs: Lichtman, A proof of the Erdős primitive set conjecture, arXiv:2202.02384

title: Banks–Ford–Tao: probabilistic prime models fail → refine the ES zero law
connection: BFT (Invent. 2023) show Cramér-type random models of primes mispredict large gaps and propose corrected models; the campaign's (J)97 lottery zero law for ES failures is a random model of the same kind.
why: Siblings fail less than the zero law predicts (G4); a BFT-style correction (sieving by small primes first) could explain it.
first_step: Rebuild the ES lottery model with residue-class sieving by primes ≤ z (BFT 'Granville model') and refit to S_{n,−4} and ES_Q1 failure data.
refs: Banks–Ford–Tao, Large prime gaps and probabilistic models, arXiv:1908.08613

title: Random multiplicative function model of (·/p) on divisor-generated sets (Harper's low moments)
connection: Model (·/p) restricted to S₃(p) by a random multiplicative function f. Then ES₅ failure is 'f ≡ 1 on a structured set'. Harper showed better-than-square-root cancellation for Σ f(n) (low moments), so multiplicative structure reduces fluctuations.
why: It is the native probabilistic model for character values with multiplicative constraints; it gives a heuristic failure probability that respects multiplicative dependencies among elements of S₃(p).
first_step: Compute the multiplicative dependency rank of S₃(p) (dimension of the F₂-span of its exponent vectors over primes). The failure probability under the model is 2^{−rank}; compare with observed.
alt_first_steps: [tools-0036] Model R(p) as Σ_C Σ_{d | 4Cp+1} 1_{d≡−1 (4C)} with prime factorizations randomized, and compute its lower-tail exponent by simulation vs Harper-type predictions.
refs: Harper, Moments of random multiplicative functions, I (Forum Math Pi 2020)
Harper, Moments of random multiplicative functions, I: low moments, better than squareroot cancellation, and critical multiplicative chaos, arXiv:1703.06654

title: Kozma–Samotij lower tails via relative entropy for R(p)
connection: Kozma–Samotij prove lower-tail large deviations for subgraph counts via relative entropy; R(p) is a count of 'arithmetic subgraphs' (divisor relations) in a random-like structure.
why: ES's core difficulty is the one-sided lower tail R(p) ≥ ε·M_BM(p); entropy methods are the modern lower-tail tool.
first_step: Map the ES certificate count to a polynomial in independent-ish Bernoulli variables (ℓ | 4Cp+1) and check the KS hypotheses (bounded influence) on data.
refs: Kozma–Samotij, Lower tails via relative entropy, arXiv:2104.04850

title: Harel–Mousset–Samotij upper tails via entropic stability (dual for R(p))
connection: HMS 'Upper tails via high moments and entropic stability' gives sharp upper tails for subgraph counts; for ES, upper-tail control of the *failure* indicator counts translates into exceptional-set bounds.
why: Exceptional-set results are upper tails of a 'number of uncovered p' variable.
first_step: Write E(N) as a polynomial count and check whether HMS-type moment methods give anything beyond Vaughan-type bounds.
refs: Harel–Mousset–Samotij, Upper tails via high moments and entropic stability, Duke Math. J. (2022), arXiv:1904.08212

title: Granville–Soundararajan pretentiousness of the 'class of divisors' character
connection: Pretentious theory: a multiplicative function f is small on average unless it pretends to be n^{it}χ(n); the indicator of 'N has a divisor in class −1 mod m' expands via characters χ mod m into Σ_χ χ̄(−1) Σ_{d|N} χ(d).
why: The ES failure set is where all such character divisor sums conspire; pretentious distance gives a language for 'conspiracy'.
first_step: For each failing N (no divisor ≡ −1 mod m), compute the pretentious distance D(χ_m-twisted divisor sums) and see whether failures cluster at a pretentious character (e.g. the real character mod m).
refs: Granville–Soundararajan, Large character sums: pretentious characters and the Pólya–Vinogradov theorem, JAMS 20 (2007)

title: Koukoulopoulos–Maynard GCD-graph compression for the dependency structure across levels
connection: The Duffin–Schaeffer proof controls sets of integers with many pairs of large gcd by iterative 'GCD graph' compression. ES levels C are coupled through gcd(4Cp+1, 4C′p+1) | C′ − C. A GCD-graph style structure theorem might show that simultaneous failure of many levels forces a structured (compressible) configuration.
why: It is a modern combinatorial-analytic technique for exactly the 'many dependent arithmetic events' situation, and it has not obviously been tried.
first_step: Read Koukoulopoulos–Maynard (Ann. Math. 2020) §§5–7; formulate the ES level-failure configuration as a weighted graph on levels with edge weights from shared primes.
alt_first_steps: [tools-0042] Build the GCD graph on ES certificates at a hard prime (vertices = (C,d), edges weighted by gcd of the p-tied integers) and test KM's 'quality increment' lemma numerically.
[upgrades-0065] Over primes p ≤ 10⁸ estimate P(E_C ∩ E_C′)/(P(E_C)P(E_C′)) as a function of gcd(C,C′) and C/C′; fit a Duffin–Schaeffer-type overlap model.
refs: Koukoulopoulos–Maynard, On the Duffin–Schaeffer conjecture (Ann. Math. 2020)
Koukoulopoulos–Maynard, On the Duffin–Schaeffer conjecture, Ann. Math. 192 (2020), arXiv:1907.04593

title: Effective Duffin–Schaeffer (Koukoulopoulos–Maynard–Yang) quantitative overlap
connection: KMY give an effective version with explicit error terms; ES needs quantitative dependency bounds.
why: Quantitative control of overlaps among rational approximations is directly re-usable in second-moment ES arguments.
first_step: Read KMY's main quantitative lemma and extract its statement for sets of moduli of the form 4Cp+1 divisors.

title: Ustinov's Kloosterman-sum method for continued-fraction length statistics
connection: Ustinov computes asymptotics of the number of a/b with prescribed CF statistics by reducing to lattice-point counts with Kloosterman sums; ES₅ is λ(p) ≤ 3 (a length-3 CF event).
why: Gives exact averaged main terms with power savings for CF-length events, possibly pointwise-in-p with a C-average.
first_step: Reproduce Ustinov's count of (a,b) with a/b having CF length 3 and specialize to b tied to p.

title: Petrow–Young Weyl bound for Dirichlet L-functions and character sums mod 4C
connection: Petrow–Young (Annals 2020) prove the Weyl-strength subconvex bound L(1/2,χ) ≪ q^{1/6+ε} for all Dirichlet χ; ES counts expand over characters mod 4C.
why: Subconvexity controls the character-sum error terms in Type I/II counts at fixed C.
first_step: Write the ES count at fixed (p,C) via Σ_χ mod 4C and determine whether subconvexity in q = 4C (small) or in the p-aspect is the bottleneck.

title: Burgess-type bounds via Hanson–Petridis Stepanov method for structured residue sets
connection: Hanson–Petridis improve the Paley-graph clique bound to √(p/2)+1 using Stepanov's polynomial method; the repo found χ-product cliques sit in a QR coset and that |A|-only Hoffman/Huang bounds fail below (p−1)/2.
why: Stepanov's method uses more than |A| — multiplicative structure — which is what the χ-product clique obstruction asks for.
first_step: Apply the Hanson–Petridis polynomial to the repo's χ-product clique family and see whether it gives a bound depending on the generating set.
refs: Hanson–Petridis, Refined estimates concerning sumsets contained in the roots of unity, arXiv:1905.09134

title: Thorner–Zaman effective Chebotarev for least prime with prescribed Frobenius
connection: Thorner–Zaman give unconditional bounds for the least prime in a Chebotarev class ≪ D^{c}; ES forcing lines (F_q: '(q/p) = −1 ⇒ ES(p)') need a small prime with prescribed splitting.
why: Quantifies how far unconditional least-prime technology is from what a fixed-q forcing line needs.

title: Pierce–Turnage-Butterbaugh–Wood effective Chebotarev in families → small split primes
connection: PTW (Invent. 2020) prove effective Chebotarev for almost all fields in families, giving ℓ-torsion bounds; ES certificates need small primes split in Q(√−d)-type fields tied to p.
why: Families of fields indexed by d or C at fixed p are exactly where 'almost all fields' results bite.

title: Explicit Burgess (Treviño) for the least non-residue ES forcing line
connection: Treviño's explicit Burgess bounds give explicit n₂(p) ≪ p^{1/(4√e)}-type constants; ES is classically settled when the least QNR is 3, 5 or 7 — the F_q line.
why: Makes the 'generic point of the least-QNR line' quantitative and checkable against 10^18 verification.
first_step: Compute, with explicit Burgess, how large p must be before n₂(p) ≤ 13 can fail and record it alongside the ES verification bound.

title: Platt–Trudgian / explicit zero-free regions for explicit exceptional-set constants
connection: Recent explicit zero-free regions and RH verification to large heights (Platt–Trudgian 2021) feed explicit prime-counting in APs; the repo's exceptional-set bounds are ineffective-constant.
why: Explicit E(N) bounds combined with verification could say 'no counterexample below X with a given property' — calibration, not a proof.

connection: The local OAI dump claims all Dirichlet L-functions are zero-free for Re s > 7/8; the repo's GRH-conditional ES statements (least-QNR, M_gen lower bounds) could become unconditional with fixed-strip exponents.

connection: Linnik's theorem with L = 5 bounds the least prime in an AP mod q by q^5; ES Type II with a prime denominator needs primes in classes tied to p.

title: Drappeau–Pratt–Radziwiłł one-level density beyond (−2,2) via Kloosterman sums
connection: DPR extend one-level density support for Dirichlet L-functions using sums of Kloosterman sums (Deshouillers–Iwaniec spectral input); ES counts reduce to sums over characters mod 4C at fixed p.
why: Shows a pathway where spectral Kloosterman bounds give information about families of characters — the ES character expansion is such a family.

title: Pascadi exceptional Maass form large sieve → ES dispersion
connection: Pascadi (2024) proves large sieve inequalities for exceptional Maass forms improving dispersion estimates (primes in APs to large moduli); the repo's exceptional-set argument uses dispersion-type steps.
why: Better exceptional-eigenvalue control improves level of distribution in the Type II dispersion step.

title: Kelley–Meka density increment on the multiplicative group (ℤ/e)^×
connection: Kelley–Meka get quasi-polynomial bounds for 3-AP-free sets via almost-periodicity + spectral positivity; the ES e-slice asks whether −1 lies in the quotient set Q = {ab⁻¹ : ab | N} ⊂ (ℤ/e)^×, an additive-combinatorial (multiplicative-group) statement.
why: KM's 'sifting' / dependent random choice finds structured pieces of a set with large Fourier mass; applied multiplicatively it might force Q to contain a coset of a large subgroup.
first_step: Compute |Q| and the multiplicative energy of the divisor set of N in (ℤ/e)^× at hard primes, and check whether Q is ever 'KM-structured' (large spectrum).

title: Bloom–Sisask log-barrier Roth bound and its almost-periodicity
connection: Bloom–Sisask broke the logarithmic barrier in Roth's theorem using Croot–Sisask almost periodicity; ES certificate sets are sumsets/product sets of divisor sets.
why: Croot–Sisask almost-periodicity is a general tool for showing A·B (here divisor quotients) contains long structured pieces.
first_step: Apply Croot–Sisask to the convolution 1_D * 1_{D^{-1}} on (ℤ/e)^× with D = divisor set of N and quantify the approximate periods.
refs: Bloom–Sisask, Breaking the logarithmic barrier in Roth's theorem on arithmetic progressions, arXiv:2007.03528

title: Balandraud's sharp subset-sum theorem in ℤ/p for the 'target −1' problem
connection: Balandraud: subset sums of k distinct nonzero residues mod a prime cover ≥ min(p, k(k+1)/2+1) elements; taking discrete logs, ES's subset-products of prime factors of N in (ℤ/e)^× is a subset-sum problem in ℤ/(e−1).
why: Gives the exact 'how many prime factors needed to hit a target' threshold in the cyclic setting; makes the ω(N) ~ log log N shortfall precise.
first_step: Tabulate, for N = (p+e)/4 at hard primes, ω(N) versus the Balandraud/Olson threshold for (ℤ/e)^× and record the gap.
refs: Balandraud, An addition theorem and maximal zero-sum free sets in Z/pZ, Israel J. Math. 188 (2012)

title: Kemnitz/Reiher-style lattice-point zero-sum for joint (C, d) conditions
connection: Reiher's Kemnitz theorem concerns zero-sums in (ℤ/n)²; ES certificates require simultaneous congruences (on f mod 4c and mod d), i.e. zero-sums in products of cyclic groups.
why: Multi-dimensional zero-sum constants control simultaneous residue requirements.
first_step: Formulate the Type I certificate condition f ≡ −p (mod 4cd) as a zero-sum in ℤ/4c × ℤ/d of log-classes of prime factors and compute the relevant constant for small c,d.
refs: Reiher, On Kemnitz' conjecture…, Ramanujan J. 13 (2007)

title: Bourgain–Glibichuk–Konyagin exponential sums over small multiplicative subgroups
connection: BGK: subgroups H ⊂ 𝔽_p^× with |H| > p^δ have nontrivial exponential sums; the subgroup generated by small primes / prime factors of N mod e is such an H.
why: Additive equidistribution of H mod e could feed into counts of e with −1 ∈ ⟨factors of N⟩.
first_step: For e prime, compute |⟨prime factors of (p+e)/4⟩| in 𝔽_e^× at hard primes and check how often −1 ∈ H fails (equivalently |H| odd).
refs: Bourgain–Glibichuk–Konyagin, Estimates for the number of sums and products and for exponential sums in fields of prime order, J. LMS 73 (2006)

title: −1 ∈ subgroup ⇔ even order: a parity reformulation of the e-slice event
connection: For prime e, −1 ∈ H ⊂ 𝔽_e^× iff |H| is even; the e-slice needs −1 in the quotient set Q (not the generated subgroup), but −1 ∈ ⟨Q⟩ is a necessary condition expressed via 2-adic valuations of multiplicative orders.
why: Converts part of the ES event into 2-adic order statistics of primes modulo e, a theme in Artin-type problems (OAI 029, Moree).
first_step: For hard primes, compute for each e-slice whether −1 ∈ ⟨factors⟩ and whether −1 ∈ Q; quantify how often the necessary condition holds but Q misses −1.
refs: Moree, Artin's primitive root conjecture – a survey, arXiv:math/0412262

title: Sum-product in ℤ/q for composite q (Bourgain) for ES moduli 4C
connection: Bourgain's sum-product and exponential-sum bounds for arbitrary q handle composite moduli; ES moduli 4C, 4cd are composite and smooth.
why: The ES condition mixes additive (4Cp+1) and multiplicative (divisor class) structure — a sum-product configuration.
first_step: State the ES Type I condition as 'A + B ∩ product set' in ℤ/4C and check whether Bourgain's composite-modulus results say anything at C ≈ p^θ.
refs: Bourgain, Exponential sum estimates over subgroups of Z_q^*, q arbitrary, J. Anal. Math. 97 (2005)

title: Guth–Katz polynomial partitioning for real ES solution geometry
connection: Polynomial partitioning bounds incidences in ℝ^d; ES solutions are lattice points on the real cubic surface 4xyz = n(xy+yz+zx).
why: Upper bounds on lattice points near the surface across many n bound pair correlations of f(n).
first_step: Bound #{(n, x,y,z) : n ≤ N} incidences with the one-parameter family of surfaces via partitioning and compare with known Σ f(n)² ≍ N log^? estimates.
refs: Guth–Katz, On the Erdős distinct distances problem in the plane, Ann. Math. 181 (2015)

title: Slice-rank of the ES 'certificate tensor' modulo q
connection: The cap-set proof bounds sets avoiding a pattern via the slice rank of the pattern's indicator tensor. Consider the tensor T(u, B, C) = 1[4uBC − u − B ≡ p (mod q)] over F_q³; its slice rank bounds how large a product set of parameter values can avoid certificates mod q.
why: Gives polynomial-method bounds on 'certificate-avoiding parameter sets' mod q, a local statement with sharp constants.
first_step: Compute the slice rank (or a polynomial-method upper bound) of T for small q and compare with the largest avoiding product sets found by search.
alt_first_steps: [tools-0069] Compute the slice rank of T_n(x,y,z) = 1[4xyz = n(xy+yz+zx)] over 𝔽_ℓ for small ℓ and compare with the size of solution-free sets.

title: Combinatorial Nullstellensatz for ES congruence certificates
connection: Alon's Nullstellensatz guarantees nonvanishing points in grids given a top-degree coefficient; mod-m versions of ES (local solubility with restricted coordinates) are polynomial non-vanishing questions over grids.
why: A grid-restricted solution mod many m simultaneously is a step toward ES with size-constrained denominators.

title: Huang sensitivity / interlacing on the ES certificate hypercube
connection: Huang's proof uses a signed adjacency matrix of the hypercube and Cauchy interlacing to force a high-degree vertex in any large induced subgraph; ES certificates live on a product of small 'choice' cubes (choice of prime factors into a,b).
why: Interlacing arguments convert 'large set' into 'has a forced structure' — the repo noted Hoffman/Huang bounds depending only on |A| fail; a signed-matrix variant with the χ structure is still open.

connection: Park–Pham relate thresholds to expectation thresholds. The repo measures ≈ (0.44 → 0.97)·log p expected hit levels (critical regime). Compute, in a random model matching ES's level statistics, the threshold for 'some level hits' and see whether ES sits above it by a growing margin.

title: Frankston–Kahn–Narayanan–Park fractional expectation thresholds / spread measures
connection: FKNP show spread measures on hypergraph edges imply threshold behaviour; ES certificates could be weighted by a spread measure over (C,d) pairs.

title: Alweiss–Lovett–Wu–Zhang sunflowers among minimal ES solutions → identity families
connection: ALWZ improved sunflower bounds to (log w)^{w(1+o(1))}; families of ES solutions across many n, encoded as sets of prime-power factors of (x,y,z), contain sunflowers, which correspond to shared 'cores' i.e. parametric identity families.

connection: Iterative absorption converts near-perfect structures into perfect ones by pre-reserving absorbers; ES knows almost-all results, and the missing step is exactly almost-all → all.

title: Szemerédi regularity / arithmetic regularity (Green; Green–Tao) for the failure set
connection: Arithmetic regularity decomposes any set into structured + pseudorandom parts; the ES failure set E is divisor-closed and scales from q ≡ 3 (mod 4) can't fill an AP.

title: Green–Tao relative Szemerédi / dense model for ES-good primes
connection: Green–Tao transference finds structure in dense subsets of primes; the set of ES-hard primes (not covered by identities of modulus ≤ M) is a structured subset of primes.
why: Could prove infinitely many patterns (APs) among primes p whose ES solutions have a specific shape — an existence-of-structure statement.

Conlon–Fox–Zhao, A relative Szemerédi theorem, GAFA 25 (2015)

title: Leng–Sah–Sawhney quasipolynomial inverse theorem for Gowers norms
connection: LSS give quasi-polynomial bounds in the U^k inverse theorem and Szemerédi; linear-form correlations of ES indicators are controlled by Gowers norms.
why: Quantitative inverse theorems are needed for any averaged ES correlation estimate with power-of-log savings.
first_step: Identify the Gowers norm controlling the ET average Σ_{p≤x} f(p) along linear forms in (c,d,e) and estimate the loss with LSS bounds.
refs: Leng–Sah–Sawhney, Improved bounds for Szemerédi's theorem, arXiv:2402.17995

title: Green–Tao–Ziegler linear equations in primes for prime-denominator ES solutions
connection: GTZ count prime solutions of finite-complexity linear systems; ES solutions with prime denominators reduce to linear equations after fixing products (e.g. Type II with x = (p+e)/4 prime-parametrised).
why: Counting prime-denominator ES solutions across p gives averaged statements with primes in all slots.
first_step: Enumerate ES solution shapes where all three denominators are of the form (linear form in parameters) and identify a finite-complexity linear system in primes.
refs: Green–Tao, Linear equations in primes, Ann. Math. 171 (2010)

title: Peluse–Prendiville polynomial Szemerédi with power saving
connection: Peluse–Prendiville give power-saving bounds for sets avoiding x, x+y, x+y² etc.; ES identities often involve quadratic expressions in the parameter (Mordell families).
