why: Degree-lowering for polynomial configurations could detect quadratic ES families within dense sets of n.
first_step: List Mordell-family identities as polynomial configurations (n, n+P1(t), …) and check whether they are of PP type.
refs: Peluse, Bounds for sets with no polynomial progressions, Forum Math. Pi 8 (2020), arXiv:1909.00309

title: Liu–Sawhney further unit-fraction questions (Erdős problems)
connection: Liu–Sawhney (2024) resolve several Erdős–Graham unit-fraction questions with refinements of Bloom's method; ES is a fixed-length unit-fraction problem.
why: Most transferable pieces: control of unit-fraction sums over smooth numbers with prescribed denominators.
first_step: Read Liu–Sawhney and list each lemma that works for a fixed small number of terms.
refs: Liu–Sawhney, On further questions regarding unit fractions, arXiv:2404.07113

title: OAI 025 short Egyptian fractions O(log log b) (claimed) — length-3 specialization
connection: OAI family 025 claims every a/b is a sum of O(log log b) distinct unit fractions, sharp; ES asks for exactly 3 terms at a = 4.
why: The construction's mechanism (how denominators are chosen) could expose a 'small number of terms' greedy-plus-smooth technique; calibration of what length is cheap.
first_step: Read the OAI 025 build sources and record which step needs Θ(log log b) terms; check whether for a = 4 the construction degenerates to fewer terms.
refs: oai-math family 025 (CLAIMED, Lean-formalized per scope page)

title: Moreira monochromatic {x, x+y, xy} and Hindman sums/products (OAI 164)
connection: Moreira (Annals 2017) found monochromatic {x, x+y, xy}; OAI 164 claims Hindman's finite sums and products conjecture; ES mixes additive (4Cp+1) and multiplicative (divisor) operations.
why: Ergodic sum-product Ramsey results show additive and multiplicative structure can be forced together.
first_step: Phrase ES Type I as a configuration {p, C, 4Cp+1, d, (4Cp+1)/d} with additive and multiplicative relations and check whether it is a 'sum-product configuration' in Moreira's sense.
refs: Moreira, Monochromatic sums and products in N, Ann. Math. 185 (2017), arXiv:1605.01469

title: Erdős reciprocal-sum conjecture (OAI 159, claimed) applied to the failure set
connection: OAI 159 claims every set with divergent reciprocal sum contains arbitrarily long APs; the ES failure set E ⊂ primes has convergent reciprocal sum already (Vaughan), so the theorem gives no constraint — a calibration that the failure set is too sparse for density Ramsey theory.
why: Records a negative transfer explicitly so later lanes don't repeat it; also suggests which sparser Ramsey statements (for primes with Σ1/p convergent) would be needed.
first_step: Verify Σ_{p∈E} 1/p < ∞ from the repo's E(N) bound and note the threshold density for Green–Tao-type relative results.

title: Campos–Griffiths–Morris–Sahasrabudhe 'book algorithm' as a structured search heuristic
connection: The exponential improvement for diagonal Ramsey uses a book-building algorithm controlling red/blue densities; ES certificate search is a two-colour (residue/non-residue) structure problem on divisor sets.
why: The book algorithm is a template for finding large structured objects in a 2-coloured complete structure.
first_step: Colour pairs of prime factors of N by whether their product ratio class is a QR mod e; search for a 'book' configuration implying −1 ∈ Q.
refs: Campos–Griffiths–Morris–Sahasrabudhe, An exponential improvement for diagonal Ramsey, arXiv:2303.09521

title: Mattheus–Verstraëte algebraic pseudorandom graphs (R(4,t)) from Hermitian unitals
connection: MV built optimal R(4,t) lower bounds from algebraic graphs over 𝔽_{q²}; ES-like 'sterile' residue structures are algebraic objects avoiding configurations.
why: Suggests constructing explicit algebraic sterile structures as candidates for counterexample-shape tests.
first_step: Check whether the repo's sterile residue patterns (STERILE_EXPLICIT.md) define an algebraic graph with Hermitian-unital-like incidence.
refs: Mattheus–Verstraëte, The asymptotics of r(4,t), arXiv:2306.04007

title: Expander mixing on Cayley graphs of (ℤ/e)^× generated by prime factors of N
connection: Alon–Roichman: O(log|G|) random generators give an expander; the ES e-slice uses the Cayley graph on (ℤ/e)^× generated by the ω(N) ≈ log log N prime factors of N.
why: Quantifies precisely why one integer's factors are too few to force −1 (B2) and what extra generators (other slices) would need to be pooled.
first_step: Compute spectral gaps of Cayley graphs of (ℤ/e)^× with generators = prime factors of N and also with pooled generators from several slices sharing e.
refs: Alon–Roichman, Random Cayley graphs and expanders, Random Struct. Alg. 5 (1994)

title: Breuillard–Green–Tao approximate groups for the divisor quotient set
connection: BGT classify approximate groups as near nilpotent cosets; in abelian (ℤ/e)^× this is Freiman–Green–Ruzsa; the ES quotient set Q is a product set.
why: If Q is an approximate group, it is near a coset progression, and −1 ∈ Q becomes an explicit lattice question.
first_step: Test on data whether divisor quotient sets are approximate groups (|Q·Q| ≤ K|Q| for small K).
refs: Breuillard–Green–Tao, The structure of approximate groups, Publ. IHES 116 (2012)

title: Golsefidy–Varjú superstrong approximation for the ES₅ semigroup
connection: Salehi Golsefidy–Varjú prove expansion for perfect groups' congruence quotients; ES₅ words generate a semigroup in SL₂(ℤ) whose Zariski closure and congruence images are computable.
why: Determines whether the ES₅ semigroup has full congruence image mod every q (local-global input).
first_step: Compute the Zariski closure and mod-q images of the semigroup generated by the ES₅ letters for small q.
refs: Salehi Golsefidy–Varjú, Expansion in perfect groups, GAFA 22 (2012)

title: Magee–Oh–Winter uniform congruence counting for Schottky semigroups
connection: MOW give uniform spectral gap/congruence counting for thin Schottky semigroups; underlying tool for Zaremba-type local-global.
why: If ES₅ admits a Schottky-semigroup formulation with unbounded alphabet truncated at height T, uniform counting mod q gives local-global for almost all.
first_step: Check whether truncating ES₅ letters to digits ≤ A yields a Schottky semigroup and compute its Hausdorff dimension δ_A as A grows.
refs: Magee–Oh–Winter, Uniform congruence counting for Schottky semigroups in SL2(Z), Crelle 753 (2019)

title: Kontorovich–Nakamura crystallographic packings ↔ ES integral geometry
connection: Kontorovich–Nakamura classify crystallographic sphere packings via integral Lorentzian reflective lattices; ES has lattice/quaternion reformulations and a cubic integral surface.
why: Packing local-global problems (Apollonian) are the main family with proved reciprocity obstructions akin to T1.
first_step: Check whether any ES lattice L_ρ (LATTICE_MEETING.md) is a reflective Lorentzian lattice.
refs: Kontorovich–Nakamura, Geometry and arithmetic of crystallographic sphere packings, PNAS 116 (2019)

title: Bourgain–Fuchs / Bourgain–Kontorovich density-one Apollonian method for ES siblings
connection: Positive-density and density-one results for Apollonian curvatures use thin-orbit circle methods with a quadratic subfamily (shifted binary forms); ES certificates are also quadratic-form values (p² + 4c²d).
why: Transfer of the 'quadratic subfamily + large sieve' trick to ES certificate families.
first_step: Identify a sub-family of ES certificates that is a shifted binary quadratic form in two free parameters at fixed p, and apply the BK almost-all argument.
refs: Bourgain–Kontorovich, On the local-global conjecture for integral Apollonian gaskets, Invent. Math. 196 (2014)

title: Erdős–Szemerédi sum-product / Solymosi for ES additive-multiplicative mixing
connection: Sum-product phenomenon: A+A or A·A large; the ES integer families {4Cp+1} are additive shifts while certificates are multiplicative.
why: Sum-product heuristics predict that additive families can't stay multiplicatively structured, supporting divisor-class equidistribution.
first_step: Measure multiplicative energy of {4Cp+1 : C ≤ X} vs random integers of the same size.
refs: Solymosi, Bounding multiplicative energy by the sumset, Adv. Math. 222 (2009)

title: Discretised projection (Bourgain) / Furstenberg sets (Ren–Wang) for p-adic or real ES geometry
connection: Bourgain's discretised projection theorem and Ren–Wang's Furstenberg set resolution give sum-product in ℝ at scale δ; ES solution ratios (x:y:z) live on a real curve family.
why: Could bound concentration of solution directions, relevant to size-window (FORCED_WINDOW) statements.
first_step: Express the set of normalized ES solutions (x/n, y/n, z/n) as a δ-discretised set and test projection-dimension statistics numerically.
refs: Ren–Wang, Furstenberg sets estimate in the plane, arXiv:2308.08819
Bourgain, The discretized sum-product and projection theorems, J. Anal. Math. 112 (2010)

title: Decoupling/energy for the hyperbolic ES surface {4uBC − u − B}
connection: BDG decoupling bounds moments of exponential sums over curves. Additive energy of the ES-word set (#{w₁ = w₂} with w = 4uBC−u−B ≤ N) controls the second moment Σ_n R(n)².
why: Second-moment control is the ingredient of every almost-all → pointwise attempt via variance; decoupling-type bounds for this specific surface could be sharp.
first_step: Compute the energy E(N) = Σ_{n≤N} R(n)² for N up to 10⁷ and fit N·(log N)^a; compare with what a decoupling inequality for (u, B, uB) would predict.
alt_first_steps: [tools-0105] Write Σ_n f(n) e(nα) as an exponential sum over the surface and identify a moment-curve-like structure for decoupling.
refs: Bourgain–Demeter–Guth, Proof of the main conjecture in Vinogradov's mean value theorem for degrees higher than three, Ann. Math. 184 (2016), arXiv:1512.01565
alt_titles: [tools-0105] Bourgain–Demeter–Guth decoupling for ES-type exponential sums

title: Wooley efficient congruencing / nested efficient congruencing for ES moments
connection: Efficient congruencing gives sharp mean values via p-adic concentration iteration; ES solution counts mod prime powers have a p-adic concentration structure (Hensel lifts of certificates).
why: Moment bounds Σ f(n)^k with sharp exponents constrain the distribution of R(p).
first_step: Compute numerically Σ_{n ≤ N} f(n)^2, f(n)^3 and fit exponents of log N; compare with decoupling-type predictions.
refs: Wooley, Nested efficient congruencing and relatives of Vinogradov's mean value theorem, Proc. LMS 118 (2019)

title: U_n's closure is the Cayley 4-nodal cubic σ₃(x,y,z,w)=0 — log CY pair with a triangle through 3 nodes
connection: Substituting w = −4w′/n turns 4xyz = nw(xy+yz+zx) into σ₃(x,y,z,w′) = xyz+w′(xy+yz+zx) = 0, the Cayley cubic (checked: singular exactly at the 4 coordinate points). U_n = Cayley cubic minus the triangle w=0 through three nodes; the Markoff k=4 surface is the same cubic minus a triangle avoiding the nodes.
why: Places ES next to Markoff in the classification of log Calabi–Yau cubic pairs and pins down the one geometric difference (boundary through vs. away from nodes) — any Markoff-type tool must explain what it does at the nodes.
first_step: Write the explicit projective equivalence to x²+y²+z²−xyz = 4 closure and map the U_n boundary triangle and the integral structure (w′ = −n/4) across; record which Markoff automorphisms preserve the ES boundary.
refs: Bright–Loughran, Brauer–Manin obstruction for Erdős–Straus surfaces, Bull. LMS 52 (2020)

title: U_n as a Looijenga pair: Gross–Hacking–Keel theta functions on the ES log CY surface
connection: The projective closure 4xyz = nw(xy+yz+zx) minus the triangle w = 0 is a log Calabi–Yau surface with a toric model: P² blown up at three collinear boundary points (GEOMETRY_ES Prop 2.1). GHK construct a canonical basis of theta functions on the mirror family of any Looijenga pair, indexed by integral points of the tropicalisation.
why: Theta functions give canonical regular functions with positive structure constants. If positive integer points of U_n correspond to positivity of some theta function's values, the native existence tools are scattering diagrams.
first_step: Compute the scattering diagram of the Looijenga pair (Y_n, D) (three collinear blow-up points). Check whether ES's special position (collinearity) makes it finite (cluster-type) or infinite.
alt_first_steps: [tools-0109] Read GHKS 'The mirror of the cubic surface' and check whether the nodal (Cayley) degeneration with boundary through nodes is covered; compute the tropicalisation of U_n.
refs: arXiv:1106.4977 (Gross–Hacking–Keel, Mirror symmetry for log Calabi–Yau surfaces I)
Gross–Hacking–Keel–Siebert, The mirror of the cubic surface, arXiv:1910.08427
Gross–Hacking–Keel–Kontsevich, Canonical bases for cluster algebras, JAMS 31 (2018), arXiv:1411.1394
alt_titles: [tools-0109] Gross–Hacking–Keel(–Siebert) theta bases for the ES log CY surface

title: Reciprocal plane / Orlik–Terao algebra viewpoint
connection: In inverted coordinates (u,v,w) = (1/x,1/y,1/z), U_n is the plane u+v+w = 4/n; its closure in the x-coordinates is the reciprocal plane of an affine hyperplane (Proudfoot–Speyer), whose coordinate ring is an Orlik–Terao algebra.
why: Reciprocal linear spaces have explicit Gröbner bases, Hilbert series and degenerations (broken circuits); a combinatorial degeneration could organise integral points.
first_step: Compute the Orlik–Terao / Proudfoot–Speyer presentation for the arrangement {u,v,w,u+v+w−4/n} and see whether integral points correspond to lattice points in a broken-circuit fan.
refs: Proudfoot–Speyer, A broken circuit ring, Beiträge Algebra Geom. 47 (2006)
Kummer–Vinzant, The Chow form of a reciprocal linear space, Michigan Math. J. 68 (2019)

title: Harpaz–Wittenberg fibration method along the x-fibration of U_n
connection: HW prove that the Brauer–Manin obstruction is the only one for fibrations over P¹ whose fibres satisfy it, under a fibration hypothesis (proved in many cases); fixing x gives a fibre ((4x−n)y − nx)((4x−n)z − nx) = (nx)², a split torus-like curve whose integral points are divisors of (nx)².
why: Makes precise the sense in which ES is 'a fibration whose fibres are divisor problems' and which hypothesis (Schinzel/HL-type) would be needed.
first_step: State the HW-type conjecture for integral points of this fibration and identify the exact divisor-problem hypothesis it needs at n = p.
refs: Harpaz–Wittenberg, On the fibration method for zero-cycles and rational points, Ann. Math. 183 (2016), arXiv:1409.0993

title: Skorobogatov–Sofos: Schinzel's Hypothesis on average → ES certificate families
connection: SS prove Schinzel's Hypothesis H for 100% of polynomials in families ordered by coefficient height and deduce Hasse principle for 100% of fibred varieties; ES certificates are values of polynomials in (c,d,e) tied to p.
why: Gives a rigorous 'almost all polynomials in a family behave' statement, the polynomial analogue of 'almost all p'.
first_step: Embed the ES Type I certificate polynomial family into a family indexed by coefficients and check which statement of SS transfers (likely 'ES for 100% of a coefficient family', not ES itself).
refs: Skorobogatov–Sofos, Schinzel Hypothesis on average and rational points, Invent. Math. (2023), arXiv:2005.02998

title: Browning–Sofos–Teräväinen Bateman–Horn & polynomial Chowla with probability 1
connection: BST prove Bateman–Horn and polynomial Chowla for almost all polynomials in large families and deduce Hasse principle with probability 1 for families of varieties.
why: ES conditional results use Dickson/Bateman–Horn-type inputs (CONDITIONAL_ES.md); BST says such inputs hold for random polynomials.
first_step: List every polynomial whose Bateman–Horn behaviour would imply ES-type statements in CONDITIONAL_ES.md and check whether it lies in a BST family.
refs: Browning–Sofos–Teräväinen, Bateman–Horn, polynomial Chowla and the Hasse principle with probability 1, arXiv:2212.10373

title: Browning–Matthiesen norm forms equal to products of linear polynomials
connection: BM prove HP/weak approximation for N_{K/ℚ}(x) = ∏ L_i(t) using additive combinatorics (GT linear equations machinery); ES Type I reads f | N(p + 2c√−d) — divisors of norms of linear forms in (c,d).
why: Additive combinatorics replaced sieve hypotheses in BM — the same could make averaged ES certificate counts in (c,d) unconditional.
first_step: Rewrite the Type I event as the solubility of N_{ℚ(√−d)/ℚ}(α) = f·g with α linear in parameters and match to BM's setting.
refs: Browning–Matthiesen, Norm forms for arbitrary number fields as products of linear polynomials, Ann. Sci. ENS 50 (2017), arXiv:1307.7641

title: Harpaz–Skorobogatov–Wittenberg: Hardy–Littlewood (finite complexity) ⇒ rational points on fibrations
connection: HSW use Green–Tao–Ziegler to prove HP for fibrations with split degenerate fibres over linear polynomials; ES fibrations have degenerate fibres over linear forms in x.
why: Unconditional finite-complexity linear prime patterns are available — the cheapest unconditional input to fibration methods.
first_step: Identify the degenerate fibres of U_n → A¹_x and test whether they are 'split over linear polynomials' in HSW's sense.
refs: Harpaz–Skorobogatov–Wittenberg, The Hardy–Littlewood conjecture and rational points, Compositio 150 (2014), arXiv:1304.3333

title: Whang: nonlinear descent on moduli of local systems → is U_n a relative character variety?
connection: Whang proves structure theorems for integral points on moduli of SL₂ local systems on surfaces (Markoff-type) via mapping class group descent; the Cayley cubic is the SL₂ character variety of the four-holed sphere at special boundary traces.
why: If U_n is (an integral model of) a relative character variety, mapping-class-group descent gives finiteness of orbits of integral points.
first_step: Match U_n to the Fricke cubic of the four-holed sphere: find boundary traces (a,b,c,d) making the Fricke cubic projectively equal to 4xyz = n(xy+yz+zx) with the ES boundary.
refs: Whang, Nonlinear descent on moduli of local systems, arXiv:1710.01848
Whang, Arithmetic of curves on moduli of local systems, arXiv:1803.04583

title: OAI 027 potential integral density on curve character varieties (claimed)
connection: OAI 027 claims integral points become Zariski dense (after finite extension) on SL_n character varieties of curves; if U_n is a character-variety component, potential density of integral points is known type.
why: Potential density is weaker than ES, but structural info about how integral points arise could be imported.
first_step: After the previous item's identification, read OAI 027's mechanism for producing integral points.

title: Lawrence–Venkatesh p-adic period maps for families of ES curves
connection: LV prove finiteness of S-integral points on hypersurfaces/curves via big monodromy of p-adic period maps; ES Type I/II fibres (fix one denominator) are genus-0 curves, but auxiliary curves (fix two certificate parameters with extra integrality) may have higher genus.
why: LV-type finiteness would be a disproof-shape tool (bounding structured solution families) rather than an existence tool.
first_step: Identify any naturally occurring higher-genus curve in the ES certificate space (e.g. requiring two simultaneous ES solutions with a shared denominator) and compute its genus.
refs: Lawrence–Venkatesh, Diophantine problems and p-adic period mappings, Invent. Math. 221 (2020), arXiv:1807.02721

title: Dimitrov–Gao–Habegger uniform Mordell for curves in the ES certificate space
connection: DGH (Annals 2021) bound the number of rational points on genus ≥ 2 curves uniformly in terms of genus and rank; ES auxiliary curves (multiple simultaneous ES conditions) have such genus.
why: Uniform bounds limit how many n can share a structured multi-solution pattern — informative for repeated-certificate statistics.
first_step: Construct the curve 'n has two ES solutions sharing x and y-ratio t' and compute its genus as a function of the constraints.
refs: Dimitrov–Gao–Habegger, Uniformity in Mordell–Lang for curves, Ann. Math. 194 (2021), arXiv:2001.10276

title: Pila–Wilkie / Binyamini–Novikov sharply o-minimal counting for ES real-analytic families
connection: Pila–Wilkie counts rational points on transcendental parts of definable sets; Binyamini–Novikov(–Zack) give effective polylog versions for sharply o-minimal structures. ES counting functions involve log-like main terms in a definable family (the real points of U_n as n varies).
why: The count M_BM(p) ≍ log² p is polylogarithmic — the same scale as sharply o-minimal point counts; a structural explanation of 'polylog' could come from there.
first_step: Check whether the set {(n, x/n, y/n, z/n)} is definable in ℝ_exp after a log-scaling and whether its algebraic part is all of it (then Pila–Wilkie says nothing).
refs: Binyamini–Novikov–Zack, Sharply o-minimal structures and sharp cellular decomposition, arXiv:2209.10972
Pila–Wilkie, The rational points of a definable set, Duke Math. J. 133 (2006)

title: Uniform dimension growth (Castryck–Cluckers–Dittmann–Nguyen) for upper bounds on f(n)
connection: CCDN prove uniform polynomial-in-degree bounds for rational points of bounded height on projective varieties (determinant method); f(n) is a count of integral points of bounded height on U_n.
why: Uniform upper bounds f(n) ≪ n^ε are inputs for second-moment/variance arguments.
first_step: Compare the CCDN bound applied to U_n with the trivial divisor bound f(n) ≪ n^{ε}; see whether it gives anything uniform in a range of heights.
refs: Castryck–Cluckers–Dittmann–Nguyen, The dimension growth conjecture, polynomial in the degree and without logarithmic factors, arXiv:1904.13109

title: Corvaja–Zannier degeneracy of integral points via the subspace theorem
connection: CZ (Annals 2004) prove non-density of integral points on affine surfaces whose boundary has many components; U_n's boundary has 3 lines (log CY), the borderline case where integral points may be dense.
why: Adding extra boundary (e.g. requiring x,y,z to avoid primes in a set S, i.e. S-integral constraints) pushes into the CZ degenerate regime — giving finiteness of 'too-structured' solution families.
first_step: Determine the number of boundary components needed for CZ when imposing 'xyz is S-smooth' and deduce a finiteness lemma for S-smooth ES solutions across n.
refs: Corvaja–Zannier, On integral points on surfaces, Ann. Math. 160 (2004)

title: S-unit equation finiteness: ES solutions with all denominators S-smooth
connection: If x, y, z, n are all S-units for a fixed finite set S, then 4/n = 1/x+1/y+1/z is an S-unit equation with finitely many non-degenerate solutions (Evertse–Schlickewei–Schmidt).
why: Gives a rigorous negative: no fixed finite set of primes can supply the denominators for infinitely many primes n — a clean barrier for 'smooth-denominator' constructions.
first_step: Write the S-unit equation and its explicit Evertse bound; compare with the data on smoothness of ES denominators at p ≤ 10^7.
refs: Evertse–Schlickewei–Schmidt, Linear equations in variables which lie in a multiplicative group, Ann. Math. 155 (2002)

title: Chabauty–Kim / quadratic Chabauty on ES-derived S-unit curves
connection: Chabauty–Kim computes integral points on P¹ − {0,1,∞} (S-unit equations) and higher-genus curves (Balakrishnan–Dogra–Müller–Tuitman–Vonk); ES-derived S-unit curves appear when two denominators are constrained to be S-units.
why: Explicit computation of the finitely many exceptions would turn the S-unit barrier into data.
first_step: For S = {2,3,5,7}, compute all solutions of 4/n = 1/x+1/y+1/z with x,y,z,n S-units by brute force / known S-unit solvers.
refs: Balakrishnan–Dogra–Müller–Tuitman–Vonk, Explicit Chabauty–Kim for the split Cartan modular curve of level 13, Ann. Math. 189 (2019)

title: Universal torsors of the Cayley cubic for parametrising ES solutions
connection: Integral points on singular del Pezzo surfaces are parametrised via universal torsors (Derenthal, Colliot-Thélène–Sansuc); the Type I/II divisor forms are presumably the torsor equations of U_n.
why: A torsor parametrisation makes integral points into lattice points with coprimality — the setting for geometry-of-numbers and circle-method counts.
first_step: Compute the Cox ring of the minimal resolution of the Cayley cubic (blow-up of P² in 6 points of a complete quadrilateral) and write the torsor equation with the ES boundary.
refs: Derenthal, Singular del Pezzo surfaces whose universal torsors are hypersurfaces, Proc. LMS 108 (2014)
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Santens / Wilsch integral Manin conjecture applied to U_n
connection: Santens proves Manin's conjecture for integral points on toric varieties; Wilsch counts integral points on log Fano threefolds; Chambert-Loir–Tschinkel give the predicted shape. f(n) is a count of integral points on the log CY U_n (not log Fano) with growing n.
why: The log CY case predicts polylog growth — matching M_BM ≍ log²; an integral-Manin framework could give a conceptual main term.
first_step: Compute Chambert-Loir–Tschinkel's predicted exponent of log B for integral points on the Cayley cubic minus triangle and compare with log² p.
refs: Santens, Manin's conjecture for integral points on toric varieties, arXiv:2312.13914
Wilsch, Integral points of bounded height on a log Fano threefold, arXiv:1901.08503

title: Browning–Le Boudec–Sawin: Hasse principle for random Fano hypersurfaces
connection: BLS prove HP for 100% of Fano hypersurfaces of fixed degree and dimension ordered by height; ES gives a one-parameter family (in n), not a random family.
why: Calibrates: one-parameter families are exactly where 'random family' methods do not apply.
first_step: Record the family dimension needed in BLS's argument and compare with the ES family {U_n} (dimension 1).
refs: Browning–Le Boudec–Sawin, The Hasse principle for random Fano hypersurfaces, Ann. Math. 197 (2023), arXiv:2006.02356

title: Sections of the ES fibration over 𝔽_q(t) via free rational curves (Browning–Sawin)
connection: Browning–Sawin use the function-field circle method to count/describe spaces of rational curves on hypersurfaces; ES polynomial identities are sections of U → A¹_n, i.e. rational curves on the total space.
why: Counting sections of bounded degree over 𝔽_q(t) quantifies the Mordell–Schinzel barrier and might find all identity families of a given degree.
first_step: Set up the moduli of degree-d sections of the ES total space over 𝔽_q(t) and compute its dimension; compare with known Mordell/Schinzel identity families.
refs: Browning–Sawin, Free rational curves on low degree hypersurfaces and the circle method, arXiv:1810.06882
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Graber–Harris–Starr sections exist over ℂ(t): why identities exist geometrically but not integrally
connection: GHS: rationally connected fibrations over curves have sections; U → A¹_n has rational fibres, so sections exist over ℂ(n) and ℚ(n) (identities with rational denominators), but Mordell–Schinzel shows none integral covering square classes.
why: Makes the integrality defect precise: it's an 'integral section' problem, whose obstructions are at the special fibres (n = square).
first_step: Compute the degenerate fibres of the integral model over Spec ℤ[n] and interpret the Mordell–Schinzel barrier as nonexistence of integral sections through specific fibre components.
refs: Graber–Harris–Starr, Families of rationally connected varieties, JAMS 16 (2003)

title: Bhargava–Gauss composition of x²+4dy² values in Type I
connection: Type I needs f | p² + 4c²d: values of the form X² + 4dY² at (p,c); divisors of represented values are represented by forms in the same genus/class group (composition).
why: Recasts the Type I event as a class-group statement about the ideal above f in the order of discriminant −16d — where Bhargava cubes / composition laws act.
first_step: For hard primes, compute the class-group element of each prime divisor of p²+4c²d and see whether the failure is explained by class-group parity.
refs: Bhargava, Higher composition laws I, Ann. Math. 159 (2004)

title: Ellenberg–Venkatesh–Westerland homological stability & Cohen–Lenstra over 𝔽_q(t)
connection: EVW prove Cohen–Lenstra-type statistics over function fields via homological stability of Hurwitz spaces; ES over 𝔽_q[T] has proved variants and class-group input in its Type I.
why: Class-group distribution in the function-field ES certificate families could be computed exactly via Hurwitz-space methods.
first_step: Identify which class groups (of 𝔽_q[T][√(−D(T))]) enter the function-field ES Type I and check whether EVW-type results give their 2-parts.
refs: Ellenberg–Venkatesh–Westerland, Homological stability for Hurwitz spaces and the Cohen–Lenstra conjecture over function fields, Ann. Math. 183 (2016)
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Landesman–Levy Cohen–Lenstra moments over function fields via stable homology
connection: Landesman–Levy (2024) prove the Cohen–Lenstra moments over 𝔽_q(t) (for q large relative to the moment) via the stable homology of non-splitting Hurwitz spaces; function-field ES is a natural test bed for such random-model predictions.
why: Large-q limits often make 'every n' statements provable (Lang–Weil); here they could validate the ES random-model zero law in a sibling.
first_step: Formulate the function-field ES lower-tail statement as a point count on a Hurwitz-type space and check whether stability arguments apply.
refs: Landesman–Levy, The Cohen–Lenstra moments over function fields via the stable homology of non-splitting Hurwitz spaces, arXiv:2410.22210
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Smith's Rédei-symbol / governing-field method for distributions of 'sterility' across p
connection: A. Smith's work on 2^∞-Selmer and class groups uses governing fields and additive combinatorics on Boolean cubes of twists to get distributions of higher Rédei symbols; ES T1 is a reciprocity (Rédei-type) obstruction and repo memos treat Rédei matrices.
why: Could prove that 'sterility patterns' up to depth k have the predicted distribution across p — a structured 100%-type statement.
first_step: Model ES sterility at depth k (fixed moduli) as a Rédei-matrix event and compute its distribution over p ≤ 10^8; compare with a Smith-type uniform model.
refs: Smith, The distribution of ℓ^∞-Selmer groups in degree ℓ twist families I, arXiv:2207.05674

title: Koymans–Pagano Stevenhagen conjecture (negative Pell) — '−1 as a target' analogy
connection: Koymans–Pagano proved Stevenhagen's conjecture on the density of D for which x² − Dy² = −1 is solvable; negative Pell asks whether −1 is a norm of a unit, ES's B2 asks whether −1 lies in the divisor quotient set.
why: Both are '−1 hitting' problems whose obstructions are 2-adic/Rédei; the negative-Pell proof technology handles exactly the −1 target.
first_step: Write the e-slice event for e prime as 'class of −1 in a ray class group generated by primes dividing N' and compare with the negative-Pell 4-rank/8-rank framework.

title: Chan–Koymans–Milovic–Pagano negative Pell lower bounds via 8-rank
connection: CKMP get the lower bound side of negative Pell densities via 8-ranks; template for proving lower bounds for '−1 attained' events.
why: ES needs a lower-bound (existence) statement — the side negative-Pell work had to prove separately.
first_step: Read the CKMP argument and identify the step converting 'distribution of ranks' into 'at least this proportion attain −1'.
refs: Chan–Koymans–Milovic–Pagano, On the negative Pell equation, arXiv:1908.01752

title: Pierce et al. ℓ-torsion & Ellenberg–Venkatesh lemma: many small split primes ⇒ small torsion
connection: The EV lemma converts many small split primes into ℓ-torsion bounds; ES Type I needs small split primes in Q(√−d) in specific classes.
why: Reverse direction: class-group structure (small 2-torsion) forces many small primes in many classes, possibly including the ES-needed class.
first_step: For d ≤ 100 and hard p, compute the classes of small split primes in Cl(−16d) and whether the Type I-needed class is hit.
refs: Ellenberg–Venkatesh, Reflection principles and bounds for class group torsion, IMRN 2007

title: Mordell–Weil / elliptic fibrations on the Cayley cubic resolution
connection: The minimal resolution of the Cayley cubic is a weak del Pezzo of degree 3; pencils of anticanonical sections give elliptic fibrations whose fibres carry group laws.
why: Group laws on fibres could produce new ES solutions from old (chord–tangent) with integrality tracked — a source of solution-generating operations.
first_step: Pick a pencil of plane sections through a node, compute the elliptic fibration, and test whether adding a torsion section maps integral ES points to integral ES points.

title: Cremona symmetries of the Cayley cubic and ES solution moves
connection: The Cayley cubic's automorphism/birational symmetry group includes S₄ on the nodes and quadratic Cremona maps (inversion x ↦ 1/x relates to the reciprocal plane); ES only uses S₃ permutations.
why: Any extra symmetry preserving the integral structure would give the missing ES 'group action' (cf. Chen/Markoff).
first_step: List the birational automorphisms of σ₃ = 0 commuting with w′ = const and test their action on ES solutions for small n.

title: Igusa / Denef–Loeser uniform p-adic integration for local densities of U_n
connection: Uniform p-adic integration (Cluckers–Loeser motivic integration) computes local densities σ_ℓ(n) uniformly in ℓ and n; the ES main term M_BM is an Euler product of such densities.
why: Uniformity in n of local densities is needed for any pointwise main-term statement.
first_step: Compute σ_ℓ(n) symbolically for the Cayley-cubic model and check uniformity across n mod ℓ^k.
refs: Cluckers–Loeser, Constructible motivic functions and motivic integration, Invent. Math. 173 (2008)

title: Perfectoid tilting Q_p(p^{1/p^∞}) ↔ 𝔽_p((t^{1/p^∞})) for local ES statements (honest low-value item)
connection: Scholze's tilting equivalence relates étale covers in mixed and equal characteristic; ES over 𝔽_q[T] has proved variants, but tilting is a local (p-adic) statement and ES's difficulty is global.
why: Recorded for completeness: the only ES-side objects it can touch are local solubility and local densities, which are already known.
first_step: Check whether any repo statement uses a local-at-p fact over 𝔽_q((t)) that lacks a mixed-characteristic counterpart; if none, close this item.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Condensed/analytic-stack adelic formalism for the integral BM set (honest low-value item)
connection: Clausen–Scholze condensed mathematics gives a uniform framework for topological algebra over all places; the integral Brauer–Manin set of U_n is an adelic topological object.
why: Only a formalism; possibly useful for a clean statement of 'non-BM integral HP failure' families, not for existence.
first_step: Check whether a condensed formulation changes anything in BL's computation; most likely not — record and close.

title: Fargues–Scholze / local Langlands — no natural ES object (recorded)
connection: Geometrisation of local Langlands (Fargues–Scholze) concerns representations of p-adic groups; ES has no evident reductive-group or Galois-representation object attached.
why: Recording the null result prevents later re-proposal; the nearest real link would go through automorphic forms attached to ES counts (theta series), which are GL₂/GL₁ and need no geometrisation.
first_step: Ask whether any ES count is a Fourier coefficient of an automorphic form on a group of rank ≥ 2; if not, close.
refs: Fargues–Scholze, Geometrization of the local Langlands correspondence, arXiv:2102.13459

title: Geometric Langlands over function fields (Gaitsgory et al.; OAI 014) for function-field ES counts
connection: Over 𝔽_q(t), Hecke eigensheaves geometrise automorphic forms; function-field ES counts are point counts on varieties over 𝔽_q whose cohomology might be automorphic.
why: Function-field ES has proved variants; a sheaf-theoretic count could give exact formulas for solution numbers in degree d.
first_step: Compute the ℓ-adic cohomology (Betti numbers) of the variety of degree-d function-field ES solutions for small q,d by point counts over 𝔽_{q^k}.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Motivic / Grothendieck-ring class of U_n and its point counts
connection: The class [U_n] in K₀(Var) and its point counts #U_n(𝔽_ℓ) are computable (Cayley cubic minus triangle); integral-point main terms are built from such local counts.
why: Exact point counts mod ℓ give exact local densities and identify any 'local sterility' structure for free.
first_step: Compute #U_n(𝔽_ℓ) symbolically as a function of n mod ℓ and verify it's ℓ² − 3ℓ + c(n,ℓ) style.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Integral points on hyperplane-arrangement complements (very affine varieties) via tropical compactification
connection: The torus part of U_n (all coordinates nonzero) is P² minus 4 lines in reciprocal coordinates — a very affine variety; tropical compactifications (Tevelev) and Huh's likelihood geometry study such varieties.
why: Tropicalisation shows which valuation patterns (sizes of x,y,z relative to n) integral points can have — a size-pattern classification of ES solutions.
first_step: Compute the tropical variety of the reciprocal plane and compare its cones with the observed (log x, log y, log z)/log n patterns of ES solutions at p ≤ 10^6.
refs: Tevelev, Compactifications of subvarieties of tori, Amer. J. Math. 129 (2007)
Huh, The maximum likelihood degree of a very affine variety, Compositio 149 (2013)

title: Lindenstrauss–Mohammadi–Wang polynomially effective unipotent equidistribution
connection: LMW (2022) give polynomially effective equidistribution for one-parameter unipotent orbits in SL₂(ℝ)×SL₂(ℝ)/Γ and SL₂(ℂ)/Γ-type spaces; ES Type II solutions are SL₂(ℤ) matrices [[f,a],[b,f′]] with ab = 4c²dp and f ≡ f′ ≡ −1 (mod 4cd), i.e. lattice points in a thin region of SL₂.
why: Effective rates are the prerequisite for counting lattice points in shrinking/thin regions (polylog many expected).
first_step: Write the Type II count as a count of Γ₀(4cd)-points in a region of SL₂(ℝ) depending on p and estimate its volume vs LMW error terms.
refs: Lindenstrauss–Mohammadi–Wang, Effective equidistribution for some one parameter unipotent flows, arXiv:2211.11099

title: Type II as SL₂(ℤ) matrices with prescribed off-diagonal product (hyperbolic lattice counting)
connection: ff′ − ab = 1 with ab = 4c²dp: Type II certificates are integer matrices of determinant 1 with diagonal ≡ −1 (mod 4cd) and off-diagonal product fixed — a hyperbolic lattice-point problem in Γ(4cd)-cosets.
why: Spectral counting in congruence subgroups (Selberg 3/16, Kim–Sarnak 7/64) applies; the fixed product ab is a 'divisor-split' constraint.
first_step: Count matrices in a coset of Γ(4cd) with |entries| ≤ T and ab = 4c²dp numerically, compare with the spectral main term.
refs: Iwaniec, Spectral Methods of Automorphic Forms (2002)
Kim–Sarnak, appendix to Kim, Functoriality for the exterior square of GL4…, JAMS 16 (2003)

title: Einsiedler–Margulis–(Mohammadi–)Venkatesh effective equidistribution of closed semisimple orbits
connection: EMV/EMMV give effective equidistribution of closed orbits of semisimple groups (e.g. SO(Q) for ternary Q) with polynomial rates; ES has ternary-form and quaternion reformulations.
why: Closed-orbit equidistribution yields local-global for representations of large integers by forms — with effective rates, potentially of a whole genus.
first_step: Pick the repo's ternary/quaternion ES reformulation (QUATERNION_ES.md) and identify the closed orbit whose equidistribution would give the needed representations.
refs: Einsiedler–Margulis–Venkatesh, Effective equidistribution for closed orbits of semisimple groups on homogeneous spaces, Invent. Math. 177 (2009), arXiv:0708.4040
Einsiedler–Margulis–Mohammadi–Venkatesh, Effective equidistribution and property (τ), JAMS 33 (2020), arXiv:1503.05884

title: Aka–Einsiedler–Shapira joint equidistribution of integer points and their orthogonal lattices
connection: AES prove joint equidistribution of primitive integer points on spheres together with the shape of their orthogonal lattice; ES certificates carry both a 'point' (solution) and an associated lattice (L_ρ).
why: Joint equidistribution could say the ES-relevant lattice shape is generic, so short vectors in cones (ES) exist for most representations.
first_step: Formulate the ES lattice L_ρ at p as the orthogonal lattice of a vector and check whether AES's setup matches.
refs: Aka–Einsiedler–Shapira, Integer points on spheres and their orthogonal grids, arXiv:1411.1272
Aka–Einsiedler–Shapira, Integer points and their orthogonal lattices, arXiv:1502.04209

title: Duke's theorem / torus packets (OAI 015 higher-dim Duke, claimed) for ES lattices
connection: Duke's theorem: class-group orbits (CM points, closed geodesics) equidistribute as discriminant → ∞; OAI 015 claims higher-degree torus-packet equidistribution. ES Type I lives in class groups of discriminant −16d tied to p.
why: Equidistribution of class-group packets is a pointwise-in-discriminant statement — at one discriminant, all of the packet equidistributes.
first_step: Find a discriminant D(p) → ∞ such that ES(p) follows from some ideal class in the packet hitting a fixed open set of the modular surface.
refs: Duke, Hyperbolic distribution problems and half-integral weight Maass forms, Invent. Math. 92 (1988)

title: Blomer–Harcos hybrid subconvexity for effective ternary representations
connection: Blomer–Harcos give hybrid subconvexity for twisted L-functions, enabling effective representation results for ternary forms (with Siegel caveats); ES's ternary analogues would need such input.
why: Effective bounds combined with 10^18 verification are the only way a ternary route could close a range.
first_step: Quantify the size beyond which Blomer–Harcos yields representations, for the discriminants arising in any ES ternary reformulation.
refs: Blomer–Harcos, Hybrid bounds for twisted L-functions, J. reine angew. Math. 621 (2008)

title: Li–Zhang's theorem on Kudla–Rapoport: unitary special cycles and an arithmetic Diff-parity
connection: KUDLA_ES links T1 to oddness of Kudla's Diff(T). In the unitary setting, Li–Zhang proved the Kudla–Rapoport conjecture (arithmetic intersection numbers = derivatives of local densities).
why: If ES certificates are special cycles on a unitary Shimura variety, intersection numbers have exact local formulas, and positivity is geometric.
first_step: Check whether the ES local densities (BM factors) match the local densities in KR for some hermitian lattice of rank 2 or 3 over Q(√−p) or Q(i).
alt_first_steps: [tools-0163] Identify which ES count, if any, appears as a degree of a special cycle (positive by geometry), per KUDLA_ES.md.
refs: arXiv:1908.01701 (Li–Zhang, Kudla–Rapoport cycles and derivatives of local densities)
Li–Zhang, Kudla–Rapoport cycles and derivatives of local densities, JAMS 35 (2022), arXiv:1908.01701
alt_titles: [tools-0163] Kudla programme / arithmetic Siegel–Weil (Li–Zhang Kudla–Rapoport) for ES theta quotients

title: Duke–Imamoḡlu–Tóth cycle integrals for ES₅ geodesic data
connection: DIT express traces of modular functions over closed geodesics (indefinite forms) as coefficients of mock modular forms; ES₅/CF-length data is geodesic (Hirzebruch–Jung, Dedekind) data of rationals tied to p.
why: A mock-modular generating function for CF-statistics could encode ES₅ counts with exact modular transformation laws.
first_step: Compute the DIT-style generating function Σ_D Tr_D(f) for f = indicator-like modular function and check whether CF length-3 counts appear.
refs: Duke–Imamoḡlu–Tóth, Cycle integrals of the j-function and mock modular forms, Ann. Math. 173 (2011)

title: Rademacher symbol (conjugacy-invariant) = linking number of the modular knot with the trefoil (Ghys)
connection: Ghys: for hyperbolic γ ∈ SL₂(ℤ), the Rademacher symbol (the conjugacy-invariant version of Rademacher's function Φ, differing by a sign/trace correction) equals the linking number of the closed geodesic (modular knot) in SL₂(ℝ)/SL₂(ℤ) = S³ − trefoil with the trefoil. If the ES sign is a function of Φ(γ_w), it becomes a linking number.
why: A topological meaning for the sign would bring knot-theoretic positivity/counting (Ghys's theorem) to ES; at least it is an exact dictionary.
first_step: Compute Φ(γ_w) for words (from the cutting sequence) and test whether Φ mod 4 determines the slot-lemma sign.
alt_first_steps: [tools-0165] Compute Rademacher symbols Ψ(M) for ES₅ certificate matrices at many p and look for a forced value range.
refs: Ghys, Knots and dynamics, Proc. ICM 2006
alt_titles: [tools-0165] Ghys modular knots / Rademacher symbol linking numbers for CF-length events

title: Weight-1 Eisenstein coefficients: ES class-divisor counts as Eisenstein Fourier coefficients along an AP
connection: #{d | N : d ≡ −1 (mod m)} = φ(m)^{−1} Σ_χ χ̄(−1) Σ_{d|N} χ(d), and Σ_{d|N} χ(d) are Fourier coefficients of Eisenstein series (weight 1 for odd χ); ES Type I at fixed p sums these at N = 4Cp+1 along C.
why: Turns ES into sums of automorphic Fourier coefficients along arithmetic progressions — a setting with spectral (shifted-convolution) technology and exact main terms.
first_step: Write R(p) explicitly as Σ_C Σ_{χ mod 4C} χ̄(−1) a_{E_χ}(4Cp+1) and separate the χ = principal/real contributions to see the main term and the T1-relevant piece.
refs: Diamond–Shurman, A First Course in Modular Forms (2005), ch. 4

title: Shifted convolution sums (Blomer, Holowinsky) for Σ_C r(4Cp+1)-type ES sums
connection: Shifted convolution sums Σ a(n)b(n+h) of automorphic coefficients have spectral asymptotics; ES Type I/II correlate divisor-class counts at N and N + (shift) across slices.
why: Second moments of ES counts over C at fixed p are shifted convolutions of Eisenstein coefficients.
first_step: Express Σ_C R_C(p)² as a shifted convolution and compute its main term numerically vs data.
refs: Blomer, Shifted convolution sums and subconvexity bounds for automorphic L-functions, IMRN 2004
Holowinsky, A sieve method for shifted convolution sums, Duke Math. J. 146 (2009)

title: Holowinsky–Soundararajan: sieve + subconvexity combo for 'large on average, so not zero' at one form
connection: Holowinsky–Soundararajan proved mass equidistribution for holomorphic Hecke forms by combining two weak methods (sieve bounds for shifted sums, Soundararajan's weak subconvexity) that each fail alone; ES's pointwise lower tail resists every single method.
why: Template for 'two complementary partial methods cover all cases' — e.g. one method for p with many small factors in 4Cp+1, another for the rest.
first_step: Split hard primes by an 'anatomy' parameter (e.g. number of small prime factors of the first slices) and check whether different repo methods cover complementary regimes.
refs: Holowinsky–Soundararajan, Mass equidistribution for Hecke eigenforms, Ann. Math. 172 (2010)

title: Nelson / Michel–Venkatesh subconvexity for Type I class-group twisted sums
connection: Subconvexity for GL₂ twists by class-group characters (Michel–Venkatesh) gives equidistribution of Heegner/CM objects; Type I class-group sums at discriminant −16d are such twisted sums.
why: Michel–Venkatesh-type bounds are what Duke-type equidistribution at a single discriminant needs.
first_step: Write the Type I count at fixed (p,d) as Σ_{ψ ∈ Ĉl(−16d)} ψ(stuff)·L-values and identify which subconvexity bound would give positivity.
refs: Michel–Venkatesh, The subconvexity problem for GL2, Publ. IHES 111 (2010)
Nelson, Bounds for standard L-functions, arXiv:2109.15230

title: Hecke-like transport between f(n) and f(ℓn)
connection: Solutions for n lift to ℓn (multiplicativity); a Hecke operator T_ℓ on solution sets would also need an adjoint pulling solutions from ℓn back to n, which is exactly the missing direction for primes.
why: If solution counts satisfied Hecke-type relations (f(ℓ²n) related to f(n), f(ℓn)), one could deduce f(p) > 0 from composite data.
first_step: Compute f(n), f(ℓn), f(ℓ²n) for n prime ≤ 10^5, ℓ ≤ 13 and fit linear relations; check whether any Hecke-type identity holds.

title: Supersingular isogeny graphs: certificates as short cycles / collisions in the ℓ-isogeny graph mod p
connection: Maximal orders in B_{p,∞} ↔ supersingular curves over F̄_p. Embeddings of CM orders ↔ endomorphisms. ES Type I ⇔ a CM-order collision, which might be a short closed walk in an isogeny graph (Pizer graphs, Ramanujan).
why: Ramanujan-graph expansion gives existence of short walks between any vertices, which is a pointwise existence mechanism (T-type thick object of size ~p/12).
first_step: For p < 500, compute which supersingular j-invariants have endomorphism rings containing the orders Λ_{d,m} and how ES levels map to isogeny degrees.
alt_first_steps: [tools-0172] Identify the quaternion algebra/order in QUATERNION_ES.md and check whether ES certificates are paths of fixed length in a Brandt/isogeny graph.
refs: Pizer, Ramanujan graphs and Hecke operators (1990)
Pizer, Ramanujan graphs and Hecke operators, Bull. AMS 23 (1990)
alt_titles: [tools-0172] Supersingular isogeny graphs (Pizer Ramanujan graphs) for ES quaternion data

title: Marcus–Spielman–Srivastava interlacing families: existence of one good member
connection: MSS proved bipartite Ramanujan graphs of every degree exist by showing the expected characteristic polynomial's root bounds the root of some member (interlacing families); ES needs one good member (certificate) among a family.
why: Interlacing gives existence beyond first-moment counting when the quantity is a polynomial root — an unusual existence mechanism worth checking for ES polynomial encodings.
first_step: Encode ES certificates at p as roots/zeros of a family of real-rooted polynomials (e.g. via the lattice L_ρ's theta function restricted to a line) and test interlacing.
refs: Marcus–Spielman–Srivastava, Interlacing families I: bipartite Ramanujan graphs of all degrees, Ann. Math. 182 (2015), arXiv:1304.4132

title: OAI 178 deterministic nonbipartite Ramanujan graphs (claimed) — explicit expanders for ES search
connection: OAI 178 claims deterministic constructions of Ramanujan graphs of all fixed degrees; explicit expanders give derandomised search/sampling over large certificate spaces.
why: Computational: deterministic sampling of (C,d) certificate grids with guaranteed coverage could make adversarial ES searches (DISPROOF_AVENUES) more efficient.
first_step: Check whether an expander walk over C ∈ [1, X] gives better coverage of ES certificates per factoring call than linear scan on hard primes.

title: Siegel–Rogers mean value / random-lattice model for ES lattices L_ρ
connection: Siegel's mean value theorem and Rogers' higher moments give the distribution of lattice-point counts in random lattices; ES(p) ⟺ some lattice L_ρ(p) has a vector in a cone (LATTICE_MEETING).
why: A random-lattice model predicts P(no vector in cone) and its p-dependence — a cleaner heuristic than divisor lotteries.
first_step: Compute covolume and cone volume for L_ρ(p) and compare empirical 'empty cone' frequency with Rogers' Poisson prediction.
refs: Rogers, Mean values over the space of lattices, Acta Math. 94 (1955)

title: Strömbergsson–Venkatesh small solutions to linear congruences
connection: Strömbergsson–Venkatesh study the distribution of the smallest solution of linear congruences via equidistribution of lattices; ES certificates are small solutions of congruences with modulus tied to p.
why: Gives the limiting distribution of 'smallest certificate size', comparable with ES's forced windows.
first_step: Write the ES Type II certificate as a small solution of a linear congruence system mod 4cd and compare its size distribution with SV's limit law.
refs: Strömbergsson–Venkatesh, Small solutions to linear congruences and Hecke equidistribution, Acta Arith. 118 (2005)

title: Browning–Vinogradov effective Ratner for SL(2,ℝ)⋉ℝ² (gaps in √n mod 1) for affine ES lattices
connection: Browning–Vinogradov make Ratner equidistribution effective on ASL(2) to count affine-lattice events; ES Type I/II with a fixed shift (p) are affine-lattice problems (L + p·v).
why: Affine lattices capture the inhomogeneous p-dependence that homogeneous equidistribution misses.
first_step: Formulate the ES certificate set as points of an affine lattice in a region and check the BV setup.
refs: Browning–Vinogradov, Effective Ratner theorem for SL(2,R)⋉R^2 and gaps in √n modulo 1, J. LMS 94 (2016), arXiv:1311.6387

title: Geodesic-flow coding (Series) of γ_w: ES₅ as a closed geodesic with 3 cusp excursions of prescribed depths
connection: Caroline Series' coding links the cutting sequence of a geodesic to its CF expansion, so cusp-excursion depths correspond to partial quotients. A word gives a closed geodesic whose (HJ) coding has 3 blocks of depths (v, t, u), plus a p-condition.
why: Shrinking-target and logarithm-law results (Sullivan) describe cusp excursions statistically. Prescribed exact-depth triples relate to 'periodic orbits with prescribed excursions' counts (Pollicott, Lalley).
first_step: Count closed geodesics whose coding is exactly a 3-block HJ word with depths in given ranges; compare with the word count via the p-constraint.
alt_first_steps: [tools-0178] Draw, for hard primes, the Farey path of the relevant rationals and record the minimal crossing count; compare with the length-3 requirement.
refs: Series, The modular surface and continued fractions (J. LMS 1985)
Series, The modular surface and continued fractions, J. LMS 31 (1985)
alt_titles: [tools-0178] Series coding of geodesics: ES₅ as short cutting sequences

title: Katz equidistribution of Kloosterman angles for fixed-modulus ES counts
connection: Katz: Kloosterman angles at a fixed prime modulus equidistribute w.r.t. Sato–Tate as the argument varies; ES fixed-modulus counts (FIXED_MODULUS_SHOTS) reduce to Kloosterman-type sums.
why: Gives exact variance/distribution of ES residue counts across p mod ℓ.
first_step: Compute the ES count mod a prime ℓ as a function of p mod ℓ and test Sato–Tate statistics of its fluctuating part.
refs: Katz, Gauss Sums, Kloosterman Sums, and Monodromy Groups (1988)

title: Murmurations for ES counts (He–Lee–Oliver–Pozdnyakov; Zubrilina)
connection: Murmurations: averages of Frobenius traces a_p over families ordered by conductor show oscillations in p/N, explained by Zubrilina via trace formula; ES counts f(p) averaged over p in a window with normalisation by a scale (e.g. 4C ~ p^θ) might show analogous oscillations.
why: A murmuration-type oscillation would reveal a hidden spectral term in ES counts — new structure for heuristics.
first_step: Plot normalised ES counts f(p)/log²p averaged over p in windows against p mod M / p modulo small structures and against p/X for X ranges; look for oscillatory patterns.
refs: He–Lee–Oliver–Pozdnyakov, Murmurations of elliptic curves, arXiv:2204.10140

title: Keating–Snaith / random-matrix models for families in the ES character expansion
connection: RMT predicts moments of L-function families; ES counts expand over Dirichlet characters mod 4C, i.e. involve families of L-values / character sums.
why: If the ES count's fluctuating part is governed by an L-function family, RMT predicts its distribution, including lower tails.
first_step: Identify the family of L-functions (if any) whose values weight the ES count (via Eisenstein coefficients) and check its symmetry type.
refs: Keating–Snaith, Random matrix theory and ζ(1/2+it), Comm. Math. Phys. 214 (2000)
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Rudnick–Soundararajan lower bounds for moments → 'at least one large term'
connection: Rudnick–Soundararajan prove lower bounds for moments of L-function families by a simple Hölder trick; ES needs lower bounds for a count of certificates.
why: Moment lower bounds (≥ expected order) for R(p) over a C-family at fixed p would show certificates are not all absent — but only if the family is at fixed p.
first_step: Apply the RS Hölder trick to Σ_C R_C(p) with weights and see whether it gives Σ_C R_C(p) ≫ main term at a single p.
refs: Rudnick–Soundararajan, Lower bounds for moments of L-functions, PNAS 102 (2005)

title: Heap–Radziwiłł–Soundararajan sharp fractional moments → lower tails
connection: HRS give sharp upper bounds for fractional moments of ζ; small-moment control is equivalent to lower-tail information for log-normal-like quantities.
why: If log R(p) were approximately Gaussian (log-normal counts), fractional moments of R would control P(R small).
first_step: Fit the distribution of log R(p) at p ≤ 10^8 (data exists) and test log-normality; compute fractional moments.
refs: Heap–Radziwiłł–Soundararajan, Sharp upper bounds for fractional moments of the Riemann zeta function, Q. J. Math. 70 (2019)

title: Nicolas–Serre Hecke algebra mod 2 for parity of ES counts
connection: Nicolas–Serre describe coefficients of modular forms mod 2 via a nilpotent Hecke algebra; the repo PROVED complement pairing makes level counts even and R(p)/2 mod 2 looks like a fair coin.
why: If ES counts relate to Eisenstein coefficients, their parities might be governed by mod-2 modular forms rather than randomness.
first_step: Compute R(p)/2 mod 2 and the parity of class-divisor counts at 4Cp+1 and compare with the mod-2 behaviour of the corresponding Eisenstein coefficients.
refs: Nicolas–Serre, Formes modulaires de niveau 1 en caractéristique 2…, C. R. Math. 350 (2012)

title: Radchenko–Viazovska Fourier interpolation applied to ES lattice theta data (speculative)
connection: Fourier interpolation reconstructs f from values at √n and f̂ at √n; ES lattice reformulations have theta series whose coefficients count certificates.
why: Interpolation formulas give exact identities linking counts at different scales — potentially forcing a nonzero coefficient.
first_step: Check whether ES certificate counts are coefficients of a theta series of a fixed-dimension lattice; if not, close.
refs: Radchenko–Viazovska, Fourier interpolation on the real line, Publ. IHES 129 (2019), arXiv:1701.00265

title: Pila–Shankar–Tsimerman André–Oort heights for the CM tetrahedron of the Cayley cubic
connection: PST proved André–Oort via canonical height bounds; the Cayley cubic/Markoff CM dictionary in the repo (cayley_markoff_cm) relates special points to CM data.
why: Height bounds for special points might constrain which CM points carry ES solutions (a finiteness/distribution statement).
first_step: Locate the CM-point parametrisation in cayley_markoff_cm.md and check whether ES integral points map to special points of bounded height.
refs: Pila–Shankar–Tsimerman, Canonical heights on Shimura varieties and the André–Oort conjecture, arXiv:2109.08788

title: Bruinier–Funke theta lifts / Borcherds products for ES generating functions
connection: Theta lifts produce modular generating functions of traces/cycle counts; Borcherds products give automorphic forms with prescribed divisors. ES counts across p could be coefficients of such a lift if they are traces over class groups.
why: A Borcherds-type product with zeros encoding ES failures would turn ES into a divisor statement for an automorphic form.
first_step: Test whether Σ_p f(p) q^p (or a class-group-trace version) is the holomorphic part of a weak harmonic Maass form by checking coefficient growth and congruences.
refs: Bruinier–Funke, On two geometric theta lifts, Duke Math. J. 125 (2004)

title: Effective Oppenheim (Lindenstrauss–Margulis–Mohammadi–Shah) for indefinite ternary ES forms
connection: LMMS give effective density of values of indefinite ternary forms at integer points; the quadratic part n(xy+yz+zx) of U_n is an indefinite ternary form.
why: Effective value-distribution of the quadratic part near targets proportional to xyz may constrain solution geometry.
first_step: Write ES as Q(x,y,z) = (4/n)·xyz with Q = xy+yz+zx and see whether effective Oppenheim-type counting with a cubic weight is meaningful.
refs: Lindenstrauss–Margulis–Mohammadi–Shah, Quantitative behavior of unipotent flows and an effective avoidance principle, arXiv:1904.00290

title: Hyperbolic circle problem in Γ₀(N) for e-slice counts
connection: Counting Γ₀(N)-orbit points in hyperbolic discs has spectral asymptotics with error controlled by exceptional eigenvalues; e-slice certificates ab | N with a ≡ −b (mod e) can be phrased via matrices with lower-left entry divisible by e.
why: Moves the e-slice count into a standard spectral counting problem.
first_step: Construct the matrix encoding of e-slice certificates and count numerically vs Γ₀(e) disc-count predictions.
refs: Iwaniec, Spectral Methods of Automorphic Forms (2002), ch. 12

title: Theta quotient / eta-quotient identities for ES counts (exact formulas)
connection: Eta-quotient identities give exact divisor-sum formulas for representation numbers (e.g. r₄, r₈); ES has theta-quotient reformulations in the repo.
why: An exact formula (sum of divisor functions) for some ES-adjacent count would make positivity checkable.
first_step: Search the ES theta-quotient reformulation for a modular form of small level whose coefficients equal an ES sub-count; test by computing 200 coefficients.
refs: Köhler, Eta Products and Theta Series Identities (2011)

title: Hirzebruch–Jung / Dedekind sums reciprocity as a forcing identity
connection: Dedekind-sum reciprocity s(a,c)+s(c,a) = (a/c + c/a + 1/(ac))/12 − 1/4 relates HJ continued fractions of a/c and c/a; ES certificates have HJ/CF data (DEDEKIND_ES).
why: Exact reciprocity laws are the only kind of 'charge identity' that work pointwise; the repo found the Dedekind–HJ discharging charge χ-blind.
first_step: Look for a twisted Dedekind sum (with a character mod 4C) whose reciprocity law is χ-sensitive and test on ES certificates.

title: LLL / Coppersmith small roots for ES Type I certificates at fixed p
connection: Coppersmith's method finds small roots of modular polynomials; Type I asks for f | p² + 4c²d with f ≡ −p (mod 4cd), a small-root problem for a polynomial in (c,d) modulo an unknown divisor (Howgrave-Graham variant).
why: Turns certificate search into lattice reduction with provable size ranges; complements factoring-based search at 10^18–10^25.
first_step: Implement Howgrave-Graham's 'approximate common divisor / unknown divisor' lattice for N(c) = p² + 4c²d, d fixed, and compare its hit rate with brute force at p ~ 10^20.
refs: Coppersmith, Small solutions to polynomial equations, and low exponent RSA vulnerabilities, J. Cryptology 10 (1997)
Howgrave-Graham, Approximate integer common divisors, CaLC 2001

title: ECM/GNFS-free certificate search: choose C so 4Cp+1 is smooth-friendly
connection: Certificate search is bottlenecked by factoring p-tied integers; ES only needs some divisor in a class, so partial factorisation (ECM to bound B) suffices for most C.
why: Practical speed-up for adversarial searches beyond 10^25, giving better 'hardest prime' calibration data.
first_step: Measure on hard primes the fraction of certificates found using only ECM with B1 = 10^4 on the first X slices; estimate cost per certificate.
refs: Lenstra, Factoring integers with elliptic curves, Ann. Math. 126 (1987)

title: Harvey–van der Hoeven O(n log n) multiplication / fast sieving for verification beyond 10^18
connection: Asymptotically optimal integer multiplication and modern segmented sieving speed up the ES verification pipeline (Salez 10^17, Mihnea–Dumitru 10^18).
why: Extending verification is calibration only, but cheap engineering improvements shift the 'explicit range' needed by any analytic tail.
first_step: Profile the repo's verify.py on a 10^9 block at 10^18 and identify whether multiplication, sieving, or modular inversion dominates.
refs: Harvey–van der Hoeven, Integer multiplication in time O(n log n), Ann. Math. 193 (2021)

title: Lean-checked certificate verifier for ES solutions at specific hard primes
connection: A Lean `decide`/`norm_num` proof that 4/p = 1/x+1/y+1/z for explicit p is trivial; a verified checker for large batches (with external computation) mirrors certified-SAT practice.
why: Turns computational evidence (e.g. 10^18 claims) into checkable artefacts — important since the 10^18 claim is an unrefereed preprint.
first_step: Write a Lean function checking ES solutions given (p,x,y,z) and run it on the repo's hard-prime certificates.

title: AlphaProof / LLM provers on campaign lemmas
connection: AI provers (AlphaProof 2024; DeepSeek-Prover, Kimina, Aristotle) solve olympiad-level formal problems; the campaign has many small formal lemmas (sterility, forcing lines, GT1) that are olympiad-like.
why: Automating the verification of small PROVED items frees effort and might find counterexamples to mis-stated lemmas.
first_step: Extract 10 short PROVED lemmas from DISCOVERIES.md into Lean statements and run an available open prover on them.

title: Davies et al. ML-guided intuition: which features predict f(p)?
connection: Davies et al. (Nature 2021) used attribution on trained models to discover knot-invariant and Kazhdan–Lusztig relations; the repo has f_I, f_II for all p ≤ 10^8.
why: A saliency analysis might find an unexpected invariant (beyond p mod small moduli) controlling low-count primes — e.g. a CF or class-number feature.
first_step: Train gradient-boosted trees on features (p mod q for q ≤ 100, n₂(p), class numbers h(−p), h(−4p), CF of √p, Legendre symbols) to predict f(p)/log²p; inspect feature importance.
refs: Davies et al., Advancing mathematics by guiding human intuition with AI, Nature 600 (2021)

title: PatternBoost / Wagner RL for counterexamples to ES sub-conjectures
connection: Wagner (2021) and PatternBoost (Charton–Ellenberg–Wagner–Williamson 2024) find counterexamples to combinatorial conjectures via RL/transformer-guided local search; ES sub-conjectures (U(n) sporadic set, S_{n,k} zero patterns, sibling failures) are searchable.
why: Finding new sporadic exceptions in siblings refines the zero law; finding none strengthens conjectural lists.
first_step: Run local-search guided by a learned score over n ≤ 10^12 restricted to low-count residue cells for U(n) and S_{n,−4}.
refs: Wagner, Constructions in combinatorics via neural networks, arXiv:2104.14516

title: Ramanujan Machine-style search for polynomial-CF identities producing ES₅ words
connection: The Ramanujan Machine (Raayoni et al., Nature 2021) searches polynomial continued fractions for constant identities; ES₅ solutions are short CF words with entries polynomial in parameters (Mordell families).
why: Automated search over polynomial CF word families could find new parametric families covering more residue classes.
first_step: Enumerate length-3 ES₅ words whose entries are degree-≤2 polynomials in t with small coefficients and record which residue classes mod 840·k they cover.
refs: Raayoni et al., Generating conjectures on fundamental constants with the Ramanujan Machine, Nature 590 (2021)

title: Hilbert's tenth problem over ℚ (OAI 004, claimed) and Koenigsmann: logical status of ES variants
connection: OAI 004 claims H10 over ℚ is undecidable; Koenigsmann defined ℤ in ℚ by a universal formula. ES is a Π₁ statement once solution sizes are bounded (x ≤ 3n/4, etc.).
why: Being Π₁, ES is 'decided by a counterexample if false'; logic tools say nothing about truth, but undecidability results for families (e.g. 'given polynomial family, does every n have an Egyptian representation') calibrate generality.
first_step: Write ES explicitly as a bounded-quantifier Π₁ sentence and note which generalisations (k/n with arbitrary k, unbounded term count) cross into undecidable territory.
refs: Koenigsmann, Defining ℤ in ℚ, Ann. Math. 183 (2016)

title: Single-fold Diophantine representations (OAI 242, claimed) — uniqueness promise versions of ES
connection: OAI 242 claims every r.e. set has a single-fold Diophantine representation; ES counts solutions (f(n) ≍ polylog), the opposite of single-fold.
why: Records a logic/arithmetic contrast: ES's richness (many solutions) is what makes it plausibly true; single-fold encodings show uniqueness is achievable in general.
first_step: None beyond reading the OAI statement; close unless a uniqueness variant of ES ('exactly one solution of shape X') becomes interesting.

title: Complexity of finding an ES solution: factoring-oracle reduction
connection: Given p, an ES solution is found by factoring a few p-tied integers until a divisor lands in the class; expected polylog many integers. So ES-search is (heuristically) in ZPP^{FACTOR}, and in BQP via Shor.
why: A complexity statement 'ES search is as hard as factoring' (or easier) would be a novel angle; a proof that search is easy for all p would be a constructive ES proof.
first_step: Formalise the reduction and test whether ES certificates can be found without any factoring (e.g. via Coppersmith) for random large p.
refs: Shor, Polynomial-time algorithms for prime factorization…, SIAM J. Comput. 26 (1997)

title: OAI 142 deterministic polynomial factorisation over 𝔽_p (claimed) for deterministic ES search mod p
connection: OAI 142 claims deterministic polynomial-time factoring of polynomials over prime fields; deterministic square roots mod p appear in Type I (p² ≡ −4c²d mod f).
why: Derandomising the local steps of ES search; minor but concrete.
first_step: Identify randomised steps in the repo's ES search code (square roots mod primes) and note whether deterministic alternatives matter.

title: Interval/ball arithmetic certified analytic constants (Arb/FLINT) for explicit exceptional sets
connection: Arb provides rigorous numerics; explicit versions of the repo's exceptional-set or main-term constants need certified evaluation of Euler products and integrals.
why: Needed for any explicit statement (calibration with verification).
first_step: Compute M_BM(p)'s Euler-product constant with Arb to 30 digits with certified error.
refs: Johansson, Arb: efficient arbitrary-precision midpoint-radius interval arithmetic, IEEE Trans. Comput. 66 (2017)

title: Flag-algebra / SDP certificates for density inequalities on ES residue menus
connection: Razborov's flag algebras prove density inequalities via SDP; finite residue-menu questions ('what fraction of classes mod M can a menu of shape X cover') are density optimisation problems.
why: SDP duality gives certified upper bounds on coverage — sharpening B1-type statements quantitatively.
first_step: Formulate menu coverage mod M as an LP/SDP and compute the dual bound for small menus.
refs: Razborov, Flag algebras, J. Symbolic Logic 72 (2007)

title: Integer linear programming for minimal sterile residue systems
connection: Sterile residue classes (STERILE_*) are CRT systems where all certificates of bounded size fail; ILP can find minimal-modulus sterile systems or prove none exist below a bound.
why: Calibrates how deep sterility can go — the disproof-shape analogue of covering systems.
first_step: Encode 'class r mod M is sterile for all certificates with C ≤ K' as constraints and minimise M with an ILP solver for K ≤ 20.

title: Equational-theories-project-style crowdsourced + automated exploration of ES variants
connection: Tao's Equational Theories Project (2024) combined ATPs, Lean and crowdsourcing to settle ~22 million implications; ES has a large lattice of variants (k/n, number of terms, sign constraints, rings) with implication structure.
why: Mapping the implication lattice among ES variants (which imply which; which fail where) is mechanical and ATP-friendly.
first_step: List 50 ES variants in the repo (siblings, coprime/non-coprime, Type I/II, ES₅, I3) and compute an implication matrix with counterexamples from data.
refs: Tao et al., The Equational Theories Project, arXiv:2512.07087
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Proof mining / Kohlenbach: extracting bounds from ineffective ES-adjacent proofs
connection: Proof mining extracts explicit bounds from ineffective proofs (Kohlenbach); ES-adjacent results (Siegel-dependent exceptional-set bounds) are ineffective.
why: May yield explicit forms without new analytic input.
first_step: Identify the ineffective step in the repo's 3/4-exponent note and check whether it's a Siegel zero use (needs real effectivity) or a compactness argument (minable).

title: Distributed GPU search for counterexamples in Mordell-hard cells beyond 10^18 (targeted, not exhaustive)
connection: Exhaustive verification is at 10^18; targeted search in the lowest-count residue cells (DISPROOF_AVENUES) at 10^20–10^30 is feasible on GPUs with Type II e-slice tests.
why: Calibration of the zero law at much larger scales where expected counts are still polylog.
first_step: Port the e-slice test to CUDA for a fixed cell and benchmark primes per second at 10^24.

title: Probabilistic primality + certification (ECPP) for adversarial hard primes
connection: Hard primes beyond 10^18 are BPSW-probable; ECPP certificates make them rigorous primes.
why: Small but necessary hygiene for any claimed record-hard prime.
first_step: Produce ECPP certificates (Primo/CM) for the repo's hardest primes (e.g. 2054098191162848070241).
refs: Atkin–Morain, Elliptic curves and primality proving, Math. Comp. 61 (1993)

title: Natural-proofs-style meta-barrier for ES
connection: Razborov–Rudich formalise why 'natural' combinatorial properties can't prove circuit lower bounds; the campaign's barrier theorems (B1–B9) are informal analogues for ES proof strategies.
why: A formal meta-barrier would classify proof strategies by a property (e.g. 'treats the p-tied integer as random') and prove they can't succeed against a pseudorandom model where ES fails.
first_step: Construct a random model (consistent with all known local and average facts) in which ES fails for a positive proportion of p, and list which proof techniques are 'relativising' to it.

title: Fake-ES models: same local statistics, almost-all holds, infinitely many failures
connection: Kahane–Katznelson show a.e. results can be sharp for any null set. Build synthetic 'ES-like' problems (random divisor data with ES's congruence statistics, or ES with a perturbed rule) where Vaughan's proof goes through verbatim but failures are infinite; the real proof must use a feature the fakes lack.
why: Identifies which properties of the integers any ES proof must use — the constructive face of the barrier map.
first_step: Construct a random model of 'divisors of 4Cp+1' with independent prime-factor classes, run the almost-all argument, and check what pointwise statement fails.
alt_first_steps: [tools-0219] Build a model: random integers with correct local divisibility but with an added sparse 'conspiracy' making all certificates fail for p in a thin set; check consistency with ET averages and Vaughan.
refs: Kolmogorov, Fund. Math. 4 (1923)/ C. R. 1926 (everywhere divergent L^1 Fourier series)
alt_titles: [tools-0219] Pseudorandomness of the Liouville/divisor patterns vs ES: 'random model where ES fails' construction

upgrade: Large values / Kolmogorov counterexample (a.e. cannot be upgraded)

title: Kolmogorov-complexity view: a least counterexample has a short description
connection: The least ES counterexample (if any) is defined by a short Π₁ formula, so has low description complexity; probabilistic models treat failing p as 'random'.
why: Low-complexity numbers are not random-like; a heuristic tension worth stating (cf. Chaitin) but unlikely to give mathematics.
first_step: Record as a heuristic remark; no computation.
refs: Li–Vitányi, An Introduction to Kolmogorov Complexity (2019)

title: Persistent data releases + OEIS-style sequence mining for ES statistics
connection: Many breakthroughs came from noticing sequences (OEIS); ES statistics (min-count primes, record-hard primes, sibling failure lists) could be matched against OEIS.
why: Cheap: an OEIS hit could connect ES failure sets of siblings to known sequences (e.g. S_{n,−4} failures {2,9,21,165,945,1197}).
first_step: Query OEIS for the sibling failure lists and U(n)'s sporadic set {105, 2961, 3985, 25305, 111969, 978145}.

title: Statistical change-point tests on hardness vs p (detecting new obstruction scales)
connection: Change-point and extreme-value statistics detect regime shifts; ES min-count/log²p over p ≤ 10^8 and adversarial data at 10^25 could reveal a scale where hardness behaves differently.
why: A detected trend in normalised minimum would inform P(ES false) calibrations.
first_step: Fit an extreme-value (Gumbel/GEV) model to block minima of f(p)/log²p over dyadic ranges and extrapolate the expected minimum at 10^30.
refs: Coles, An Introduction to Statistical Modeling of Extreme Values (2001)

title: OAI 012 joint Dickman law for consecutive integers ↔ consecutive Type II slices
connection: OAI 012 claims log P⁺(n)/log n and log P⁺(n+1)/log n are asymptotically independent (Erdős–Pomerance). At fixed p the Type II slices N_e = (p+e)/4, e = e₀, e₀+4, …, are consecutive integers N, N+1, N+2, …
why: Joint anatomy of consecutive integers is exactly the joint law of successive ES slices at one p; independence-type theorems for consecutive integers are the right genre (though they average over n, here n ≈ p/4 + small).
first_step: Measure, at hard primes, the joint distribution of (ω, P⁺, smoothness) of N, N+1, …, N+K for the first K slices vs random consecutive integers near p/4; read OAI 012's method for short-range uniformity.

title: OAI 011 Poisson–Dirichlet law for prime factors of p−1 → law for factors of p+e
connection: OAI 011 claims the ordered normalised log prime factors of p−1 converge to PD(1); the e-slice integers (p+e)/4 are shifted primes for fixed e.
why: A PD(1) law for shifted primes p+e (fixed e) gives the distribution of the 'generator set' of the ES quotient set across p — the right random model for e-slice success.
first_step: Compute the empirical law of prime-factor log-ratios of (p+3)/4 for p ≤ 10^8 and compare with PD(1); then simulate e-slice success under PD(1).

title: OAI 007 ordinary two-point Chowla (claimed) for λ-weighted ES counts
connection: OAI 007 claims Σ_{n≤X} λ(a₁n+b₁)λ(a₂n+b₂) ≪ X/(log X)^c for fixed affine forms; ES certificate counts can be twisted by λ of the p-tied integers to detect parity structure.
why: Parity of Ω(4Cp+1) correlates with whether its divisors can split into classes; ordinary (non-log) two-point Chowla removes the log-averaging that blocked earlier transfers.
first_step: Check whether 'number of divisors ≡ −1 (mod 4) of N' correlates with λ(N) for N in an AP, and if so formulate the needed correlation along the forms (4Cp+1, 4C′p+1).

title: OAI 029 Artin primitive roots for every admissible base (claimed) — order-2-adic statistics
connection: OAI 029 claims ≫ x/log²x primes p < 2x with a primitive mod p; for the ES e-slice with prime e, −1 ∈ ⟨ℓ⟩ ⟺ ord_e(ℓ) even, and a primitive root ℓ | N gives −1 = ℓ^{(e−1)/2} (but the exponent must be realised inside N).
why: Primitive-root abundance controls how often a single prime factor generates −1 multiplicatively — a precondition (not sufficient) for e-slice success.
first_step: For hard primes, count slices where some prime factor of N is a primitive root mod e, and how often −1 is then in Q.
