title: OAI 021 quadratic Jacobsthal bound (claimed) for slices avoiding bad primes
connection: OAI 021 claims every interval of C·k²/(log log k)² integers contains one coprime to any m with ≤ k prime factors; ES e-slices form an interval of consecutive N_e.
why: Guarantees, within a short window of slices, an N_e coprime to any prescribed bad modulus — e.g. avoiding primes that obstruct (−1 ∉ Q). It forces avoidance, not hitting, but is a pointwise every-interval statement.
first_step: Identify a finite set of 'obstructing primes' for e-slice success at a hard prime and compute whether Jacobsthal-avoidance within the first slices helps.

title: Iwaniec / Ford–Green–Konyagin–Maynard–Tao Jacobsthal & large-gap sieves for sterile windows
connection: Large-gap constructions (FGKMT) sieve out long intervals by choosing residue classes cleverly; ES sterile windows (all slices in a window fail) are analogous 'sieved-out' intervals.
why: The machinery (hypergraph covering, Maynard weights) for building long sifted intervals tells how long a sterile slice window could be.
first_step: Compute the longest run of failing e-slices at hard primes and compare with a FGKMT-type construction of residue classes killing a window.
refs: Ford–Green–Konyagin–Maynard–Tao, Long gaps between primes, JAMS 31 (2018)

title: OAI 026 positive lower density of large prime gaps (claimed) — calibration for sterile runs
connection: OAI 026 claims a positive proportion of prime gaps exceed C log p for any C; analogous 'long sterile runs' of slices at positive density would be a calibration point for ES heuristics.
why: Shows how 'rare-event at a fixed scale with positive density' results are proved — compare with ES's polylog windows.
first_step: Read the OAI 026 mechanism and test whether long failing slice-runs at fixed length have positive density among primes in data.

title: OAI 020 squarefree values of quartics (claimed) — squarefreeness of p-tied quadratics
connection: OAI 020 claims squarefree density for irreducible quartics; ES p-tied integers p² + 4c²d are quadratic/quartic in parameters, and square factors matter for divisor structure (T1 is a square phenomenon).
why: Squarefreeness of p² + 4c²d in c is classical (quadratic); quartic families arise when c and d are tied (d = c² etc.).
first_step: Check the frequency of square factors in Type I values at hard primes and whether failures correlate with square divisors.

title: OAI 023 Patterson cubic Gauss sum first moment (claimed) — cubic analogue of ES characters
connection: OAI 023 claims Patterson's first-moment asymptotic unconditionally; ES's 'class of divisors' uses quadratic/Dirichlet characters, while 4/n ↔ cubic forms suggest cubic residue structure (cubic surface).
why: Low expectation; recorded because ES's cubic surface could have a cubic-character layer the campaign hasn't probed.
first_step: Test whether ES counts f(p) for p ≡ 1 (mod 3) correlate with the cubic residue character of 2 or 4 mod p.
refs: Dunn–Radziwiłł, Bias in cubic Gauss sums: Patterson's conjecture, arXiv:2109.07463

title: OAI 013 Ostmann inverse Goldbach (claimed) — additive irreducibility of ES-good sets
connection: OAI 013 claims the primes are not A+B up to finite modification; ES-type sets (n with Type I solution of a shape) have additive/multiplicative decomposition questions.
why: Not a route to ES, but a structural fact about sets of n defined by divisor events: the set of n covered by a family is a set of multiples (multiplicatively decomposable).
first_step: Record and close unless an additive decomposition of the covered set appears.

title: OAI 028 Gaussian moat (claimed) — ES_Q1 Gaussian sibling geometry
connection: OAI 028 claims no infinite bounded-step walk through Gaussian primes; ES_Q1 over ℤ[i] has failures at Gaussian primes 2+5i, 4+5i, …
why: Coverage-transfer technique (sieve on Gaussian primes in sectors) might bound or locate Gaussian ES_Q1 failures by angle.
first_step: Plot ES_Q1 failure Gaussian primes by argument and norm; check for angular structure (the repo killed one angular-pinching claim).
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: OAI 006 Goldfeld densities (claimed) — rank-parity as a model for ES parity layers
connection: OAI 006 claims Goldfeld's conjecture for quadratic twists; ES's parity layers (R(p)/2 mod 2 fair coin) resemble root-number parity statistics in twist families.
why: Root numbers are local products — a fully local parity; ES parity looks random — comparing clarifies whether an ES 'root number' exists.
first_step: Test whether R(p)/2 mod 2 is predicted by any product of local symbols (p/ℓ) for small ℓ via logistic regression.

title: OAI 138 Subset Sum in 2^{0.49n} (claimed) — e-slice as subset-product search
connection: e-slice success is a subset-product problem: choose a sub-multiset of prime factors of N whose product ratio is −1 mod e; with ω(N) small, brute force is trivial, but for highly composite N or pooled factors it's subset-sum in ℤ/(e−1) (discrete logs).
why: Fast subset-sum algorithms matter only if one pools many factors (e.g. across slices) — a computational lens on pooled certificates.
first_step: Estimate typical ω(N) at slices; if pooled designs push it past ~40, benchmark meet-in-the-middle subset-product search.

title: OAI 182 power savings for polynomial differences at primes (claimed)
connection: OAI 182 claims power-saving Sárközy-type bounds for differences P(p), p prime; ES certificate polynomials evaluated at primes are a polynomial-at-primes family.
why: Weak link; records that difference-set methods at prime arguments now have power savings.
first_step: Check whether any ES certificate condition is a 'difference set avoids P(primes)' statement; likely close.

title: OAI 018 Margulis–Platonov (claimed) — normal subgroups of SL₂ over global fields for ES words
connection: OAI 018 claims Margulis–Platonov over number fields; normal-subgroup structure of arithmetic groups matters for congruence-subgroup and thin-group questions about ES₅ words.
why: Very indirect; listed for completeness of the SL₂-word line.
first_step: Close unless an ES SL₂ formulation needs non-congruence normal subgroups.

title: OAI 002/030 BSD formula & modularity over imaginary quadratic fields (claimed) — ES has no elliptic curve
connection: These claimed results concern elliptic curves; ES's surface is rational (Cayley cubic) with no natural attached elliptic curve except via chosen fibrations.
why: Null result recorded; the only conceivable link is through elliptic fibrations of the Cayley cubic resolution (separate item).
first_step: Close.

title: OAI 024 asymptotic count of totients (claimed) — value-set counting technique
connection: OAI 024 claims an asymptotic for V(x) = #{φ(n) ≤ x}; Ford's anatomy of totients machinery counts value sets of multiplicative functions — ES's 'set of n with an ES solution of shape S' is a value set problem.
why: Value-set counting with structured preimages mirrors 'set of 4/n reachable by shape S'.
first_step: Read OAI 024 introduction for the method and see if 'n = 4xyz/(xy+yz+zx)' value-set counting fits.
refs: Ford, The distribution of totients, Ramanujan J. 2 (1998)

title: Bergström–Diaconu–Petersen–Westerland moments of L-functions over function fields
connection: BDPW compute all moments of quadratic L-functions over 𝔽_q(t) for q large via homological stability; function-field ES counts expand over quadratic/Dirichlet characters.
why: Exact function-field moment formulas would test any ES lower-tail heuristic precisely.
first_step: Identify the character family in the function-field ES count and compare with BDPW's families.
refs: Bergström–Diaconu–Petersen–Westerland, Hyperelliptic curves, the scanning map, and moments of families of quadratic L-functions, arXiv:2302.07664
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Katz monodromy of the function-field ES certificate cover
connection: Over 𝔽_q(t), the variety of ES certificates over the space of prime polynomials of degree n has a monodromy group; big monodromy ⇒ equidistribution ⇒ positive counts for large q.
why: Computing this group exposes the function-field analogue of T1 (failure at squares = monodromy degeneracy?).
first_step: Compute Frobenius cycle types of the certificate cover over 𝔽_q for small q,n numerically to guess the monodromy group.
refs: Katz–Sarnak, Random Matrices, Frobenius Eigenvalues, and Monodromy (1999)
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Sawin square-root cancellation for factorisation-type functions in short intervals over 𝔽_q[T]
connection: Sawin proved square-root cancellation for sums of arithmetic functions depending on factorisation type in very short intervals over 𝔽_q[T]; 'has a divisor in a class' depends on factorisation plus residues.
why: Short-interval control over 𝔽_q[T] is exactly the slice-window statement needed in a function-field ES lower tail.
first_step: Check whether 'N has a divisor ≡ −1 (mod M)' is a 'factorisation function' in Sawin's sense (it depends on residues of factors, so needs his twisted version).
refs: Sawin, Square-root cancellation for sums of factorization functions over short intervals in function fields, Duke Math. J. 170 (2021)
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Bary-Soroker: Hypothesis H over 𝔽_q[T] for large q → function-field ES conditional lines unconditional
connection: Bary-Soroker proved Schinzel's Hypothesis H over 𝔽_q[T] in the large-q limit; repo CONDITIONAL_ES lines (Dickson/H ⇒ ES-type statements) transfer to function fields unconditionally.
why: Validates the conditional mechanism in a sibling and checks for hidden errors.
first_step: Translate each CONDITIONAL_ES statement to 𝔽_q[T] and verify numerically for q = 101, small degrees.
refs: Bary-Soroker, Irreducible values of polynomials, Adv. Math. 229 (2012)
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Kubilius model / PD anatomy for the p-tied integer 4Cp+1
connection: The Kubilius model replaces ω-type statistics of integers by independent prime indicators; Granville's anatomy shows prime factors follow PD(1).
why: A precise anatomy model of 4Cp+1 (C varying, p fixed) predicts the full distribution of R(p), including the lower tail.
first_step: Simulate R(p) under a Kubilius/PD model with the exact local factors at small primes and compare its lower tail with data at p ≤ 10^8.
refs: Granville, Anatomy of integers and permutations (2008 lecture notes)

title: Gaussian multiplicative chaos limit for divisor-class counting functions
connection: Critical GMC describes limits of random multiplicative functions' partial sums and of |ζ| on short intervals (Saksman–Webb); the ES count is a divisor-sum over a random-like factorisation.
why: GMC is the established mechanism behind non-Gaussian lower tails of such sums.
first_step: Compute the random-model R(p) distribution and check for GMC-type log-correlated structure (variance ~ log log).
refs: Saksman–Webb, The Riemann zeta function and Gaussian multiplicative chaos: statistics on the critical line, Ann. Prob. 48 (2020)

title: Smooth-number restriction (Vaughan–Wooley) with smooth moduli in APs (Drappeau/Harper)
connection: Smooth numbers drove progress on G(k). ES: restrict certificates to smooth (u,B) or smooth 4C, where distribution in progressions to large moduli is better (friable Bombieri–Vinogradov beyond 1/2).
why: Smooth moduli are where the strongest level-of-distribution results live; ES certificates are numerically often smooth.
first_step: Drappeau, 'Théorèmes de type Fouvry–Iwaniec pour les entiers friables', Compositio 151 (2015), arXiv:1307.7554 (verified) gives beyond-√ distribution for friable integers; check whether it applies to sums Σ_{C smooth} #{d | 4Cp+1, d ≡ −1 (4C)}; measure numerically the fraction of (★) solutions with y-smooth C for y = p^{0.1}.
alt_first_steps: [tools-0252] Measure what fraction of certificates at hard primes have P⁺(C) ≤ log² p; if substantial, target smooth-number technology.
refs: Harper, Bombieri–Vinogradov and Barban–Davenport–Halberstam type theorems for smooth numbers, arXiv:1208.5992
Drappeau, Théorèmes de type Fouvry–Iwaniec pour les entiers friables, Compositio 151 (2015)
alt_titles: [tools-0252] Smooth numbers in APs (Harper; Drappeau) for the C-smooth ES sub-family

title: Barban–Davenport–Halberstam variance for ES counts in APs of p
connection: BDH gives the variance of prime counts over all residue classes; an analogous variance for ES counts f(p) across p mod q would quantify residue-class structure of hardness.
why: The repo's 'failure profile carries nothing beyond p mod M' claim is a variance statement in disguise.
first_step: Compute Σ_{a mod q} (Σ_{p≡a, p≤x} f(p) − expected)² for q ≤ 1000 and compare with a BDH-type prediction.
refs: Montgomery, Primes in arithmetic progressions, Michigan Math. J. 17 (1970)

title: Turán–Kubilius inequality for R(p) across C: second-moment pointwise statements
connection: Turán–Kubilius bounds variance of additive functions; R_C(p) summed over C is a sum of divisor-class indicators, whose variance over C at fixed p might be bounded by a Turán–Kubilius-type argument.
why: A variance bound Var_C ≪ (mean)² /K at fixed p would imply many C succeed — pointwise in p, averaged over C.
first_step: Compute mean and variance over C ≤ X of R_C(p) at hard primes; test whether Var/mean² decays with X.

title: Selberg–Delange for class-restricted divisor generating functions
connection: Selberg–Delange gives asymptotics for Σ a(n) when Σ a(n)n^{−s} ≈ ζ(s)^z G(s); the indicator 'N has no divisor ≡ −1 (mod m)' has Dirichlet series with a fractional zeta power (prime factors in a subgroup).
why: Exact asymptotics for counts of N with no class-divisor give the baseline failure probability per slice.
first_step: Compute the Selberg–Delange exponent z for 'all prime factors in a subgroup H ∌ −1 of (ℤ/m)^×' and the resulting density x(log x)^{z−1}.
refs: Tenenbaum, Introduction to Analytic and Probabilistic Number Theory (3rd ed. 2015), II.5

title: Granville–Harper–Soundararajan Halász with explicit structure for failure-indicator twists
connection: GHS give a quantitative Halász theorem with explicit dependence on the pretentious distance; failing slices have divisor sums conspiring with characters mod 4C.
why: A quantitative pretentiousness bound for class-divisor sums would say failures are 'character-pretentious' only on thin sets.
first_step: Compute, for failing N, max_χ |Σ_{d|N} χ(d)|/τ(N) over χ mod 4C and its distribution.
refs: Granville–Harper–Soundararajan, A new proof of Halász's theorem, and its consequences, Compositio 155 (2019)

title: Ford–Konyagin–Luca / multiplicative structure of shifted primes p+e for e-slice generators
connection: Results on prime factors of shifted primes (Baker–Harman largest prime factor of p−1, Fouvry; Erdős–Pomerance) control whether N_e = (p+e)/4 has many small factors (good for generating −1).
why: Shifted-prime anatomy across all p is known in averaged forms; a fixed-p statement over e is needed.
first_step: Compute the fraction of hard primes p for which the first 10 slices N_e are all y-rough (no factors ≤ y) and compare with independence.
refs: Baker–Harman, Shifted primes without large prime factors, Acta Arith. 83 (1998)

title: Weighted dilation graphs / smooth shifted primes (OAI 'Weighted dilation graphs', claimed)
connection: The OAI paper claims x^{1−o(1)} primes p ∈ (2x,5x] with p−1 being x^δ-smooth via weighted dilation graphs; ES slices benefit from smooth N_e (many small generators).
why: Smooth shifted primes in abundance give structured slices; the dilation-graph technique is a new combinatorial counting tool.
first_step: Read the dilation-graph construction; test whether it can produce primes p with a smooth slice N_e for some small e.

title: Inverse Littlewood–Offord (Tao–Vu, Nguyen–Vu) for signed subset products hitting −1
connection: For squarefree N = ∏ℓ_i, the e-slice quotient ab⁻¹ (ab | N) is ∏ ℓ_i^{ε_i} with ε_i ∈ {−1,0,1} — a signed 'Littlewood–Offord walk' in (ℤ/e)^×. Inverse LO theorems say a walk concentrates on one value only if the steps are structured (lie in a small GAP/subgroup).
why: Gives the right language for ES's e-slice: the hitting probability of −1 vs the generic 1/|group|, and what structure is needed for systematic failure.
first_step: For hard primes compute, per slice, the distribution of ∏ℓ_i^{ε_i} over all 3^ω sign patterns and compare P(−1) with 1/φ(e); identify slices where steps lie in an index-2 subgroup.
refs: Tao–Vu, Inverse Littlewood–Offord theorems and the condition number of random discrete matrices, Ann. Math. 169 (2009)
Nguyen–Vu, Optimal inverse Littlewood–Offord theorems, Adv. Math. 226 (2011)
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Littlewood–Offord in finite abelian groups (Juškevičius–Šemetulskis) — exact anti-concentration
connection: Sharp LO bounds in arbitrary abelian groups bound max_x P(Σ ε_i v_i = x) given that steps avoid small subgroups; ES needs a LOWER bound on P(= −1), the converse direction.
why: Clarifies that LO gives upper (anti-concentration) bounds; for ES a 'local limit theorem' (equidistribution of the walk) is needed — a different but standard tool.
first_step: Compute the local-limit error for the ±1/0 walk with ω ≈ log log N steps in (ℤ/e)^×; note the step count is far below the mixing time ~ log e.
refs: Juškevičius–Šemetulskis, Optimal Littlewood–Offord inequalities in groups, arXiv:1707.01085

title: Gowers' quasirandom groups: ABC = SL₂(𝔽_q) for dense A,B,C — local covering for ES₅ words
connection: Gowers (and Nikolov–Pyber) show that if |A||B||C| > |G|³/m (m = minimal nontrivial representation dimension) then ABC = G; ES₅ certificates are length-3 products of letters from fixed sets.
why: Gives a clean local (mod q) surjectivity criterion for length-3 words — the local layer of ES₅ — and quantifies how dense the letter sets must be mod q.
first_step: Compute the reductions mod q of the ES₅ letter sets A, B, C (with entries bounded by p-dependent ranges) and check the Gowers inequality for q ≤ 50.
refs: Gowers, Quasirandom groups, Combin. Probab. Comput. 17 (2008)
Nikolov–Pyber, Product decompositions of quasirandom groups and a Jordan type theorem, JEMS 13 (2011)

title: Word-map surjectivity (Larsen–Shalev; Ore conjecture) for ES₅ word shapes
connection: Larsen–Shalev show word maps w: G^k → G are surjective (or nearly) for large finite simple groups; ES₅ is a specific word shape with constrained letters in SL₂.
why: Surjectivity of the ES word map on SL₂(𝔽_q) (with letter constraints) is the local-at-q statement; failures at small q explain local obstructions.
first_step: Define the constrained ES₅ word map over 𝔽_q and compute its image size for q ≤ 100.
refs: Larsen–Shalev, Word maps and Waring type problems, JAMS 22 (2009)

title: Helfgott growth in SL₂(𝔽_p) for the set of ES₅ letters
connection: Helfgott: generating sets A of SL₂(𝔽_p) satisfy |AAA| ≥ |A|^{1+δ} unless A is nearly the group; the ES₅ letter set at p is a specific subset.
why: Growth explains how quickly length-k words cover the group; ES fixes k = 3 so the growth exponent needed is computable.
first_step: Measure |A|, |A²|, |A³| mod small primes for the ES₅ letter set restricted to letters of height ≤ p.
refs: Helfgott, Growth and generation in SL2(Z/pZ), Ann. Math. 167 (2008)
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Bourgain–Lindenstrauss–Michel–Venkatesh effective ×a×b for multiplicative semigroups mod q
connection: BLMV give effective equidistribution of orbits of the multiplicative semigroup ⟨a,b⟩ acting on ℤ/q (Furstenberg ×2×3 discrete analogue); ES e-slices ask whether −1 lies in a product set built from a few multiplicative generators mod e.
why: Shows when a 2-generator multiplicative semigroup fills (ℤ/q)^× — the 'enough generators' threshold relevant to pooling slices.
first_step: Compute, for e-slices at hard primes, the size of the semigroup generated by the two smallest prime factors of N mod e.
refs: Bourgain–Lindenstrauss–Michel–Venkatesh, Some effective results for ×a×b, Ergodic Theory Dynam. Systems 29 (2009)

title: Dias da Silva–Hamidoune restricted sumsets for distinct-factor products
connection: Erdős–Heilbronn (Dias da Silva–Hamidoune): |h^∧A| ≥ min(p, h|A| − h² + 1) for restricted h-fold sums in ℤ/p; ES uses products of distinct prime factors (restricted products).
why: Exact lower bounds for restricted product sets in cyclic groups of prime order (take discrete logs mod e−1 when e−1 is prime-ish).
first_step: Compute restricted product set sizes of prime factors of N mod e and compare with the DdS–H bound.
refs: Dias da Silva–Hamidoune, Cyclic spaces for Grassmann derivatives and additive theory, Bull. LMS 26 (1994)

title: Szemerédi–Vu long APs in subset sums → structure of rich divisor sets
connection: Szemerédi–Vu: subset sums of a set of size ≫ √n contain long APs; highly composite slices have rich subset-product sets.
why: For slices with large ω(N) the quotient set contains long 'geometric progressions' mod e, which may be forced to contain −1.
first_step: Identify slices with ω(N) ≥ 8 at hard primes and test whether their quotient sets contain long GPs in (ℤ/e)^×.
refs: Szemerédi–Vu, Long arithmetic progressions in sumsets: thresholds and bounds, JAMS 19 (2006)

title: Heath-Brown delta-method circle method for Σ_{n≤N} f(n) with power saving
connection: Heath-Brown's delta method counts integral points on quadrics/cubics with Kloosterman refinement; the total count of ES solutions over n ≤ N is an integral-point count on the 3-fold 4xyz = n(xy+yz+zx).
why: Power-saving asymptotics for the total count, and for counts restricted to n in APs, feed variance and exceptional-set arguments.
first_step: Set up the delta-method count for #{(n,x,y,z): n ≤ N} with a smooth weight and identify the singular series (should match ET's main term).
refs: Heath-Brown, A new form of the circle method, and its application to quadratic forms, J. reine angew. Math. 481 (1996)

title: Browning–Heath-Brown / Browning–Vishe circle method over function fields for ES threefold
connection: Browning–Vishe developed the function-field circle method (cubic forms over 𝔽_q(t)); the ES threefold's point counts over 𝔽_q[t] (function-field ES averaged over n) fit.
why: Exact function-field asymptotics for averaged counts test the ET main term heuristics in a sibling.
first_step: Formulate the averaged function-field ES count and check Browning–Vishe's applicability to non-homogeneous cubics.
refs: Browning–Vishe, Rational points on cubic hypersurfaces over F_q(t), GAFA 25 (2015)
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Munshi's delta-method variants (DFI δ with conductor lowering) for ES character sums
connection: Munshi's conductor-lowering trick proves subconvexity by inserting extra averaging; ES counts at fixed p could use an artificial extra average (over a dummy modulus) to gain cancellation.
why: Conductor lowering creates averages where none exist — precisely ES's 'no free average' problem.
first_step: Insert a dummy average over auxiliary primes q ~ Q into the fixed-p ES count expansion and see whether Poisson summation yields a gain.
refs: Munshi, The circle method and bounds for L-functions III: t-aspect subconvexity for GL(3) L-functions, JAMS 28 (2015)

title: Lenstra integer programming in fixed dimension for 'certificate in a box' decisions
connection: Lenstra/Kannan: integer feasibility in fixed dimension is polynomial; certificate existence with bounded parameters is a low-dimensional integer program with a divisibility constraint (non-linear).
why: Linearising divisibility via auxiliary variables gives an IP; feasibility algorithms could replace factoring in searches.
first_step: Model 'f·g = 4Cp+1, f ≡ −1 (4C), C ≤ X' as a quadratic IP and test whether branch-and-bound beats factoring at p ~ 10^20.
refs: Lenstra, Integer programming with a fixed number of variables, Math. Oper. Res. 8 (1983)

title: Tao's Collatz 'almost bounded orbits' technique for greedy-with-choice Egyptian algorithms
connection: Tao (2019) analysed a 3-adic Syracuse random variable to show almost all Collatz orbits attain almost bounded values; ES solutions are produced by greedy-type algorithms (choose x ≈ n/4, recurse on the remainder) whose residue dynamics resemble Syracuse.
why: A stabilisation argument for the remainder's residue distribution could show 'greedy with bounded look-ahead succeeds for almost all n in log density' — and identify the structure of failures.
first_step: Implement the greedy-with-choice algorithm (x = ⌈n/4⌉ + k, k ≤ K) and record the residue distribution of remainders at each step for p ≤ 10^7.
refs: Tao, Almost all orbits of the Collatz map attain almost bounded values, Forum Math. Pi 10 (2022), arXiv:1909.03562

title: Erdős discrepancy (Tao) — sign-sequence view of ES parity layers
connection: Tao proved every ±1 sequence has unbounded discrepancy along HAPs, via entropy decrement + Fourier on multiplicative functions; ES parity data (R(p)/2 mod 2) is a ±1 sequence on primes.
why: If ES parity were completely multiplicative-like, discrepancy theorems would constrain it; mainly a calibration lens.
first_step: Compute discrepancy of the sequence (−1)^{R(p)/2} along APs of primes for p ≤ 10^8.
refs: Tao, The Erdős discrepancy problem, Discrete Analysis 2016:1, arXiv:1509.05363

title: Tao–Teräväinen odd-order log-Chowla & Klurman–Mangerel–Teräväinen sign patterns
connection: Tao–Teräväinen proved odd-order log-averaged Chowla; KMT studied sign patterns of multiplicative functions; ES certificates at consecutive slices involve λ/divisor patterns of consecutive integers N, N+1, …
why: Patterns of multiplicative data on consecutive integers are exactly what Type II slices are.
first_step: Tabulate (λ(N_e), λ(N_{e+4}), …) patterns at hard primes vs random and test for bias.
refs: Tao–Teräväinen, The structure of logarithmically averaged correlations of multiplicative functions, with applications to the Chowla and Elliott conjectures, Duke Math. J. 168 (2019)

title: Sarnak Möbius disjointness: is the ES-hardness sequence 'deterministic'?
connection: Sarnak's conjecture: μ is orthogonal to zero-entropy sequences; the indicator of 'ES-hard p' (low normalised count) is a sequence of unknown complexity.
why: Testing correlation of ES-hardness with μ(p−1)-type data or with low-complexity sequences gauges whether hardness has hidden deterministic structure.
first_step: Compute correlations of the hardness indicator with μ((p−1)/4), λ((p+3)/4) and with Sturmian sequences of p.
refs: Sarnak, Three lectures on the Möbius function, randomness and dynamics (2011)

title: Host–Kra / Frantzikinakis ergodic structure for multiplicative ES colourings
connection: Host–Kra factors describe multiple ergodic averages; Frantzikinakis–Host apply them to multiplicative functions; the colouring of n by 'ES shape type' is multiplicatively closed (solutions lift to multiples).
why: A Furstenberg-correspondence model of the ES shape colouring could show forced configurations in each colour class.
first_step: Define the colouring n ↦ (minimal certificate type) and test partition-regularity-type configurations numerically.
refs: Host–Kra, Nonconventional ergodic averages and nilmanifolds, Ann. Math. 161 (2005)

title: Lorentzian polynomials (Brändén–Huh) / log-concavity of certificate-count sequences
connection: Lorentzian polynomials prove log-concavity of combinatorial sequences (matroid independent sets, etc.); ES certificate counts by size class or by number of prime factors used form sequences whose log-concavity could constrain zeros.
why: Log-concavity + positive endpoints ⇒ no internal zeros: a positivity mechanism that is pointwise.
first_step: For hard primes, compute the sequence a_k = #certificates using C with ω(C) = k (or certificate size buckets) and test log-concavity; if robust, look for a Lorentzian generating polynomial.
refs: Brändén–Huh, Lorentzian polynomials, Ann. Math. 192 (2020), arXiv:1902.03719

title: Adiprasito–Huh–Katz Hodge theory for matroids: positivity from combinatorial Hodge–Riemann
connection: AHK proved log-concavity (Rota/Heron/Welsh) via Hodge–Riemann relations on matroid Chow rings; U_n in reciprocal coordinates is a hyperplane-arrangement object (matroid of {u,v,w,u+v+w}).
why: Matroid Hodge theory gives positivity of combinatorial invariants of the arrangement; whether any ES count is such an invariant is the question.
first_step: Compute the characteristic polynomial / Chow ring of the arrangement for U_n and check whether any coefficient relates to solution counts (likely not; record).
refs: Adiprasito–Huh–Katz, Hodge theory for combinatorial geometries, Ann. Math. 188 (2018)

title: Markov/Markoff via cluster algebra of the once-punctured torus — ES analogue?
connection: Markoff triples are cluster variables of the once-punctured torus cluster algebra; the Cayley cubic ↔ four-punctured sphere character variety; ES's U_n shares the Cayley cubic.
why: If U_n's integral points are cluster-like for the four-punctured sphere (Fomin–Shapiro–Thurston surface cluster algebras), mutation provides the missing group action.
first_step: Compute the cluster algebra of the four-punctured sphere and its exchange relations; test whether ES solution triples satisfy any mutation relation.
refs: Fomin–Shapiro–Thurston, Cluster algebras and triangulated surfaces I, Acta Math. 201 (2008)

title: Elsholtz-style generalised windmills for x² + ny² as templates for ES windmills
connection: Zagier's one-sentence proof generalises (Elsholtz; Jackson et al.) to involution proofs that primes in certain classes are represented by x² + 2y², x² + 3y², etc. These are verified parity proofs for 'one representation exists' at primes in classes.
why: These are the closest proved windmill-type pointwise theorems. Their combinatorial skeleton (sets of triples with linear involutions) is the template that WINDMILL/INVOLUTION_ES look for, so the known catalogue tells what forms are reachable.
first_step: Collect the known windmill proofs (x² + ny², n ∈ {1,2,3,…}) and their set definitions; check whether the ES Type II data (4abd = pe + 1) can be fitted to any of their shapes.
alt_first_steps: [tools-0285] Search computationally for involutions on finite ES-related sets (e.g. bounded certificate tuples) whose fixed-point count is odd exactly when p ≡ 1 (mod 4) and not a square.
[upgrades-0281] Read the paper; list the equations handled (x² + ky², etc.) and try its windmill construction on the (★) set or on {(u,B,C) : 4uBC − u − B = p}.
refs: Elsholtz, A combinatorial approach to sums of two squares and related problems (2010; check)
Zagier, A one-sentence proof that every prime p ≡ 1 (mod 4) is a sum of two squares, Amer. Math. Monthly 97 (1990)
Elsholtz, A combinatorial approach to sums of two squares and related problems (2010)
alt_titles: [tools-0285] Elsholtz windmill generalisations (Zagier one-sentence) for ES involutions
[upgrades-0281] Elsholtz's windmill framework for sums of two squares and related problems

title: Chatterjee–Dembo nonlinear large deviations for R(p) as a low-complexity polynomial
connection: Nonlinear large deviation theory handles functions of independent variables with low-complexity gradient (Chatterjee–Dembo; Eldan); R(p) under a random-factorisation model is such a function.
why: Mean-field LDP gives the lower-tail rate function — the probability that R(p) = 0 — in models.
first_step: Write R(p) in the Bernoulli model and estimate its gradient complexity (covering number of gradients).
refs: Chatterjee–Dembo, Nonlinear large deviations, Adv. Math. 299 (2016), arXiv:1401.3495

title: Shearer / entropy inequalities for joint divisibility of slices
connection: Shearer's lemma bounds joint entropy by marginals; the joint divisibility profile of slices (N_e mod small primes for e in a window) is a random vector whose entropy controls how many 'independent chances' ES gets.
why: Quantifies effective number of independent slices at a fixed p.
first_step: Compute empirical entropies of divisibility profiles across windows of slices at hard vs typical primes.
refs: Chung–Graham–Frankl–Shearer, Some intersection theorems for ordered sets and graphs, JCTA 43 (1986)

title: Hypothesis-testing view: sequential probability ratio of certificate search
connection: Wald's SPRT gives optimal stopping for detecting an effect; certificate search at p is a sequential search with known per-slice success probabilities.
why: Gives the expected search cost and a principled 'hardness score' for primes, standardising adversarial data.
first_step: Define per-slice success probabilities from the random model and compute the likelihood ratio of 'p is hard' after K failed slices for data primes.

title: Gallagher's larger sieve with prime-power moduli to bound sterile p
connection: The larger sieve bounds sets missing many residue classes modulo prime powers; sterile primes must lie in non-covered classes modulo many moduli 4C simultaneously.
why: A direct quantitative bound on the number of primes ≤ X sterile to depth K.
first_step: Compute, for each modulus m ≤ M, the number of residue classes of p that are sterile for certificates of modulus m, and plug into the larger sieve.
refs: Gallagher, A larger sieve, Acta Arith. 18 (1971)
Croot–Elsholtz, On variants of the larger sieve, Acta Math. Hungar. 103 (2004)

title: Heath-Brown square sieve on the ES failure set (non-squareness exploitation)
connection: Heath-Brown's square sieve counts squares in a sequence via characters; T1 says Type I/II fail at squares — the square sieve could quantify 'how square-like' a non-square must be to fail.
why: Makes T1 quantitative: failure at non-squares requires mimicking squares at many primes ℓ ((p/ℓ) = 1).
first_step: Correlate f(p) with the number of small ℓ with (p/ℓ) = 1 (QR-richness) on data.
refs: Heath-Brown, The square sieve and consecutive square-free numbers, Math. Ann. 266 (1984)

title: Baker's linear forms in logarithms: bounds for exceptional structured solutions
connection: Baker/Matveev bound linear forms in logs; ES solutions with denominators in multiplicatively structured families (powers, S-units) lead to exponential Diophantine equations.
why: Gives explicit bounds for the S-unit/smooth barrier items, making them computational.
first_step: Write the ES equation with x,y,z restricted to ⟨2,3,5,7⟩ and solve completely via Baker + LLL reduction.
refs: Matveev, An explicit lower bound for a homogeneous rational linear form in logarithms, Izv. Math. 64 (2000)

title: Bilu–Tichy / Hilbert irreducibility for 'identity families' over ℚ(t)
connection: Bilu–Tichy classify when f(x) = g(y) has infinitely many integral solutions; ES identity families are polynomial solutions; Hilbert irreducibility explains when parametric families give integral specialisations.
why: A classification of integral polynomial families for ES in one parameter (Bilu–Tichy style) would make the Mordell–Schinzel barrier complete.
first_step: Classify one-parameter families n(t), x(t), y(t), z(t) ∈ ℤ[t] via the curve of ES solutions over ℚ(t) and Siegel's theorem (genus 0, ≤ 2 points at infinity).
refs: Bilu–Tichy, The Diophantine equation f(x) = g(y), Acta Arith. 95 (2000)

title: Siegel's theorem on integral points of curves for one-parameter ES slices
connection: A curve C ⊂ U_n (e.g. x fixed as polynomial in a parameter) has infinitely many integral points only if genus 0 with ≤ 2 points at infinity; ES certificate curves are genus 0 with specific boundary.
why: Counting points at infinity classifies which 1-parameter certificate families can be infinite — a structural census.
first_step: For each certificate family in the repo, compute genus and number of points at infinity of the associated curve.
refs: Siegel, Über einige Anwendungen diophantischer Approximationen (1929)

title: Ihara zeta / non-backtracking spectra of ES certificate graphs
connection: Ihara zeta functions encode cycle structure and Ramanujan property of graphs; the bipartite graph (C-values) ↔ (primes dividing 4Cp+1) at fixed p is a natural graph.
why: Spectral gap of this bipartite graph controls how dependent certificates are (Janson Δ).
first_step: Build the bipartite graph at a hard prime for C ≤ 10^4 and compute its non-backtracking spectrum.

title: Selberg Λ² upper-bound sieve for the number of sterile p ≤ X at depth K
connection: Λ² sieve gives sharp upper bounds for sifted sets; 'p sterile for all certificates with C ≤ K' is a sifting condition on p modulo the moduli 4C and auxiliary primes.
why: Gives E_K(X) ≪ X/(log X)^{g(K)} with explicit g, the cleanest depth-K exceptional bound.
first_step: Compute the sieve dimension of the depth-K sterility condition from the densities of sterile classes mod primes ℓ.

title: Duke–Friedlander–Iwaniec bilinear forms with Kloosterman fractions (classic) for ES dispersion
connection: DFI bound Σ α_m β_n e(a m̄/n) nontrivially in all ranges; ES dispersion involves e(h·\overline{4C}/f)-type fractions.
why: The basic input for Type II dispersion in divisor-of-quadratic problems.
first_step: Locate where the repo's exceptional-set work uses Weil bounds instead of DFI and assess the gain.
refs: Duke–Friedlander–Iwaniec, Bilinear forms with Kloosterman fractions, Invent. Math. 128 (1997)

title: Ramaré's local models / Ramaré–Walker for one-integer certificate densities
connection: Ramaré's local-model technique gives explicit lower bounds for sifted sums by matching local densities; the deep catalogue lists Ramaré–Walker as a thin-count precedent.
why: Template for explicit lower bounds with a small number of witnesses.
first_step: Re-read the deep catalogue entry and check whether ES's one-integer event fits Ramaré's 'local model' assumptions.
refs: Ramaré–Walker, Products of primes in arithmetic progressions: a footnote in parity breaking, J. Théor. Nombres Bordeaux 30 (2018)

title: Hasse norm principle / Tate cohomology for ray-class formulations of Type I
connection: Type I as 'an ideal of norm f in a ray class mod 4cd in ℚ(√−d)' invokes norm groups; Hasse's norm theorem (cyclic) gives local–global for norms.
why: Turns part of the Type I condition into class field theory, possibly identifying a reciprocity layer (T1) as a ray-class character.
first_step: Compute the ray class group mod 4cd of ℚ(√−d) and identify the subgroup the Type I condition requires, for small c,d.
refs: Neukirch, Algebraic Number Theory (1999), ch. VI

title: PARI/Magma class-field computations: explicit 'ES ray class fields' for small (c,d)
connection: Computer algebra computes ray class fields explicitly; ES Type I certificates for fixed (c,d) correspond to primes f splitting in a specific ray class field with a twist by p.
why: Explicit fields allow Chebotarev-density computations of the per-(c,d) success probability, sharpening M_BM.
first_step: Compute with PARI bnrinit for d ≤ 10, c ≤ 5 and list Frobenius conditions.

title: Inverse Littlewood–Offord for I3 at fixed t: walks in (ℤ/t)^×
connection: For I3 at fixed t, success needs a divisor of tn+1 ≡ −1 (mod t) — a signed subset-product hitting −1 in (ℤ/t)^× (t small!).
why: Small t means a tiny group: random-walk/local-limit arguments are much stronger than for ES's large e; I3 might be provable where ES isn't, isolating why.
first_step: For n ≤ 10^9 and t ≤ 20, measure the fraction of (n,t) with the event and the dependence across t at fixed n.

title: Target-Davenport constants for I3 at small t: forcing −1 from enough prime factors
connection: In (ℤ/t)^× with t ≤ 20, a sequence of prime factors of tn+1 of length ≥ D(G) has a nonempty subproduct ≡ 1; the I3 event needs a divisor ≡ −1, so a 'target' Davenport constant is the forcing threshold.
why: Combined with 'tn+1 has many prime factors for some t ≤ T' (provable for most n?), could give I3 for many n deterministically.
first_step: Compute target constants for G = (ℤ/t)^×, t ≤ 30, and the fraction of n where some t ≤ 30 has ω(tn+1) above the threshold.

title: Brauer–Manin for the pencil S_{n,k} at k = −4 (sibling failures {2,9,21,165,945,1197})
connection: The repo proved a BM obstruction on S_{n,k} for positive squares k; at k = −4 failures exist but no invariant is known; Colliot-Thélène–Xu style integral BM with negative k is untried.
why: Explaining sibling failures by a BM class would refine the zero-law calibration and test whether ES-type failures are always 'lottery'.
first_step: Compute Br S_{n,−4} and evaluate the candidate quaternion classes at the failing n.
refs: Colliot-Thélène–Xu, Brauer–Manin obstruction for integral points of homogeneous spaces and representation by integral quadratic forms, Compositio 145 (2009)

title: Function-field transfer of T1: odd squares in 𝔽_q[T] and the reciprocity obstruction
connection: T1 (no Type I/II at odd squares) should have a function-field analogue with polynomial reciprocity; FF_ODD_ABSENCE/FF_STERILE memos study function-field sterility.
why: In function fields the obstruction might be explained by monodromy, giving a conceptual T1 proof that could suggest a 'prime T1' test.
first_step: Verify T1 for squares of irreducible polynomials over 𝔽_3, 𝔽_5 numerically and compute the monodromy of the certificate cover at a square.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Kloosterman/KMS bounds applied to the I3 count averaged over t
connection: I3's divisor event involves tn+1 with class −1 mod t; averaging over t ≤ T at fixed n gives Kloosterman-type sums with modulus t (small).
why: Fixed-n averages over t is the I3 analogue of fixed-p averages over C — test bed for bilinear Kloosterman input.
first_step: Write Σ_t Σ_{d | tn+1} 1_{d ≡ −1 (t)} via Fourier in d mod t and identify the Kloosterman sums.

title: Gaussian ES_Q1 count growth log³N vs log²N: Lang–Weil / local densities explanation
connection: z52 found ES_Q1 counts grow like log³N (EVIDENCE) against the board's log²N; integral-Manin-type predictions depend on the rank of the relevant Picard/boundary data over ℚ(i).
why: A geometric explanation (extra boundary component splitting over ℚ(i)) would validate the log-power heuristics used for ES itself.
first_step: Compute the Chambert-Loir–Tschinkel exponent for U_n over ℚ(i) vs ℚ (Galois action on boundary/nodes) and compare with 3 vs 2.
refs: Chambert-Loir–Tschinkel, Igusa integrals and volume asymptotics in analytic and adelic geometry, Confluentes Math. 2 (2010)
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Maynard–Tao weights over the slice index e at fixed p
connection: At fixed p the slices N_e = (p+e)/4 are consecutive integers; MT weights over admissible tuples of slices could force several slices to be 'structured' (e.g. have a small prime factor in a chosen class) simultaneously.
why: Fixed-p, average over e: legitimate without averaging over p — and MT weights are designed for consecutive-integer tuples.
first_step: Choose an admissible k-tuple of slice offsets and compute (numerically) the MT weighted proportion of windows where ≥ 2 slices succeed.
refs: Maynard, Small gaps between primes, Ann. Math. 181 (2015)

title: Matomäki–Radziwiłł for divisor-class functions on the slice window (N, N+H) at fixed p
connection: The Type II slices are the short interval [p/4, p/4 + H]; MR-type theorems give almost-all-short-interval behaviour, but here the interval is one specific interval (fixed by p).
why: Precisely localises the B2-type gap as 'one specific short interval near p/4' — any 'all short intervals' theorem for the divisor-class function would prove ES.
first_step: Check the strongest known 'all intervals of length H' result for multiplicative functions (e.g. Teräväinen/MR 'every interval' results for smooth numbers) and compare H with ES's polylog window.

title: Smooth numbers in all short intervals (Matomäki–Radziwiłł; Teräväinen) → smooth slice existence
connection: MR prove every interval [x, x + C√x] contains x^ε-smooth numbers? (check exact statement); a smooth slice N_e has many small prime factors and likely succeeds.
why: An 'every interval' smooth-number theorem is a pointwise tool; the slice window near p/4 is short (polylog?) so the needed length must be compared.
first_step: Check the exact current record for smooth numbers in every short interval and compare with the number of slices available at p (e < some bound).
refs: Matomäki–Radziwiłł, Multiplicative functions in short intervals, Ann. Math. 183 (2016), §1 (smooth numbers in short intervals)

title: Green–Sawhney-type Type II information for p² + 4c²d with d prime
connection: Restricting to prime d makes p² + 4c²d a sparse polynomial family close to Green–Sawhney's p² + nq² setting.
why: Sub-family selection to reach a known bilinear estimate; the count loses only a log factor.
first_step: Measure how often Type I certificates with d prime exist at p ≤ 10^7.

title: Duke–Imamoḡlu–Tóth-style traces for I3's t-family (closed geodesics of discriminant t²n²+…)
connection: (tu−1)(tv−1) = tn+1 relates to binary forms of discriminant depending on (t,n); traces over these classes could be mock-modular generating functions.
why: Same speculative mechanism as for ES₅, but I3's single free parameter t makes the family cleaner.
first_step: Identify the binary quadratic form whose representation gives I3 at (t,n) and compute its discriminant.

title: Koukoulopoulos–Maynard GCD graphs for I3 overlaps across t
connection: I3 events for different t at fixed n share prime factors through gcd(tn+1, t′n+1) | (t−t′)… structure; GCD graphs quantify such overlaps.
why: Second-moment control at fixed n over t is the key missing step; GCD-graph compression is designed for that.
first_step: Compute gcd(tn+1, t′n+1) statistics for t,t′ ≤ 100 at the hardest I3 n values.

title: Rosser–Iwaniec semi-linear sieve for I3 at t = 4: 'tn+1 has a divisor ≡ 3 (mod 4)'
connection: At t = 4, the I3 event needs a divisor of 4n+1 that is ≡ −1 (mod 4) (plus size constraints): it fails iff all prime factors of 4n+1 are ≡ 1 (mod 4) — a semi-linear sifted set of density ≍ (log n)^{−1/2}.
why: Exact density of the t = 4 failure set; combining t = 4, 8, 12 … failures gives a sieve-dimension computation for I3's exceptional set.
first_step: Compute the joint failure probability for t ∈ {4, 8, 12, 16} under independence and compare with data.

title: Chen–Stein Poisson approximation for I3 counts at fixed n
connection: I3 counts at fixed n over t, u, v are sums of weakly dependent divisor events; Poisson approximation predicts P(count = 0).
why: I3 is verified to 10^9 with a known largest exception 2 433 600 — calibrates Poisson-model predictions of the largest exception.
first_step: Fit the Poisson model on n ≤ 10^8 and predict the largest exception; compare with 2 433 600.

title: Extreme-value prediction of ES's 'last hard prime' scale from sibling data
connection: Siblings with known last exceptions (I3: 2 433 600; U(n): 978145?) calibrate extreme-value models mapping expected count μ(n) to the largest failing n.
why: If the same model predicts ES's last failure below 2 (i.e. none), it quantifies P(ES false) consistently across siblings.
first_step: Fit log P(fail at n) ≈ −μ(n)·κ on siblings, then evaluate Σ_{p > 10^18} exp(−κ μ(p)).

title: Bhargava-style 'average over a family then sieve to the subfamily' for ES over n in APs
connection: Bhargava's method: count over a big family with geometry of numbers, then sieve to squarefree/maximal subfamilies via uniformity estimates; ES averaged over n in APs mod M is a sieve to sub-families.
why: Uniformity estimates ('tail' bounds) are exactly what pass from averages to subfamilies like Mordell-hard classes.
first_step: Compute averaged ES counts over n ≡ r (mod 840) for each Mordell-hard r and check uniformity in r of the main-term constant.
refs: Bhargava–Shankar, Binary quartic forms having bounded invariants, and the boundedness of the average rank of elliptic curves, Ann. Math. 181 (2015)

title: SAT/ILP search for a 'prime T1': a non-square class where all certificates of bounded shape fail
connection: A 'prime T1' (structured family of primes with no Type I/II certificates of a bounded shape) is the campaign's sought disproof-shape; SAT/ILP can search residue systems where all bounded-shape certificates fail.
why: Either finds sterile families to a given depth or certifies none exist below a modulus — sharp data for the sterility question.
first_step: Encode depth-K sterility for certificate shapes with C ≤ K as a CRT-consistency SAT instance and search moduli up to 10^6.

title: Davies-style ML on sibling failures: which local features predict S_{n,−4} and ES_Q1 failures?
connection: Sibling failures (S_{n,−4}: n ≡ 0 mod 3 odd failures; ES_Q1: Im n ≡ 1 mod 4 cell) were partly explained by low-count cells; attribution on a classifier could find further features.
why: If failures are fully explained by local count-lowering features, the lottery reading is strengthened.
first_step: Train a classifier on n ≤ 10^5 with local features (n mod q, Legendre symbols) to predict S_{n,−4} counts; inspect feature importance.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Murmuration-type averages of I3 counts against n mod t
connection: Average I3 counts as a function of n's residue pattern across t could show oscillations analogous to murmurations.
why: Exposes hidden structure that residue-class fits might miss.
first_step: Plot normalised I3 counts averaged in windows vs n/X and residues mod 840.

title: Kahn–Kalai / Park–Pham on the I3 random model (small groups, many events)
connection: I3's events per n are many (t ranges) with small moduli; threshold theory could predict exactly when 'expected ≥ 1' implies 'present w.h.p.'.
why: I3 is proved-false-free beyond 2 433 600 in data; matching threshold predictions is a sanity test of the method before ES.
first_step: Compute expectation thresholds for I3 events at n ~ 10^6–10^9 in the random model.

title: Effective Chebotarev in the ES Type I ray class fields (explicit success density per (c,d))
connection: For fixed (c,d), the density of primes p having a Type I certificate with that (c,d) and a prime f is a Chebotarev density in a field tied to (c,d); summing gives M_BM's constant.
why: Explicit densities let one compute the exact main term and the variance contributed by each (c,d).
first_step: Compute the Chebotarev density for (c,d) ∈ {(1,1),(1,2),(2,1)} via PARI and compare with empirical frequencies.
refs: Lagarias–Odlyzko, Effective versions of the Chebotarev density theorem (1977)

title: Quantitative Hilbert irreducibility (Cohen; Castillo–Dietmann) for ES certificate covers
connection: Quantitative HIT bounds the number of specialisations where a Galois group drops; ES certificate covers over the p-line have Galois groups whose specialisations at p determine certificate existence.
why: If the cover's Galois group stays large at all but few p, Chebotarev-type positivity follows for most p — and exceptional p are 'thin sets'.
first_step: Compute the Galois group of a single Type I certificate cover (fixed c,d) over ℚ(p) and its thin-set exceptions.
refs: Castillo–Dietmann, On Hilbert's irreducibility theorem, Acta Arith. 180 (2017)

title: Expander walk sampling + Ramanujan graphs for Monte Carlo estimates of M_BM constants
connection: Expander-walk Chernoff bounds give sharp concentration for Monte Carlo with few random bits; estimating Euler-product-type constants and certificate densities by sampling primes benefits.
why: Minor computational gain; listed as a concrete use of Ramanujan-graph technology.
first_step: Implement expander-walk sampling of primes in [X, 2X] and compare variance of estimates of mean f(p) with i.i.d. sampling.
refs: Gillman, A Chernoff bound for random walks on expander graphs, SIAM J. Comput. 27 (1998)

title: Spectral sparsification / effective resistance on certificate dependency graphs
connection: Spielman–Srivastava sparsification approximates graphs by sparse ones preserving quadratic forms; the Janson Δ is a quadratic form on the certificate dependency graph.
why: Allows computing/approximating Δ for huge certificate families at large p.
first_step: Compute Δ exactly for p ~ 10^7 and approximately via sparsification at p ~ 10^12.
refs: Spielman–Srivastava, Graph sparsification by effective resistances, SIAM J. Comput. 40 (2011)

title: Kelley–Meka sifting for pooled multi-slice certificates
connection: Pooling several slices with a common modulus e (e.g. N_e and N_{e′} with e | stuff) creates larger generating sets; KM-type density increments find large structured pieces in the pooled divisor sets.
why: Pooling is the natural escape from B2's 'one integer' constraint; additive-combinatorial structure theorems are the tool to exploit pooled sets.
first_step: Identify ES certificate shapes that legitimately combine prime factors of two different p-tied integers in one group, if any (check SIGNED_REFACTOR.md / COMPOSITION_ES.md).

title: Bloom/Liu–Sawhney machinery for few-term Egyptian representations with dense denominators
connection: Bloom: positive density sets contain S with Σ1/n = 1, via counting with main term + exponential sums on integers with structured anatomy. Ask what the machinery gives for k-term representations of 4/p (k fixed, small) with denominators restricted to structured sets (multiples of p with smooth cofactors).
why: Bloom's framework is the modern Fourier-analytic engine for unit-fraction existence; checking where it breaks for k = 3 localises ES's difficulty.
first_step: Read Bloom's §§2–4 and identify the minimal number of terms the method needs; check if it can handle 4/p = Σ_{i≤k} 1/n_i with k ~ 10 and n_i in a set of density zero.
alt_first_steps: [tools-0333] Track, in Bloom's argument, the minimal number of terms needed for the Fourier step and how it scales.
refs: arXiv:2112.03726 (Bloom, On a density conjecture about unit fractions)
alt_titles: [tools-0333] Bloom unit-fraction method for 'k/n with prescribed smooth denominators' — 3-term specialisation test

upgrade: Bloom: unit fractions in dense sets

title: Mixing of the greedy/odd-greedy Egyptian map as a Markov chain on residues
connection: The map n ↦ remainder after subtracting the greedy unit fraction acts on residues; as a Markov chain its mixing describes the distribution of remainders (cf. Tao's Syracuse analysis).
why: Mixing estimates give 'almost all' success of fixed-depth greedy-with-choice algorithms and pinpoint residue traps.
first_step: Compute the transition matrix of the remainder residue mod M for the 2-step greedy-with-choice ES search and its spectral gap.

title: ES₅ as a sandpile-group pairing condition on a 4-vertex fan multigraph
connection: The chain matrix M = [[v,−1,0],[−1,t,−1],[0,−1,u]] is the reduced Laplacian of the multigraph: path a–b–c plus a sink s joined to a, b, c by v−1, t−2, u−1 parallel edges. It has det M = tuv−u−v = p spanning trees, a cyclic sandpile group ℤ/p, and its discriminant (monodromy) pairing has self-pairing (M⁻¹)₁₁ = A/p. So ES₅(p) (∃ t,u,v ≥ 2, tuv−u−v = p, (A/p) = −1 with A = tu−1; sufficient for ES(p)) ⇔ some fan multigraph of this shape with p spanning trees has a sandpile pairing in the non-square class.
why: Sandpile groups with their pairings are a mature field (Lorenzini, Shokrieh, Bosch–Lorenzini) with classification results for pairings on cyclic critical groups; this gives ES₅ a purely graph-theoretic statement.
first_step: Script: for p ≡ 1 (4) < 10⁵, enumerate all graphs on ≤ 5 vertices with p spanning trees and record which pairing classes occur; is the non-square class reached by 4-vertex fans exactly when ES₅(p) holds, and always by 5-vertex graphs?
refs: arXiv:2311.06367 (Lorenzini, The critical polynomial of a graph)

title: Relaxing the fan: which pairing classes occur among graphs with p spanning trees and k vertices
connection: Generalise item 1: the graph-theoretic analogue of 'ES with more terms' is 'some graph with ≤ k vertices and τ(G) = p has a non-square sandpile pairing'. ES₅ is the k = 4 fan case. (Not via cycles/trees: a tree has trivial critical group, and C_p has pairing class −1/p, which is a square for p ≡ 1 (4). For large k a non-square class should come from longer chains, i.e. from λ(p) ≤ k − 1, which is known for k ≫ log p.)
why: Gives a ladder of relaxations parametrised by vertex count, with a known extremal theory for τ(G) values (Sedláček's α(n)); the threshold k(p) at which the non-square pairing first appears is a new invariant to compare with λ(p).
first_step: Compute k*(p) = least vertex count with a non-square pairing and τ = p, for p < 10⁴; compare with λ(p) and with Stong/Azarija–Škrekovski bounds for α(p).
refs: Stong, Minimal graphs with a prescribed number of spanning trees, Australas. J. Combin. 82 (2022)
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Spanning-tree values and Zaremba (Chan–Kontorovich–Pak) applied to fan graphs
connection: Chan–Kontorovich–Pak prove exponential growth of the set of spanning-tree counts of n-vertex planar graphs via continued fractions, thin orbits and Zaremba. ES₅ asks the same kind of question for continuants of length 3 with a sign condition.
why: It is the nearest proved theorem in which spanning-tree counts and continued fractions are linked through thin-orbit methods. Their graphs realise numerators of CFs, as our fan does for HJ length 3.
first_step: Read arXiv:2411.18782 §2 (graph ↔ CF dictionary). Check whether their construction realises a prescribed numerator p with a prescribed denominator class (A/p) = −1 at bounded length.
refs: arXiv:2411.18782 (Chan–Kontorovich–Pak, Spanning trees and continued fractions)

title: Modular spanning-tree realisation (Alon–Bucić–Gishboliner) as a model for the sign condition
connection: Alon–Bucić–Gishboliner show every residue u mod N is τ(G) mod N for some planar G on O(log N) vertices. ES₅ is a 'τ(G) = p exactly and pairing class prescribed' statement on 4 vertices.
why: Their short combinatorial proofs control τ(G) modulo N with few vertices; a version controlling the pairing class (a mod-p quadratic datum) would be a graph-theoretic analogue of an ES-type sign theorem.
first_step: Read arXiv:2503.23648; check whether their gadgets allow simultaneous control of τ(G) and the square class of the sandpile pairing.

title: Idoneal numbers in spanning-tree extremal problems vs U(n)/I3 sporadic lists
connection: Azarija–Škrekovski: α(n) ≤ (n+4)/3 iff n ∉ {3,4,5,6,7,9,10,13,18,22}, a subset of Euler's idoneal numbers. U(n)/I3 have finite sporadic failure lists for tuv−u−v representations, also continuant/spanning-tree statements.
why: The appearance of idoneal numbers (class-group exponent ≤ 2) in a spanning-tree problem suggests the U(n) sporadics {105, 2961, 3985, 25305, 111969, 978145} might have a class-group characterisation.
first_step: Compute the class groups Cl(−4n), Cl(−n) for the U(n) sporadics and for I3 failures; test exponent-2 / genus-one patterns.

title: Effective resistance A/p of a 3-node ladder network
connection: In the fan network with unit conductances, the effective resistance between a and the sink is (M⁻¹)₁₁ = A/p. So ES₅(p) ⇔ a three-node ladder network with integer conductances to ground and total 'tree count' p has R_eff(a,s) = A/p with A a non-residue mod p.
why: Electrical-network theory has exact theorems on which rationals are resistances of networks with k unit resistors (series–parallel ↔ continued fractions). The ES sign becomes a residuosity property of a physical quantity.
first_step: Enumerate rational resistances of networks with ≤ 12 unit resistors (OEIS A048211 family); check whether non-residue numerators A/p appear at small resistor counts for every p ≡ 1 (4) < 2000.

title: Linking form of the double branched cover of a 2-bridge link with a 3-vertex plumbing description
connection: L(p,A) is the double branched cover of the 2-bridge link b(p,A). The ES₅ sign is the isometry class of the linking form of Σ₂(b(p,A)), and HJ length 3 means a 3-vertex linear plumbing (negative-CF) description. Note this is not an 'even' continued fraction: three even HJ digits would give an even determinant.
why: Knot theory has exact formulas tying linking forms, Goeritz matrices and signatures (Gordon–Litherland). If σ mod 8 detects (A/p), the ES sign becomes a knot signature on a 3-parameter knot family.
first_step: Compute σ(b(p,A)) by Murasugi's formula Σ_{i<p} (−1)^{⌊iA/p⌋} for p < 500. Check whether σ mod 8, together with p mod 8, determines (A/p) (a van der Blij / Gauss-sum reciprocity).
refs: Gordon–Litherland 1978, On the signature of a link

title: Heegaard Floer d-invariants of L(p,A) as an obstruction/selector for 3-chain plumbings
connection: d-invariants of lens spaces satisfy an explicit recursion (Ozsváth–Szabó), d(L(p,q),i) via d(L(q, p mod q), j). Plumbing length 3 constrains the negative-definite fillings, and the ES sign is the homotopy class.
why: d-invariants are a native tool for deciding which lens spaces bound which definite 4-manifolds (Lisca's rational-ball classification itself used Donaldson's theorem and lattice embeddings; d-invariants give complementary obstructions). They might give a closed-form test of 'some 3-chain filling exists in the non-square class'.
first_step: Implement the Ozsváth–Szabó recursion. For p < 2000, compare Σ_i d(L(p,A),i) statistics over the classes A with r(p/A) = 3 between (A/p) = ±1.

title: Casson–Walker invariant / Dedekind sum of L(p,A) restricted to HJ-length-3 A
connection: λ_CW(L(p,q)) is a Dedekind sum s(q,p) up to normalisation, and Rademacher-type congruences tie 12p·s(q,p) mod 8 to (q/p). On words, s(A,p) has a closed form in (t,u,v) by Dedekind reciprocity.
why: It gives an explicit integer-valued topological invariant of the word whose residue mod 8 is the ES sign. Sums over words then become sums of a topological invariant.
first_step: Derive s(tu−1, p) in closed form from three applications of reciprocity; compare with DEDEKIND_ES §4.

title: Rational balls bounded by lens spaces (Lisca) vs 3-chain plumbings
connection: Lisca classified lens spaces bounding rational homology balls (p = m², specific q). Square p is exactly where ES-type certificates vanish (T1), and rational-ball bounding is tied to the linking form being metabolic.
why: T1 (obstruction at odd squares) and 'bounds a rational ball' are both 'linking form is split/hyperbolic' phenomena. A Lisca-style lattice-embedding argument could explain T1 topologically and show why primes escape it.
first_step: Read Lisca math/0701610 §§2–3 (lattice embeddings). Check whether the T1 square-class obstruction is equivalent to the metabolic linking form of L(m², A) for the relevant A.
refs: arXiv:math/0701610 (Lisca, Lens spaces, rational balls and the ribbon conjecture)

title: Lattice embedding of the 3-chain into the diagonal lattice ℤ^k (Donaldson-style)
connection: If a definite filling can be glued to another definite filling (of the reversed manifold) to give a closed definite 4-manifold, Donaldson's theorem forces the combined intersection lattice to be diagonal, so the plumbing lattice embeds in −ℤ^k (Lisca's method). For the chain (v,t,u), embeddings into ℤ^3 or ℤ^4 are explicit combinatorics, and the ES sign is a property of the complement lattice's discriminant.
why: This is the native toolbox of 4-dimensional topology for lens spaces, and it turns ES₅ into a finite combinatorial embedding question at each p.
first_step: Enumerate embeddings of chain lattices with det p into ℤ⁴ for p < 500; check whether the orthogonal complement's discriminant square class equals the ES sign.

title: Cyclic quotient singularity 1/p(1,A) with a 3-curve resolution and non-residue A
connection: p/A = [[v,t,u]] is the minimal resolution chain (−v,−t,−u) of the cyclic quotient singularity 1/p(1,A). ES₅(p) ⇔ some 1/p(1,A) with (A/p) = −1 has exactly 3 exceptional curves.
why: Singularity theory controls resolution lengths via Riemenschneider duality, P-resolutions and smoothing components (KSB). The ES sign is a Galois-type datum: is 1/p(1,A) isomorphic over a quadratic twist to 1/p(1,1)?
first_step: Compute embedding dimension and Riemenschneider dual lengths for A ∈ L₃(p); test whether the dual-chain length distribution differs between (A/p) = ±1.

title: Kollár–Shepherd-Barron P-resolutions and Wahl singularities 1/m²(1, ma−1) as the T1 locus
connection: T-singularities 1/(dm²)(1, dma−1) have ℚ-Gorenstein smoothings with Milnor number d − 1; the Wahl case d = 1, i.e. 1/m²(1, ma−1), has rational-homology-disk (QHD) smoothings. These sit at square orders m², exactly where T1 kills certificates. KSB P-resolutions of 1/p(1,A) are counted by zero continued fractions.
why: The T1 obstruction may be the shadow of 'square-order cyclic quotients admit QHD smoothings'. Smoothing theory would then give a geometric reason for the square/prime dichotomy.
first_step: Compute, for A ∈ L₃(m²), whether 1/m²(1,A) is a Wahl singularity or admits a QHD smoothing, and compare with the T1 certificate emptiness.

title: Hacking–Prokhorov degenerations of P² to P(a²,b²,c²) and Markov-type equations for ES
connection: Hacking–Prokhorov: toric degenerations of P² to weighted projective planes with T-singularities are governed by Markov triples a²+b²+c² = 3abc, generated by mutations. ES's Markoff-type surface S_{n,D}: nA²+B²+D = ABC is a twisted analogue.
why: Mutation trees of degenerations give an infinite combinatorial structure over a Markov-type equation, and U_n has no comparable mutation structure (only coordinate permutations), while S_{n,D} has only Vieta-type involutions such as B ↦ AC − B (and A ↦ BC/n − A when n | BC). This is a place to look for a hidden mutation.
first_step: Check whether S_{n,D} solutions arise as weights of Q-Gorenstein degenerations of some del Pezzo (degree depending on n); start from HP's classification table.

title: Toric surface with three boundary curves: HJ-length-3 cones as compact toric surface data
connection: A 2-dim cone of type 1/p(1,A) whose resolution has 3 rays corresponds to a toric surface patch. ES₅ asks for a smooth fan refinement with 3 new rays whose self-intersections (−v,−t,−u) give p, with a twist class.
why: Toric geometry turns the condition into lattice-polygon combinatorics (Oda's 12/24 theorem for complete fans), which might give global constraints linking different A's.
first_step: Write the 3-ray refinement condition as a lattice-polygon statement; check whether completing the fan to a compact toric surface forces relations between v, t, u and A (mod 4).
refs: Oda, Convex bodies and algebraic geometry (1988)

title: Tridiagonal ternary lattice of determinant p in the non-square genus
connection: The Gram matrix M(t,u,v) defines a positive definite ternary lattice of determinant p with basis e₁,e₂,e₃, e₁·e₃ = 0, e₁·e₂ = e₂·e₃ = −1. Its discriminant form is A/p on ℤ/p. ES₅(p) ⇔ the genus of ternary lattices of det p with non-square discriminant form contains a lattice admitting such a chain basis with norms ≥ 2.
why: This is the native language of ternary quadratic forms: genus/class tables (Brandt–Intrau), Siegel mass, and representation of binary sublattices. It brings Duke–Schulze-Pillot style tools.
first_step: For p < 2000, list the reduced ternary forms of det p in each genus (Eisenstein reduction). Count the classes admitting a chain basis, and check whether the non-square genus always has one iff ES₅(p).

title: Chain basis ⇔ representation of the binary lattice [[v,−1],[−1,t]] with a prescribed orthogonal vector
connection: A chain basis exists iff the ternary lattice L contains a primitive binary sublattice ≅ [[v,−1],[−1,t]] whose orthogonal complement direction meets L appropriately. This is a 'representation of binary forms by ternary forms' problem with an extra condition.
why: Representation of binary forms by ternary/quaternary forms has deep equidistribution results (Ellenberg–Venkatesh; Einsiedler–Lindenstrauss–Michel–Venkatesh). These give existence for large discriminant, but with growing discriminant here.
first_step: Formulate: for each binary form b of disc ≈ 4tv−4 ≤ X, is b represented by a ternary of det p in the non-square genus with the extra e₃ condition? Compare with the Ellenberg–Venkatesh hypotheses.
refs: Ellenberg–Venkatesh, Local-global principles for representations of quadratic forms (Invent. 2008)

title: Frobenius-class form: uv | n+u+v ⇔ n is in the 'Frobenius shadow' of the numerical semigroup ⟨u,v⟩
connection: n = tuv−u−v ⇔ n ≡ −(u+v) (mod uv). If gcd(u,v) = 1 (automatic for interior words at a prime n), Popoviciu's formula gives exactly t−1 representations of n as au+bv (a,b ≥ 0), and uv−u−v is the Frobenius number. Without coprimality this fails (t = u = v = 2, n = 4). ES₅ words are pairs (u,v) whose denumerant at n is in the Frobenius residue class, plus a sign condition.
why: The theory of numerical semigroups and denumerants (Popoviciu, Sylvester, Ramírez Alfonsín) gives a new vocabulary for the forest F_p (uv | p+u+v), with generating-function tools.
first_step: Express the ES₅ sign in terms of (u,v,n) via denumerant data; check whether Σ_{(u,v)} sign·q^n has a Popoviciu-type generating function (∏ 1/(1−q^u)(1−q^v) restricted to a class).
refs: Ramírez Alfonsín, The Diophantine Frobenius Problem (2005)

title: Sylver coinage / numerical-semigroup games on the forest's Frobenius classes
connection: The forest edge relation uv | p+u+v identifies p as a 'Frobenius-shadow' point of ⟨u,v⟩. Conway's Sylver coinage is a game whose positions are numerical semigroups; P-positions are related to Frobenius data.
why: Game positions give a different combinatorial calculus on pairs (u,v); an ES-relevant invariant might appear as a Sprague–Grundy value. Low prior but not meaningless.
first_step: Compute Sprague–Grundy-type data for two-generator Sylver positions ⟨u,v⟩ with uv | p+u+v; look for any correlation with (uv/p).

title: Christoffel/Sturmian word of slope A/p with three runs
connection: HJ length r(p/A) is a run-length statistic of the Christoffel word of slope A/p (equivalently the cutting sequence of the segment to (p,A)). ES₅ asks for a non-residue A whose Christoffel word has the minimal 3-block structure.
why: Combinatorics on words has exact results on Christoffel words, palindromes and standard factorizations, which might give explicit constructions of A with prescribed structure, for instance via palindromic closure.
first_step: Express r(p/A) = 3 as a factorisation condition on the Christoffel word; test whether the Lothaire standard factorisation relates the two halves to (A/p).
refs: Lothaire, Algebraic Combinatorics on Words, ch. 2

title: Goeritz matrix of an alternating 2-bridge diagram equals the chain matrix
connection: For the plumbing description, the Goeritz form of a suitable 2-bridge link diagram should be (up to sign and stabilisation) the tridiagonal chain matrix (check the diagram convention: plumbing digits are not the same as twist-region counts of the standard diagram). Gordon–Litherland gives σ = sign(G) − μ.
why: This pins ES₅ to an explicit knot diagram: a 3-twist-region 2-bridge knot of determinant p. Knot tables could be scanned for the sign.
first_step: Check against KnotInfo: for 2-bridge knots with det p ≡ 1 (4), p < 200, and 3 twist regions in even CF form, record the linking-form class.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Quantum (WRT) invariants of lens spaces: Gauss sums carrying (A/p)
connection: Jeffrey's formula for the Witten–Reshetikhin–Turaev invariant of L(p,q) involves Dedekind sums and quadratic Gauss sums whose evaluation produces Jacobi symbols in q. The ES sign may appear as a phase of a quantum invariant of L(p,A).
why: Quantum topology has exact formulas (and quantum modularity results) for WRT invariants of Seifert/lens spaces. A sum over words of a quantum invariant could be a computable object.
first_step: Write τ_r(L(p,A)) (Jeffrey 1992). Check whether some level r makes the phase equal to (A/p), and evaluate Σ_{A ∈ L₃(p)} τ_r(L(p,A)).
refs: L. Jeffrey, Chern–Simons–Witten invariants of lens spaces and torus bundles (CMP 1992)

title: Plumbing calculus moves (blow-up/blow-down of ±1 curves) as certificate transport
connection: Kirby calculus moves change a plumbing chain without changing the boundary lens space. The boundary words (letters = 1) of LENGTH_THREE are formal words that become interior after blow-downs.
why: This gives a topological interpretation of the repo's boundary/interior word distinction and of 'transport' moves between certificates (boundary-preserving blow-ups do not change |det|, so transport between different n needs a non-boundary-preserving move such as a surgery/cobordism step; identify which).
first_step: Map LENGTH_THREE formal words (letter 1) to blow-down sequences; check whether ES transport laws (TRANSPORT_LAW.md) are Kirby moves.

title: Hyperbolic triangle billiards / Veech triangles with prescribed area
connection: Billiards in the hyperbolic (π/x, π/y, π/z) triangle unfold to the triangle group's tiling of H² (not to Euclidean translation surfaces). Separately, Euclidean rational triangles unfold to translation surfaces, and Veech's lattice triangles are special shapes there. ES is a statement about the area spectrum of reflection-group triangles.
why: A genuine dynamics translation of the original equation, but probably only a restatement. Recorded for breadth.
first_step: Check whether the area/angle condition has any known role in Veech-group classification (Kenyon–Smillie, Ward triangles).

title: Kirchhoff/Brooks–Smith–Stone–Tutte: squared rectangles from planar networks with p spanning trees
connection: A planar network with τ = p spanning trees gives a rectangle tiled by squares with sides of total scale p (BSST). The fan graph of item 1 is planar, so ES₅ gives a squared rectangle of a specific shape whose aspect ratio encodes the resistance A/p.
why: Squared-rectangle theory has a 'reduced side' (= τ) and aspect ratios = resistances. ES₅ becomes: some 4-vertex-network squared rectangle with reduced side p has aspect class non-residue.
first_step: Compute BSST rectangles for the fan networks at small p; check whether the aspect-ratio numerator class is visible geometrically (e.g. via tile parity).

title: Domino/strip tilings counted by continuants with a parity weight
connection: Positive continuants count tilings of a strip by monominoes and dominoes with weights. The negative continuant K(v,t,u) = tuv−u−v is a signed count, equivalently det of the chain matrix as a weighted path-matching count. The ES sign is the class of the cofactor.
why: Tiling enumeration has transfer-matrix and involution machinery. A sign-reversing involution on tilings might isolate a non-residue cofactor.
first_step: Write tuv−u−v and tu−1 as tiling counts of a 3-cell strip with weights; look for a sign-reversing involution whose fixed points carry the class of tu−1 mod p.
refs: Benjamin–Quinn, Proofs that Really Count (continuants ch. 4)

title: Matrix-tree theorem with signed/twisted weights: the ES sign as a determinant of a twisted Laplacian
connection: (A/p) for the fan graph equals the Legendre symbol of a principal cofactor of the reduced Laplacian M (principal cofactors of the full Laplacian all equal p). Twisted Laplacians (connection Laplacians with ℤ/2 or ℤ/4 holonomy) compute signed spanning-forest counts (Kenyon's cycle-rooted spanning forests).
why: Kenyon's vector-bundle Laplacian theory computes topological invariants of forests via determinants. A ℤ/4 connection might encode the slot-lemma condition '4 | some pentagon entry'.
first_step: Put a ℤ/4 connection on the fan graph; compute det of the connection Laplacian and compare with the slot-lemma indicator over all words for p < 1000.
refs: Kenyon, Spanning forests and the vector bundle Laplacian (Ann. Probab. 2011)
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Hoffman/spectral bound on the forest F_p with Legendre colouring (bichromatic edge existence)
connection: ES₅ for p ≡ 1 (8) ⇔ the word forest F_p has a bichromatic edge under v ↦ (v/p). Spectral graph theory bounds the size of monochromatic (independent-type) sets via eigenvalues.
why: It is the textbook first tool for 'every 2-colouring with given class sizes has a bichromatic edge'. The Legendre colouring has known sizes inside intervals (Burgess), but F_p is sparse.
first_step: Compute the spectrum of F_p for p < 10⁴; compare λ_max/λ_min with the size of the QR set inside vertices to see if Hoffman-type bounds are anywhere near.

title: Isoperimetry/expansion of the forest components vs character-sum smoothness
connection: If the component of 1 in F_p has edge expansion h and contains a QNR, then a bichromatic edge exists. Combinatorial expansion of an arithmetic forest is a graph-theory question.
why: 'The component containing 1 reaches a QNR' is a sufficient (not necessary) condition for ES₅, the arithmetic analogue of a percolation/connectivity statement. FRONTIER §3 records that under Dickson it fails infinitely often (e.g. p = 409 has a monochromatic component of 1 but a negative word (15,4,7)).
first_step: Compute the component sizes of F_p and the least QNR inside the component of 1, for p < 10⁶.

title: Ising model on F_p: ES₅ failure = zero-energy configuration of a frustrated ferromagnet
connection: Put spins σ_v = (v/p) on F_p. ES₅ failure (no bichromatic edge) means the Legendre configuration is a ground state of the ferromagnetic Ising Hamiltonian on F_p. Statistical mechanics has Peierls/contour arguments for when ground states must have domain walls.
why: A Peierls-type argument combines an 'external field' (Legendre symbol bias on short intervals) with graph connectivity. It is a native tool not obviously tried.
first_step: Compute, per component of F_p, the fraction of +spins; check how large monochromatic components get (ES₅ only needs one bichromatic edge somewhere, so monochromatic components are compatible with ES₅).

title: ℤ/2 gauge field on F_p plus multiplicative edges: the Legendre colouring as a flat connection
connection: F_p is a forest, so its own critical group is trivial and colourings carry no holonomy. Adding 'multiplicative' edges u ~ qu (q a small prime, weight (q/p)) creates cycles. The Legendre colouring is then a ℤ/2 gauge configuration that is flat around every cycle by multiplicativity, and ES₅ failure means it is also constant along every forest edge.
why: Speculative: combining the forest's divisibility edges with multiplicative edges might force a contradiction for a flat ℤ/2 connection that is trivial on forest edges, i.e. a global consistency obstruction that a single forest cannot carry.
first_step: Build the augmented graph for p < 2000 (forest + edges u ~ 2u, 3u, 5u); compute the space of ℤ/2 colourings that are multiplicative on the added edges and constant on forest edges, and its dimension.

title: Farey-graph geodesic of length 3 in the non-residue class
connection: HJ length r(p/A) is (up to normalisation) a combinatorial distance-type statistic in the Farey graph from ∞ to p/A via a specific path type. ES₅ asks whether the Farey ball of 'HJ radius 3' around ∞ contains a vertex p/A with A a QNR.
why: The Farey graph is hyperbolic geometry's combinatorial skeleton, and its metric theory (Beardon–Hockman–Short) is well developed.
first_step: Compare r(p/A) with Farey distance d(∞, p/A) for p < 10⁴; check whether the ES₅ condition is a Farey-distance condition for a known metric.

title: Ford circles: A/p lies in a horoball of 'depth-3' chain
