connection: r(p/A) = 3 means the Ford circle chain from ∞ to A/p has three tangency steps of HJ type. ES₅ becomes: some non-residue A has A/p inside the union of depth-3 Ford horoball chains.
why: The Ford circle picture makes the condition a covering-by-horoballs statement, where hyperbolic volume arguments live.
first_step: Draw/compute the union of depth-3 HJ horoball chains intersected with {A/p}; measure its proportion and its correlation with QR.

title: Closed horocycle at height 1/p: equidistribution of (a + i)/p and cusp excursions
connection: Every closed horocycle of length → ∞ equidistributes (Sarnak/Hejhal; sparse versions by Venkatesh, Strömbergsson). Points (a + i)/p, a mod p, lift ES₅-type continued-fraction data of a/p; ES₅ needs a point whose cusp excursion has a specific deep shape.
why: Puts ES₅ into the horocycle-equidistribution world where every-p statements exist — but probably at too deep a cusp scale (B2), which this item would quantify.
first_step: Translate λ(p) ≤ 3 into a statement on the cusp depth/shape of some (a + i)/p and compare with the scales reachable by effective equidistribution.
alt_first_steps: [translate-0040] Compute the measure of the 'HJ-length ≤ 3' cusp region in the unit tangent bundle; compare with the count |L₃(p)| ≈ log²p to see the scale.
refs: Strömbergsson, On the uniform equidistribution of long closed horocycles (Duke 2004)
alt_titles: [translate-0040] Closed horocycle of period p: depth-3 cusp excursion at a non-residue point

title: Closed geodesic of γ_w on the modular surface: trace N−m and word length 3
connection: γ_w is hyperbolic when |A+A*| > 2. Its closed geodesic has a cutting sequence of length governed by the word. Prime geodesic theorems with Jacobi-symbol twists (Sarnak's class-number sums) count such objects.
why: Prime geodesic theorems in conjugacy classes and with characters are fully developed; ES₅ is a twisted count of geodesics with very short cutting sequences.
first_step: Write trace(γ_w) = tu + tv − 2 = A + A* and list the conjugacy classes; check whether ES₅ is equivalent to a short-cutting-sequence geodesic of trace in a given set with a character condition.
refs: Sarnak, Class numbers of indefinite binary quadratic forms (1982)

title: A¹-curves on U_n and log Gromov–Witten counts vs polynomial ES identities
connection: GHK's theta functions are built from counts of A¹-curves (log GW invariants) meeting the boundary at one point. Integral A¹-curves in U_n are polynomial parametric families of (signed) solutions, the fixed-n analogue of Mordell identities.
why: Mordell–Schinzel says no polynomial families cover square classes. Log GW counts are an enumerative invariant of the same objects, so they might give a geometric reason for which classes are covered.
first_step: Count low-degree A¹-curves on U_n for a few n by direct polynomial search (deg ≤ 3); compare with the GHK broken-line counts.

title: Harpaz's log K3 surfaces: dP5 minus a pentagon and the frieze variety with coefficient N
connection: Harpaz classified log K3 surfaces with trivial geometric Picard group compactifiable to del Pezzos: dP5 with a boundary pentagon of (−1)-curves, which is the A₂ cluster variety. He proved non-Zariski-density of integral points when the Galois action is trivial. The ES₅ frieze (Ptolemy relations with frozen sides (1,1,1,1,N)) is a one-parameter deformation of this variety.
why: It is the closest proved arithmetic theorem about integral points on the exact variety class carrying ES₅ words, and it shows how Brauer–Manin fails to be the only obstruction there.
first_step: Check whether the N-fibre of the pentagon-with-coefficients variety is again dP5 minus a pentagon (a twisted A₂ cluster variety), and read Harpaz §§4–5 for the non-BM obstruction mechanism.
refs: arXiv:1511.01285 (Harpaz, Geometry and arithmetic of certain log K3 surfaces)

title: Frieze patterns with coefficients (Cuntz–Holm–Jørgensen) for boundary (1,1,1,1,N)
connection: CHJ develop friezes with coefficients and prove finiteness: for given boundary there are finitely many friezes with entries in a discrete set. They also obtain them by cutting subpolygons out of triangulated polygons. ES₅ words are exactly the positive integral friezes of the pentagon with boundary (1,1,1,1,N) (FRIEZE_ES).
why: Their 'cutting out subpolygons from Conway–Coxeter friezes' construction could realise each ES₅ word inside a classical triangulation of an (N+…)-gon, giving a triangulation model of the sign.
first_step: Read arXiv:1909.02332 §§3–5. Represent each word for p < 200 as a cut-out from a Conway–Coxeter frieze and check whether the sign (4 | quiddity entry) is visible on the triangulation.

title: Conway–Coxeter triangulation count with a mod-4 marked quiddity entry
connection: Classical friezes ↔ triangulations (Conway–Coxeter). The slot lemma says the ES sign is −1 iff 4 divides one of the five pentagon entries (t,u,v,tu−1,tv−1). So ES₅ asks for a frieze with coefficients having an entry ≡ 0 (mod 4).
why: 'Some quiddity entry ≡ 0 mod 4' is a reduction-mod-4 condition, and friezes over ℤ/4 (or SL₂(ℤ/4) Farey complexes) are finite objects with full classifications.
first_step: Enumerate the mod-4 reductions of all positive words for p < 10⁵ and record which mod-4 frieze types occur per p; compare with Morier-Genoud's counts of friezes over finite rings.
refs: Morier-Genoud, Counting Coxeter's friezes over a finite field via moduli spaces (check arXiv id)

title: Lyness 5-cycle with a coefficient: integrable map whose integer orbits are ES₅ words
connection: The pentagon Ptolemy relations with one frozen side N give a period-5 birational map (a Lyness-type recurrence x_{k+1}x_{k−1} = x_k + c_k with c ∈ {1,N}). Integer orbits are words. Lyness maps have an invariant cubic (elliptic) fibration.
why: Discrete integrable systems give invariants and elliptic fibrations of such maps; the invariant of the coefficient-N Lyness cycle gives each word a 'conserved energy', possibly with arithmetic meaning.
first_step: Compute the invariant rational function of the (1,1,1,1,N) Lyness cycle (sympy). Evaluate it on words and look for a link with the sign or with t.

title: Tropical frieze / tropicalisation of the pentagon-with-coefficient
connection: Replacing (×,+) by (+,max) gives a tropical frieze: 2-adic valuations of the pentagon entries satisfy the tropical Ptolemy relations only as inequalities (v₂(a+b) ≥ min, with equality unless there is cancellation, e.g. 1 + 1 = 2), so they give tropical constraints, not a tropical frieze. The slot lemma condition is a 2-adic valuation event (v₂(entry) ≥ 2).
why: Tropical friezes are piecewise-linear and fully classifiable, so they might give a necessary-and-sufficient 2-adic shape of sign-(−1) words.
first_step: Compute the 2-adic valuation vectors (v₂ of the 5 entries) of all words for p < 10⁵ and the allowed tropical patterns; check whether every p has a pattern with some v₂ ≥ 2.

title: Laurent phenomenon: all frieze entries as Laurent polynomials in an initial seed (c, m) with coefficient N
connection: In a cluster algebra with frozen N, every entry is a Laurent polynomial in an initial cluster. ES words are integrality (positivity) points of these Laurent polynomials, so ES₅ is an 'integer specialisation of a cluster algebra' problem.
why: The theory of integer points of cluster varieties (positivity, theta bases, Fock–Goncharov) is native here, and may give parametrisations of all words by a seed.
first_step: Write the five entries as Laurent polynomials in (c,m) with N; the integrality condition is (cm−1) | (N + c). Record that the frieze reproduces the hyperbola/divisor condition, and check whether any other seed gives a different divisor condition.

title: SL₂-tilings (Bergeron–Reutenauer) containing a row of five with boundary N
connection: SL₂-tilings are infinite arrays of 2×2 minors 1; friezes are bounded tilings. A word gives a finite SL₂-pattern; Bergeron–Reutenauer parametrise tilings by bi-infinite paths in the Farey graph.
why: It turns words into Farey-graph path pairs, where the ES sign might be a holonomy in SL₂(ℤ/4) along the path pair (SVZ already looked at mod-4 contractibility).
first_step: Compute the Bergeron–Reutenauer path pair of each word; check whether the mod-4 holonomy distinguishes signs.
refs: Bergeron–Reutenauer, SL_k-tilings of the plane (Illinois J. 2010)

title: Positive points of cluster varieties ↔ tropical points (Fock–Goncharov duality) for the ES frieze
connection: Fock–Goncharov: positive-integer tropical points of a cluster X-variety parametrise a canonical basis of the dual A-variety. ES words are positive integer points of an A-type frieze variety with coefficient.
why: If ES words were tropical points of a dual variety, existence would become 'a certain polyhedral cone contains an integer point', which is linear.
first_step: Identify the dual (X-variety) of the A₂-with-coefficient frieze variety; compute its tropical points relevant to N; check whether the A-integer points (words) are in bijection with them.
refs: Fock–Goncharov, Cluster ensembles, quantization and the dilogarithm (2009)

title: Quiver representations of A₂ with dimension-vector data equal to a word
connection: Friezes of type A_n categorify via Caldero–Chapoton maps on cluster categories of A_n. Frieze entries are Euler characteristics of quiver Grassmannians. Coefficients correspond to frozen vertices (Frobenius categories).
why: Categorification gives representation-theoretic meaning to every entry, so 'entry ≡ 0 mod 4' becomes 'Euler characteristic of a quiver Grassmannian ≡ 0 mod 4'.
first_step: Find the Frobenius 2-CY category categorifying friezes with coefficients (Holm–Jørgensen line of work), and identify which objects give entries t,u,v,tu−1,tv−1.

title: Integral points on log CY surfaces: counting conjecture of order (log B)^k and the U_n fibre
connection: For log K3/log CY surfaces the expected integral point count up to height B is a power of log B (Harpaz; Wilsch-type works on integral points of bounded height). U_n has finitely many positive points, but its signed integral points can be counted.
why: The ES expected count ≍ log²n matches 'log-power' heuristics for log CY. Translating the n-dependence into height may connect ES's count to a Manin-type conjecture for integral points.
first_step: Count signed integral points on U_n of height ≤ B for fixed n and growing B (numerically); compare with a (log B)^b law and identify b with the boundary's dual-complex dimension.
refs: Wilsch, Integral points of bounded height on a log Fano threefold (check arXiv)

title: Total family U → A¹_n: integral points on a threefold and Manin–Peyre for the total space
connection: The total space 𝒰 = {4xyz = n(xy+yz+zx)} ⊂ A⁴ is a threefold. ES says the projection 𝒰(ℤ_{>0}) → ℤ_{≥2} is surjective. Integral points on the threefold are counted asymptotically (Elsholtz–Tao averages), so surjectivity is a 'fibre-wise' strengthening.
why: This is the standard 'surjectivity of a morphism on integral points' question, related to Serre's thin-set / Hilbert irreducibility for integral points. The fibres here are log CY rather than rational curves.
first_step: Look up results on 'integral points: surjectivity onto the base' (e.g. Corvaja–Zannier thin sets, integral Hilbert irreducibility) to locate the nearest theorem.
refs: Corvaja–Zannier, On the Hilbert property and the fundamental group (check)

title: The pencil S_{n,k}: 4xyz − n(xy+yz+zx) = k as a K3-type family with a singular fibre at k = 0
connection: Z52 proved a BM obstruction for k = m² (with congruence conditions) that dies at k = 0. In degeneration theory, the k = 0 fibre is the central fibre of a family of affine cubic surfaces. Brauer classes can extend over the family or ramify at k = 0.
why: Specialisation of Brauer classes in families (purity/residue maps) is a native tool. The residue along the exceptional conic was computed; nearby fibres give limiting information.
first_step: Compute Br of the generic fibre of the pencil over Q(k), and the residues at k = 0 and k = ∞; record whether any class survives as an unramified class on the k = 0 fibre's resolution.

title: Integral points via the universal torsor: ES as lattice points satisfying a system of coprime divisibilities
connection: Torsor descent turns 4xyz = n(xy+yz+zx) into the classical parametrisation x = abd·…, which has the shape of ET's (a,b,c,d) Type I/II data. Torsor coordinates are the standard native coordinates.
why: It explains the ET parametrisations as torsor coordinates, and opens the use of the torsor's own symmetry group, a torus.
first_step: Match ET (2.1)–(2.7) with the Cox ring of the minimal desingularisation of the closure; list any extra torus action not used so far.
refs: Derenthal, Cox rings of singular del Pezzo surfaces (check)

title: Integral Hasse principle for U_n relative to a group action at infinity (ℝ⁺ component)
connection: BL treat the positive real component U_n(ℝ)⁺. Positivity of solutions is an archimedean condition; BM evaluation can see real connected components (as in BL's U_n(ℝ)⁺ version), but not finer positivity structure inside a component. Strong approximation with an archimedean constraint is studied for homogeneous spaces.
why: The repo's T1 is a reciprocity obstruction coupling the archimedean and finite places. The native tool is a 'Brauer–Manin with archimedean condition' (BL's U(ℝ)⁺ version).
first_step: Re-read BL §§5–7 for the exact role of U_n(ℝ)⁺; record which Brauer classes have non-constant evaluation on U_n(ℝ)⁺.

title: ES over number fields with unit-rank ≥ 1 (unit orbits as infinite families)
connection: Over O_K with infinite unit group, U_n(O_K) may have unit-orbit families. UNIT_ORBIT_ES studied these; the native field is Diophantine equations over rings of integers (unit equations, S-unit theorems).
why: Shows what infinite symmetry does to the problem. The S-unit equation theory (Evertse–Győry) gives finiteness or infinitude results for the related unit equations.
first_step: Check whether some ES equivalent form is an S-unit equation in disguise (e.g. after fixing a factorisation pattern) and apply the S-unit counting bounds.
refs: Evertse–Győry, Unit Equations in Diophantine Number Theory (2015)
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Elliptic fibration of the ES cubic by planes x + y + z = s
connection: Intersecting the projective closure with the pencil of planes x + y + z = sw gives plane cubic curves, an elliptic fibration (after base-point blow-ups). ES points are integral points on these elliptic curves with positive coordinates.
why: The elliptic-curve toolbox applies fibrewise: Mordell–Weil ranks, Néron–Tate heights and integral points. Ranks along the family could produce infinitely many signed points.
first_step: Compute the Weierstrass model of the s-fibre for fixed n (sympy), and the Mordell–Weil rank of the generic fibre over Q(s).

title: Conic bundle over the x-line: Châtelet-surface toolbox (descent, Schinzel's hypothesis)
connection: The x-fibration is a conic bundle with split degenerate fibres. Châtelet surfaces and conic bundles have Hasse principle results conditional on Schinzel's hypothesis (Colliot-Thélène–Sansuc–Swinnerton-Dyer) and unconditional ones in some degrees (Browning–Matthiesen–Skorobogatov).
why: It is the canonical way the field produces points fibrewise. Integral and positivity constraints are what is missing, but the fibration method with additive combinatorics (Green–Tao input) is a powerful modern variant.
first_step: Write the x-fibration's degenerate fibres as linear forms in x. Check whether Browning–Matthiesen–Skorobogatov's linear-forms setting applies to integral points with x in a short range.
refs: Browning–Matthiesen–Skorobogatov, Rational points on pencils of conics and quadrics with many degenerate fibres (Ann. Math. 2014)

title: Vojta/abc for integral points on U_n: what does 'log Kodaira dimension 0' predict
connection: Vojta's conjecture predicts degeneracy of integral points only for log general type. U_n is log CY (κ̄ = 0), so integral points may be dense, and no prediction of existence follows.
why: This is a calibration: it explains why no conjectural Diophantine machine gives ES, unlike Markoff (log CY too) where Ghosh–Sarnak found failures.
first_step: Note as calibration. Check whether 'log CY with BM set non-empty but positive points absent' is known to occur infinitely often in a family (Loughran–Mitankin for Markoff).
refs: Loughran–Mitankin, Integral Hasse principle and strong approximation for Markoff surfaces (IMRN 2021; check)

title: Arakelov/height view: ES solutions have height ≤ n³-type bound, a Π⁰₁ statement
connection: Positive solutions satisfy x ≤ 3n/4, y ≤ n²-ish and z ≤ n⁴-ish (Curtiss-type bounds), so ES is a Π⁰₁ arithmetic sentence. Heights in Arakelov theory bound points; existence of small-height points is a Siegel-lemma question.
why: Siegel's lemma or geometry of numbers on the torsor might produce small points if a linear structure is present (e.g. Type II at fixed C is linear in some coordinates).
first_step: State precisely the height bounds for positive solutions. Check whether any linear sub-system at fixed (C,d) has a Siegel-lemma solution of the right size.

title: Toric degeneration of U_n to the torus complement xyz ≠ 0 and the Newton polytope
connection: As n varies, 4xyz = n(xy+yz+zx) degenerates (n → 0, n → ∞) to toric strata. Newton polytope methods (Bernstein–Kushnirenko, Khovanskii) count solutions in tori over finite fields; positive integer solutions relate to the polytope's interior lattice points.
why: Newton-polytope/tropical methods give exact solution counts over F_q (Ax–Katz divisibility of point counts) and might give mod-2 parity of solution counts.
first_step: Compute #U_n(F_q) exactly via the toric model and check Ax–Katz-type q-divisibility; record whether any parity information survives to positive integer points.

title: Motivic/Igusa zeta function of U_n: local densities and the BM main term
connection: The BM main term is a product of local densities, each the limit of #U_n(ℤ/p^k)/p^{2k}. Igusa's local zeta function encodes these densities as rational functions with poles governed by an embedded resolution.
why: The exact local factors (especially at 2) control the T1/sign phenomena. Igusa poles might give a uniform closed form for the BM constant, which is already exact.
first_step: Compute Igusa zeta of 4xyz − n(xy+yz+zx) at p = 2 and p | n via the toric resolution; compare with BM_CORRECTED_COUNT local factors.

title: Hasse principle for the 'Type II at fixed level' variety: d | 4Cn+1, d ≡ −1 (mod 4C) as a norm-form/torus variety
connection: At fixed C, a solution is a factorisation 4Cn+1 = d·d′ with d ≡ −1 (mod 4C). This is an integral point on a torus-type variety (norm form for the trivial extension, with level structure). Ray-class-field reciprocity says the class of d is constrained.
why: Torus-variety integral points with level structure are governed by class field theory (ray class groups). ES at fixed C is exactly a ray-class question, B2.
first_step: Record the ray class group mod 4C whose Frobenius class decides it, and the explicit list of p's covered for C ≤ 20 (sanity link to Mordell covering).

title: Integral points on the affine quadric family: Type I as a sum-of-squares/norm condition in ℤ[√−d]
connection: QUATERNION_ES Lemma 1.1: Type I at level d ⇔ (1+2aw)(1+2bw) = e(2cw − p) in ℤ[w], w = √−d. This is a factorisation problem in an imaginary quadratic order.
why: Factorisation in quadratic orders is governed by the class group and genus theory, and the repo uses it in LATTICE_MEETING. The native next step is a Heegner-point/CM-points equidistribution input.
first_step: Express the condition as 'a specific ideal of norm e lies in a class of order ≤ 2·something'; test which genus characters are forced.

title: Bhargava cubes: the Type II cube point (c,d,j) as a 2×2×2 integer cube
connection: FIXED_MODULUS_SHOTS packages Type II data as a cube point; Bhargava's cube law composes three binary quadratic forms. If certificates are cubes with a fixed corner, composition gives relations among certificates of different n.
why: Bhargava's parametrisations come with orbit-counting (geometry of numbers on prehomogeneous spaces), which gives averages but sometimes also exact class-group relations.
first_step: Write a certificate as an explicit 2×2×2 cube and compute its three binary forms; check which one has discriminant related to p and what composition does to certificates.
refs: Bhargava, Higher composition laws I (Ann. Math. 2004)

title: Prehomogeneous vector space view: averages are easy, pointwise is the problem (calibration)
connection: Orbit-counting on prehomogeneous spaces gives averages over discriminants (Davenport–Heilbronn style). ES's averages are known (Vaughan, ET), and the pointwise question has no prehomogeneous analogue.
why: This calibrates what arithmetic statistics can give: possibly a positive-proportion statement in the n-aspect with explicit constants, not ES.
first_step: Skip unless a pointwise parametrisation arises. Note as a calibration entry.

title: Multiplicative subgroup generated by prime factors: Frobenius / Chebotarev form of 'divisor in coset'
connection: A divisor d of N in the class −1 mod 4C exists iff a subset product of the prime factors of N hits −1 in (ℤ/4C)^×. This is a zero-sum / subset-product problem in a finite abelian group (Davenport constant).
why: The Davenport constant D(G) says any sequence of length ≥ D(G) has a zero-sum subsequence. Subset-product hitting −1 needs ω(N) about D((ℤ/4C)^×) primes in general position.
first_step: For p < 10⁶ and C ≤ 30, compute ω(4Cp+1) and whether the prime classes' subset products cover −1; compare with Davenport-constant thresholds.

title: Olson/Erdős–Ginzburg–Ziv-type theorem for 'subset product = −1' in (ℤ/4C)^×
connection: Zero-sum theory has inverse theorems: sequences with no zero-sum subsequence are structured (lie in a coset). ES failure at fixed C forces the prime factors of 4Cp+1 to lie in an index-2-type structure that avoids −1.
why: Inverse zero-sum theorems give explicit structure of failing configurations, which is a different angle from sieve counting.
first_step: State: the subset products of ω primes avoid −1 ⇒ all lie in a subgroup H not containing −1 or the configuration is short. Check against data for p < 10⁶.
refs: Gao–Geroldinger survey, Zero-sum problems in finite abelian groups (2006)

title: Vinogradov's least-QNR conjecture as a sufficient hypothesis for the BM layer only
connection: SYNTHESIS_SPARKS9: the BM layer is pointwise free, i.e. some level 4 | t ≤ 4ℓ(p) has a positive main term. The remaining question is the class of the divisor inside a coset. Least-QNR bounds control the first layer only.
why: This calibrates what 'standard conjectures' buy; the second layer needs a different hypothesis (equidistribution of divisor classes of one integer).
first_step: Formulate the minimal second-layer hypothesis ('divisors of tp+1 equidistribute in (ℤ/t)^× for some t ≤ T') and compare it with the known Erdős–Hall/Montgomery-type results on divisor class distribution.

title: Kloosterman-sum form of the word count R_t(p) and Weil-bound positivity
connection: #{(X,Y): XY = tp+1, X ≡ Y ≡ −1 (t), sizes} is a divisor-in-progression count. Its sign-twisted version Σ(A/p) is a sum of Jacobi symbols over divisors, expressible by Kloosterman/Salié sums after Poisson summation.
why: Weil's bound is the native positivity tool. It needs long sums, and the word count per level is O(1), which is the B3 issue in native terms.
first_step: Write the χ-twisted level-t count as a Salié sum expression and record the length vs modulus ratio.

title: Burgess-type bounds for character sums over 'divisor sets' (multiplicative structure)
connection: ES₅ needs χ_p to be non-constant on S₃(p) = {A : r(p/A) = 3}, a set of size ≈ log²p built from divisors. Character sums over multiplicatively structured sets (products of two sets) admit Burgess/bilinear bounds.
why: S₃(p) = {(p+u)/v : v | p+u, …}: if it contains a product set A·B mod p with |A|,|B| ≫ p^ε, bilinear character-sum bounds would force a non-residue.
first_step: Check computationally whether S₃(p) (or the larger S_L(p)) contains large product sets A·B mod p.

title: Sum-product / Bourgain–Glibichuk–Konyagin for the set S_L(p) as L grows
connection: S_L(p) = {A : r(p/A) ≤ L} grows like p^{c(L)} for L ≫ log p. Sum-product theory says sets of size p^δ generate F_p in bounded steps. ES₅ fixes L = 3, where |S₃| ≈ log²p.
why: It is the native additive-combinatorics frame for why L = 3 is hard (polylog sets have no sum-product leverage) and where L-ladders become easy.
first_step: Tabulate |S_L(p)| and the least L with S_L(p) ⊄ QR for p < 10⁶ (this is λ(p)); fit L_min growth.

title: Hidden Number Problem formulation: recover/obtain A from partial information on A·x mod p
connection: Boneh–Venkatesan's HNP finds α from approximations of α·t_i mod p. The ES₅ condition r(p/A) = 3 says A/p lies near 1/v with a prescribed error structure (A = (p+u)/v), an approximation statement about A mod p.
why: HNP and lattice-reduction tools are native for 'find an element mod p with given approximate multiples'. Reversing them (choose A with small multiples) is a geometry-of-numbers existence question.
first_step: Write the ES₅ word condition as 'vA ≡ u (mod p) with uv small, (u,v) in a hyperbolic region'; check the Minkowski bound for the lattice {(x, y) : y ≡ Ax mod p} restricted to non-residue A.

title: The lattice Λ_A = {(x,y) : y ≡ Ax (mod p)}: ES₅ ⇔ a non-residue A whose lattice has a short vector in a hyperbolic region
connection: vA ≡ u (mod p) with v | p+u means (v, u) ∈ Λ_A with uv small. By Minkowski every Λ_A has a vector with |x||y| ≤ p. ES₅ needs (v, u) with vA − u = p exactly (not just mod p) and positive.
why: It is geometry of numbers in its native form: minima of the family of lattices Λ_A over A ∈ QNR. Successive minima of Λ_A relate to CF data, with a Hecke-type averaging over A.
first_step: For p < 10⁵ compute λ₁(Λ_A) for all A and the minimum over non-residue A of the product-norm minimum; relate to λ(p).

title: Klein polygons / sails of the cone for p/A: HJ length = number of sail vertices
connection: The HJ digits of p/A are read off the boundary of the convex hull of the non-zero lattice points in the cone of the toric model of 1/p(1,A) (e.g. cone((0,1),(p,−A)) up to orientation convention; Klein's sail). The boundary lattice points are the HJ convergents (r(p/A) + 2 Hilbert-basis points), and geometric vertices are the points with digit ≥ 3. So r(p/A) = 3 means exactly 3 interior boundary points.
why: Arnold's statistics of sails and multidimensional continued fractions are a native toolbox. Sails with few vertices are rare and structured.
first_step: Express 'sail of cone(p,A) has 3 interior vertices' and count over A ∈ QNR; compare with Arnold's predictions for random cones.

title: Vallée's dynamical analysis of Euclidean algorithms (by-excess algorithm) with a quadratic character
connection: The HJ expansion is the 'by-excess' Euclidean algorithm. Vallée's transfer-operator method gives limit laws for costs such as length. ES₅ asks for the extreme value: min length over A in the non-residue class equals 3.
why: It is the native analysis-of-algorithms framework; twisting transfer operators by Dirichlet characters is done in Baladi–Vallée-type works.
first_step: Look up whether the by-excess algorithm's length distribution has been studied with a character twist (Baladi–Vallée 2005 for Gauss map; Dolgopyat estimates).

title: Backward-CF (Rényi-type) map T(x) = ⌈1/x⌉ − 1/x: infinite invariant measure and orbit length 3
connection: The HJ expansion is generated by a backward-CF (Rényi-type) map with an infinite invariant measure (parabolic fixed point). The coordinate convention matters: in the variable x = A/p the map T(x) = ⌈1/x⌉ − 1/x reproduces the HJ step, whereas the map x ↦ 1/(1−x) − ⌊⋯⌋ started at A/p does not (5/17 takes 4 steps, but its HJ length is 3). Short orbits to 0 in 3 steps are the ES₅ words.
why: Infinite-ergodic-theory tools (Aaronson, Thaler) describe return statistics near the parabolic point, and ES words are 'fast escapes', the complementary regime.
first_step: Compute the measure of points with exactly 3-step Rényi orbits to the cusp at resolution 1/p; compare with |L₃(p)|/p.
refs: Aaronson, An Introduction to Infinite Ergodic Theory (1997)

title: Mayer/Gauss–Kuzmin–Wirsing transfer operator twisted by (·/p): spectral gap for character sums over CF sets
connection: Character sums over sets defined by CF conditions can be studied by transfer operators with a character twist (as in Bourgain–Kontorovich and Dolgopyat). A spectral gap gives cancellation in Σ_{A: CF condition} χ(A).
why: It is the native way to get cancellation for CF-defined sets, but works for growing lengths, not length 3. Recorded as the nearest tool.
first_step: Record the length threshold L(p) beyond which twisted transfer-operator methods give non-trivial Σ_{A ∈ S_L(p)} (A/p); compare with λ(p) data.
refs: Mayer 1991 (transfer operator of the Gauss map)

title: Farey-fraction spin chain (Kleban–Özlük) partition function and the ES words
connection: Kleban–Özlük's Farey spin chain has a partition function built from products of matrices [[1,0],[1,1]] and [[1,1],[0,1]], and its states are Farey fractions. ES words correspond to specific length-3 HJ blocks, so a restricted partition function counts them.
why: Statistical mechanics of number-theoretic chains has exact phase-transition results; a 'Legendre-field' coupling would make the ES sign a magnetization.
first_step: Define Z_p(β, h) = Σ_{A} e^{−β·r(p/A)} (A/p)^{h}; compute for p < 10⁴ and look at the h-derivative at β → ∞ (the min-length sign).
refs: Kleban–Özlük, A Farey fraction spin chain (CMP 1999)

title: Knauf's number-theoretic spin chain and Riemann ζ: a ζ-like Dirichlet series for HJ lengths
connection: Knauf's spin chain partition function is ζ(s−1)/ζ(s). An analogous chain with HJ (by-excess) matrices and a quadratic-character field might have a Dirichlet-series partition function whose coefficients encode λ(p).
why: If the partition function is an L-function quotient, analytic properties (zeros/poles) would control its coefficients.
first_step: Compute Σ_{p,A} p^{−s} x^{r(p/A)} (A/p) numerically and try to identify it as an L-function combination.
refs: Knauf, On a ferromagnetic spin chain (CMP 1993)

title: Hecke operators on the space of words: does T_ℓ map ES₅ words of p to words of ℓp or ℓ²p?
connection: Hecke operators act on SL₂(ℤ)-cosets/matrices with fixed determinant structure. Words are SL₂ matrices with upper-right entry p. Hecke correspondences relate matrices with entry p to entry ℓp.
why: It is the modular-forms-native way to get relations between different n. A Hecke-equivariant structure on certificates would allow induction.
first_step: Apply the coset representatives of T_2 to γ_w and check which images are words (positive, upper-right p or 4p) and how the sign transforms.

title: Kudla Diff-parity and T1: incoherent Eisenstein series derivative as a 'certificate counting function'
connection: KUDLA_ES: T1 ⟺ oddness of Kudla's Diff(T). The derivative of an incoherent Eisenstein series at the centre has Fourier coefficients that are arithmetic degrees of special cycles (Kudla–Rapoport–Yang).
why: If ES certificate counts were arithmetic degrees on a Shimura curve or variety, the arithmetic Siegel–Weil formula would give exact identities, with positivity coming from geometry.
first_step: Check whether certificates of level d correspond to special 0-cycles Z(T) on a quaternionic Shimura curve; compare degrees with KRY's formula numerically.
refs: Kudla, Central derivatives of Eisenstein series and height pairings (Ann. Math. 1997)

title: Gross–Keating / arithmetic intersection of CM cycles as certificate counts
connection: Gross–Keating compute intersection numbers of Hecke correspondences on modular curves in terms of quadratic forms. QUATERNION_ES shows Type I ⇔ an x = 2 collision of CM orders in B_{p,∞}, i.e. an intersection of CM points.
why: Intersection numbers are positive and given by explicit local formulas, which is a geometric positivity mechanism. The question is whether some intersection number equals (or bounds below) a certificate count.
first_step: Express the 'collision of CM orders' count as an intersection T_m · T_n of Hecke correspondences (Gross–Keating) for small p; compare with ES counts.
refs: Gross–Keating, On the intersection of modular correspondences (Invent. 1993)

title: Brandt matrices: theta series of ternary lattices of maximal orders and the representation number of certificates
connection: Brandt matrix entries are representation numbers of the norm forms of ideals in B_{p,∞}; their traces relate to class numbers of imaginary quadratic orders (Eichler trace formula). Certificate counts at level d may be Brandt-matrix entries.
why: Eichler's trace formula is an exact class-number identity. If certificate counts are traces, they become class-number sums, and class numbers are positive.
first_step: Compute Brandt matrices B(m) for p < 200 (Sage/Magma) and correlate entries with ES level counts.
refs: Gross, Heights and special values of L-series (1987) §§1–2
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Duke–Schulze-Pillot: ternary forms represent all large n in their spinor genus — applied to the chain lattice
connection: DSP proved every sufficiently large integer (primitively, locally represented, outside spinor exceptions) is represented by a positive definite ternary form. ES₅ is not 'a fixed form represents p' but 'some form of det p has a special basis'; the dual question 'which binary forms does a ternary represent' (Ellenberg–Venkatesh) is closer.
why: It records the nearest pointwise representation theorem with ternary forms and why it does not apply directly (the form varies with p).
first_step: Find a reformulation where a fixed ternary form must represent a p-tied number with a sign (e.g. via QUATERNION_ES Λ_{d,m}) and check DSP's ineffectivity/effectivity.
refs: Duke–Schulze-Pillot, Representation of integers by positive ternary quadratic forms (Invent. 1990)

title: Gauss's three-squares theorem as a template: r₃(n) ≍ h(−n) and the ES sign as a genus character
connection: Gauss: r₃(n) = 12h(−4n) (n ≡ 1,2 mod 4, squarefree) is an exact class-number formula for a pointwise existence theorem. THREE_SQUARES links the ES sign to three-squares data.
why: It is the canonical example where pointwise existence follows from an exact identity plus positivity of class numbers. ES lacks such an identity (SIGN_IDENTITY).
first_step: Look for a combination Σ_level c_t·(certificate count at level t) that equals a positive class-number expression (e.g. h(−tp) type) at primes; fit numerically.

title: Hurwitz class numbers and the level count M_t^lev(n) = (τ(N) − σ_{χ_{−t}}(N))/φ(t)
connection: The BM level count is a difference of divisor functions twisted by χ_{−t}. Sums over t of such twisted divisor sums resemble Hurwitz class-number relations (Kronecker–Hurwitz Σ_t H(4n − t²)).
why: Class-number relations are exact and positive. If Σ_t over BM levels matches a Hurwitz-type sum, the BM layer gets an exact formula.
first_step: Compute Σ_{t ≤ T} M_t^lev(n) and compare with Σ H(4tn − s²)-type expressions numerically for n < 10⁴.

title: Waldspurger/Kohnen–Zagier: squares of half-integral-weight coefficients as central L-values
connection: SIGN_IDENTITY Prop 2.4 restricts the Waldspurger route. In native terms: if the ES count (or its sign part) were |c(p)|² for a weight-3/2 form, nonvanishing would be L(f⊗χ_p, 1/2) ≠ 0, which is known for positive proportions (Iwaniec–Sarnak type) but not pointwise.
why: Calibration: shows the best automorphic route yields positive proportion, unless a root-number obstruction is absent and an exact formula exists.
first_step: Record calibration; check whether any weight-3/2 form's coefficients correlate with N₋(p) on p < 10⁵ (it should be ruled out by size).

title: Shimura curve / quaternion Shimura lift of the ES theta series
connection: The theta multiplier sign (bsB_theta_multiplier) is weight-1/2 data. The Shimura correspondence maps half-integral to integral weight. ES's sign function on certificate matrices might lift to a function on a Shimura curve's CM points.
why: It would place the sign inside an automorphic representation where nonvanishing theory exists. Zero-propagation was refuted (O175), so only the lifting is new.
first_step: Look at O175 notes (bsB_theta_multiplier) and identify which level and character a 'certificate theta series' would have; compute the first 50 coefficients.

title: Markoff-type surface S_{n,D}: Vieta jumping (olympiad technique) as a descent on certificates
connection: S_{n,D}: nA² + B² + D = ABC has the Vieta involution B ↦ AC − B (always integral) and A ↦ BC/n − A (integral only when n | BC). Where the involutions stay integral and positive, Vieta jumping descends solutions towards fundamental ones (IMO 1988 Q6 style); unrestricted integral descent is not automatic here.
why: Vieta jumping is the elementary native tool for Markoff-type equations. It gives finite fundamental sets per (n, D) and transports positivity along orbits.
first_step: For n = p < 500, compute the fundamental (minimal) solutions under Vieta jumping on S_{p,D} and check whether ES certificates (2D | C) appear among fundamental solutions or in their orbits.

title: Composition on V_n as ideal multiplication in ℤ[2√f]: certificates as a 'box' in a narrow class group
connection: COMPOSITION_ES: V_n values at μ are the fibre over a fixed order-2 narrow class δ of the box of primitive ideals of norm dividing μ. ES ⇔ the box meets δ with an extra condition (B = 1).
why: Class-group 'boxes' (ideals of bounded norm generating/hitting a class) are a native class-field-theory question, with results via Bach's bound under GRH and unconditional Lamzouri-type results.
first_step: Calibrate: for μ in a window, size of box vs narrow class number; check whether GRH-Bach bounds would put the box onto δ (they handle generation, not hitting one class with norm constraints).

title: Heegner points / CM points equidistribution (Duke) for the lattice meeting point
connection: LATTICE_MEETING moves the slice inside Cl(−4p); Duke's theorem says CM points of discriminant −4p equidistribute on the modular curve. Certificates are CM points landing in a thin region (near the cusp, Y small).
why: Duke's theorem with explicit rates (Iwaniec's bound for half-integral-weight coefficients) is a pointwise-in-p existence statement for regions of size ≫ p^{−δ}. ES needs regions of size ≈ p^{−1/2}·polylog.
first_step: Compute the hyperbolic area of the 'certificate region' for CM points of disc −4p and compare with the best-known equidistribution error p^{−1/28}-type.
refs: Duke, Hyperbolic distribution problems and half-integral weight Maass forms (Invent. 1988)

title: Subconvexity for L(1/2, f × χ_{−4p}) and shrinking-target CM equidistribution
connection: Equidistribution of CM points in shrinking targets reduces (via Waldspurger) to subconvexity for twisted L-functions. ES certificates live in a target of measure ~p^{−1/2+o(1)}.
why: It gives the precise exponent gap: Weyl-strength subconvexity yields shrinking targets of size p^{−1/12}-ish, far from p^{−1/2}. It is a clean calibration.
first_step: Compute the target measure exactly, then the required subconvexity exponent; record the gap.
refs: Michel–Venkatesh, The subconvexity problem for GL₂ (Publ. IHES 2010)

title: Genus theory and the 2-part of Cl(−4p): ES sign as a genus character value
connection: For p ≡ 1 (4), Cl(−4p) has 2-rank 1, and genus characters are (·/p) and χ_{−4}. Certificate ideals of norm e must lie in a principal genus or its complement; the slot lemma's mod-4 condition may be the 4-rank (Rédei) symbol.
why: Rédei symbols and 4-ranks are explicit and computable. If the ES sign is a Rédei symbol of the certificate ideal, the structure is governed by governing fields (Stevenhagen, Smith).
first_step: For p < 10⁵, compute the Rédei-matrix data of Q(√−p), Q(√−2p) and compare with p's ES₅ certificate statistics (sign distributions by level).
refs: Stevenhagen, Rédei reciprocity, governing fields and negative Pell (2018; check)

title: Fermat two-squares via Thue's lemma (pigeonhole) as a template for ES at primes ≡ 1 (4)
connection: Thue: given ρ² ≡ −1 mod p, pigeonhole gives x ≡ ρy with |x|,|y| < √p, hence p = x² + y². ES's lattice L_ρ(g) uses ρ² ≡ −p mod g, a Thue-type lattice; certificates are short vectors with extra divisibility.
why: It is the most elementary pointwise prime theorem from a thick object (lattice of covolume p). ES needs the short vector to hit a divisor condition, which is where pigeonhole breaks.
first_step: Formulate the ES lattice-point condition as 'a short vector of L_ρ(g) lies in a sublattice of index k' and compute the pigeonhole threshold vs the actual vector lengths.

title: Quaternion order Λ_{d,m}: reduced-norm representation of p by a ternary sublattice
connection: QUATERNION_ES Lemma 1.2: Λ_{d,m} = ℤ⟨u,v⟩ with u² = −d, v² = −m, uv + vu = 1 is an order. Type I data are elements of prescribed norm/trace. ES becomes 'p is represented by a specific ternary norm form attached to (d,m)'.
why: Representation by ternary forms attached to orders has a theory: Gross lattices, Eichler orders, spinor genera. A family over (d,m) gives many forms, any of which suffices.
first_step: For each (d,m) ≤ 20 compute the Gross lattice (trace-zero part) and its genus; check whether p's representability by that genus is automatic (local conditions only) and whether spinor exceptions arise.

title: Siegel–Weil formula for the certificate genus: average over the genus is the BM main term
connection: Siegel–Weil: the genus-averaged representation number is a product of local densities, i.e. an Eisenstein coefficient. BM's main term is exactly such a product. The difference from a single class is a cusp-form coefficient.
why: In the quadratic-form toolbox, pointwise lower bounds come from 'Eisenstein main term ≫ cusp error'. ES's analogue has main term log²p, too small for cusp bounds; this is the native statement of the B3 obstacle.
first_step: Compute the ratio of BM main term to the trivial cusp-form bound in the best available quadratic encoding (rank 4, QUATERNION_ES); record the exponent gap.
alt_first_steps: [upgrades-0181] Express M_BM as Π of local densities (singular series) for the (★) variety and compare with the BL Brauer-corrected Siegel–Weil heuristics; look for the 'classes' whose average it is.
alt_titles: [upgrades-0181] Is M_BM a Siegel–Weil mass? A genus/class decomposition of certificates

upgrade: Tartakowsky / Kloosterman: quadratic forms in >= 4-5 variables

title: Borcherds products / divisors of automorphic forms with zeros at CM points
connection: A Borcherds product has explicit divisor supported on Heegner/CM points. If ES failure at p corresponded to a CM point where some form must vanish, the Borcherds lift might prohibit it.
why: It is the native 'existence via zeros of modular functions' tool, with exact divisor formulas. Speculative but categorically meaningful.
first_step: Read BRAINSTORM/bsC_valence_borcherds.md for the prior attempt; identify which weakly holomorphic input (principal part) would encode certificate data.
refs: Borcherds, Automorphic forms with singularities on Grassmannians (Invent. 1998)

title: Dedekind eta multiplier and the ES sign: (A/p) as an eta-multiplier value on γ_w
connection: The eta multiplier ε(γ) is given by Dedekind sums, and Rademacher's formulas relate it to Jacobi symbols. The ES sign is the theta multiplier on γ_w (bsB_theta_multiplier), and θ and η multipliers are related (θ = η⁵/(η²η²)-type identities).
why: Expressing the sign via η multipliers gives a conjugacy-invariant (Rademacher Φ function / class invariant), which might be easier to sum over words.
first_step: Compute Rademacher's Φ(γ_w) (and separately the Rademacher symbol) for words at p < 1000 and check whether either, mod 8 or 24, determines the sign.

title: Hilbert modular / Hirzebruch–Zagier cycles for the pair (A, A*) with AA* = tp+1
connection: Hirzebruch–Zagier cycles T_N on Hilbert modular surfaces have intersection numbers given by class numbers. Pairs (A,A*) with AA* = tp + 1 are points of a 'norm' condition that might be intersection points of T_N with a modular curve.
why: Hirzebruch–Zagier gives exact intersection numbers as coefficients of modular forms; if certificates are intersection points, their count is a known modular coefficient.
first_step: Check whether pairs (A, A*) with A ≡ A* ≡ −1 (mod t) and AA* = tp+1 are naturally CM points / intersection points on X(1) × X(1) (i.e. on a Hecke correspondence T_{tp+1}).
refs: Hirzebruch–Zagier, Intersection numbers of curves on Hilbert modular surfaces (Invent. 1976)

title: Hecke correspondence T_{tp+1} on X(1) × X(1) and ES words as its points with level structure
connection: Pairs of lattices with cyclic isogeny of degree N_t = tp+1 form the modular curve X₀(N_t). A word is a factorisation N_t = A·A* with congruences mod t, which is a Γ₀/Γ₁-level datum.
why: It gives ES₅ a moduli interpretation: level-t structures on isogenies of degree tp + 1. Moduli-theoretic counts (Riemann–Hurwitz on X₀) are exact.
first_step: Write the bijection {words of level t} ↔ {points on a specified cover of X₀(N_t) over ℤ}; check whether the sign is a Galois/Atkin–Lehner action.

title: Bounded arithmetic: is the Mordell covering (ES for n ∉ hard classes) provable in IΔ₀ + Ω₁?
connection: Bounded arithmetic proves elementary NT statements whose witnesses are polynomial-time computable. ES for the easy residue classes has explicit polynomial witnesses (Mordell identities), so it is provable in very weak systems.
why: Proof-complexity calibration: a proof of full ES in a weak system would yield a polynomial-time witness algorithm (Buss witnessing). Conversely, if no poly-time deterministic witness algorithm exists, any proof must use strong axioms or non-constructive steps.
first_step: State the witnessing theorem consequence: ES provable in S¹₂ ⇒ a poly-time algorithm outputs (x,y,z) from n. Check whether any deterministic poly-time ES algorithm is known (likely not without factoring).

title: Existential theory of (ℕ, +, |) (Lipshitz/Bel'tyukov) and fixed-C Type II statements
connection: At a fixed level C, 'p has a certificate' is ∃d,k: d | 4Cp+1 ∧ d = 4Ck − 1, an existential formula in (ℕ,+,|) with parameter p. Lipshitz proved the existential theory of (ℤ,+,|) decidable; the ∀p∃ fragment is a different matter.
why: It locates the logical complexity of finite-menu ES statements. A decidable ∀∃ fragment would make 'ES via levels C ≤ C₀' algorithmically decidable, although B1 says such statements are false.
first_step: Check the literature on the decidability of ∀∃ sentences of (ℕ,+,|) (Bel'tyukov, Lipshitz); record whether multiplication becomes definable there.
refs: Lipshitz, The Diophantine problem for addition and divisibility (Trans. AMS 1978)

title: Legendre-PRF-style pseudorandomness of (·/p) on S₃(p): a crypto-flavoured heuristic for ES₅
connection: The Legendre PRF (Damgård) uses a secret key shift, x ↦ ((x+k)/p), and is conjectured pseudorandom; the unshifted symbol (·/p) is public, so this is only an analogy. ES₅ failure at p means (·/p) is identically +1 on the explicitly enumerable set S₃(p) (size ≈ log²p). A naive 'no efficiently enumerable set is monochromatic' hypothesis is false (enumerate squares), so any useful hypothesis must restrict to sets defined without reference to residuosity.
why: It translates ES₅ into crypto language: infinitely many failures form a 'weak key' class. Crypto hardness assumptions are heuristic and asymptotic, so this gives density, not all p.
first_step: Formulate a restricted hypothesis (e.g. sets S_p defined by additive/divisor conditions of bounded complexity, without multiplicative-character structure) and check whether it is consistent with known structured monochromatic sets (squares, products of squares); compare with the Legendre-PRF cryptanalysis literature (Khovratovich; Beullens et al.).
refs: Damgård, On the randomness of Legendre and Jacobi sequences (CRYPTO 1988)

title: Quadratic residue codes: ES₅ failure as S₃(p) ⊂ support of the QR idempotent
connection: The QR code of length p is defined by the QR set. ES₅ fails at p iff S₃(p) ⊆ QR. Coding theory studies which structured sets sit inside QR (e.g. minimum-weight words, automorphism group PSL₂(p) acting on QR codes).
why: The QR code's automorphism group PSL₂(F_p) is large. Words (as SL₂ data) act naturally, so S₃(p) ⊆ QR might be translated into a code-automorphism statement.
first_step: Check whether S₃(p) is a union of orbits of some subgroup of PSL₂(F_p) stabilising QR; if so, failure would be forced or forbidden group-theoretically.
refs: MacWilliams–Sloane, The Theory of Error-Correcting Codes, ch. 16

title: Gauss-sum / Fourier coefficient of 1_{S₃(p)} at the quadratic character
connection: ES₅(p) ⇔ Σ_{A ∈ S₃(p)} (A/p) < |S₃(p)|. In coding/Fourier terms, the quadratic Fourier coefficient of 1_{S₃} must not be maximal. Uncertainty principles (Tao's prime-field uncertainty, Biró–Meshulam) bound how concentrated a set and its Fourier transform can be.
why: Tao's uncertainty principle for F_p says |supp f| + |supp f̂| ≥ p + 1. Indicator sets that are subsets of QR have structured Fourier transforms, which gives a potential contradiction with S₃'s known Fourier structure.
first_step: Compute the Fourier transform of 1_{S₃(p)} for p < 5000; check whether 'S₃ ⊆ QR' would force a Fourier property contradicted by S₃'s divisor structure.
refs: Tao, An uncertainty principle for cyclic groups of prime order (MRL 2005)

title: F₂-linear algebra: ES₅ failure ⇔ a linear system over F₂ in the Legendre symbols of small primes
connection: (A/p) = ∏ (q/p)^{v_q(A)}. ES₅ failure ⇔ all A ∈ S₃(p) have Σ v_q(A)·ε_q ≡ 0 (mod 2), where ε_q = [(q/p) = −1]. This is a linear system over F₂ in the unknown vector ε (the 'quadratic character of p on primes').
why: The exact linear-algebra form shows that failure is consistent iff the exponent-vector matrix of S₃(p) has the actual ε in its right kernel. Rank considerations give a sharp combinatorial necessary condition.
first_step: For p < 10⁶ compute rank_F₂ of the exponent matrix of S₃(p) (over primes dividing elements) and the codimension of the failure space; record the minimum over p.

title: Statistical-mechanics partition function over all ES solutions and Lee–Yang zeros
connection: Define Z_n(β) = Σ_{solutions} (xyz)^{−β}. ES(n) ⇔ Z_n ≢ 0. Lee–Yang-type theorems locate zeros of partition functions with ferromagnetic structure. A family Z(n, β) analytic in n-related variables might have provably non-vanishing coefficients.
why: Speculative, but it is the stat-mech native form of 'nonempty'; the Dirichlet series Σ_n Z_n(β) n^{−s} is a height zeta function of the threefold 𝒰.
first_step: Compute the height zeta function Σ_n Σ_{sol} n^{−s}(xyz)^{−β} numerically; check for Euler-product structure.

title: Height zeta function of the threefold 𝒰 and its analytic continuation
connection: Σ_{(n,x,y,z) ∈ 𝒰(ℤ_{>0})} H(n,x,y,z)^{−s} counts all ES solutions. Its rightmost pole gives the log²-order average count (ET). Its analytic structure, e.g. as a sum of Eisenstein-type series via the torsor, is native to Manin-conjecture methods (Chambert-Loir–Tschinkel).
why: Analytic continuation gives secondary terms, which control the lower tail in short intervals of n, a step towards almost-all-with-rates.
first_step: Write the height zeta function via ET's parametrisation as a multiple Dirichlet series and identify its polar structure.
refs: Chambert-Loir–Tschinkel, Igusa integrals and volume asymptotics (2010)

title: Large deviations / lower-tail of the certificate count: Poisson vs Gaussian regime
connection: The certificate count N(p) has mean ≍ log²p. P(N(p) = 0) is a lower-tail large deviation. In random-graph theory (Janson–Łuczak–Ruciński) lower tails are governed by Janson's inequality and are exponential in the mean.
why: The lower-tail exponent ≈ mean gives P(0) ≈ p^{−c log p}, summable over p: ES true heuristically. Native LDP theory would quantify the needed dependence structure.
first_step: Fit log P(N = 0 | mean M) from data (repo has it) against the Janson prediction −M/(1+Δ/M); record Δ.

title: Branching-process / tree-search model of the certificate search (Galton–Watson survival)
connection: Searching levels C = 1,2,… and divisor splits gives a search tree; the probability of finding no certificate is an extinction probability of a branching process with offspring ~ divisor counts.
why: Branching processes give exact extinction-probability equations, which give a sharper heuristic than Poisson when certificates cluster.
first_step: Model the per-level offspring distribution from data; solve the extinction equation and compare with observed zero frequencies for ES₅.

title: Percolation on the forest F_p: giant component reaching a QNR
connection: If F_p behaves like a random graph above the percolation threshold, the component of 1 is giant and contains a QNR. ES₅ (p ≡ 1 mod 8) follows from 'the component of 1 contains a QNR'.
why: Percolation-native: thresholds are sharp, and arithmetic graphs (divisor graphs) have percolation results (e.g. random divisor graphs). The forest might be supercritical in a window of small vertices.
first_step: Compute the degree distribution and component structure of F_p restricted to vertices ≤ X for p < 10⁷; locate the effective percolation threshold.

title: Maker–Breaker / Erdős–Selfridge criterion for covering-system strategies
connection: View 'adversary chooses p's residues prime by prime, prover covers with certificates' as a Maker–Breaker game on a hypergraph of congruence certificates. The Erdős–Selfridge criterion Σ 2^{−|e|} < 1/2 gives Breaker (adversary) a win.
why: It turns B1 (no finite covering) into a game-theory calculation and might quantify how large the certificate hypergraph must be for a covering, compared with the actual size.
first_step: Compute the Erdős–Selfridge potential of the certificate hypergraph up to level C₀ (edges = residue-class conditions on p); see where it crosses 1/2.

title: Kolmogorov-complexity view of the sporadic lists (U(n) and Rickards–Stange-type exceptions)
connection: Finite sporadic lists in local-global problems (U(n): six values; RS: 15) have low Kolmogorov complexity only if explained by structure. An algorithmic-information test can flag 'structured' vs 'random' sporadics.
why: Exploratory: a compressible sporadic list suggests a hidden obstruction that might also act at primes.
first_step: Factorisations (computed): 105 = 3·5·7, 2961 = 3²·7·47, 3985 = 5·797, 25305 = 3·5·7·241, 111969 = 3³·11·13·29, 978145 = 5·7·27947. All are ≡ 1 (mod 8); mod 840 they are 105, 441 = 21², 625 = 25², 105, 249, 385, so two lie in square classes mod 840. Next: test whether every sporadic lies in a class mod 840·k that is 'square-like' for U's local model.

title: Machine-learned certificate selectors: features that predict the first working level
connection: Train a classifier on p ↦ least working level (or least u in I3_𝒞), with features such as Legendre symbols of small primes, p mod small moduli and factorisations of p+small. Interpretable models (sparse logistic, decision trees) may expose a structure.
why: This is the data-science native lens. Many repo results (I3_𝒞 u ≤ 39) suggest the selector is simple; a sparse rule could be a conjecture or a lemma candidate.
first_step: Using repo data for p ≤ 10⁹, fit a depth-6 decision tree predicting the least certifying u in I3_𝒞 from (q/p) for q ≤ 50; report accuracy and the tree.

title: Garsia–Milne involution principle for a bijective ES-count identity
connection: The involution principle builds a bijection from two sign-reversing involutions. If N₋(p) = (count of a simple positive set) − (count of another) via explicit involutions, Garsia–Milne yields a bijection and hence positivity whenever the simple set is bigger.
why: It is the enumerative-combinatorics native machine for turning signed identities into injections. Positivity of ES would follow from an injection from a set of known size ≥ 1.
first_step: Look for any signed identity for N₋ (SIGN_IDENTITY lists the known ones); check whether its terms are counts of explicit finite sets amenable to involutions.

title: Lindström–Gessel–Viennot: words as non-intersecting lattice path families with determinant tuv−u−v
connection: det M(t,u,v) can be read as a signed count of path systems in a planar network (LGV). If the planar network can be chosen so that the count is non-negative termwise, the cofactor A and its class get a path interpretation.
why: LGV gives combinatorial meaning to determinants and cofactors, the same objects as the ES sign (cofactor A mod p). Positivity of path counts is automatic.
first_step: Construct the planar network whose LGV matrix is M(t,u,v); interpret A = tu−1 as a path count and the slot-lemma 4-divisibility as a parity/symmetry of path families.

title: Kasteleyn/Pfaffian orientations: ES count as a Pfaffian of a skew matrix built from p
connection: Perfect matchings of planar graphs are Pfaffians. Windmill-type 'odd number of fixed points' arguments are mod-2 Pfaffian/determinant arguments. A planar graph G_p with ES certificates as matchings would give #certificates = |Pf(K_p)|.
why: Exact Pfaffian formulas give closed-form counts, and nonvanishing of a determinant is checkable algebraically (e.g. via its value mod a prime).
first_step: Attempt to realise the forest F_p's edges or the words as perfect matchings of a planar graph; compute det mod 2 for small p.

title: Smith theory / ℤ/2-equivariant topology: fixed points of an involution on a ℤ/2-acyclic certificate complex
connection: Smith theory: an involution on a mod-2 acyclic finite complex has a non-empty mod-2 acyclic fixed set. A simplicial complex on solutions (or near-solutions) that is provably ℤ/2-acyclic, with an involution whose fixed points are certificates, would give existence.
why: It is the topological generalisation of 'odd number of fixed points', more flexible than plain parity because acyclicity can be proved by shellability or discrete Morse theory.
first_step: Define a complex on words of all p′ ≤ p (or on near-certificates) with faces from shared letters; compute mod-2 homology for small p.

title: Discrete Morse theory / matching on the poset of near-solutions
connection: Acyclic matchings on a poset (Forman) count critical cells, and Euler characteristic = alternating count of critical cells. If an ES-defined poset has Euler characteristic ≠ 0, a critical cell (certificate) must exist.
why: It is a combinatorial-topology tool that generalises sign-reversing involutions with a global acyclicity condition, a strictly richer version of the windmill route.
first_step: Define a poset of partial certificates (e.g. levels/divisor pairs ordered by divisibility) and compute its Euler characteristic as a function of p (small p).
refs: Forman, Morse theory for cell complexes (1998)

title: Lefschetz number of a map on a 'certificate space' with ES-certificate fixed points
connection: Lefschetz fixed-point theorem: L(f) ≠ 0 ⇒ fixed point. A continuous or algebraic self-map of a compact space whose fixed points are ES certificates and whose Lefschetz number is computable would prove existence.
why: It is the classic topological existence engine; the windmill is its discrete special case. A finite-field version (Lefschetz trace for Frobenius) counts points over F_q, not integral points.
first_step: Record the attempts in invol_topological.md; look for algebraic maps on U_n's compactification whose fixed loci are positive points (e.g. the cyclic permutation composed with a birational involution).

title: Sperner / KKM / Tucker lemmas for a labelled triangulation whose 'rainbow cell' is a certificate
connection: Sperner's lemma gives an odd number of fully labelled simplices. If the triangle {x+y+z = const} or the (u,v) quadrant can be triangulated with labels from p-arithmetic (e.g. Legendre symbols and divisibility), a rainbow cell might encode a word with the right sign.
why: It is the combinatorial-topology native parity engine with geometric flexibility. The forest bichromatic-edge statement is already a 1-dimensional Sperner-type statement (path from QR to QNR has a bichromatic edge).
first_step: Write the 1-D Sperner argument behind H4/forest bichromatic edges explicitly; then look for a 2-D labelling that encodes the extra divisibility.

title: Borwein–Choi's xy+yz+zx theorem as the closest proved sibling of I3/U(n)
connection: Borwein–Choi: there are at most 19 integers not of the form xy+yz+zx (x,y,z ≥ 1). Eighteen are known, and the 19th is excluded under GRH. The form is classified via class groups of Q(√−n), using (x+z)(y+z) = n + z². I3 is n = tuv−u−v ⇔ (tu−1)(tv−1) = tn+1.
why: It is structurally parallel (a factorisation of n + (shift) with constraints) and is proved up to one possible exception via idoneal-type class-number arguments. The I3/U analogue would be 'finitely many failures, all but one effective'.
first_step: Read Borwein–Choi (Exp. Math. 9 (2000)) and translate: for which discriminants does 'tn+1 has no factorisation (tu−1)(tv−1)' force a class-group condition (exponent ≤ 2) on Q(√−?)?
refs: Borwein–Choi, On the representations of xy+yz+zx, Exp. Math. 9 (2000) 153–158

title: Class-number-one-type ineffectivity: is I3's exceptional list finite by a Siegel-type argument?
connection: Chowla proved finiteness of idoneal numbers via Siegel's (ineffective) class-number bound. If I3 failure at n forced a large class group to have a small exponent (an 'idoneal-type' condition), Siegel–Tatuzawa would give finiteness of exceptions up to one.
why: It is the only known mechanism turning a 'polylog-witness' representation problem into a pointwise theorem (with ineffectivity). It is the (R)-rigidity type of FRONTIER's meta-finding.
first_step: Look for a map: I3 failure at n ⇒ the class group of some order of disc −D(n) has exponent ≤ 2 (or bounded); test on the known I3 exceptions.
refs: Chowla, An extension of Heilbronn's class-number theorem (1934)

title: Lorenzini's critical-polynomial question (W) and the A₃ graph: I3 as a sandpile statement
connection: LORENZINI_W: (W) asks that every n outside a finite set is xyz − x − z (x,y,z ≥ 2), which comes from critical groups of A₃-type graphs. I3 (t,u,v ≥ 3) is a strengthening.
why: This is the graph-theory native home of I3. Lorenzini's and Wang–Lu's density-1 results are its nearest theorems.
first_step: Check Wang–Lu (EJC 2026) methods for density 1 and whether they extend to the I3 lower bound t,u,v ≥ 3 (repo has an unconditional rate).
refs: Wang–Lu, The critical polynomials of simple connected graphs, EJC 33(3) (2026)

title: Restricted-denominator ES: which congruence restrictions on x, y, z keep ES true?
connection: Breusch/Stewart: every rational with odd denominator is a sum of distinct odd unit fractions (many terms). For three terms, all-odd is impossible (parity: 4xyz = p(xy+yz+zx) forces an even denominator). Classify restrictions (x,y,z in prescribed classes mod m) that are consistent with ES for all small p, and test which ones look 'every p'.
why: Restricted versions that hold numerically are stronger statements that may carry more structure for a proof (or reveal new obstructions).
first_step: For m = 3, 4, 5, 8 and all class-restriction patterns, compute the failure set among p ≤ 10⁶.
alt_first_steps: [translate-0168] Read arXiv:1108.6118 and arXiv:1606.02117; tabulate which three-term restricted variants of 4/n are known false and true.
refs: Breusch, A special case of Egyptian fractions, Amer. Math. Monthly 61 (1954) 200-201
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings
alt_titles: [translate-0168] Egyptian fractions with restricted denominators (Chen–Elsholtz–Jiang) and ES variants

title: Function-field ES: Weil-bound positivity as the model where pointwise ES is provable
connection: Over F_q[T], ES-type statements have proved variants (FUNCTIONFIELD_ES*). The native reason is that Weil's RH gives square-root cancellation in short character sums, which is unavailable over ℤ.
why: It records the 'what does RH give' calibration: whether ES_q holds for all P of large degree by Weil bounds, and which step uses RH for curves.
first_step: Re-read FUNCTIONFIELD_ES3 / FF_STERILE_* for the exact proved statements and the step where the Weil bound enters; state the ℤ-analogue hypothesis needed.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Drinfeld modules / Carlitz module: ES_q certificates as torsion points
connection: DRINFELD_ES: degree-k Diff-parity over F_q(T) via rank-k Drinfeld modules. Carlitz torsion gives cyclotomic function fields where Frobenius of P is explicit.
why: In function fields, 'divisor of 4CP+1 in a class' is a Chebotarev statement in Carlitz cyclotomic extensions, with effective Chebotarev (Weil). This is the native tool.
first_step: State the function-field Type II at fixed level C as a Chebotarev condition in F_q(T)(Λ_{4C}) and compute the effective error.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Large-q limit (Katz–Sarnak) of the ES_q certificate count distribution
connection: As q → ∞ with deg P fixed, counts of certificates become equidistributed statistics governed by monodromy groups (Katz's equidistribution). The probability of zero certificates in the limit is computable.
why: It gives an exact 'random model' limit of the ES count distribution, a rigorous analogue of the Poisson heuristic, and possibly a proof of ES_q for q large relative to the degree.
first_step: Identify the monodromy group of the certificate-counting sheaf (divisor-in-class conditions) and compute the limiting P(count = 0) for small degrees.
refs: Katz–Sarnak, Random Matrices, Frobenius Eigenvalues, and Monodromy (1999)
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Power ladder ES_(k): cubic and higher rungs collapse to finite coverings
connection: POWER_LADDER_ES: for odd k, ES_(k) (x, y integers; the third term 1/z with z RATIONAL whose reduced denominator is Q^k, Q odd, gcd(Q,n) = 1; equivalently a third term Q^k/Z) is a finite congruence covering mod 4, while even k returns to ES^□. The native field is power-residue symbols and Waring-type coverings.
why: Calibration item: it shows exactly which relaxations are trivially true. A new rung (e.g. denominators in a norm group of a cyclic field) can be tested the same way.
first_step: Generalise: third denominator in N(K^×) for an abelian field K; find the index condition that makes the rung a finite covering.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: I3 at 2^k ± 1 by exponent coverings: Sierpiński-number technique
connection: I3 holds on 2^k ± 1 etc. by exponent coverings (I3_DEEP). This is exactly the Sierpiński/Riesel-number covering technique for k·2^n + 1 compositeness.
why: Covering congruences in the exponent are a native tool that is complete for its families. Extending to 'n = a·b^k + c' families tests how far exponent coverings go.
first_step: Try families n = 3^k ± 2, 5·3^k + 1 with exponent coverings for I3; record which ones close.

title: Additive basis view of I3: tuv−u−v as a 'thin basis' of order 1 with three free parameters
connection: The set W₃ = {tuv − u − v : t,u,v ≥ 3} has counting function ≍ N (it is almost everything), but the representation function is only ≍ log²n. Thin-basis theory (Erdős–Tetali; Nathanson) studies bases with small representation functions.
why: Erdős–Tetali gives random bases with r(n) ≍ log n that are bases for all large n. Deterministic thin bases with full coverage are rare; I3 would be a natural deterministic example.
first_step: Survey known deterministic 'thin bases' with polylog representation functions and full coverage; check whether any proof technique applies to multiplicative shapes.
refs: Erdős–Tetali, Representations of integers as the sum of k terms (1990)

title: Goldbach-type circle method for I3? The minor arcs for tuv − u − v
connection: The circle method treats additive representations. I3 is multiplicative-additive (tuv − u − v), so its exponential-sum generating function Σ e(α(tuv−u−v)) factors through divisor sums. The major arcs give the local density (Haar survival).
why: It gives the analytic-NT native attempt and shows the minor-arc problem is like the ternary divisor problem in progressions (d₃ in APs), which has level of distribution results (Friedlander–Iwaniec, Heath-Brown).
first_step: Write the singular series for I3 and compare with I3_DEEP's Haar survival; record the minor-arc bound needed for a pointwise result (polylog main term ⇒ impossible).

title: Erdős #306-type Fourier counts (Li 2609.32140) and why abundance is needed
connection: Recent AI/Lean-assisted solutions of Erdős problems (e.g. Li's #306) use Fourier counts over exponentially many configurations. ES has polylog witnesses.
why: Calibration: these tools apply to ES variants with many more terms (k ≥ log n unit fractions). They locate the minimal k where Fourier methods work.
first_step: Find the smallest k(n) for which '4/n is a sum of k unit fractions with denominators ≤ n^C' is provable by a Fourier count; compare with k = 3.

title: Unit-fraction graph on ℚ: 3-step walks from 0 to 4/n
connection: Define the graph on ℚ_{>0} with r ~ r + 1/k. ES(n) ⇔ dist(0, 4/n) ≤ 3. Farey neighbours a/b, c/d satisfy c/d − a/b = 1/(bd), so unit steps between Farey neighbours are edges.
why: It gives a metric-geometry view of Egyptian fractions. Bounds on the graph's diameter on {m/n : m ≤ 4} are exactly ES-type statements, and 'every m/n at distance ≤ c·log log n' results are known.
first_step: Compute the distance-2 neighbourhood of 4/p (pairs 1/y + 1/z) and its overlap with {4/p − 1/x}; record which Farey structure produces most certificates.

title: Fractional quantum Hall hierarchy: the chain matrix as a K-matrix and the ES sign as an anyon-theory class
connection: Haldane–Halperin hierarchy states have tridiagonal K-matrices whose filling is an HJ continued fraction. The anyon theory is the discriminant form of K on ℤ^r/Kℤ^r (here ℤ/p). ES₅(p) ⇔ a 3-level hierarchy state with det K = p whose ℤ/p anyon braiding form is in the non-square class.
why: Abelian Chern–Simons theory classifies anyon theories with ℤ/p fusion into two classes (by the Gauss sum and chiral central charge). Physics constraints such as Gauss–Milgram relate the class to the signature and to spin structure.
first_step: Write the topological spins θ_x = e^{πi x²A/p} for the fan K-matrix; compute the Gauss–Milgram sum (odd/fermionic version) and relate it to the slot lemma.
refs: Wen, Quantum Field Theory of Many-Body Systems ch. 7 (K-matrix)

title: Slot lemma as a van der Blij / Gauss–Milgram formula for odd lattices (characteristic covectors)
connection: For an odd lattice, the Gauss sum of the discriminant form is governed by σ − w² mod 8, where w is a characteristic covector (van der Blij, Brown invariant). For the chain lattice, w has coordinates (v,t,u) mod 2 and w² has denominator p. This plausibly yields (A/p) as a function of p mod 8 and the parity pattern of (t,u,v,tu−1,tv−1), i.e. the slot lemma.
why: It would give the slot lemma a structural (lattice-theoretic) proof and a generalisation to chains of any length, i.e. an exact sign rule for λ(p) ≤ L words.
first_step: Compute σ − w² mod 8 symbolically for the 3-chain and compare with the slot-lemma indicator over all parity classes of (t,u,v) mod 8; then do the 4-chain.
refs: van der Blij, An invariant of quadratic forms mod 8 (1959)

title: q-deformed rationals [p/A]_q (Morier-Genoud–Ovsienko) and Jones polynomials of 2-bridge links
connection: MGO's q-rationals have numerator polynomials with positive coefficients, which equal (up to normalisation) Jones polynomials of 2-bridge links (Kogiso–Wakui). The fan graph is the Tait graph, so the Jones polynomial is a Tutte specialisation. ES₅ concerns the class of A, i.e. which 2-bridge link has numerator p.
why: A root-of-unity specialisation detecting (A/p) would make the ES sign a quantum invariant with positivity structure (q-rationals), possibly giving inequalities.
first_step: Compute [p/A]_q numerators for p < 300 and evaluate at q = i, e^{iπ/4}, e^{2πi/8}; test whether any evaluation's phase equals (A/p) on words.
refs: Morier-Genoud–Ovsienko, q-deformed rationals and q-continued fractions (Forum Math. Sigma 2020; check)

title: Tutte polynomial of the fan graph: evaluations beyond T(1,1) = p
connection: The fan multigraph's Tutte polynomial T(x,y) has T(1,1) = p. Other evaluations count forests, acyclic orientations, recurrent sandpile levels (Merino) and, via Thistlethwaite, the Jones polynomial of the associated alternating link.
why: It is a single polynomial carrying graph, sandpile and knot data. The ES sign might be an evaluation (e.g. T(−1,−1) or a root-of-unity value).
first_step: Compute T(x,y) symbolically for the fan in terms of (t,u,v) and evaluate at small roots of unity; correlate with the slot-lemma sign.

title: ES₅ words as integral points of a twisted M₀,₅ (A₂ cluster surface birational to M₀,₅)
connection: The A₂ cluster variety is M₀,₅ (configurations of 5 points on P¹), up to passing to open subsets (the A2 cluster surface is dP5 minus a pentagon of lines, whereas M_{0,5} is dP5 minus all ten boundary lines, so the relationship is birational/open-subset, not equality). Positive integral friezes correspond to special integral points. The coefficient-N pentagon is a twist/deformation. Integral points of M₀,₅ over ℤ[1/S] are governed by S-unit equations.
why: This brings the S-unit equation toolbox (finiteness, effective bounds, counting) and the cross-ratio coordinates of M₀,₅ to ES₅ words.
first_step: Write the five frieze entries as cross-ratios of 5 points on P¹ and identify the N-twist; check whether words correspond to points of M₀,₅ with cross-ratios in a multiplicative set related to N.

title: Pentagon identity of the dilogarithm on the coefficient-N pentagon
connection: The Rogers dilogarithm satisfies the 5-term relation along A₂ mutations: Σ L(X_i/(1+X_i)) = π²/2 on the positive real locus. With frozen coefficient N the relation acquires N-dependent terms. Words give rational points.
why: Dilogarithm identities encode K₂/Bloch-group data of the points. For rational points, Bloch-group elements are torsion, which gives exact identities; the sign might appear as a torsion class.
first_step: Compute Σ L over the five X-coordinates of each word for p < 100 numerically; look for a pattern in N and in the sign.

title: Stern's diatomic sequence: (p, A) = (s(k), s(k+1)) and HJ length as a binary-run statistic of k
connection: Every coprime pair occurs exactly once as consecutive Stern values, and the CF of p/A is encoded by the run lengths of k's binary expansion. ES₅ ⇔ some k with s(k) = p, s(k±1) ≡ non-residue, and k's binary word in a 3-run HJ pattern.
why: This makes ES₅ a statement about binary words, so automata/regular-language tools (automatic sequences, Stern's sequence is 2-regular) apply.
first_step: Find the exact HJ-run encoding (LORENZINI_W §7 has a Stern coding); enumerate k with ≤ 3 HJ-runs and s(k) = p, check the sign.

title: Commute time / escape probability on the fan: A/p as a random-walk quantity
connection: For the fan graph, R_eff(a,s) = A/p, so the commute time between a and the sink is 2|E|·A/p and the escape probability from a is 1/(v·R_eff) = p/(vA). The ES sign is a residuosity property of a commute time numerator.
why: Random-walk interpretations allow coupling/monotonicity arguments (Rayleigh monotonicity: adding edges decreases resistance), which could organise words by a partial order.
first_step: Use Rayleigh monotonicity to order words of p by resistance; check whether the sign changes monotonically along chains (data p < 10⁵).
refs: Doyle–Snell, Random Walks and Electric Networks (1984)

title: Hilbert basis of a 2-dimensional cone: ES₅ ⇔ a cone of index p in the non-residue class with a 5-element Hilbert basis
connection: The Hilbert basis of cone((0,1),(p,−A)) consists of the HJ convergents, so it has r(p/A) + 2 elements. ES₅ ⇔ some cone of type 1/p(1,A) with (A/p) = −1 has Hilbert basis of size 5.
why: Integer-programming/commutative-algebra native: Hilbert-basis sizes and normal semigroup rings (embedding dimension). Toric-ideal theory gives explicit invariants.
first_step: Compute the semigroup-ring invariants (Hilbert series, a-invariant) of the 5-element cones and test whether the sign is a ring-theoretic invariant (e.g. class group element of the toric ring).

title: Divisor class group of the toric ring k[σ^∨ ∩ M] ≅ ℤ/p and the canonical class: the sign as an Atiyah–Bott/Gorenstein index datum
connection: The cyclic quotient 1/p(1,A) has class group ℤ/p generated by a boundary divisor D₁. The canonical class K corresponds to −(1 + A)·[D₁]-type data, so the 'position of K in ℤ/p' is a quadratic-residue question about 1 + A or A.
why: Native singularity invariants (Gorenstein index, canonical class position) are computable and might rephrase the sign as 'K is a square multiple of a generator'.
first_step: Compute [K] ∈ Cl = ℤ/p for 1/p(1,A) and express its square class via A; compare with (A/p).

title: Arithmetic topology (Morishita): Legendre symbol as mod-2 linking number of prime knots
connection: In arithmetic topology (q/p) is the mod-2 linking number of 'prime knots' p and q in Spec ℤ. (A/p) = Σ_q v_q(A) lk(p,q) mod 2, and Rédei symbols are Milnor triple-linking numbers. ES₅ asks p to link oddly with the 'certificate link' of some word.
why: The dictionary might suggest topological constructions (Seifert surfaces = genus-theory objects) that force an odd linking. Speculative, but categorically sound.
first_step: Read Morishita, Knots and Primes ch. 4–8; translate the slot lemma into linking-number language and see whether a Seifert-surface argument suggests a certificate.

title: Multiplicative generation of F_p^* by forest edge products
connection: A = (p+u)/v ≡ u/v (mod p), so (A/p) = (uv/p) on forest edges. ES₅ fails ⇒ every edge product uv lies in the QR subgroup ⇒ the group generated by edge products is ≠ F_p^*. So ES₅(p) ⇐ 'edge products generate F_p^*'.
why: Generation of (ℤ/q)^× by small structured sets is now proved for almost all q (Klurman–Shparlinski–Teräväinen). Edge products are small integers with a divisibility constraint; this links ES₅ to the 'small sets generate' literature.
first_step: Compute the index of ⟨uv : (u,v) edge of F_p, u,v ≤ X⟩ in F_p^* as X grows, p < 10⁶; compare the least X needed with the least QNR.

title: s-form: ES(p) ⇔ ∃ s ∈ ℕ³ with lcm_i 4s_i/gcd(4s_i, S) = p (value of an arithmetic function)
connection: GEOMETRY_ES: positive points ↔ primitive s with 4s_i | nS, and ES(p) ⟺ ∃ s with m(s) = lcm_i 4s_i/gcd(4s_i,S) = p. ES says the arithmetic function m on primitive triples hits every prime.
why: Surjectivity of an explicit arithmetic function on ℕ³ is the native form for additive/multiplicative combinatorics (value sets of lcm/gcd expressions, like the problem of values of lcm(a,b)/gcd(a,b)-type maps).
