title: Recursive product constructions: certificates for p from certificates for pieces of 4Cp + 1
connection: Bose–Shrikhande–Parker built orthogonal Latin squares of composite orders from smaller ones. For ES, 4Cp + 1 = N₁N₂ (coprime): if N₁ has a divisor ≡ a (mod 4C) and N₂ one ≡ b with ab ≡ −1, the product is a certificate. Study 'recursive' constructions splitting N and combining class information from each piece.
why: Product constructions are the combinatorial counterpart of the Kneser/product-set items, with an explicit recursive structure.
first_step: For hard p, enumerate coprime splittings of 4Cp + 1 and compute the class sets of divisors of each piece; count combinations giving −1.

upgrade: Euler's 36 officers: orthogonal Latin squares for every n != 2, 6

title: Surgery on near-certificates: local modifications that remove a single obstruction
connection: Perelman's surgery removes singularities and continues the flow. For a near-certificate at level C (a divisor d of 4Cp + 1 in a class ≠ −1), define 'surgeries' changing one prime factor (moving to another level C′ sharing that factor via CRT) and study whether repeated surgery reaches a certificate.
why: Gives a local-move graph on near-certificates across levels, linked by shared prime factors.
first_step: Build the graph (nodes: (C, d); edges: share a prime factor q, C ≡ C′ (mod q)) for small p and search paths to certificates.
refs: arXiv:math/0211159 (Perelman, The entropy formula for the Ricci flow)

title: Current-graph-style explicit constructions for one residue class mod a large modulus
connection: Ringel–Youngs used 'current graphs' — compact algebraic data generating a whole family. For one Mordell-hard class r mod M (M large, e.g. 840·1001), search for compact algebraic data (a finite list of certificate templates with parameters depending on p's residues mod M′) covering all primes in that class up to 10⁹.
why: Even if B1 forbids bounded templates for all p, the minimal template count per class reveals growth rates and hidden structure.
first_step: Run a greedy set-cover of primes in the class by parametric templates (Type II with C | M′) and plot template count vs X.

title: Landau–Siegel 'at most one exceptional modulus' analogue for ES levels
connection: Landau: at most one real character mod q ≤ Q has L(1,χ) tiny. ES analogue: among the characters χ_{−4uB} driving M_BM, show at most one (or boundedly many) can be 'exceptional' at p (strongly biased), so M_BM stays large except via one identifiable character whose effect can be handled separately.
why: The 'at most one exception' structure is what makes Siegel-type arguments work; ES's main term is a sum over many real characters.
first_step: Model T(p) as a sum over real characters and quantify how much a single character can reduce M_BM; compare with the observed minima of M_BM/L².

upgrade: Siegel's theorem (average class numbers -> individual lower bound)

title: Polynomial congruence certificate: an identity in ℤ[X]/(X^r − 1, p) detecting ES
connection: AKS used a polynomial congruence that holds iff n is prime. Ask whether ES(p) has a characterisation by a polynomial identity modulo (X^r − 1, p) or modulo auxiliary moduli (e.g. a product over levels of polynomials whose evaluation detects certificates), testable deterministically.
why: Odd: algebraic characterisations sometimes admit clean counting proofs (as in AKS's group-size argument).
first_step: Construct the generating polynomial P_p(X) = Π_{C ≤ K} (1 − X^{[level C fails]}) style objects and look for algebraic relations they satisfy for all p.

upgrade: PRIMES is in P (randomized / conditional -> deterministic unconditional)

title: Thin-semigroup local-global with the ES constraint t ∈ 4ℤ ∪ (8ℤ − p): local obstructions?
connection: Bourgain–Kontorovich require knowing the local (congruence) obstructions of the semigroup before counting. Compute the reductions mod q of the ES-word set with the constraint on t (4ℤ for one branch, 8ℤ − p for the other, which depends on p!) and determine exactly which residues of p are locally admissible; check that only squares-related obstructions appear (T1-type).
why: The p-dependent constraint (8ℤ − p) is unusual for thin-orbit theory; its local analysis is a concrete, finite task.
first_step: For q ≤ 200 compute the set of p mod q (and mod 8q) hit by words with each constraint branch.

title: Strong approximation mod p for the ES surface fibre U_p (BGS-style) — sanity check
connection: BGS proved Markoff surfaces satisfy strong approximation mod p for most p. For ES, check the analogous local statement: does U_n(ℤ) → U_n(ℤ/q) have dense image for various q (it is BM-obstructed for strong approximation by BL)? Quantify the BL obstruction concretely on data.
why: Makes BL's 'BM obstruction to strong approximation always exists' concrete and shows which residue patterns ES solutions avoid.
first_step: For small n with many solutions, compute the reductions of solutions mod q and compare with U_n(ℤ/q).
refs: arXiv:2011.12940 (Chen, Nonabelian level structures, Nielsen equivalence, and Markoff triples, Ann. Math. 2024)

title: Erdős–Vaaler-type restricted versions: ES with levels restricted to squarefree or prime C
connection: Before Duffin–Schaeffer was proved in general, restricted cases (ψ supported on special sets) were proved first. Restrict ES (★) to prime levels C (or squarefree C): the overlap structure simplifies (gcd(C, C′) = 1). Study the prime-level-only (★) failure set and its overlap model.
why: Restricted versions with clean overlap structure are the natural first targets of a Duffin–Schaeffer-type method.
first_step: Compute (★) restricted to prime C for p ≤ 10⁹ and list failures; fit an independence model.

title: Divisor sum over shifted primes reversed: Σ_{q prime} 1[q | p + m] for structured m
connection: The Titchmarsh divisor problem counts divisors of shifted primes. The trial form needs prime (or general) divisors of p + u in the class −1 mod (stuff tied to u); reverse the roles: for fixed p, count primes q ≡ 3 (4) with q | p + u and q = 4uC − 1 for some C — a 'Titchmarsh problem with a tied modulus' at a single p.
why: Relates single-prime certificates to the distribution of prime divisors of p + u, a classical object.
first_step: Count, for fixed p, pairs (u, q) with q | p + u, q ≡ −1 (mod 4u), q prime; compare with heuristic Σ_u τ*/φ(4u).

title: Siegel–Weil for indefinite ternary forms with congruence: ES's SL₂ quadric
connection: For indefinite forms in ≥ 3 variables representing a number, Siegel–Weil and strong approximation (spin groups) give local-global with spinor exceptions. The SL₂ form ad − pc = 1 is an affine quadric with degenerate quadratic part (rank 2, linear in c), so spin-group strong approximation does not apply as is; the ES congruence a ≡ d ≡ −1 (mod c) is not a lattice coset condition (modulus = coordinate), so classical theory does not apply directly. Find a reformulation where the congruence becomes a fixed-modulus coset condition.
why: If achieved, strong approximation for spin groups (no spinor obstruction ⇒ every locally represented integer is represented) would be the closing theorem.
first_step: Try substitutions a = ck − 1, d = cl − 1 and fix c's residue class; examine whether the resulting variety in (k, l, c) is homogeneous for a group with strong approximation.

upgrade: Tartakowsky / Kloosterman: quadratic forms in >= 4-5 variables

title: No minor arcs: positivity lets ES discard all but the smallest levels
connection: Goldbach-type proofs must bound minor arcs because terms cancel. ES counts are sums of nonnegative level counts, R(p) = Σ_C D_C(p) ≥ Σ_{C ≤ K} D_C(p); so ES ⟸ a certificate among levels C ≤ K = (log p)^A, where the expected count is still ≍ (log p)·(log K) → ∞. The whole problem is a lower bound for a short, explicit 'major-level' sum.
why: Reframes which part of the analytic machinery is needed: only lower bounds on a few explicit structured counts, no cancellation estimates for the bulk.
first_step: For p in the hard lists, find the least K(p) such that some level ≤ K(p) carries a certificate, and fit K(p) against (log p)^A.

title: Baseline: a single level already gives density one
connection: Level C = 1 works for p iff 4p + 1 has a prime factor ≡ 3 (mod 4) (it then automatically has two, so both cofactors are ≥ 3); the primes p for which 4p + 1 has only prime factors ≡ 1 (mod 4) have density zero (an upper-bound sieve gives ≪ X/(log X)^{3/2}; the matching order is the heuristic — check a source for the asymptotic). So 'almost all p' is cheap; all information sits in how fast the exceptional set of K levels decays.
why: A sanity baseline for every almost-all statement in this list: improvements must be measured in exceptional-set decay, not in 'density one'.
first_step: Compute the counting function of primes failing all levels C ≤ K for K = 1..10 up to 10⁹ and fit X/(log X)^{α_K}; compare α_K with Σ_{C≤K} δ_C from Landau–Ramanujan-type densities.

title: Sieve of growing dimension: when do the thin sets S_C (C ≤ K) exhaust all primes?
connection: Failing levels 1..K means 4Cp + 1 ∈ S_C for all C ≤ K, an intersection of thin multiplicative sets of total 'dimension' Σ_{C≤K} δ_C. Upper-bound sieves for such intersections are standard for fixed K; ES needs K growing with p until the expected number of survivors near X is < 1 — a sieve problem of growing dimension.
why: Puts the ES exceptional-set question in the language of high-dimensional sieves (Diamond–Halberstam–Richert), where the dependence on dimension is explicit.
first_step: Compute Σ_{C≤K} δ_C as a function of K and the K(X) at which X·(log X)^{−Σδ} < 1; compare with the observed least K(p).

title: Pretentious distance D((·/p), 1; y) as the controlling statistic for ES difficulty
connection: Tao's EDP and Granville–Soundararajan's pretentious theory organise multiplicative functions by their distance to characters. The BM main term (via T(p)) and the least non-residue are governed by how much the Legendre symbol (·/p) 'pretends' to be 1 on small primes. Test whether all ES sub-route difficulty is a function of D((·/p), 1; y) for suitable y.
why: If one pretentious distance controls difficulty, the problem reduces to the 'pretentious case' (p a QR mod many small primes), where structure is strongest.
first_step: Compute D² = Σ_{ℓ ≤ y} (1 − (ℓ/p))/ℓ for primes ≤ 10⁹ and correlate with R(p)/M₀(p), least certificate C, and sub-route failures.

title: Affine-sieve strengthening: certificates with prime or almost-prime parameters
connection: Bourgain–Gamburd–Sarnak's affine sieve produces almost-primes in orbits once expansion is known. Ask whether every p has a (★) certificate with u, B (or 4uC − 1, 4BC − 1) prime or with ≤ r prime factors; if true numerically, sieve methods on the word set apply and the strengthened statement has more structure.
why: Strengthenings with prime parameters connect ES to the affine-sieve toolkit and to Chen-type almost-prime results.
first_step: For p ≤ 10⁸ compute the least r such that a certificate with Ω(4uC − 1) ≤ r and Ω(4BC − 1) ≤ r exists; find primes needing large r.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Supersingular points and maximal orders: ≈ p/12 objects attached to every p
connection: Every prime p has ≈ p/12 supersingular j-invariants, in bijection (Deuring) with left ideal classes of a fixed maximal order of the quaternion algebra ramified at p and ∞ (maximal-order types correspond to j up to Frobenius conjugation). These always exist, like Elkies's CM values; map them (or their small-norm elements, Eichler orientations) to ES certificate data.
why: Supplies power-many canonical objects for every p; if any natural map lands in certificates with positive probability, existence follows from their number.
first_step: Read the repo's supersingular/Eichler memos; for small p compute the maximal orders' reduced norms forms and test whether ES certificates appear as small vectors.

upgrade: Elkies: every elliptic curve over Q has infinitely many supersingular primes

title: Large deviations of Euclid's algorithm at a fixed denominator (Hensley, Baladi–Vallée)
connection: The CF length of a/v is asymptotically Gaussian with mean ≍ log v (Heilbronn for the mean at fixed denominators; Hensley, Baladi–Vallée via transfer operators — reviewer repair: Baladi–Vallée average over denominators v ≤ N with rate O(1/√log N), not a fixed denominator). ES₅ (λ(p) ≤ 3) asks for an extreme left-tail event (length 3, prescribed shape). Large-deviation estimates for fixed p from the dynamical analysis of Euclid's algorithm would give lower bounds in exactly this quantifier order.
why: The dynamical analysis of Euclid's algorithm is 'every p' by construction (it averages over a, not p); the question is how far into the tail its estimates reach.
first_step: Find fixed-denominator large-deviation statements (Hensley's work on fixed-denominator Euclid statistics; check) beyond Baladi–Vallée's denominator-averaged ones; compare the reachable tail with length-3 events (count ≍ log²p out of p).

title: Reduction theory for ES solutions and congruence exclusion of all reduced representatives
connection: In Ghosh–Sarnak failures every orbit has a reduced representative in a bounded region, and congruence conditions can exclude all of them. ES: every solution has x ∈ (p/4, 3p/4] (x minimal); the 'reduced representatives' are the pairs (x, m = 4x − p). Ask whether congruence conditions modulo a fixed M can exclude all reduced representatives for infinitely many p (that would be a non-BM obstruction).
why: A concrete search space for genuinely new obstructions; if impossible for structural reasons, that fact is itself a (small) theorem.
first_step: For M = 840·k, compute which residues of p mod M admit a reduced representative whose two-term remainder is locally solvable mod M; check that no non-square class is fully excluded.
refs: arXiv:1706.06712 (Ghosh-Sarnak, Integral points on Markoff type cubic surfaces, Invent. Math. 229 (2022))

title: Search for F_q[T] counterexamples to the direct ES analogue at small q
connection: Function-field analogues sometimes fail at small q (as Artin's C₂ fails for small p). If the direct analogue of ES over F_q[T] (with a suitable positivity replacement, e.g. degree constraints) fails for some small q, the failure mechanism is an explicit structure that ℤ-ES must avoid; if it holds for all tested q, the F_q[T] proof (repo) is the template.
why: Cheap exhaustive computation with high information value (8/131-type test in the function-field world).
first_step: For q = 2, 3, 4, 5 and irreducible P of degree ≤ 12, search solutions of 4/P = 1/X + 1/Y + 1/Z (with the repo's degree conventions) and list failures.
refs: Effinger-Hayes, Additive Number Theory of Polynomials over a Finite Field (1991)

title: Positive proportion before density one (Bourgain–Fuchs) for bounded-shape certificates
connection: Bourgain–Fuchs proved a positive proportion of integers are Apollonian curvatures before density one. For ES, bounded-shape certificate families (u, B ≤ U fixed) cover a positive proportion of primes by Dirichlet; quantify the proportion covered by shapes with u, B ≤ U as U grows, versus the full ES density one.
why: Measures how much of ES is 'explained' by bounded shapes (Mordell-type) vs growing ones — the shape-growth rate needed for density one.
first_step: Compute coverage of primes ≤ 10⁹ by (★) with u, B ≤ U for U = 1..100.

title: Third-method insurance: find a family whose success is uncorrelated with both (★) and b=1
connection: Holowinsky–Soundararajan needed exactly two complementary methods. ES data show (★) ∪ b=1 never fail together ≤ 10⁸, but a proof-grade argument may need a third family whose success correlates with neither (e.g. ES₅, Type I lines, small windows). Measure correlations of success indicators among 6–8 families.
why: Identifies the minimal robust family set for a complementary-methods proof.
first_step: Compute the correlation matrix of family success indicators (and of their counts) over primes ≤ 10⁸ in Mordell-hard classes.
refs: arXiv:0809.1636 (Holowinsky-Soundararajan, Mass equidistribution for Hecke eigenforms)

title: Which almost-all ES results are sharp in the Kolmogorov sense?
connection: Kolmogorov's divergent Fourier series shows some a.e. theorems are optimal. For each ES-type almost-all theorem (single levels, (★), b=1, ES₅), decide whether infinitely many failures are known/expected (then the almost-all result is 'sharp') or not; only the latter are candidates for every-p upgrades.
why: Avoids attempting upgrades of statements that are actually false infinitely often (like single-level or (★)-only versions may be).
first_step: For each sub-route, estimate Σ_p P(fail) under the calibrated model; classify as 'expected finitely many' vs 'expected infinitely many' failures.
refs: Kolmogorov, Fund. Math. 4 (1923)/ C. R. 1926 (everywhere divergent L^1 Fourier series)

title: Average over p of Schinzel-type events for the polynomials 4Cp + 1 in C
connection: Skorobogatov–Sofos average over polynomial families. At fixed p, the family {4Cp + 1 : C} is a linear polynomial in C; averaging over p (with C free) gives Schinzel-on-average-type statements on factorisations of 4Cp + 1 that underlie the almost-all ES theorem. Make explicit which 'Schinzel on average' input the almost-all proof uses and whether a pointwise-in-p version is a known open problem.
why: Locates ES exactly within the Schinzel-on-average landscape (what is averaged, over what).
first_step: Rewrite Vaughan's almost-all proof as a statement about factorisations of 4Cp + 1 averaged over p; identify the pointwise analogue.
refs: arXiv:2005.02998 (Skorobogatov-Sofos, Schinzel Hypothesis on average and rational points)

title: Twists by characters mod 4C as 'twisted point counts' with an exactly known total
connection: Weil-type lower bounds use that twisted counts sum to an exact total. At level C, Σ_{χ mod 4C} χ(−1)·#{d | N : χ(d)…} expansions give D_C^−(N) = (1/φ(4C)) Σ_χ χ̄(−1) σ_χ(N) exactly; the trivial character gives τ(N)/φ(4C), others are twisted divisor sums. A lower bound needs |Σ_{χ ≠ 1} …| < τ(N): bound the twisted divisor sums σ_χ(N) pointwise (multiplicative, |σ_χ(q^a)| ≤ a + 1).
why: Pointwise bounds on σ_χ(N) are trivial-to-moderate; the issue is how many characters and how cancellation among them behaves for structured N = 4Cp + 1.
first_step: For hard p and small C, compute |Σ_{χ ≠ 1} χ̄(−1)σ_χ(N)| vs τ(N) and record how close it gets.

title: Kaplansky-type ternary forms with conditional (GRH) complete lists as structural analogues
connection: Beyond Ramanujan's form, several ternary forms have GRH-conditional complete lists of exceptions (Ono–Soundararajan type). Their exception lists are finite but sporadic; ES-adjacent statements with sporadic exceptions (U(n) list, b=1 failures) might be 'ternary-form-like'. Test whether the U(n)/b=1 exceptions are represented/non-represented by specific ternary forms.
why: A direct dictionary between sporadic ES-adjacent exceptions and ternary-form exceptions would import Waldspurger/GRH technology.
first_step: For the known sporadic exception lists, test representability by all reduced positive ternary forms of discriminant ≤ 500.

title: Switching between the two cofactors of 4Cp + 1 and the two ES types
connection: Chen's switching replaces a hard count by a dual count where the roles of variables swap. In (★), 4Cp + 1 = (4uC − 1)(4BC − 1) is symmetric; the b=1 line uses p + 4d with a divisor ≡ −1 (mod 4d). Find an explicit bijection/switch between near-certificates of one line and of the other, so that an upper bound for near-misses of one yields a lower bound for hits of the other.
why: Switching is the concrete mechanism behind complementary-route arguments.
first_step: Search for maps (u, B, C) ↦ (d, w) between (★) data and b=1 data for the same p, and test on hard primes.

title: Zero-free region analogue: a range of levels where no 'conspiracy' is possible
connection: Linnik's theorem uses a zero-free region near s = 1 for all characters of modulus ≤ Q. For ES, find a range of small levels (C ≤ C₀(p)) where the relevant characters (mod 4C) are so few that a full conspiracy against certificates would force p into explicit square-like residue classes (contradiction for non-squares).
why: Small levels have few characters; a 'no conspiracy at small levels' lemma would be the ES zero-free region.
first_step: For C ≤ 30, characterise the residues of p (mod lcm(4C)) for which all these levels fail; compute the density of such residues and whether they are squares.

title: Box principle for windows: two windows with the same residue data combine
connection: Thue's lemma is a box principle. Pigeonhole windows e by the residue vector of p modulo small primes and the factorisation shape of N_e; two windows with equal data might combine (via CRT) into a certificate at the window e·e′ or at lcm, if a combination law exists.
why: Pigeonhole needs a combination law; windows have CRT structure that may supply one.
first_step: Test on data: for pairs of failing windows e, e′ with compatible data, check whether e·e′ (or another derived window) succeeds more often than random.

upgrade: Thue's lemma / pigeonhole for x^2 + y^2

title: Exact formulas for divisor-class counts: Ramanujan sums expansion of D_C^−(N)
connection: Rademacher-type exact expansions use Kloosterman/Ramanujan sums. The class-restricted divisor count D^−_{4C}(N) has an exact finite Fourier expansion over additive characters mod 4C (Ramanujan sums c_q(·)); for the all-level sum this becomes a series Σ_q c_q-type terms, an ES 'singular series' with exact tail.
why: An exact Ramanujan-sum expansion of R(p) separates the main (BM) part from the rest explicitly and may be summable in closed form at small q.
first_step: Write R(p) = Σ_q A_q(p) with A_q built from Ramanujan sums; compute A_q(p) numerically for q ≤ 100 and the remainder.

upgrade: Rademacher exact formula (asymptotic -> exact for every n)

title: Commutator-style 'every element' from character ratios: target −1 in (ℤ/e)* via products of few divisor classes
connection: Ore-type results show every element is a product of few commutators using character bounds. Analogue for windows: when the prime-factor classes of N_e generate a large subgroup H ∋ −1, show −1 is a product of a bounded number of them (with ±1 exponents) using additive-combinatorics in abelian groups (Cauchy–Davenport/Kneser iterated), i.e. a bound on the 'diameter' of H w.r.t. the generating multiset.
why: Reduces window certificates to a diameter bound in a Cayley graph of an abelian group — fully finite and checkable.
first_step: Compute the ±1-diameter of (ℤ/e)* w.r.t. the multiset of prime-factor classes of N_e for hard (p, e), versus ω(N_e).
refs: Liebeck-O'Brien-Shalev-Tiep, The Ore conjecture, J. Eur. Math. Soc. 12 (2010) 939-1008

title: Finite base + closure: what finite verification would an ES closure theorem need?
connection: Graham's 77-theorem needed a finite check (78–333) plus closure maps. If any closure/transfer system for ES certificates were found (see closure items), compute the minimal 'base' of verified instances it needs; ES is verified to 10¹⁸, so any closure system with base ≤ 10¹⁸ would finish.
why: Turns closure-map searches into a concrete success criterion.
first_step: For each candidate closure map found by search, compute the set of primes it reaches from primes ≤ 10⁶ and check whether its complement thins out.

title: Syracuse-type random variable for ES: the 2-adic/3-adic structure of minimal certificates
connection: Tao's Collatz proof analysed the distribution of a 3-adic 'Syracuse random variable'. ES certificates carry 2-adic data (4 | t; 8ℤ − p branch) and 3-adic data (Mordell classes mod 3). Define the analogous random variable (residues of minimal certificate parameters mod 2^k, 3^k) and study its distribution and mixing as p varies.

title: Linear recurrences for minimal certificates along exponential families
connection: SML-type structure suggests that along n_s = a·b^s + c the minimal certificate parameters may follow linear recurrences in s on residue classes of s. Detect such recurrences for the proved families (3·2^s + 1, 63·2^s + 1) and use them to predict certificates for open families.

title: Reducibility check automation: verify 'configuration ⇒ certificate' lemmas by computer
connection: The four-colour proof verified each configuration's reducibility by computer. For ES, configuration lemmas of the form 'if p ≡ r (mod M) and 4Cp + 1 has factorisation pattern π then a certificate exists' can be verified symbolically for each (r, π); automate generation and checking of such lemmas.
why: Builds a library of machine-checked partial results that any case-analysis proof would need.

title: Stickiness analogue: certificates at nearby levels share prime factors
connection: Wang–Zahl handled 'sticky' Kakeya sets where tubes cluster coherently across scales. For fixed p, near-certificates at levels C and C + kq share the prime q (CRT); study whether certificate data are 'sticky' across levels (coherent families sharing primes) and whether non-sticky configurations are easier to force.
why: A structural dichotomy (sticky vs non-sticky) that may split the problem into two tractable halves.

title: Limit objects of normalised divisor-class data as p → ∞ (Sendov's limiting measures)
connection: Tao's Sendov proof studies limiting zero distributions. For ES, attach to p the empirical measure of (log d / log N, class of d mod 4C) over levels C ≤ K and divisors d of 4Cp + 1; study its limit as p → ∞ (should be a product of uniform measures) and the rate; a counterexample sequence would converge to a measure avoiding a fixed 'certificate region'.
why: Gives a concrete limit object for compactness arguments.
first_step: Compute these empirical measures for p ~ 10⁶, 10⁸, 10¹⁰ and measure distance to the product-uniform model.
